noticias.titulo: The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
noticias.resumen: From legal-tech to healthcare, dozens of Indian AI start-ups are solving uniquely Indian challenges.
noticias.texto:
The AI start-ups fixing India's broken roads and messy land records
- Published
In 2020, Sanjay Mandava flew down from Chicago to Chennai in southern India to resolve a personal land dispute.
Over the next few months, he was running around between government offices to access a dozen records that would conclusively prove that the property belonged to his family.
Just a sale deed dating back to when his parents bought the land was not enough. Authorities asked him to produce a string of other documents.
Frustrated by the experience, he built Landeed - an AI-led digital platform that enables users to aggregate fragmented, multi-source land-records, verify titles and conduct legal checks at the click of a few buttons, across 24 states in India.
He's solving a problem that is uniquely Indian.
"In the US or UK, when you purchase a property, the government verifies ownership. In India by contrast, we follow presumptive titling - the buyer is responsible for establishing ownership. A sale deed merely records the transaction - multiple other documents may be needed to prove title," Mandava told the BBC.
These include building certificates, property tax receipts and land survey maps among others.
The system is rife for misuse - property disputes account for a bulk of civil litigation cases in the country where some 80% of household wealth is held in real estate.
Landeed has mapped large swathes of India using geo-spatial technology and data from state land revenue departments, registration offices, survey records and municipal databases.
Using this, it has linked registered properties to their official land identification and survey numbers and ownership records.
An additional AI-layer can read these titles, extract information and spot inconsistencies within minutes - a process that takes lawyers and brokers several days.
With the largest repository of title data in the country, consisting of 1.8 billion documents, the app is now used by millions of individual and enterprise customers while doing real estate transactions.
The app is among a burgeoning list of Indian start-ups trying to address some of India's most complex challenges in sectors ranging from legal-tech to healthcare, infrastructure, education and agriculture using AI.
Unlike the US and China which have a global dominance in building frontier language models like ChatGPT, India's AI revolution is happening downstream in data centre infrastructure and consumer applications rather than in research.
Start-ups are solving issues for everything from pothole detection to tribal language translation to assisting overworked public-health professionals with medical tasks - often working with highly fragmented, multilingual datasets in extremely cost sensitive industries.
Bengaluru-based YouTube teacher Gaurav Sen's AI app detects potholes using a dash-cam, satellite-based navigation and an AI vision model to analyse images.
It then identifies civic officials responsible for fixing them and sends them this data. He got viral attention recently given how widespread the menace of potholes is across India's urban sprawls.
On last count, there are at least half a dozen other similar offerings that map and report road damage to authorities across the country.
"A municipal corporation can take the app and use it on public buses and taxis, to access real-time, updated data on road conditions," Sen told the BBC.
In Mumbai on India's western coast, Fractal Analytics - among the few Indian listed AI companies - has deployed its AI tool "Vaidya" in hospitals run by the local civic authority.
The app allows citizens to receive AI-generated, simplified summaries of their lab reports in multiple languages, identify nearby healthcare facilities based on their needs and gives doctors AI-guided pre-consultation support such as medical history and medication details of patients.
It also provides hospital administrators with a public health dashboard based on aggregated, anonymous insights from lab reports accessed through its tie-up with municipal hospitals, giving them crucial visibility into emerging infections or other disease trends.
This boom has led to a surge in funding for AI start-ups - up 265% year-on-year according to Inc42, external, a start-up information platform. They raised over $1bn in the first nine months of this year amid a relatively muted fundraising environment for the broader ecosystem.
Yet, these companies face an uphill task in commercialising their ideas and taking them beyond pilot.
"The cost of building in India is sometimes much higher than what Indian customers are willing to pay," Fractal's co-founder Srikanth Velamakanni told the BBC at his sprawling office overlooking Mumbai's film city.
"The computing power needed to run an AI model is the same whether it is built in India or the US - but American customers have a far bigger paying capacity than those here."
Indian AI founders are also being forced to build around scarcity, with availability of high quality chips at the right scale and price, a major impediment for many.
"I believe I am building one of the most impactful things for this country," says Mandava.
"But I am starved for GPUs [chips that perform millions of calculations and help train AI models]. I have a hellish time trying to acquire them," he says.
The country has promised its start-ups 38,000 GPUs through its government-led AI mission, external, but demand for this compute power is far greater than supply.
Cumbersome regulation and bureaucracy are other major challenges.
Without these fundamental issues being addressed, there's a risk that Indian AI companies will build shallow solutions that a next generation of founders will immediately make redundant, say experts.
"Someone like a Google will probably laugh if I tell them of my pilot. To make it sustainable and hard to replicate, it will have to be much more sophisticated," says Sen, displaying a self-awareness of where his product currently stands.
From a lack of experienced talent to the struggle to turn successful pilots into recurring government contracts to heavy dependence on expensive foreign technology, Indian founders are powering through many odds.
"We can still do it. We don't want protection, but propel us, give us the weapons to compete against the best," Mandava says, when asked what he wants from policymakers.
"To quote Jay-Z - I can't help the poor if I'm one of them," he adds.
Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

noticias.titulo: Portugal coach Jorge Jesus responds to criticism from Ronaldo’s mother
noticias.resumen: Ronaldo's mother said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat after he had 'deceived' her son.
noticias.texto:
Portugal coach Jorge Jesus responds to criticism from Ronaldo’s mother
Ronaldo’s mother Dolores Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat after her son had been ‘deceived’ by him.
Portugal coach Jorge Jesus believes he will still be responding to questions about Cristiano Ronaldo next year, after he was asked for his thoughts on scathing comments by the football great’s mother.
“Now I have to respond to Cristiano Ronaldo’s mother?” Jesus asked on Tuesday, addressing the media before Portugal’s final Nations League group fixture away to Wales.
“I don’t know when it is going to stop. If you guys ask the questions, I have to answer. If you ask about Ronaldo next year, I will answer.”
Jesus’s frustration stemmed from his lingering tensions with Ronaldo following the recent international retirement of football’s all-time greats.
The 72-year-old head coach responded to comments from Ronaldo’s mother in the wake of the team’s latest defeat – their first since the 41-year-old forward quit national duties.
Jesus wondered when he would stop being peppered about Ronaldo after a 4-1 Nations League defeat to Denmark prompted criticism from the five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s mother, Dolores Aveiro.
Aveiro said she was glad to see Jesus suffer his first defeat since taking charge after the World Cup as Ronaldo had been “deceived” by the former Benfica boss.
Ronaldo’s decision to hang up his boots for country followed a falling out with Jesus, who was previously the superstar’s coach at Saudi club Al-Nassr.
The ex-Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus star accused Jesus of broken promises after he was asked to warm up during a match against Norway in September without being introduced as a substitute.
Ronaldo left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and a token fine.
He apologised and was expected to return to the Portugal squad, but instead brought down the curtain on a 23-year international career.
His 234 appearances and 146 goals are both world records in the men’s game.
Ronaldo’s lack of mobility was often pinpointed as a factor in a richly talented Portugal squad falling short in recent major tournaments.
Jesus’s side had made a perfect start with four consecutive wins prior to Saturday’s shock defeat to the Danes.
“After the game against Denmark, everyone is asking me about different individuals, not about the team or winning here,” added Jesus.
“We played one bad game and it’s harder to move on when we have a result like that, but we are going to try and win the game.”
Portugal only need a point in Cardiff to secure top spot in Nations League group A4 against a Wales side that will finish bottom of the section.
“You were all having a go at him for playing, and then as soon as he retires, suddenly it’s all hell breaking loose!” Wales boss Craig Bellamy told the Portuguese media.
“He is one of the best players that has ever played the game. We’re all going to miss him.”

noticias.titulo: The new French malaise
noticias.resumen: The ongoing student protests in France are a symptom of a much larger crisis affecting French society.
noticias.texto:
The new French malaise
The ongoing student protests in France are a symptom of a much larger crisis affecting French society.
Fifty years ago, Alain Peyrefitte, who served as a spokesperson for French President Charles de Gaulle, published a book entitled Le Mal français (The French Malaise). In the book, Peyrefitte wrote that the progress of the French nation was impeded by the lack of trust – within society and between society and state institutions. In reaction, the state exercised excessive control through rules, bureaucracy and centralisation, which resulted in stagnation.
Today, the French malaise persists, but its symptoms are quite different from the ones observed by Peyrefitte. We now have the dramatic protests by French students as well as workers and other disaffected groups, which at times have turned violent.
But these demonstrations are only the tip of the iceberg. The malaise runs much deeper.
A threat to the Republic
Following the events of October 17, in which symbols of state authority were attacked – including the town halls of Limoges and Marseille and an official building in Lyon – and businesses were looted, French President Emmanuel Macron stated that these acts sought “to tear down our institutions”.
The use of such strong words reminds one of the rhetoric employed by the French government during the protests of May 1968, when students challenged the established order, and their actions were portrayed as an “attack on the Republic”.
There is, in fact, a tendency to compare the current wave of demonstrations with the events of May 1968. Yet the two movements differ. The protesters of 1968 were calling for more freedom, while today’s protesters are demanding equality and dignity. The former demonstrations were led by privileged youth; the latter are driven by those who have been left behind.
Perhaps a more relevant episode to examine is the upheaval of 2005 in the suburbs of Paris and other major cities following the deaths of two teenagers, Bouna and Zyed, who were pursued by the police.
For three weeks, residents of impoverished neighbourhoods, living on the fringes of society both geographically and socially, expressed their anger at police violence and their own marginalisation.
Two elements of the French malaise were already apparent at the time. First was the deep divide between two segments of society: the prosperous urban population and the marginalised, racialised poor, living in the underdeveloped and underserviced outskirts.
The second was the French police itself, which has overwhelmingly focused on policing the latter with ever-growing brutality.
In any country, a citizen-oriented police force can help build the bonds that unite a nation. But in France, the police is tasked with defending the state, not protecting the citizens.
It does not contribute to the cohesion of a nation. It does not abide by proportionality in the use of force or opt for de-escalation; it openly practises a discriminatory approach to policing which differentiates between affluent neighbourhoods and impoverished areas, between the white majority and the communities of colour.
It is no wonder that upwards of 60 percent of the police and military forces of France vote for the far right.
The French archipelago
In 2019, French political scientist Jérôme Fourquet wrote a book entitled The French Archipelago: The birth of a diverse and divided nation. In it, he argues that France has undergone a societal shift which has fundamentally altered people’s relationship with themselves and with the “other”. As a result, French society has split into small “islands” which are increasingly isolated from one another.
This transformation cannot be attributed solely to immigration. It is, above all, the result of the secession of the elite, which has grown distant and indifferent to the fate of the rest of the nation. This includes the political left, who are now commonly referred to as the gauche caviar (the caviar left).
It has been the elite’s abandonment and self-isolation that has caused the revolt of the masses, rather than the other way around.
The institutions that traditionally fostered socialisation between various groups, bestowing a sense of belonging, including schools, summer camps and compulsory military service, are no longer functioning effectively, or are cancelled.
In this fragmented society, one segment has been picked as a scapegoat for all problems, diverting attention from the real roots of the malaise.
Islamophobia is flourishing in France, as is the belief in the “Great Replacement”, a conspiracy theory that people of colour are meant to “replace” the white majority. Islamophobia has even become institutionalised through legislation and a political culture that has transformed blasphemy into something resembling a duty.
The paradox is that France – compared with its neighbours – has a smaller immigrant population while it espouses a much louder rhetoric about “integration”.
And there is a considerable gap between rhetoric and reality. While those in power demand that people of immigrant background “integrate”, very little is done by the state to actually drive this process.
As a result, some French citizens feel they are French only on paper. They understand that citizenship cannot be reduced to a political discourse. Without genuine access to rights, which necessarily entails social justice and human dignity, there can be no meaningful citizenship.
In 2005, a group of activists went as far as declaring themselves the “Natives of the Republic” and calling for its decolonisation. Indeed, anyone familiar with French society can recognise that France has reproduced a colonial order within.
The country that gave birth to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen has failed to treat some of its own people as full citizens. And that stands at the core of the new French malaise.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Will Netanyahu lose this time?
noticias.resumen: The Israeli prime minister has manoeuvred out of tough situations to retain power. But he may find it hard this time.
noticias.texto:
Will Netanyahu lose this time?
The Israeli prime minister has manoeuvred out of tough situations before to retain power. But he may find it hard this time.
I have been covering Benjamin Netanyahu for more than 30 years. I was in Washington when, as a young opposition leader, he worked hand in glove with the Republicans to embarrass Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and sabotage the Oslo Accords. I have seen him cornered before. I have never seen him cornered like this.
The numbers are merciless. His bloc won 53 seats, eight short of a majority. Sixty-seven members of the new Knesset recommended former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, who now has up to 42 days to form a government. For Netanyahu, they may be the longest 42 days of his political life.
The stakes are political, but above all personal. His corruption trial continues, and he faces a possible prison sentence. His pardon request has been gathering dust on President Isaac Herzog’s desk for months. Eisenkot’s bloc has already tabled bills for a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 attacks and for prime-ministerial term limits.
A state inquiry would strip him of the title he covets the most: “defender of Israel”. For Netanyahu, the chair is not a job. It is a lifeline. His trial, under way since May 2020, is in its final stretch. A sitting prime minister can be removed only after a final conviction.
From his office, he can stall hearings and lean on the justice system. Out of office, he is just another defendant.
To survive, Netanyahu does not need to build a government. He needs time to keep his rivals from building one. To buy it, he is pulling three levers.
The first is his proposal for a “national unity government” of all the parties that support Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people. Translation: the Arab parties, representing 21 percent of the population, are out. The Jewish supremacists, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are in. So are the anti-Zionist Haredi parties. This is unity, Netanyahu-style.
He has gift-wrapped the offer in the old rhetoric of the Iranian nuclear threat, with one catch: He would not give up the premiership or agree to a rotation.
Eisenkot has called the offer “another spin”, yet he has agreed to negotiate with Likud. He knows a refusal would only feed the spin machine: They will talk to Arab supporters of Hamas, but not to Jewish patriots, the Netanyahu camp would claim.
He also knows to beware of a diversion designed to burn through the days the president has allotted him.
The second lever is incitement. At the Knesset’s opening session, Netanyahu branded Ra’am and the Joint List “terror supporters” and “haters of Israel”. A government depending on them, he declared, “must not be formed”. The goal is to strangle an Arab-backed government in its cradle, and to scare the Haredi parties, which are currently part of his bloc, away from joining the “enemy”.
But this time the incitement has a hole in it. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas says Netanyahu’s confidant Natan Eshel sounded him out on the bill to bar an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Joint List lawmaker Ahmad Tibi went on live television with WhatsApp messages he said came from Eshel. “Terror supporters”, it seems, are good enough for a quiet chat.
The third lever is escalation. According to media reports, Netanyahu has been pressing US President Donald Trump for another wave of strikes on Iran. A return to full-scale war could help him form an emergency government.
In a media interview, former Prime Minister Ehud Barak laid out the scenario: a blatant provocation that forces Iran to respond, and a war that would disrupt or prevent the establishment of a new government. Lebanon, Gaza or the West Bank could serve just as well. The mantra is well-known: The enemy must see that we are united.
Here, too, there are limits. A former chief of staff of the army, Eisenkot spent many years in uniform and has no shortage of sources in the army. They are likely telling him there is no urgent need for another round of war with Iran. And Trump has hinted that he wants that war over.
If all three levers fail, Netanyahu has a familiar fallback: another election, next spring. Between 2019 and 2022, he dragged Israelis to the polls five times rather than give up the chair. Tibi has revealed that one of Netanyahu’s ministers tried to convince him his party would be better off “going to elections” than joining Eisenkot’s bloc.
Eisenkot has a problem of his own. He campaigned on three pledges: no Netanyahu, no Haredi parties, no Arab parties. He cannot keep all three. Politics is the art of choosing which promise to break.
The first path available to Eisenkot runs through the Haredim. His bloc has 48 seats; Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) would add 13, for exactly 61, the number he needs to secure a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. A softened draft law is reportedly on the table. But UTJ’s rabbis want all 48 members of the bloc to sign a pledge exempting Haredim from military service, with an override clause to shield the law from the Supreme Court. Eisenkot has pledged not to back down on military service for all.
The second path is a minority government, backed by the Arab parties from outside the coalition. Eisenkot is reportedly willing to do it, and so is one of his allies, Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats. Another ally, Naftali Bennett, is believed to oppose it. The big obstacle is Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, who rules out the Arab parties, a minority government and new elections. Three noes in a single breath.
The third path is Likud without Netanyahu, or with him in a diplomatic role. No Likud lawmaker has broken ranks so far. And for Netanyahu, a junior partnership would be not a retirement plan but a launching pad: From inside the cabinet, he could stall the bills on a state inquiry and term limits, undermine the government and bring it down at a moment of his choosing. Just ask Benny Gantz, whose 2020 rotation deal with Netanyahu never brought him to the prime minister’s chair.
This is a game of chicken. Netanyahu is betting that Eisenkot’s partners will squabble over the draft, the Arab parties and the portfolios until the clock runs out, forcing a seventh election since 2019 — one he would fight from the Prime Minister’s Office, his finger on the trigger. Eisenkot’s best weapon is the one Netanyahu fears the most: a government, any government, sworn in before the 42 days are up.
Eisenkot’s camp has already taken over the Knesset building. Netanyahu’s camp will do everything it can to keep it from taking over the government buildings. They will not give up without street battles.
The last time incitement spilled into the streets, in November 1995, it ended with the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin. It paved the way for the comeback of the Israeli right, led by a young, charming Revisionist.
Will November 2026 mark the end of the Netanyahu era and a return to Rabin’s path of peace?
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Palestine Weekly: Israel’s political reshuffle as the occupation grinds on
noticias.resumen: As Eisenkot’s bloc moves to form a government and courts the ultra-Orthodox, Gaza genocide and settler pogroms continue.
noticias.texto:
Palestine Weekly: Israel’s political reshuffle as the occupation grinds on
As Eisenkot’s bloc moves to form a government and courts the ultra-Orthodox, the Gaza genocide and settler pogroms continue.
Israel’s parliament speaker is due to be replaced on Tuesday, one of several signs that power is being rearranged as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s bloc angles to lead the government.
But for Palestinians, the machinery of occupation, dispossession and deprivation keeps running. Israeli attacks killed at least 37 people in Gaza in the past week, while in the occupied West Bank, settlers attacked whole villages with little to stop them.
Gaza: Two narratives of daily killing under the “ceasefire”
The past week saw numerous Israeli attacks and killings in Gaza, as military claims of targeting fighters were weighed against accounts of people killed in tents, filling water containers and driving to a wedding photo shoot. According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, as of November 16, Israel has killed 1,650 Palestinians since the October 2025 “ceasefire”.
On November 12, an Israeli bomb hit the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis. The hospital’s surgery building was struck, killing six people, including surgeon Rizq Abu Shaira, and wounding dozens. The Israeli military said it targeted Hamas’s Khan Younis Brigade commander, Muhammad Abu Ismail, and accused Hamas of running a command centre in the hospital. In the days that followed, the foreign ministers of 18 Arab and Muslim-majority countries condemned the attack as a violation of international humanitarian law.
Beyond the hospital bombing, the Israeli military told Israeli media it had killed 10 Hamas operatives in the past week. Among them was Samir Abu Younis, whom the army named as Hamas’s Rafah Brigade commander, killed in a drone strike in al-Mawasi on November 14, which Hamas confirmed. The strike hit a tent for displaced people, wounding two. Over the weekend, in Jabalia camp, two men were killed in a strike the army said targeted “terrorists”, and a separate strike on a Gaza government security post in al-Mawasi, Rafah, killed two people, according to Wafa.
At the same time, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in circumstances that offered little indication of any military target:
- A tank shell hit an apartment in the al-Qastal towers in Deir el-Balah on November 13, where mourners had gathered. Israeli tanks then fired on people fleeing, killing at least three, including 12-year-old Ahmed Abu Daher, and wounding at least 20, according to local activist Hamza al-Masri and Gaza Now.
- According to Wafa, a man was killed by a drone on November 11 as he filled water containers on his Gaza City roof. The next day, a driver taking a groom to a wedding photo shoot in Deir el-Balah was killed by Israeli fire.
- On November 16, a man was shot dead at displacement tents in Jabalia, while three people, including a child, were separately wounded by gunfire inside a school south of Khan Younis, Wafa reported.
This week, Gaza’s Health Ministry recorded the winter’s first death from hypothermia – a nine-month-old baby – following the devastation of last week’s rains. Israel’s Prime Minister’s Office claimed more than 91,000 tents and 8,200 trucks of winter supplies have been delivered, the Times of Israel reported, and blamed Hamas for the suffering. The United Nations, however, reported this week that aid-truck offloads have fallen about 42 percent after Israel suspended the Egyptian corridor.
The United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and Italy called conditions in Gaza “catastrophic” and urged that 150,000 tents be allowed into the territory.
West Bank: Settler attacks, closures and two pogroms
The most violent olive harvest on record continues in the occupied West Bank, as OCHA counted 410 harvest-related attacks this year as of November 9. The week saw several kinds of attacks by settlers and soldiers unfold repeatedly across the West Bank:
- Harvest and land: Residents reported settlers attacking pickers at Deir Istiya, Abu Nujeim, Wadi Saif near Beit Fajjar, Beit Dajan and Deir Jarir. On November 10, dozens of masked settlers attacked Rabbis for Human Rights volunteers and farmers at Qusra, injuring six, the Times of Israel reported. Settlers also bulldozed farmland at Marj Arzal and Sinjil and uprooted olive trees at as-Sawiya, according to Israeli field monitor Jonathan Pollack and local residents.
- Arson and vandalism: Settlers burned a Bedouin tent at Deir Qaddis, set a car ablaze in Taybeh while spray-painting “Death to Arabs”, and destroyed beehives at Atara, according to Wafa and Pollack.
- Closures and raids: In al-Mughayyir, settlers pitched a tent in a zone closed to Palestinians, and that night, troops sealed the village, raiding a wedding hall and arresting the groom and three guests. Forces also imposed a curfew on Beit Ummar and closed ad-Dhahiriya’s main entrance, Wafa reported.
But in the past week, two settler attacks escalated into full-blown pogroms against Palestinian communities. Late on November 10, more than 50 masked settlers set fire to a scrapyard, a workshop and cars beside homes in al-Lubban Asharqiya, south of Nablus, burning more than 100 vehicles and dozens of olive trees and cutting power. Wafa put the damage from the attack at more than one million shekels ($310,000). On November 12, after soldiers evicted an outpost near Atara, north of Ramallah, settlers smashed four homes and a factory and wrecked at least three cars, injuring more than 10 residents.
The Israeli army evacuated outposts near Burqa, Wadi al-Rakhim and Jalud, and on November 11, police arrested four Israelis over a September attack by settlers on troops escorting a displaced Palestinian family, the Times of Israel reported.
Yet settlers re-established an outpost at Burqa within days, and in Wadi al-Rakhim, south of Yatta, the six-week siege of Yousef Shanaran’s home by settlers continues unimpeded. While soldiers pulled down the settlers’ tent outside Shanaran’s home on November 13, the tent was rebuilt after sunset, according to the family. On November 16, Shanaran told Al Jazeera that settlers had thrown stones at their home throughout the previous night. Soldiers were present, but did nothing. “We are alone,” he declared.
Eisenkot condemns racism, but courts the Haredim
As the occupation continues largely unchecked, early coalition negotiations suggest that a change of government might mean little more than a rearrangement of the political chairs for Palestinians. On November 10, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told the new parliament in a speech Eisenkot called “hate-filled” that Arab-led parties “seek to destroy the Jewish state”, while demanding a Zionist unity government instead of the opposition partnering with the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Meanwhile, Israel’s Channel 12 reported on November 15 that Netanyahu’s chief of staff had given police the tip behind three election-day arrests of activists from Ra’am, one of the Arab-led parties. Israel’s attorney general is probing whether Netanyahu’s office engineered the case to bolster claims that Arab parties stole the vote. Shin Bet chief David Zini also asked to wiretap five Palestinian members of the Israeli parliament, Channel 12 reported. Netanyahu’s office has called the report defamatory.
Eisenkot called the campaign against Palestinian citizens of Israel “racist and violent” and said Netanyahu was a threat to Israeli democracy who could not stay “for even one more minute”.
Yet he has ruled out a government with the Arab parties, whose 19 seats would give his bloc 67, above the 61-seat majority threshold.
Instead, the week’s moves point towards Eisenkot working with the ultra-Orthodox: right-wing anti-Netanyahu leader Avigdor Liberman, just approved as chair of the parliament’s Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee, suggested working with military leaders, the High Court and religious leaders to compromise on any ultra-Orthodox conscription bill, the Times of Israel reported.

noticias.titulo: Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon
noticias.resumen: The ongoing Israeli assault continues to have disastrous consequences for the people of southern Lebanon.
noticias.texto:
Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon
The ongoing Israeli assault continues to have disastrous consequences for the people of southern Lebanon.
Kfar Reman, Lebanon – It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of a home destroyed in an overnight air strike, searching for the bodies of two children.
Ten members of the same family, spanning three generations, had already been found in the building’s collapsed rooms, among them two survivors.
Two months later, I met 10-year-old Zainab and her eight-year-old brother Mustafa. After losing their parents and elder sister, Fatima, and their one-month-old brother, Ahmed, they now live with their grandmother. Both were thrown out of the house due to the intensity of the blast, but their physical wounds were no longer visible.
Zainab had a constant smile, but she was hiding sadness which she did not know how to express in words.
Mustafa was different. There was no smile. He is angry at Israel. When I asked him to share his story or a message to the world instead of speaking to me, he looked straight at the camera.
“What they did is they took my home and my parents from me,” Mustafa said. He paused for a few seconds and continued, “Because of them I no longer live in peace.”
More than a thousand children were injured in Israeli attacks between March and August this year, according to the United Nations.
Some lost a parent or both their parents while more than 260 were killed. That figure represents an average of seven children killed or injured every day over those six months – nearly double the number at the start of the latest on-again, off-again conflict between Hezbollah and Israel in late 2023.
We have repeatedly filmed children’s clothes, toys and school books among the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli strikes, and repeatedly attended funerals of children killed alongside their parents. It is just as difficult emotionally to talk to survivors who show signs of trauma and tell us they live in fear.
In the village of Tibnine, close to the northern edge of the area occupied by the Israeli army, 11-year-old Bannine took us to the second floor of an orphanage, to show us what a nearby Israeli air strike did to their rooms.
“We were not here when this happened,” Bannine told us in a room full of debris and broken glass. Stuffed animals and clothes were still scattered on the floor.
Hundreds of thousands of people returned to their villages in southern Lebanon because of a reduction in violence in recent months. But there is little sense of security, with Israeli strikes and home demolitions continuing in front line areas.
“We wake up and sleep to the sound of bombing and warplanes and irritating drones,” Anaya Sultan told us. Her father was killed when the Israeli military escalated the conflict earlier this year. “He was my soul … he was everything to me,” she added.
Some of the girls here are not orphans, but their parents are too poor to care for them. According to Lebanese officials, the region’s economy is in a state of collapse.
Recurring conflicts, ruined infrastructure, blocked access to agricultural land, and mass displacement are making it hard for families in southern Lebanon to sustain themselves.
The UN identified southern Lebanon – alongside impoverished northern and eastern regions such as Akkar and Baalbek – as areas of greatest concern where families are struggling to survive.
According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than 1 million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity.
“Unfortunately, so many people are displaced … many of them used to support and help us. They are not present and they themselves are struggling,” Bassima Fawaz, who helps manage the orphanage, told us as we walked through the cold hallways and rooms of the building.
“We had to cover the windows with plastic sheeting because there’s no money to replace the glass shattered by Israeli bombardment. One of our girls is in hospital with pneumonia.”

noticias.titulo: Leonid meteor shower 2026: When and where to see it from where you live
noticias.resumen: The Leonids, among the year's fastest meteor showers, peak on November 17-18. Find the best time to watch in your city.
noticias.texto:
Leonid meteor shower 2026: When and where to see it from where you live
The Leonids, among the year’s fastest meteors, peak on November 17-18. Find the best time to watch in your city.
Some of the fastest meteors in the night sky return this week, as the Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night between November 17 and 18.
Racing at about 71km (44 miles) per second, they burn up as bright streaks, sometimes leaving glowing trails that hang in the sky for seconds.
In this visual explainer, see how the shower forms as Earth crosses a comet’s dust trail, then search for your city to find the best viewing time.
What is a meteor shower?
A meteor shower happens when dozens, or sometimes hundreds, of “shooting stars” streak across the night sky. In reality, they are not stars, but tiny bits of space debris burning up in Earth’s atmosphere.
Most of this debris comes from comets, which are icy bodies that orbit the sun and shed dust as they get closer to it. When Earth’s orbit crosses one of these dust trails, the particles, called meteoroids, hit the atmosphere at high speed and heat up. They glow as meteors and usually burn up long before reaching the ground.
The Leonids come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle, whose dust trail Earth passes through every November. Drag the slider below to follow Earth through 2026 and see when it meets the stream.
What makes the Leonid meteor shower special?
The Leonids are named after the constellation Leo, the point in the sky from which they appear to come. They are known for fireballs, which are unusually bright meteors from larger bits of debris. They also produce Earth-grazers, meteors that skim the upper atmosphere at a shallow angle and leave long trails near the horizon.
What really sets them apart is their storms. Comet Tempel-Tuttle passes close to the sun about every 33 years and leaves debris behind. When that happens, the shower can produce a storm of at least 1,000 meteors an hour.
The 1833 storm over North America helped scientists work out where meteors come from. In 1966, thousands of meteors fell every minute for about 15 minutes. The most recent storms came in 1999, 2001 and 2002, and the comet next swings close to the sun in 2031.
Where in the sky should you look?
The Leonids can appear in any part of the sky, so the best approach is to find a dark spot with a wide view, lie back and take in as much sky as you can.
If you trace their paths backwards, the meteors all seem to streak out from a single point known as the radiant. This is an effect of perspective: the debris travels along roughly parallel paths, but the meteors appear to spread out from one point, much like railway tracks seem to meet in the distance.
For the Leonids, the radiant lies in the constellation Leo, which rises in the east around midnight.
When and how to watch from where you live
According to the International Meteor Organization (IMO), the Leonids are active from November 6 to 30 and are expected to peak on the night between November 17 and 18, around 23:45 GMT on Tuesday. Under clear, dark skies, the IMO expects up to about 15 meteors an hour at the peak.
The best time to watch is between midnight and dawn, as Leo climbs higher in the sky. The moon, which will be about half full on the peak night, sets around midnight in many places, leaving darker skies for the rest of the night.
Find a spot away from city lights and give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the dark.
Use the widget below to find the best viewing times in your city.
Can you see the Leonid meteor shower from both hemispheres?
Yes. The Leonids are visible from the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere, but conditions are generally better in the north, where Leo climbs higher in the sky. South of the equator, the best chance is in the hour or two before dawn.
Will the moon affect the Leonid meteor shower in 2026?
Only slightly. The moon reaches its first quarter on November 17 and sets around midnight, so it should not interfere much during the best viewing hours.
How do the Leonids compare with other meteor showers?
The Leonids are far from the busiest shower. Under ideal conditions, the IMO puts their peak rate at about 15 meteors an hour, compared with about 100 for the Perseids in August and about 150 for the Geminids in December. What they lack in numbers, they make up for in speed and their history of storms.

noticias.titulo: US bank outage: What caused Chase problems and Zelle payment delays?
noticias.resumen: A Chase software bug disrupted US banking transactions and delayed some Zelle payments. Here's what happened.
noticias.texto:
US bank outage: What caused Chase problems and Zelle payment delays?
A Chase software bug disrupted US banking transactions and delayed some Zelle payments. Here’s what happened.
Thousands of customers across the United States reported problems accessing banking services and making payments after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.
The problems on Monday affected customers at several major financial institutions, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America, while some users also reported delays with Zelle payments.
So, what caused the US bank outages, which banks were affected, and have services returned to normal?
What happened?
Thousands of US customers reported problems accessing online banking services after JPMorgan Chase said a software issue caused knock-on effects for transactions involving other banks.
The disruption extended to customers of at least five other banks, who reported issues accessing services and completing transactions.
According to the French news agency AFP, reports on outage-tracking Downdetector peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (19:00 GMT) before declining later in the day.
“JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system – it is not cyber-related,” said Joe Evangelisti, spokesperson for the bank.
Which US banks were affected by the outages?
Customers of several major US banks reported problems on Monday.
These included JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Truist and Capital One.
However, not all the banks reported problems with their own systems.
Chase confirmed experiencing technical problems, while US Bank said its own systems were not directly affected. Capital One and Truist also said their services were operating normally.
Why were US banks down?
JPMorgan Chase said that a software bug in its internal hardware systems had slowed transaction processing and may have delayed transactions involving other banks.
Some customers said they were not able to access accounts and funds, although Chase said customers continued to have access.
The bank stressed that the disruption was not systemic and that other banks may have experienced delays when processing transactions involving Chase.
Chase is the consumer banking division of JPMorgan Chase, which holds the most assets of any US bank. It handles payments involving other financial institutions, meaning a technical problem at Chase can also delay transactions for customers at other banks, even if those banks’ systems are operating normally.
“This is not a systemic issue – other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” Evangelisti added.
Is Zelle down?
Zelle is the peer-to-peer third-party payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Early Warning Services, an Arizona-based company that is itself owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
In the US, some customers also reported problems sending and receiving payments through Zelle.
However, Zelle said its network was operating normally.
The company said that customers access Zelle through participating banks and credit unions so technical problems at those institutions can affect the ability to make a payment even if Zelle’s own systems are fully operational.
US Bank said its systems were not directly affected but warned that customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving other financial institutions could experience delays.
Are the bank outages over?
JPMorgan Chase said that transactions were processing normally again following the disruption.
A Chase spokesperson said that shortly after close of business on Monday, at approximately 6:30pm (23:30 GMT), transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News.
However, the restoration of Chase’s transaction processing does not necessarily mean every delayed payment has been completed.
Are the bank outages connected to the Microsoft and FAA disruptions?
There is no confirmed connection between Monday’s outages and the recent Microsoft outage and disruptions impacting the US government’s transport agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The banking problems followed two major incidents in the US last week.
On Thursday, Microsoft experienced a widespread outage that disrupted services including Outlook. A day later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop following a technical failure affecting air traffic control communications.
The incidents had different reported causes. JPMorgan Chase said its disruption was due to a software bug, while the FAA disruption involved malfunctioning equipment.
However, Jody Westby, CEO of cybersecurity advisory firm Global Cyber Risk, told Al Jazeera that the series of incidents raised questions about the reliability and security of critical infrastructure.
“I think it’s very concerning that everyone’s just jumping to the conclusion it’s a technical issue, it’s a software bug, it was old equipment,” she said.
“I don’t think that any of that is a complete explanation the public deserves.”
Westby said she believed more detailed investigations were needed.
“My concern is that we are not diligently looking into these incidents and analysing them, and even with a global working group to make sure that we can determine whether there are any correlations.”

noticias.titulo: Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
noticias.resumen: Iran reports tanker mine strikes as a drone alert in Iraq and the arrival of a US aircraft carrier raise tensions.
noticias.texto:
Tankers hit in Strait of Hormuz as drone raises alarm at Iraq gas field
Ships struck as US reinforces its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
Fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have raised concerns over the security of energy infrastructure across the region, as tensions between the United States and Iran persist despite diplomatic efforts to end their conflict.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Monday that two oil tankers had struck naval mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the southern part of the strait through a route Tehran considers unauthorised.
Separately, Iran’s regular navy said another tanker had caught fire and become immobilised after striking a mine in restricted waters east of the strait.
The claims could not be independently verified, and Iranian authorities did not identify the vessels involved.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency separately reported two tanker attacks in the strait on Monday.
In the latest incident, a tanker was disabled and an engine room fire broke out following an attack seven nautical miles (13km) north of Khasab, Oman.
Earlier, the maritime monitoring agency said another tanker had been struck by an unidentified projectile while travelling out of the strait, also causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported.
It remained unclear whether either incident was connected to the mine strikes claimed by Iran.
The incidents followed a series of attacks on commercial vessels in recent weeks. The United Nations’ International Maritime Organization recorded 136 security incidents involving vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11, including 35 in October alone.
Drone alert at Iraq gas field
The threats to maritime energy shipments came as another security alert raised concerns over energy infrastructure elsewhere in the region.
In Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, warning sirens sounded after a drone flew over the Khor Mor gas field on Monday, Reuters reported, citing two security sources.
There were no immediate reports of a strike or damage from the latest incident.
Production at Khor Mor had already been halted the previous week following a suspected drone attack that sparked a fire and disrupted 2.8 gigawatts of electricity generation, according to United Arab Emirates-based Dana Gas, one of the facility’s operators.
The field is a major source of natural gas for electricity generation in the Kurdish region, making disruptions particularly significant for local power supplies.
It has faced repeated attacks that Iraqi Kurdish officials have blamed on Iranian-backed armed groups.
No group was identified as responsible for Monday’s drone overflight.
The developments came as the US reinforced its military presence in the Middle East, with the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt arriving in the region.
A US official confirmed its arrival to Al Jazeera on Monday, bringing the number of American aircraft carriers operating in the US Central Command area to three, as tensions with Iran remained high and diplomatic efforts to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remained stalled.

noticias.titulo: US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips amid Nvidia scandal
noticias.resumen: The Trump administration introduces export licence requirements for Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil.
noticias.texto:
US moves to block China’s remote access to AI chips amid Nvidia scandal
Trump administration introduces export licence requirements for Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Singapore and Brazil.
United States President Donald Trump’s administration has announced new restrictions on China’s access to advanced chips amid fallout from the alleged spy scandal involving AI giant Nvidia.
The rule announced by the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) on Monday aims to prevent Chinese AI developers from getting around export controls by remotely accessing data centres in third countries, particularly in Southeast Asia.
It designates Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil as countries with an “unacceptable risk of diversion” and requires anyone seeking to ship advanced chips to those destinations to obtain an export licence.
BIS, which sits under the Department of Commerce, said the change was a “logical extension” of the existing requirement for companies to obtain a licence to export or transfer chips to firms based in China.
“The United States is the global leader in advanced computing and super intelligence technology and is committed to promoting the global adoption of American technology for legitimate commercial purposes while ensuring that sensitive technologies are not exploited in ways that threaten US national security,” BIS said in a statement.
While Chinese firms are barred from importing the most advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) under US export controls, they had until now been legally able to take advantage of remote access to top-of-the-line computing power at data centres in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
Singapore, which hosts dozens of data centres, said on Tuesday that it was “studying the details of this new measure carefully”.
“We are engaging affected companies to understand the potential impact on their businesses,” the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Digital Development and Information said in a joint statement.
“We have also been engaging the relevant US authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure, as well as exploring how to facilitate trusted access for Singapore companies.”
The ministries added that they did not condone companies using Singapore to “circumvent or violate” the laws of other countries.
The restrictions come as Nvidia’s export of advanced chips is under scrutiny following claims that former CEO Jensen Huang was romantically involved with a woman recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security for espionage.
Huang, who became one of the most prominent faces of the AI boom at the helm of Nvidia, resigned last week amid a company board investigation into allegations involving the Chinese-born executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Beijing has denied the spying allegations, made by unnamed US officials in media reports, calling them “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.
Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive identified as Jensen Huang’s ex-romantic partner, has not publicly commented on the claims.
Late on Monday, the US Commerce Department and the Department of Justice publicly confirmed that investigators had opened a criminal investigation into Megaspeed.
The Commerce Department began investigating Megaspeed for potential export control violations in 2024, leading BIS officials to conduct an on-site inspection of the Singapore-based company and to interview Alice Huang the following year, the statement said.
The Justice Department subsequently took the “lead role” in the criminal investigation, according to the statement.
“The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” it said.
US tech stocks fell sharply on Monday as investors weighed the scandal’s fallout on the AI rollout.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5 percent, closing in the red for the third consecutive session.
The broader S&P 500 dropped 1.9 percent.
Shares of Nvidia, which have shed more than 30 percent of their market value over the past month, dropped 4.1 percent.
The other six companies of the “Magnificent Seven” also lost ground, with Alphabet and Amazon seeing the next-biggest declines of 4.1 percent and 3.3 percent, respectively.
The sell-off continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong closing in the red.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s Kospi closed down 1.3 percent and 2.6 percent, respectively, while the Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong dropped 0.9 percent.

noticias.titulo: Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden
noticias.resumen: Yemen's army reports 173 Houthi fighters killed or wounded as government forces reposition to defend Aden.
noticias.texto:
Yemeni army reports 661 attacks on Houthis as group advances towards Aden
The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces.
Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest.
Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks.
In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications.
He said government forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, were continuing to confront Houthi movements in the provinces of Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, while operations were also under way on southern fronts.
The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The latest operations followed a series of battlefield setbacks for government-aligned forces, which have withdrawn from strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and are repositioning to defend Aden, the temporary capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry reported that the Houthis had cut off a key government supply route along the Red Sea coast, forcing troops to abandon several positions as concerns grew over a possible Houthi offensive towards Aden.
Parliament moves to outlaw Houthis
The military escalation coincided with a political development, as Yemen’s parliament unanimously approved a bill designating the Houthis a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising their activities, financing and supply of weapons.
According to the state-run Saba news agency, the bill provides for prosecuting those involved in violations attributed to the group, freezing and confiscating affiliated assets, and imposing tougher penalties for offences, including attacks on civilians, planting landmines and targeting international shipping.
The legislation will now be submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, for enactment.
The latest developments come six weeks after government forces launched “Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, seeking to regain territory controlled by the Houthis, including the capital, Sanaa.

noticias.titulo: Irish court jails man for life over Dublin knife attack that sparked riots
noticias.resumen: Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023.
noticias.texto:
Irish court jails man for life over Dublin knife attack that sparked riots
Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023.
A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life behind bars for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin on November 23, 2023, in an attack that triggered rioting and looting in the Irish capital.
Riad Bouchaker, an Algerian national and Irish citizen, was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court in Dublin on Monday after being found guilty in July on eight charges arising from the knife attack outside a school nearly three years ago.
His victims included a five-year-old girl, a six-year-old girl, a five-year-old boy and a woman in her mid-30s.
The youngest girl was stabbed in the heart, resulting in severe disability after her brain was deprived of oxygen for 40 minutes following the attack.
The girl, who is now eight, cannot speak and communicates only by blinking. She uses a wheelchair and is fed through a tube in her stomach because she is unable to swallow safely.
Bouchaker was also found guilty of assaulting childcare worker Leanne Flynn, who suffered serious injuries as she tried to protect the children.
Speaking outside the court, Garda Superintendent Colm Murphy, the senior investigating officer, acknowledged the actions of those who intervened, the Press Association reported.
“I just want to take this opportunity to acknowledge the actions of those that immediately reacted to the situation as it unfolded, in particular to Leanne Flynn, who undoubtedly her actions on the day saved lives,” he said.
Within hours of the attack, false information about the suspect’s identity spread online, fuelling anger among anti-immigration activists and far-right groups.
The worst rioting seen in the Irish capital for decades erupted in the city centre as crowds clashed with police, set vehicles on fire and looted shops.
The violence shocked the country and triggered days of debate over immigration, online misinformation and public order.
Nearly 100 people were arrested, and more than 80 were charged with offences.
Bouchaker had pleaded not guilty to three counts of attempted murder and three counts of assault causing harm.
He also denied one count each of intentionally or recklessly causing serious harm and brandishing a dangerous weapon, a kitchen knife.
Judge Tony Hunt told the jury that two years before the attack, Bouchaker had suffered from a benign brain tumour that required surgery.
Hunt also said that due to interventions by bystanders immediately after the attack, Bouchaker suffered a head injury that required hospital treatment.
He was found fit to stand trial, and “there is no suggestion that he was suffering mental disorder at the time of the incident”, the judge said.
Evidence was heard from more than 80 witnesses, including eyewitnesses, emergency responders, police and forensic experts.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
noticias.resumen: Kushner reports progress towards a deal, but Moscow says it has not agreed to European participation in the next talks.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said there had been ‘no change in Russia’s position’ as Russia and Ukraine strike major infrastructure.
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.
“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.
Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.
Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.
US envoy reports progress, warns of difficult choices
Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.
“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.
He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.
The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.
Europe prepares to join, Moscow withholds agreement
Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.
Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.
European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.
Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”
Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.
“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.
Russia rules out a temporary respite
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.
He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.
Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.
“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”
The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

noticias.titulo: UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
noticias.resumen: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
noticias.texto:
UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says UK lost more than it gained after its divorce from the bloc.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.
During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.
“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”
The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.
Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.
The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.
The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.
Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.
Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.
“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”
Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.
Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.
Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

noticias.titulo: Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
noticias.resumen: The country's unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands.
noticias.texto:
Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
Ethiopia’s unresolved Oromia-Somali border dispute fuels renewed violence, displacing thousands.
Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement.
The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume.
The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services.
A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations.
The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal.
A territorial dispute reignites violence
According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), the latest escalation began on October 18, when Somali regional police clashed with ethnic Oromo militia members following the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed locality of Moyale.
The conflict monitor’s East Africa senior analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru, reported that a 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed during the confrontation. However, accounts of how she died differ: some people said she was caught in crossfire, while others claimed she was killed after trying to remove the flag.
Members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened and stopped the initial fighting, according to ACLED. The following day, Oromo residents staged a demonstration against the office opening and the girl’s death, blocking the main road and forcing businesses to close.
Elders and security officials from both sides later agreed to remove the Somali regional flag and suspend the office’s opening. However, the agreement did not prevent further confrontations. ACLED reported that Somali residents also demonstrated against the arrangement on October 20, closing the main road and disrupting transport services.
Fighting escalated again on October 22, when Somali regional police clashed with Oromia regional police and Oromo militia members in several locations in Moyale. ACLED also reported clashes involving Oromo and Somali militias in parts of Arero and Wachile districts.
The violence is rooted in longstanding disagreements over administrative boundaries, political representation and access to land and natural resources. These disputes have repeatedly fuelled tensions between Borana Oromo and Somali communities along the regional border.
Federal government under pressure to intervene
A security official familiar with the situation in Moyale told Al Jazeera that clashes were continuing and that attempts to broker an agreement between representatives of the Oromia and Somali regional administrations had failed. He said resolving the crisis required direct and immediate involvement by the federal government.
The federal government’s role has consequently become a central question in efforts to contain the violence. Although members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened during the initial October 18 confrontation, ACLED documented further clashes involving regional police and militia members from October 22 onwards.
The crisis has also drawn attention beyond Ethiopia’s borders. On November 9, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said he had spoken with his Ethiopian counterpart and urged the government in Addis Ababa to help restore stability so that people who had fled into Kenya could return home.
Reporting by Kenya’s The Star newspaper said Mudavadi put the number of Ethiopians who had crossed into Kenya at approximately 40,000 at the time. He said the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it would work towards restoring normality.
Unresolved boundaries and political tensions
Cameron Hudson, a political and security analyst and former director for African affairs at the US National Security Council, said the crisis reflected wider challenges facing Ethiopia’s federal system and its management of regional disputes.
Hudson said federal forces were already preoccupied with security challenges elsewhere in the country. He also pointed to a perception among Somali communities that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party favour the Oromo, Abiy’s ethnic group.
Hudson said previous mediation efforts had largely failed because the territorial dispute along the regional border remained unresolved.
The historical background includes a referendum organised on October 24, 2004, to determine the administration of 463 small communities along the Oromia-Somali regional border, according to Ethiopia’s National Election Board.
However, research by Boku Tache, published in a doctoral thesis at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences in 2008, found that the referendum was conducted in Liban and parts of Arero, while the Moyale case remained unresolved.
The research also examined how displacement, competing claims over grazing land and access to traditional resources contributed to tensions between Borana and Somali communities. These historical disputes continue to provide important context for the current confrontation.
Hudson added that successive Ethiopian governments had failed to engage local communities to address the underlying causes of territorial tensions, instead responding after violence had erupted.
The humanitarian consequences have extended beyond Ethiopia. On October 28, the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) said local authorities estimated that up to 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya since October 22 to escape the fighting. The agency said registration and verification were continuing, meaning the figure remained provisional.
Many of those arriving in Kenya were women and children, according to the UNHCR, which identified food, drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and healthcare as urgent needs.
For residents in the affected areas, immediate priorities remain the restoration of security and the resumption of livelihoods. With the territorial dispute unresolved and the two regional administrations yet to reach a lasting agreement, uncertainty continues over when affected communities will be able to return to normal life.
“The federal government is ultimately responsible for addressing violence, even along regional borders,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.

noticias.titulo: Paraguay ex-president moved to military jail amid special treatment reports
noticias.resumen: Santiago Pena has been accused of corruption following the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this month.
noticias.texto:
Paraguay ex-president moved to military jail amid special treatment reports
Santiago Pena has been accused of corruption following the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this month.
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Pena has been transferred to a military prison on a judge’s orders, following reports that he was granted special amenities while awaiting trial for a financial corruption scandal.
On Monday, Judge Osmar Legal ordered Pena to be moved from the Presidential Escort Regiment, a military base in the capital city of Asuncion.
There, media reports indicated he had a large dining room, furnishings, a private gym and a bathroom, sparking public backlash.
His new lodgings are inside Vinas Cue military prison. Pena, however, is to be held separately from the facility’s other prisoners for his safety.
Allegations against the former president are at the centre of a corruption scandal related to the collapse of a major financial lender, Ueno Bank, used by more than half of the country’s adult population.
The political crisis erupted into the public spotlight on November 3, when Paraguay’s central bank took control of Ueno after declaring it insolvent.
In doing so, it froze account activity for nearly three million people. In the months before its collapse, Ueno held roughly $850m in public funds, including money for retirement pensions.
The scandal led to the end of Pena’s presidency. A member of the conservative Colorado Party, a leading force in Paraguay’s politics, Pena saw his political allies distance themselves from him in the wake of the lender’s collapse.
His attempts to resign were rejected, as Paraguay’s Congress instead pursued impeachment proceedings against him. He was removed from office on November 6.
As criminal investigations unfolded, scrutiny fell on Pena’s role as a shareholder in Ueno’s parent company. Pena has denied wrongdoing and said he sold his shares in 2025.
Prosecutors, however, have accused Pena of using his position in office to direct public funds to the bank while it made insider loans to owners.
He faces charges including breach of trust, criminal association and administration for personal gain. Angry protests accompanied Pena’s removal, and he was ordered to be held in pretrial detention.
His former vice president, Pedro Alliana, has since been sworn in to lead Paraguay’s executive branch.
In a news conference on Monday, Alliana said he had dismissed a military official, Colonel Jose David Daiub, accused of giving Pena special treatment while in detention.
“Our priority is to guarantee the country’s stability, restore confidence, and provide concrete and rapid solutions,” said Alliana.
Paraguayans, he added, “deserve to know the truth”. Pena’s transfer to a military prison came on his 48th birthday.
