noticias.texto:
Transport for NSW is investigating allegations that a young Aboriginal mother and her family were told to leave a bus and left by the side of a regional highway because her 22-month-old child was crying.
Wiradjuri woman Kaneesha Lee Williams was travelling home from Sydney to the Riverina town of Darlington Point, 155km west of Wagga Wagga, with her young daughter, Audria, and her mother, Tamara, on Sunday.
They had been in Sydney for a family birthday and had caught the train from Sydney to Wagga Wagga, before transferring to a regional bus operated by NSW TrainLink, with tickets to Hay.
But about 15 minutes into the journey, on Coolamon Road, Williams alleges, the driver pulled over and told her and her family to disembark because her daughter was crying.
“We got on the road and my daughter Audria started getting a little bit restless so I sat her on my lap and put her to sleep because she was crying and stuff,” Williams said.
She said her daughter had just begun to settle when the driver pulled over.
“I thought, ‘why did we stop for?’ I didn’t think he was coming up to me. Then he walked up to me and he said, ‘I can’t drive this bus while that baby is crying, you’re gonna have to get off’.
“I just looked at him and I looked at my daughter and my eyes started swelling up into tears.”
She said the driver gave her no warning. “We weren’t aggressive or anything, we were more in shock … Are you really gonna kick a little baby off the bus for crying?
“She’s 22 months old, she’s overtired, overstimulated and doesn’t want to be on the bus … We had little food, no water. He didn’t even ask if we were able to get a lift or anything, he just kicked us straight off.”
Williams said they were deposited on the side of the road with low phone battery and no alternative transport arrangements. The driver did not offer to make alternative arrangements or ask if they had anyone to pick them up, she alleges. They eventually found somewhere to charge their phones to contact family, who drove more than two hours to pick them up.
Teenager Alexis Longdon, who was sitting three seats back on the opposite side of the aisle, told Guardian Australia she saw Williams and her family being asked to get off the bus, and was confused when they then left without them.
“We were just outside of Wagga and the bus driver stopped the bus and said: ‘can you get off the bus and calm her down please’, because apparently it was creating an unsafe environment for the driver,” the 14-year-old said. “And then she got off the bus and I guess she couldn’t calm her baby down, we waited five minutes maybe and then he got on the bus and left.
Williams then wrote a formal complaint to the NSW transport minister demanding an independent investigation into the incident, including an examination of all relevant CCTV, and asking whether the driver’s actions complied with TrainLink and the transport department’s policies and standards.
The letter, seen by Guardian Australia, also asked whether this would have happened to a non-Aboriginal family.
On Tuesday, the NSW minister for regional transport, Jenny Aitchison, said her office had reached out to Williams to offer support and that the “alleged behaviour of this driver was completely unacceptable”.
“It’s extremely disappointing that a mother and her young child were treated so poorly on a service that they had every right to use,” Aitchison said in a statement to Guardian Australia. “It’s not the service we accept from our bus drivers.
“I hope to speak to the family soon and reiterate my concern about this incident and apologise for what happened to them.
“I’m advised the bus driver is no longer employed by the coach operator.”
A Transport for NSW spokesperson said the incident was being investigated.
“Transport for NSW is aware of an incident involving passengers travelling on a NSW TrainLink coach service operated by Dyson between Wagga Wagga and Mildura on Sunday,” they said in a statement. “Transport for NSW takes the concerns raised extremely seriously.
“The operator is investigating the incident and Transport for NSW has requested updates as those enquiries progress.
“Passenger safety is our highest priority and we expect all operators and their employees to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism when interacting with passengers.”
Dyson was contacted for comment.

noticias.titulo: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia named as biggest CO2 exporters in history
noticias.resumen: Analysis of fossil fuel exports since 1850 differs from most assessments – which look at countries where CO 2 is released Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the three biggest exporters of carbon dioxide in history, according to analysis of fossil fuels since 1850. Russia tops the list of global exporters of fossil fuels, with its vast coal, oil and gas deposits. Accounting for the CO 2 produced by burning these exports, Russia has been responsible for more than 70 gigatonnes, up to the end of 2025. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the three biggest exporters of carbon dioxide in history, according to analysis of fossil fuels since 1850.
Russia tops the list of global exporters of fossil fuels, with its vast coal, oil and gas deposits. Accounting for the CO2 produced by burning these exports, Russia has been responsible for more than 70 gigatonnes, up to the end of 2025.
Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s biggest producers of oil and gas, comes next with about 60 gigatonnes of CO2 exported. The country has long been an obstructive force at the annual UN climate summits.
Australia is in third place, a long way behind the top two exporters, with responsibility for more than 25 gigatonnes of exported CO2, not far ahead of Venezuela. The revelation comes as Australia acts as president of this year’s UN climate summit, Cop31, which is now into its second week in Turkey. The country has yet to set an end point for the use or export of fossil fuels, which make up about two-fifths of its export economy.
Louise Hutchins, the convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said: “This analysis tells you a lot about what’s going wrong with climate negotiations. Here at Cop31, governments claim there’s not enough money to tackle the climate crisis, while Australia, Russia and Saudi Arabia, that have amassed fortunes from fossil fuels, continue to wield pivotal political power in this consensus-based process.
“Just look at Australia. Its contribution to global heating more than doubles when fossil fuel exports are counted. Yet it is co-presiding over the very negotiations where climate finance talks are once again in stalemate.
“Responsibility is on the wealthy, the powerful and the profiteers. Those who made fortunes from fossil fuels must pay for the damage.”
The analysis of historical exports of fossil fuels, conducted by Carbon Brief and seen by the Guardian, apportions responsibility for CO2 emissions based on the country extracting the fossil fuels, in contrast to most analyses, which look to the countries where the CO2 is released.
Calculating where the fossil fuels came from casts the global economy, and historical responsibilities for emissions, in a new light. Exporting countries can be relatively low on the list of global greenhouse gas emitters, because those calculations are based on fossil fuel use.
The analysis also shows that the US and China – the world’s two biggest current emitters of greenhouse gases – still bear greater responsibility for historical emissions than Russia, Saudi or Australia, because as well as importing vast quantities of fossil fuels, they have also burned their own supplies.
The Cop28 UN conference outcome in Dubai in 2023 called on all countries to contribute to a global fossil fuel transition, but set no timetable or workplan for doing so. At Cop31, on Monday afternoon, Australia issued a first draft of a potential outcome from the summit, which contained a call for “the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”.
However, many countries – including Saudi Arabia – have hardened their negotiating positions since Dubai, and the absence of the US under Donald Trump takes pressure away from them to find compromises. Many observers think the reference to the “immediate transition away” is unlikely to survive unscathed through the several more drafts of the cover decision text that are likely.
Saudi, Russia and allies in the Arab group and others are even opposing the idea of having a cover text, which could stymie negotiations further.
Climate Analytics, a thinktank, published separate analysis on Tuesday showing that Australia, despite presiding over Cop31, appeared to have no plans to curtail its own fossil fuel extraction.
Coalmines are still being permitted that would remain in operation until 2088, long after all countries are supposed to have reached net zero greenhouse gas emissions, around mid-century.
“It’s abundantly clear Australia is not ‘doing its part’ as the prime minister claimed here in Turkey last week,” said the Climate Analytics CEO, Bill Hare. “There is a deep contradiction in a government position that champions climate ambition abroad but plans for continued fossil fuel exports, with approvals for coalmines and gasfields that lock in production for decades.”
Addressing these contradictions is politically difficult for the Australian government. Anthony Albanese, the prime minister, attended Cop31 last week, but at home he is under pressure from a resurgent One Nation party that is riding high in the polls, and which spurns net zero and denies climate science.
A representative for the Saudi ministry of energy told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia accounted for approximately 1% of historical global CO₂ emissions within its borders. “Saudi Arabia exports oil to countries around the world to meet their energy needs. These countries decide how the oil is used, which technologies are employed, and how the resulting emissions are managed. It would therefore be misleading to place responsibility for those emissions on the exporting country while overlooking the role of those who consume the fuel.”
They added: “This does not absolve energy producers of their role in reducing emissions. Saudi Arabia is actively pursuing that role. Peer-reviewed research published in Science has identified Saudi crude among the lowest in upstream carbon intensity, while International Energy Agency data indicate comparatively low methane intensity in Saudi oil and gas operations.'”
Australia and Russia were approached for comment.
Asad Rehman, the chief executive of Friends of the Earth, said: “It’s time for the deadly tango between the producers of fossil fuels, and those locked into dependency on oil and gas, to have its last dance. We must turn off the tap on fossil fuels and push richer nations to commit to a fair, fast and fully funded phaseout. That means real public finance, and access to the technology that can make it possible, for the countries bearing the brunt of climate breakdown.”

noticias.titulo: Ukraine critically damages Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
noticias.resumen: Photos of bridge, built after 2014 annexation and viewed by Ukraine as illegal, suggest massive steel arch has fallen into water Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin. Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.
Footage showed a Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missile seconds before it hit the road and railway crossing, followed by an explosion. The strike follows an earlier attack on Monday that targeted an arch across its central section.
Russian forces struck two major bridges in Kyiv that straddle the Dnipro River late on Monday, along with some other critical infrastructure, amid drone and missile attacks across Ukraine.
Ukraine has declared that the Kerch bridge, built eight years ago after Vladimir Putin’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and known officially as the Crimean Bridge, is illegal. It has repeatedly attempted to destroy it, with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone strike the following year.
The latest drone and missile barrage appears to have succeeded, after months in which Ukrainian unmanned systems forces have systematically knocked out the peninsula’s multi-layered air defences.
The Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov, confirmed the bridge, which was temporarily closed on Monday, was no longer usable. “The enemy has once again attacked the Crimean Bridge. At the moment, traffic has been suspended,” he posted.
He added on Telegram: “We ask residents and visitors in Crimea to refrain from traveling toward the bridge and to take these restrictions into account when planning their routes.”
Photos on Tuesday suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.
Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.
The debris appears to have blocked the main navigable route beneath the bridge, used by maritime traffic from the Sea of Azov and the ports of Berdiansk and Mariupol. The channel is 120 metres wide and 8.3 metres deep. Submerged steel struts could prevent large vessels from passing until the debris is removed.
Ukrainian observers were gleeful at the bridge’s long-awaited destruction. They pointed out that Ukraine’s armed forces could hit the bridge again to prevent repair work from being carried out. Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to the defence ministry in Kyiv, wrote: “In response to your many questions. Yes, the bridge is fucked.”
In Kyiv, loud explosions could be heard as Russian forces struck two bridges over the Dnipro River. The mayor of the Ukrainian capital, Vitali Klitschko, wrote on Telegram that according to “preliminary information, there have been hits on the north and south bridges in the capital”. There were water and power cuts in parts of the city, he added later.
Russian forces launched a series of attacks on bridges crossing the river earlier this month and in October.
A Russian missile attack had injured three people in the region of Cherkasy and also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-biggest city, local officials said on Telegram.
Russia’s defence ministry claimed on Tuesday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, transport infrastructure in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia and the Cherkasy and Dnipropetrovsk regions.
The ministry said the strikes had also targeted energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels used by Ukraine’s armed forces.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said earlier on Monday that intelligence showed Russia’s military was planning strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday.
Russian defence ministry data from Monday showed that an overnight Ukrainian drone barrage on was the biggest since the start of full-scale war in 2022.
Zelenskyy also said on Monday that Ukraine had held new online talks with the US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as European representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia.
Kushner said progress had been made toward an agreement, though important challenges remain to end the war that Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.

noticias.titulo: Asylum seekers on final ‘one in, one out’ UK-France flight feel they are being ‘punished’
noticias.resumen: Many of those onboard are being deported for second time after fleeing threats from people smugglers in France Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation flight are people who returned to the UK fleeing threats from smugglers after they were already forcibly returned to France. Hundreds of asylum seekers who were sent back to France are thought to have returned to the UK, citing threats from smugglers who said their families still owed them money for the Channel crossing. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Many of the asylum seekers on Tuesday’s final “one in, one out” deportation flight are people who returned to the UK fleeing threats from smugglers after they were already forcibly returned to France.
Hundreds of asylum seekers who were sent back to France are thought to have returned to the UK, citing threats from smugglers who said their families still owed them money for the Channel crossing.
Asylum seekers who spoke to the Guardian described being punched, beaten or raped by the smugglers. Some said smugglers had caught them while they slept on the streets and forced them to work for them in conditions of modern slavery in a migrant camp in Calais, cleaning the smugglers’ tents and carrying water or firewood.
The charity Medical Justice, which has provided support to people detained for one in, one out, called the pilot scheme “a disaster”.
The one in, one out scheme involved forcibly returning hundreds of people who had travelled to the UK on small boats to France in exchange for bringing a similar number from northern France to the UK to claim asylum.
One asylum seeker with a ticket for Tuesday’s flight said he was captured by the smugglers after being returned to France by the Home Office earlier this year. He said he was a political dissident in Iran, and believed he would be executed if he was returned there.
“I came back to the UK a second time because the smugglers caught me in France,” he said. “I was sleeping on the streets in Paris because France did not accept my asylum case.
“Many of the people who have tickets for Tuesday’s flight are people like me, who came back to the UK a second time. I believe those of us who came back to the UK a second time are being punished by being sent back to France a second time. I believe that 100%.”
He said that although the Home Office stated that sufficient lawyers were available for asylum seekers detained for France, he and others had struggled to access good quality legal advice.
“Friends paid privately for a lawyer for me. The lawyer promised me that 24 hours before the flight, they would challenge my removal, but he has done nothing,” he said. “They do not even answer the phone although I have tried to call them 10 times.
“My mind is broken. I am scared that when I am returned to France on Tuesday, the smugglers will catch me and kill me.
“When the guards came to take me to the plane for France last time, three or four of them surrounded me and made me feel like a criminal. I have committed no crime apart from coming to UK to claim asylum.
“When I slept on the street last time the weather was warmer in France. Now it is too cold to sleep outside. I don’t know what I’m going to do.”
A second asylum seeker with a ticket for the flight, who also returned to the UK after being sent back to France, said he knew of dozens of people due to fly on Tuesday.
“All of us have bad solicitors who are not helping us,” he said. “One in, one out finished on 1 October. I do not understand why the Home Office wants to continue sending us to France.”
John Tuckett, the independent chief inspector of borders and immigration, said in a report published last week that it was not known how the Home Office would measure the success or failure of the one in, one out scheme, despite it being given the highest operational priority, with regular updates supplied to ministers and 10 Downing Street.
He cited a ministerial submission which stated that the aim of the scheme was to demonstrate that dangerous journeys on small boats were not a viable option for entry into the UK, with the aim of undermining the organised immigration crime model. Since the scheme ended on 1 October, 4,786 people have crossed the Channel in 69 small boats, according to government data.
A Medical Justice spokesperson said: “One in, one out has been a disaster, causing avoidable suffering to a vulnerable group and it has failed in the Home Office’s stated objective.
“The Home Office must start to learn lessons and put an end to dangerous detention conditions.”
Seema Syeda, of the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, said: “The UK government has forced people fleeing war, climate breakdown and persecution to take murderous and traumatising journeys across the Channel, only to treat them with brutality once they have arrived here, retraumatising them with detention and deportation.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We welcome the inspector’s recognition of the strong operational delivery of the UK-France pilot, which successfully demonstrated that a returns arrangement of this kind can work.
“The message was clear: if you returned to the UK after being transferred to France under the pilot, you would be sent back.
“The pilot has now concluded and we are taking forward lessons learned as part of wider efforts to strengthen returns. Any future operational decisions, including on evaluation and reporting, will be considered in the usual way.”

noticias.titulo: Serbia’s Student List candidates to be sworn in as MPs after election triumph
noticias.resumen: Inaugural parliamentary session comes as ousted populist Aleksandar Vučić threatens mass protests of his own Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government. The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Ser
noticias.texto:
Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, are to be sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government.
The 140 candidates – among them academics, lawyers, scientists and the odd actor – will be sworn in on Tuesday during the inaugural session of the new parliament, bringing 14 years of rule by Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) to an end.
A caretaker government under the outgoing prime minister, Ðjuro Macut, will remain in office until MPs approve the Student List’s choice of a cabinet. For now, its makeup – including the identity of a future prime minister – remains unclear.
Sarah El Sarag, a human rights lawyer and MP-elect, said the wider student movement continued to be active in the process of selecting the cabinet, along with the candidates themselves. “We are there because of them,” she said of the students. “All the time, we are doing it together.”
Parliamentary planning sessions had helped prepare the candidates, she said. “We have been having meetings and exercises for the parliament almost every day, because none of us are professional politicians. We are lawyers, doctors, professors – and it is the first time for us to do this kind of job.”
The sessions reflect the Student List’s efforts to pre-empt sceptics who question whether a group of candidates with no political experience is equipped to govern. Members of the movement that selected El Sarag and her fellow MPs-elect have reiterated that all are experts in their professional or academic fields and are better qualified than many of the people who served as ministers or MPs under Vučić.
El Sarag said her colleagues had a good idea of what to expect from Tuesday’s opening session. “People who have had some experience of politics have been making some simulated exercises for us,” she said.
She would not divulge the identity of the candidate for speaker – who will become Serbia’s acting president – let alone the name of the next prime minister.
Vučić is not accepting his new role as leader of the opposition meekly. Since the election, he has accused the Student List of instituting a regime of “naked terror” by directing “submissive prosecutors and police” to carry out unlawful detentions.
Police and prosecutors have made a series of arrests of people with links to the SNS. Last week, prosecutors targeted the owners of a well-connected construction company over a project on the site of the once-famous Hotel Jugoslavija, which was hit during the 1999 Nato airstrikes on Belgrade.
That followed the arrest of the owner of Alta Bank, which held the concession for processing bill payments on behalf of Serbia’s state-owned electricity company. Others facing charges include senior police officers accused of abuse of office, and people suspected of vote rigging and violence during the elections.
After the two years of protests which culminated in the SNS’s defeat at the ballot box, Vučić is threatening major protests of his own.
Raša Nedeljkov, the programme director of the Serbian election and democracy monitor CRTA, said the first disruptions could come during parliament’s inaugural session.
“We can expect a lot of sabotage, a lot of obstruction, a lot of circus-creating atmosphere,” he said. “If we see such scenes in parliament – including some kind of physical obstruction – that’s something which would not surprise me.”
In such an atmosphere, speed may be of the essence, he said. MPs must approve a new cabinet within 90 days of the national assembly’s inaugural session but will be motivated to name a PM well before that deadline.

noticias.titulo: Iran launches drone attacks against US military base in Bahrain
noticias.resumen: Strikes cast further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington with increasing risk of escalation Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation. Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Iran has launched drone attacks against a US military base in Bahrain, casting further doubt on peace talks between Tehran and Washington and raising the spectre of escalation.
Blasts sounded over the Gulf nation on Sunday in the second Iranian drone attack in three days in retaliation for US strikes in Iran.
Meanwhile, in Yemen, Iran’s Houthi allies advanced against pro-government forces in the south, opening a potential route to Aden. Iran also claimed that a mine sank an oil supertanker in the strait of Hormuz.
The developments deepened gloom about the chances of any diplomatic breakthrough in the region.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said they launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. Authorities in Bahrain said air defences intercepted the drones before they reached their targets.
At a press conference in Tehran the foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked if the latest strikes indicated a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
US forces have conducted a series of strikes against Iranian targets in recent weeks, including Qeshm Island in the strait of Hormuz.
Donald Trump last week called them minor strikes and said Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states had cautioned him against large-scale combat operations.
However, the president also said Washington was no longer seeking a deal with Iran and that he had instructed the vice-president, JD Vance, to switch his focus to alleged corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance – who blamed the Republicans’ loss of Congress in midterm elections on the Iran war – had requested a personal meeting with Iranian negotiators to discuss peace terms.
A conflict that began with joint US and Israeli attacks against Iran in February remains at an impasse, with the US maintaining a naval blockade and Iran its chokehold over the strait of Hormuz.
In a separate development, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed that two ships hit mines in the strait of Hormuz and that one, an oil supertanker with 2m barrels of oil, sank. The ships suffered “massive explosions and fire”, said the statement.
There was no immediate independent verification. The US military recently claimed it had cleared all mines from main routes through the waterway.
The strikes against Bahrain suggested Iran has decided on a tit-for-tat response to US attacks.
Bahrain hosts significant US bases, including a forward base that was home to the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, operating as a central support hub for military operations in the Middle East.
Tehran repeatedly targeted the kingdom until September, when there was a lull in attacks. That ended on Friday when Iran launched drones against a US radar facility. US Central Command said it shot down two drones without any injury or damage.
The attacks on Sunday prompted sirens and alerts from Bahrain’s authorities urging residents to seek shelter.
“It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them,” resident Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told Agence France Presse.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry called the resumption of attacks “heinous aggression” and a flagrant violation of international law.
The kingdom rejected Tehran’s “flimsy pretexts and baseless claims” to target its territory, it said in a statement. “The kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.”
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.
In Yemen, Saudi Arabia’s campaign against the Iranian-aligned Houthi rebels reeled when forces fighting on behalf of the Yemeni government retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb strait to defend Aden on the southern coast.
“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south said in a statement.
The admission signalled the apparent failure of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
A Houthi missile strike near Aden killed people and wounded 12 near Aden, AFP reported, citing military and government sources.

noticias.titulo: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain - as it happened
noticias.resumen: Iran has targeted airbase in Bahrain in latest resumption of strikes since september The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the c
noticias.texto:
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain
The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning.
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.
The statements are very similar, I’ve pulled out a few below:
Saudi Arabia’sMinistry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement published by the Saudi Press Agency:
The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on the Qatar news agency (QNA):
The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region.
I’m going to wrap up coverage for now. Here’s a summary of what you need to know as Iran steps up strikes against US allies in the Gulf again.
Iran launched a six-drone attack on a US airbase in Bahrain early on Sunday, prompting fears of a return to full-blown fighting after a two-month lull in strikes
Bahrain said it had intercepted “several aerial attacks” and destroyed the drones before they reached their targets, and officials did not immediately disclose any damage or injuries
However the tiny Gulf kingdom, which hosts a major US naval command, was forced to send out public warnings and sound missile warning sirens ahead of the incoming strikes
Iran said it had targeted a radar facility at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base. The US is yet to respond, but said there had been no damage from the first attempted strike on Friday.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have claimed the sinking of an oil supertanker which hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. There’s no independent verification of this yet.
The US military had claimed recently that it had cleared all mines from the main routes through the waterway.
But the IRGC said Sunday that two ships had hit its mines while travelling through the strait, “resulting in massive explosions and fire”.
It said the super tanker had been carrying more than two million barrels of oil when it sunk in the Gulf. Iran has made several announcements in recent weeks about ships hitting mines.
Tehran has heavily restricted shipping traffic through the strait since the start of the war, demanding vessels seek permission and travel via designated pathways. It has fired on ships trying to circumvent Iranian detection.
The US has been supporting ships going through the strait. In the past 24 hours, Centcomm posted on X a picture of F-16 fighter jets and said that more than 1.7 billions of crude oil “have been shipped through the Strait of Hormuz by Gulf partners with U.S. protection.”
As I mentioned earlier, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards have said its strikes this morning were retaliation for US aggression.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a press conference in Tehran on Sunday that Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states.
He was asked whether the strike on Tehran, the second this weekend, showed a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled.
Mr. Baghaei said that Iran was “not waiting for anyone” and was focused on its security.
The US has launched strikes on Iranian naval bases in the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, as well as along Iran’s southern coast. This has been seen as efforts to try and degrade Iran’s striking capability as well as offering cover for commerical ships still venturing through and out of Hormuz.
President Trump has refrained from major military escalation, describing those sporadic strikes as minor. However, American media have reported that both the US and Israel have discussed plans for a fuller resumption of strikes.
Here’s a map showing Bahrain, the smallest Gulf state, in relation to Iran and the rest of its Gulf neighbours. Tehran sent a flurry of drones across the Gulf in the early hours of Sunday morning to target a US air base south of Manama.
Bahrain is home to a major US military base, the NSA Bahrain (or Naval Support Activity Bahrain), which are headquarters for the US Fifth Fleet and US Naval Forces Central Command, and also acts as key hub of support for all operations in the region.
However the base was struck heavily during Iran’s retaliatory strikes at the start of the war, and it’s unclear whether it’s fully recovered.
American media have reported major damage to its headquarters, barracks and radar facilities.
Iran’s drones this morning were aimed at a different target- the US air base in Al-Rifaa, south of the capital.
The US has formal bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar, and access arrangements to military facilities in the United Arab Emirates, Oman, and Saudi Arabia.
In light of Iran’s latest strike attempts on US allies in the Gulf, it’s useful to look at what the US commander-in-chief has been saying in recent days, as my colleague Patrick Wintour reports.
Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews since Thursday that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.
Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
Five killed in Houthi attack near Yemeni government capital
I reported earlier that Yemeni government forces are falling back to Aden to try and secure their interim capital which is coming under pressure from Houthi forces.
A Houthi attack on a checkpoint near Aden has killed five people and injured eight others near Aden, AFP is reporting.
The missile targeted a checkpoint in Khor Omeira, Lahj province, AFP says, citing three unnamed military sources and a government source.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain
The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning.
Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.
The statements are very similar, I’ve pulled out a few below:
Saudi Arabia’sMinistry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement published by the Saudi Press Agency:
The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples.
Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on the Qatar news agency (QNA):
The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region.
Below is the full statement from Bahrain’s foreign ministry on the Iranian drone strikes today, which were intercepted and shot down. This has been published in Bahrain’s various state-controlled media outlets.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s strongest condemnation of the continued Iranian aggression against its territory, including the attack launched today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, by drones that were intercepted and destroyed by air defense systems in the Kingdom’s airspace.
This comes two days after a similar attack at dawn on Friday, November 13, 2026, by two drones that were also intercepted. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for these attacks. The Ministry praised the efficiency, vigilance, and capability of the Bahrain Defense Force in confronting today’s attack and its complete readiness to deter any aggression.
The Ministry considered these attacks a resumption of Iran’s heinous aggression against the Kingdom and countries in the region, disregarding the provisions of international law and the principles of the UN Charter.
The Kingdom views them as a blatant attack on its sovereignty and territorial integrity, a flagrant violation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on the Kingdom of Bahrain and neighboring countries and demanded their immediate cessation, a targeting of innocent citizens and residents, a sabotage of de-escalation efforts, and a serious threat to the region’s security and stability.
The Ministry affirmed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s categorical rejection of the flimsy pretexts and baseless claims put forward by the Iranian Revolutionary Guard, emphasizing that no pretext justifies aggression against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states.
It stressed that freedom of navigation and passage, by sea and air, in straits used for international navigation is a right guaranteed by the rules of international law and is not subject to the will or conditions of any state.
The Kingdom also rejects the transformation of its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks and their consequences.
The Ministry also affirmed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s inherent right, both individually and collectively, to self-defense in accordance with Article (51) of the Charter, and to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents, in close coordination with its brothers in the Gulf Cooperation Council, based on the Joint Defense Agreement, which considers an attack on any member state an attack on all, as well as with its allies and partners. The Ministry noted that the Kingdom of Bahrain, as a member of the UN Security Council, calls upon the Council to condemn these repeated attacks and demands that it assume its responsibilities and take decisive measures to ensure Iran’s full compliance with Resolution 2817, and to halt its attacks, threats, and support for proxy groups in the region. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs added that the Kingdom of Bahrain affirms that its security is a red line, that its sovereignty is non-negotiable, and that it will remain, as it has always been, a proponent of good neighborliness, respect for the sovereignty of states, and non-interference in their affairs, and is committed to the security and stability of the Arabian Gulf.
Iranian media are reporting that their foreign minister Abbas Araqchi will be in Oman on Tuesday for talks with his Omani counterpart.
Oman, along with Qatar, has been one of the key negotiators in ceasefire and peace talks between Tehran and Washington.
As both sides have settled into a strategy of exerting continued economic pain on the other, we’re yet to see any movement on a deal though.
The US is maintaining a highly expensive military operation in the Gulf, with a naval blockade that aims to stop Iranian oil ships leaving the Persian Gulf, thereby hurting the Iranian economy, and through a missile and drone operation targeting Iran’s southern coastline aimed at protecting and helping commercial ships get out. Oil flows are said to be back near their prewar level.
But Iran hasn’t strayed from its demands, and the conditions it wants to end the war: a measure of control over Hormuz, removal of the blockade and economic sanctions, having its assets unfrozen, and reparations.
Yemen government forces dropping back from Bab el-Mandeb to shore up Aden capital
I mentioned earlier the withdrawal of Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces from the areas around Bab el-Mandeb where they’ve been attempting to stave off the Houthis.
A lightning-strike offensive back in September saw the Houthis sweep almost the entire Red Sea coast and almost seize control of the critical Red Sea strait, which has become another chokepoint in the flow of oil and and energy supplies from Gulf producers.
Here’s the full statement from the Yemeni forces, who are now redeploying towards Aden, where their government is based.
The Houthis are gathering steam in the south, where most areas remain under government control.
The Souther Yemeni forces said:
The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate.
This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.
The Houthis’ stronghold currently remains most of northern Yemen, where they control the capital Sanaa and other populous areas. Since the civil war erupted in 2014, the Houthis have pushed the internationally-recognised Yemeni government south and stunned the Saudi-backed administration with their push south in September.
That prompted a military fight back operation, and Saudi Arabia striking Houthi areas in Yemen as the Houthis targeted airports and oil supplies in the Gulf kingdom.
The US thinks Iran still has between 1,500-2,500 missiles in its arsenal despite the US-Israeli damage done this year to its production facilities, reports the Wall St Journal.
They noted difficulties with tracking Iran’s stockpile, and assessing whether they’re ready for launch or remain in storage.
But they noted that Iran has appeared to manage to slowly rebuild its arsenal during the long lulls in fighting and mostly from stockpiled weapons components. Tehran has also kept up a ready supply of drones and short-range missiles.
The assessment would go against what Trump and his Secretary of Defence/War, Peter Hegseth, have been claiming repeatedly throughout the nearly-nine months of war so far; that the US has “decimated” Iran’s long-range fighting capability.
Both the US and Israel had also stated the goal of destroying Iran’s ballistic-missile capabilities when they launched war on 28 February.
Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza refugee camp
Hamas has confirmed the killing of Samir Mahmoud Hassan Abu Younis, commander of the group’s Rafah Brigade, in an Israeli airstrike on a Gaza refugee camp on Saturday night.
The Israeli military said it had taken steps to “mitigate harm to civilians” in the strike. It said it had also targeted other Hamas militants in the strike but gave no further detail.
Israel’s military first announced the killing on Sunday, saying they had targeted Younis who they said had been working on restoring Hamas and getting members to “advance and carry out terror attacks”.
Younis had been one of the senior Hamas figures who helped plan and oversee the October 7 attacks. He had only been the Rafah brigade leader role for two months, after Israel killed his predecessor, Nael Abu Obeid.
In their statement announcing his death, Hamas said Younis was “one of the most important commanders involved in planning and overseeing the 7 October attack”.
Earlier this week, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital, the largest operational hospital in southern Gaza, killed at least six people, including a surgeon and patients, and injured 30, local officials said. The IDF said it had been targeting a commander of Hamas’s armed wing.
Israel is still striking Gaza on a near daily basis despite the the US-brokered ceasefire having come into action since October last year. More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, and more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza since the war began.
Here’s a recap of what the various sides have said this morning regarding the latest Iranian strikes targeting a US air base in Bahrain.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards:
The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force.
The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry
Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain.
[Bahrain] rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks.
I’m yet to see a response from the US, but can expect Centcomm (which oversees all American military operations in the Middle East) to comment at some stage, like it did for Friday’s attack. Those strikes also targeted a radar site.
Bahrain locals: 'I was hoping this period was behind us'
After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.
Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.
It’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.
Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:
I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.
They said they had attacked the air base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. The base is about a 30-minute drive south of Manama.
US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes.
Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.
The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.
That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.
Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.
Iran has targeted an airbase inBahrainin the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.
According to Iranian media, the IRGC said it had sent six drones to attack a US radar system hosted in the US-allied island state.
Explosions were heard around the capital, Manama, but Bahrain authorities say their air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets.

noticias.titulo: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
noticias.resumen: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. noticias.texto:
The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.
What else we’re reading about
Politics | More than one-third of the international delegates – about 115 people – expected to attend the Congress party’s Bharat summit over the weekend were denied entry to India or had their visas cancelled, according to the Wire. Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
71
Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The national capital reported its most-polluted Diwali since 2021, data from the Central Pollution Control Board showed.
Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.
Get in touch
Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

noticias.titulo: UK unemployment unexpectedly eases to 4.6%, as government prepares to release Milburn report
noticias.resumen: Wage growth falls to to 3.5% in September, as ministers examine how best to get young people into work Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on young people Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release a major report on the youth jobs crisis. The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had expected it to remain at 4.7%. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release a major report on the youth jobs crisis.
The unemployment rate was 4.6% in September, dipping from 4.7% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. City economists had expected it to remain at 4.7%.
However, wage growth fell to 3.5%, excluding bonuses, in the latest official figures for the three months to the end of September, down from 3.7% in the three months to August.
With inflation also at 3.5% and expected to rise for a fourth consecutive month to 3.7% when figures are released on Wednesday, the average worker faces a fall in real wages growth to zero or even into negative territory.
The figures highlighted how difficult it will be for ministers to improve living standards as they consider the findings of a key report by the former health secretary Alan Milburn examining how to get young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) back into work, released later on Tuesday.
The jobs market has proved difficult for analysts and politicians to assess in recent years. It has been called weak after a dramatic slide in the number of vacancies, which illustrates the reticence of companies to hire new staff.
However, employment has proved resilient, with unemployment falling between July and August from 4.9% to 4.7%, indicating that few employers were ready to cut large numbers of staff.
Ministers are known to be concerned that some large employers, including several banks, have said they intend to use artificial intelligence to reduce their staffing levels.
Economists are divided over whether AI will enhance productivity across all major sectors of the economy – after signs it has boosted GDP – or lead to improvements in certain industries, such as healthcare.
Employer groups have complained that Labour’s increase in national insurance payments, a higher minimum wage and changes to employee rights have increased costs, leading to a fall in the number of advertised vacancies.
The Bank of England increased interests rates earlier this month after a rise in the consumer prices index to 3.5% in September.
It has said that its own surveys showed employers did not expect to increase pay beyond 3.5% to 4% next year, despite the higher level of inflation, and also reported little change looking ahead in their own prices.
However, a growing number of the Bank’s policymakers believe the prospect of high oil and energy prices next year as the Iran war drags on will push inflation towards 5% and force employers to offer higher pay, which will be passed on in higher retail prices.

noticias.titulo: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credi
noticias.texto:
Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.
But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest.
Anthropic’s millionaire factory promises to expand the group of tech buyers, who range from senior staff at major AI labs to founders who have sold their startups, with budgets that range from £2m to £40m, Eccles says.
Tech’s wave of wealth has already reshaped Silicon Valley – notably in San Francisco – driving up demand for already scarce housing as young entrepreneurs and engineers became millionaires overnight. Now, that money is washing up on British shores too.
Anthropic, which employs about 5,000 people worldwide, has more than 200 employees in the UK. The company, founded in San Francisco in 2021, has announced plans to expand its presence in London, with a new office that is capable of accommodating up to 800 people.
The company’s UK filings show that it spent £24.1m employing an average of 43 staff in 2024 alone – a mean average of £560,000 per person. Job listings this year have advertised base salaries of up to £630,000 before stock options for research engineers.
Salaries across Britain’s AI sector are flying: OpenAI’s staff in London each received £2.3m on average last year – about 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings. That puts them on par with partners at top law firms such as Linklaters and Clifford Chance, and ahead of some bankers in the City.
UK-based investors in these companies are also watching the value of their stakes grow at breakneck speed. Alex Gerko, the billionaire founder of the trading firm XTX and an early investor in Anthropic via the venture arms of the business, is expected to make hundreds of millions of pounds in paper gains when the company joins the stock market this week.
The flush of technology cash is already evident in London’s commercial property market. First, a wave of startups led to Shoreditch being nicknamed Silicon Roundabout, before tech firms began expanding across the capital. Now, US AI firms are expanding at pace in the UK, clustering tightly inside the King’s Cross “knowledge quarter” where Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta all work a stone’s throw from each other.
They have followed in the footsteps of Demis Hassabis, a totemic figure in AI’s breakthrough era who co-founded DeepMind in 2010 and sold it to Google for £400m four years later. He was one of the first to set up in the north London enclave. Isomorphic Labs, his AI drug discovery startup that is also now owned by the Google parent Alphabet, is in the area.
The AI gold rush is already being felt at the highest end of London’s housing market. Although tech bosses may be younger than the sector’s traditional client base, agents report that interest – while spread across London – includes plenty of familiar wealthy haunts.
In February, the Times reported that Igor Babuschkin, the billionaire co-founder of Elon Musk’s AI venture xAI, had bought a £57m penthouse overlooking Hyde Park, in one of the biggest deals in the city this year.
Meanwhile, Providence House, the Reform UK treasurer Nick Candy’s former mansion on the grounds of the Royal Hospital Chelsea in London, was reportedly sold for £270m to the founder of the quantitative investment firm Quadrature Capital, Suneil Setiya. Aidan Devane, the chief executive of the firm, attributed its success partly to its proximity to AI labs in the city, telling the Financial Times: “We are probably in the golden age of London quant.”
Tech wealth, increasingly generated by gains in the AI sector, “has become a force at the very top of the prime central London market”, according to the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates, which has a portfolio including a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park.
Jeremy Gee, a managing director at Beauchamp, says inquiries from tech and AI buyers have risen noticeably over the past year. “Some are international buyers, principally from the US, but a growing number are based here in London,” he says, adding that many have amassed their fortunes with remarkable speed.
“They tend to be younger, they move quickly and they are very clear about what they want. Location and quality matter most and they will pay a premium for something genuinely special,” he says. “London offers culture, history, world-class schools and a growing AI community of its own.”
Even the traditional bastions of old British money are adapting. According to Shona Baijal, the managing director of wealth at Coutts, the private bank long associated with the British aristocracy, the tech and AI sectors are increasingly a source of new clients. One of the key challenges, she says, is helping young entrepreneurs who are coming into vast amounts of wealth very quickly.
“A lot of people feel overwhelmed,” she says. “We have to discuss the emotional aspects of what it means to come into wealth. We might say: you’ve come into the money, but do not rush to do anything.”
Coutts found last month that eight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price.
But sellers and property agents hoping the AI industry may ride to London’s rescue face a glaring problem: much of these new AI fortunes remains on paper.
At founder level, many are “paper rich, cash poor”, Baijal says – meaning until they sell their businesses or their shares vest, their wealth is largely theoretical.
At the same time, Britain’s wider economy is growing more reliant on the sector’s momentum. Last week, official figures showed that the UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, its fastest expansion in two and a half years, almost entirely due to strong and widespread growth in services, led by the IT sector. Separate analysis by Bloomberg found that roughly a quarter of UK economic growth this year had been powered by AI.
That dependence makes the prospect of an AI bubble bursting all the more dangerous. There have been months of warnings over the valuations of AI companies, and there has been a groundswell of public opposition to datacentre construction and worries around AI safety.
Investors were reminded again of the fragility of the AI trade last week after a scandal involving extramarital affairs and an alleged Chinese spy sent shares in one of the most valuable AI companies in the US, the chip designer Nvidia, tumbling.
Other market indicators have been flashing warning lights. This year one popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE, or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings, ratio – rose to its highest level since 2000, showing that the US stock market was unusually highly valued compared with its profits. That was before the Anthropic’s blockbuster debut.
For now, the AI boom’s physical footprint is unmistakable. In San Francisco, the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 a month, up more than 25% from last year and nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.
Meanwhile in London, the transformation of King’s Cross from a railway goods yard once notorious for criminal activity into an international hub for tech and AI is well under way. Whether this new class of wealth is permanent, or a temporary flash in a historic tech bubble, is yet to be seen.

noticias.titulo: Invest in international rail services to boost UK-EU reset, Burnham urged
noticias.resumen: Campaigners call for reopening of high-speed Eurostar stations and new infrastructure for London St Pancras Britain should throw its weight behind international rail services to reset the UK-EU relationship, transport campaigners have urged the prime minister. A coalition of groups has called on Andy Burnham to commit to reopening high-speed stations for Eurostar and other services in Kent, and to support new infrastructure for passengers at London St Pancras and for rail freight. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Britain should throw its weight behind international rail services to reset the UK-EU relationship, transport campaigners have urged the prime minister.
A coalition of groups has called on Andy Burnham to commit to reopening high-speed stations for Eurostar and other services in Kent, and to support new infrastructure for passengers at London St Pancras and for rail freight.
The call came alongside research showing that annual rail passenger numbers through the Channel tunnel could more than double in five years and hit 28 million by 2040.
The report said that planned increases in services and routes, including competition to Eurostar from new operators and significant investment in rolling stock, should drive demand for international rail travel, but that the government needed to help realise the potential.
A letter to Burnham from the Campaign for Better Transport, co-signed by sustainable transport groups and train operators, said the numbers would come “only if a strategy is put in place and the barriers to growth are unlocked”. The campaigners urged him to tackle high fares and border delays and invest in more depot and station capacity.
Ben Plowden, the chief executive of the Campaign for Better Transport, said: “The Channel tunnel is one of Britain’s greatest, underused transport assets. Improving our international rail network would give people a genuine alternative to flying, making international travel more affordable and accessible, and delivering major benefits for the economy and the environment.”
According to research by the Transport and Environment (T&E) thinktank, three times as many Britons support expanding international rail rather than airports. Labour has approved expansion at London’s Stansted, Luton and Gatwick airports, although, significantly, Burnham has not expressed support for Heathrow’s third runway.
Georgia Whitaker, a rail campaigns manager at T&E, said: “If the EU and UK want to get back on track, ensuring the Channel tunnel is no longer half-used is a no-brainer.”
Gareth Williams, the general secretary of Eurostar, said: “The UK needs a big picture plan to unleash international rail growth. There is a real opportunity to deliver economic benefits through rail and to provide low-carbon connections, including direct routes as far afield as Germany and Switzerland. To get there, there’s a need to be ambitious about infrastructure investment – particularly in stations and depots that are fit for the future.”
The letter calls on Burnham to open Stratford International station in east London as a second gateway into the capital, something the government committed to providing funding for in the autumn budget.
It also urged him to commit to reopening international services at Ashford and Ebbsfleet International stations. The letter is signed by Eurostar, despite the current cross-Channel operator having deemed the Kent stations commercially unviable.
A strategic approach to international rail should mean more investment, the report said, but it also pointed to “proportionate and efficient border and security arrangements”, better connections and integrated ticketing.
The campaigners also suggested levying more taxes on aviation to reflect the climate impact of short-haul flying compared with rail.
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We also want to see a thriving, competitive international rail market that gives passengers more choice and supports economic growth.
“That’s why we’re supporting industry and local partners to deliver international services at Stratford International, Ebbsfleet and Ashford, and are exploring options for new international rail depot capacity.”

noticias.titulo: Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people
noticias.resumen: Report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis calls for welfare, education, health and employment policy shake-up Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits. In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis , Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits.
In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.
He said ministers had a choice to either carry on down a path of state and market failure or adopt a 10-year plan with an ambition to eradicate long-term youth unemployment.
