Publishing a blueprint for change in a highly anticipated review, the report calls on the government to launch a sweeping shake-up of welfare, education, health and employment policy with the aim to ensure every young person has the chance to earn or learn.
If adopted by the government, Britain could halve the number of young people neither earning nor learning, helping about 600,000 more under-25s into education, employment or training each year by 2036, according to the review.
Milburn’s report comes as Britain’s young bear the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Coupled with the legacies of the Covid pandemic and austerity, and a rise in mental ill-health and as AI upends the jobs market, the UK’s Neet rate has reached 13% – the highest level since 2014. Milburn said that rate could be lowered to 5% by 2036.
However, central to his plan would be a controversial shake-up of Britain’s benefits system to approach the under-25s as wholly separate from the working-age population at large.
Urging the prime minister not to shy away from welfare reform – after Keir Starmer was forced into a humiliating climbdown over a plan to cut disability benefits amid pressure from Labour MPs – Milburn warned the future of the next generation depended on the government making changes.
At a press conference in London on Tuesday to mark the launch of his report, he is expected to say: “It is time for a new settlement that makes work not welfare the future for the next generation.”
But Milburn also warned that crude benefit cuts would not work, arguing that changes would need upfront investment.
Burnham pledged on Sunday to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment. Writing in the Guardian, he promised that changes to benefits he was considering in response to Milburn’s review would only be accompanied by a “root and branch rethink” of youth support.
At the heart of Milburn’s blueprint would be the creation of an entirely new welfare system for young people, involving tougher eligibility criteria than for older claimants. In exchange, however, there would be a drastic step-change in support to help young people find work.
This would involve some young people with health conditions and disabilities losing access to current benefits, although they would be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment. Those with the most profound health conditions who would be unable ever to work would still get more generous financial support.
To counterbalance the changes, Milburn said upfront investment to create a new “youth opportunity service” in England should be created to deliver a drastic boost in support for young people.
Accountable to regional mayors and local leaders, the service would combine employment, careers, health and practical support. Young people would receive a personalised participation plan and a named adviser, with access to support guaranteed by two new legal guarantees.
While education, skills and health policies are devolved in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, Milburn will say at the report launch that the underlying principles in his report should also apply.
Analysis in Milburn’s report shows that for every £1 spent on helping young people into work or education, the state spent £25 on youth benefits last year. Under his proposals that figure would be rebalanced to £2 to £1, bringing Britain closer into line with the ratios in other European countries.
The changes will, however, raise fears among some Labour MPs as well as charities and campaigners that slashing youth benefits could result in plunging more young people into poverty, particularly for those who require additional financial support to manage health conditions.
As Milburn prepared to launch his review, backbenchers from the left of the party – including Nadia Whittome, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, John McDonnell, Apsana Begum, Clive Lewis and Richard Burgon – warned in a letter that an entire generation risked becoming disconnected from work and wider society.
“What young people need is not more punishment, but more opportunity,” the signatories wrote, warning that an approach relying on benefit cuts “risks further disenfranchising young people who are already struggling”.
They added: “Placing young people under threat of losing essential financial support does not address the shortage of good-quality jobs, the barriers facing disabled young people, or the lack of meaningful routes into employment.”
In a bid to ease concerns among Labour MPs after last year’s welfare rebellion threatened to rupture the party and arguably began Starmer’s downfall, Milburn held meetings with MPs on Monday alongside the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden.
McFadden told backbenchers: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR. It’s about bringing together the help young people need in one place – treating them as a person not a departmental client.”
Milburn said Britain had faced a Neet problem for 25 years and had never made a plan to end it before. “We are at a fork in the road and half measures will not do. A complete system reset is needed. A lost generation is not inevitable. A work generation is possible.”
Labour has faced fierce criticism from business groups who say its decisions – including tax increases and a rising minimum wage – have added to Britain’s crisis in youth jobs, while the Conservatives and Reform have pushed for a tougher approach on benefits.
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn’s review was “too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state”.
“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years,” she said. “Even so, there’s a long road ahead to see if it can get past welfare-loving Labour MPs.”

noticias.titulo: United Airlines says ‘widespread’ system outage resolved
noticias.resumen: Airline acknowledges ‘technology issue that delayed flight departures’ in latest high-profile outage to affect Americans United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights. “We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-relate
noticias.texto:
United Airlines said on Monday that it had resolved a widespread system outage, just three days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.
“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”
According to an internal memo from United’s pilots’ union seen by Reuters, a company-wide web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.
Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.
Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said in an interview Monday night that he did not know what caused the one-and-a-half-hour outage. “This is not an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system-wide problem,” Duffy said on Hannity on Fox News.
The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.
Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday’s outage involved United’s Unimatic system.
The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.
And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.
Microsoft said it had resolved the issue and restored service by Saturday, also issuing an apology. The office software giant did not attribute the blackout to a cybersecurity breach, identifying in an initial report on Monday that a combination of a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity sparked the outage.

noticias.titulo: Dolores Huerta honored in ceremony at California state capitol
noticias.resumen: Labor leader was remembered for her advocacy and co-founding union that would become United Farm Workers California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists, at a memorial ceremony Monday at the state capitol. They remembered her as a relentless advocate for a more just and fair world. Huerta co-founded a union that became the United Farm Workers with César Chávez and made famous her rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” – which translates to “Yes, it can be done!” Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
California officials paid tribute to Dolores Huerta, one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists, at a memorial ceremony Monday at the state capitol.
They remembered her as a relentless advocate for a more just and fair world. Huerta co-founded a union that became the United Farm Workers with César Chávez and made famous her rallying cry, “Sí, se puede!” – which translates to “Yes, it can be done!”
Huerta, 96, died of cancer at her home in Bakersfield, California, last month. A celebration of life, with an interfaith memorial service, will be held in her hometown on Friday.
Robert Rivas, the Democratic assembly speaker, had called Huerta a family friend and mentor. Rivas’ grandfather, Servando Flores, moved from Mexico to California in the 1960s and went on to organize fellow farmworkers alongside Huerta.
“She is the mother of our Latino civil rights movement,” Rivas said. “Her place in the history of our state and nation is enduring.”
Rivas stood beside fellow Democrats Xavier Becerra, the governor-elect, Monique Limón, the senate president pro tempore, and Nancy Pelosi, the former US House speaker, in the Ccapitol rotunda as they spoke about Huerta during an invitation-only ceremony. There were performances of songs that included We Shall Overcome and Put a Little Love in Your Heart before the space was opened to the public.
“As we honor one of the towering figures of our time, we make her this solemn promise: the march goes on,” said Limón, who is serving as acting governor while Gavin Newsom, the governor, is out of state.
Before the event began, Huerta’s casket was transported to the capitol by a hearse adorned with flags reading “Sí, se puede!” Hundreds of people, including union leaders, politicians and members of the public, followed behind, many with marigolds in hand.
Huerta was born in New Mexico in 1930 and raised in California’s farm-rich San Joaquin valley. She became an elementary school teacher before turning her focus to the plight of farmworkers and teaming up with Chávez to create the National Farm Workers Association in 1962, which became United Farm Workers.
Then president Barack Obama, who borrowed her rallying cry for his campaign slogan, “Yes we can,” awarded her with the nation’s highest civilian honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom, in 2012. Well into her 90s, Huerta was a familiar face at news conferences and rallies in Sacramento, where she advocated for the rights of workers, women, voters and others.
She revealed this year that she was sexually abused by Chávez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years.

noticias.titulo: Fiona the hippo under veterinary care after eating hat at Cincinnati zoo
noticias.resumen: Knit hat caught in ceiling fan and flung into enclosure eaten by Fiona, who is being closely monitored by zoo staff The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global celebrity after her premature birth nearly a decade ago, is undergoing veterinary care after swallowing a knit hat that got into her enclosure. Zoo veterinarians and staff are monitoring Fiona and working to help her pass the hat, the zoo said in a statement Monday. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The Cincinnati zoo says Fiona, its beloved hippo who became a global celebrity after her premature birth nearly a decade ago, is undergoing veterinary care after swallowing a knit hat that got into her enclosure.
Zoo veterinarians and staff are monitoring Fiona and working to help her pass the hat, the zoo said in a statement Monday.
“Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self,” the zoo said. The zoo said she received fluids and an enema Sunday to help move things through her system.
The cap got into Fiona’s habitat after it was tossed into the air by a visitor and caught by a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening above the area’s viewing windows, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley.
“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told Axios in a statement, emphasizing it was an accident. Fiona will be off the exhibit until she is in better health.
Fiona was born six weeks premature in January 2017, and her fight to survive grabbed international attention.
She initially could not stand on her own and weighed just 29lbs (13.2kg) at birth, 25lbs (11.3kg) less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
Fans followed her progress online, and she became so popular that books were written about her. She also inspired a line of beer, all sorts of clothing and an ice cream flavor.
One couple even got engaged in front of her exhibit, with Fiona getting into the picture while underwater in the background.
Other zoos contacted Fiona, showing concern for her health. Timothy, the hippo at the San Antonio zoo sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
The zoo said in a social media post it will share more information as they get it, also reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
“If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately,” the zoo said.

noticias.titulo: Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting
noticias.resumen: Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific. The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.
The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.
On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”
A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”
In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.
On 16 September, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.
Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.
“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.
“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”
As Hurricane Polo began to form in late September, researchers with the aquarium and its federal and local partners relocated the 204 eggs from the two nests to incubate in the safety of the aquarium’s animal care facility.
“As animals adapt in unexpected ways to changes in their natural world, humans will need to adapt and make space to ensure endangered and threatened species are given a fighting chance,” said Jeffrey Flocken, president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific.
“If they successfully hatch, these baby turtles will likely one day return to nest to carry on future generations on these very same beaches, giving us a remarkable opportunity to help a species expand its range and thrive.”
Even as the Huntington Beach and Seal Beach turtles have begun hatching and returned to the ocean, researchers are continuing to advise the public to be on the lookout for more nests. On 1 November, a third nest was recorded in Ventura county although those eggs were swept away by unusually high tides – likely also caused by El Niño.

noticias.titulo: Trump kicks off Asia tour ahead of major talks with Putin, Xi in China
noticias.resumen: US President Donald Trump is flying into Manila for a Quad meeting before he takes off to China for a much anticipated meet with Russian and Chinese counterparts. Follow live.
noticias.texto:
Trump kicks off Asia tour ahead of major talks with Putin, Xi in China
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 17, 2026
What you need to know
- US President Donald Trump set to arrive in Manila on Tuesday amid protests
- Trump to meet leaders of India, Japan and Australia for his first Quad meeting
- Asia tour includes highly-anticipated trilateral meet between Trump, Xi and Putin
Here are the biggest headlines from Trump's Asia tour on Tuesday, November 17:
Canada, China agree to ease tariffs amid trade rows with US
Talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen have produced deals to further reduce tariffs, Ottawa said on Tuesday.
The agreements reflect a growing rapprochement between the two countries after years of strained relations, thanks to trade tensions with Washington leading both Canada and China to seek to reduce dependence on the US.
Read the full story here.
What's on the agenda?
Trump will arrive in Manila later afternoon or early evening. Here's what he's expected to do:
- Meet with Quad leaders — a grouping of US, India, Australia and Japan — for strategic security in the Indo-Pacific
- Signing of a trade deal with Thailand in the wake of the trade war Trump launched in 2025
- A cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr
- Trump will skip the larger East Asia Summit but join a US-ASEAN 'Special Summit' meant to discuss deepening trade, security and the region's conflicts
- On Wednesday, Trump leaves for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China
- There, he will hold a trilateral meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin
Trump set to arrive in Manila amid protests
US President Donald Trump is set to arrive in Manila, Philippines on Tuesday evening for his first meeting of the Quad group of Indo-Pacific countries.
The Asia tour comes as Trump's Republican Party reels from a stunning defeat in the US midterm elections and the Nvidia spy allegations at home.
His administration likely hopes the high-profile meetings of the tour will shift the conversation away from these recent setbacks. That said, the US president is set to be greeted by protesters, angry over the US-Israeli war in the Middle East as well the "Pax Silica" supply chain initiative.
Several miles from the Southeast Asian summit venue in Manila, hundreds of leftist activists, students and indigenous people gathered for a three-day campout against Trump."Trump is a fascist, a warmonger and enabler of brutal, genocidal regimes," rights group Karapatan, one of the groups involved, said in a statement.
The group also accused Trump of pursuing policies that had caused death and destruction worldwide and criticized President Ferdinand Marcos Jr for welcoming him to the Philippines.
Welcome to our coverage
Good morning and welcome to DW's coverage of US President Donald Trump's Asia tour.
Trump is flying into the Philippines to kick off his tour — which he will be hoping makes a positive splash on the global stage and shift attention from his Republican party's deep losses in the recent US midterm elections.
The US President is arriving at the tail end of the ASEAN summit in Manila where he will also join a Quad meeting with the leaders of Japan, Australia and India.
The main attraction, however, comes on Wednesday.
After Manila, Trump will fly to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit where he will have his third face-to-face meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this year. The two will also be joined by Russian President Vladimir Putin for a highly anticipated and controversial trilateral meeting.
Stay tuned for all of this and more!

noticias.titulo: Canada, China agree to ease tariffs amid trade rows with US
noticias.resumen: The Canadian and Chinese leaders have vowed closer cooperation as both nations seek to reduce reliance on the US. Canada's government said it had agreed to further reduce tariffs on a range of products.
noticias.texto:
Canada, China agree to ease tariffs amid trade rows with US
November 17, 2026
Talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen have produced deals to further reduce tariffs, Ottawa said on Tuesday.
The agreements reflect a growing rapprochement between the two countries after years of strained relations, thanks totrade tensions with Washington leading both Canada and China to seek to reduce dependence on the US.
At the talks, Carney hailed "greater predictability and stability" in relations with China, while Xi said the cooperation between his country and Canada would "benefit not only our two countries but also Asia-Pacific and the world."
Carney said Canada had already made faster-than-expected progress toward its goal of boosting exports to China "by 50% by the end of this decade."
What have China and Canada agreed on?
According to a statement from the Canadian government, China is to reduce tariffs on Canadian pork, fish and seafood.
In exchange, Canada will prolong the current tariff exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum for another two years.
The two leaders also agreed to cooperate more closely on economic and financial matters, and to work together in the fields of education and environmental protection.
Growing China-Canada rapprochement
Xi and Carney already declared their intention to enhance bilateral ties during talks in Beijing in January.
There, they struck a deal that foresaw a reduction in tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, while Chinese electric vehicles gained easier access to the Canadian market.
Critics in Canada have, however, pointed out what they see as dangers to the country's security and values through the closer ties to Beijing.
Among other things, Canadian intelligence believes that China interfered in at least two federal elections, something Beijing denies.

noticias.titulo: India news: Modi to attend ASEAN, Quad meet in Manila
noticias.resumen: This is the first time Modi and US President Donald Trump are meeting since the US midterm elections, which changed the political scene in the US.
noticias.texto:
India news: Modi to attend ASEAN, Quad meet in Manila
November 17, 2026
What you need to know
- Modi is meeting the Quad leaders on the margins of the ASEAN summit in Manila
- Cyclone Akvan is expected to cross Andhra Pradesh coast on November 20 as a 'very severe cyclonic storm'
Here is a roundup of headlines from India on Tuesday, November 17:
PM Modi to meet Quad leaders in Manila
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to join the leaders of Australia, Japan and the US for a Quad Leaders' Summit and hold several bilateral meetings in the Philippine capital, Manila.
This is the first meeting between Modi and US President Donald Trump since the US midterm elections took place.
Modi and Trump are not expected to hold any bilateral talks on the sidelines of the summit, instead Indian news outlet The Print reported that a bilateral meeting is planned for next month in Florida, on the margins of the G20 leaders' summit.
Modi is also attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-India summit and the 21st East Asia Summit today.
At the ASEAN meet, maritime security, economic cooperation and development partnership are expected to dominate the agenda.
In his departure statement, Modi said India's relationship with ASEAN was "at the heart of India’s Act East Policy" and central to its MAHASAGAR (Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions) vision.
"Our ties, rooted in centuries of civilisational exchanges, have grown into a dynamic partnership spanning trade, connectivity, maritime security, technology and people-to-people relations," he said.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Midhat from DW's New Delhi bureau, bringing you the latest news from across India.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is in the Philippines to attend the ASEAN summit on the sidelines of which he will also attend a Quad leaders' summit.
Meanwhile, the state of Andhra Pradesh is bracing for a third cyclone after cyclones Arnab and Murasu wreaked havoc in the state. The state is facing a third cyclone within the span of three weeks.
Stay tuned as we bring you more news from India.

noticias.titulo: Mongolian President Khurelsukh to resign amid corruption allegations
noticias.resumen: Khurelsukh has said he will step down over accusations that he profited from a government railway project, but said he had been "falsely accused."
noticias.texto:
Mongolian President Khurelsukh to resign amid corruption allegations
November 17, 2026
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa said Tuesday that he would resign after the opposition Democratic Party accused him of profiting from a government railway project.
At a press conference, Khurelsukh said he was being "falsely accused and defamed" but would resign in order to "restore my good name."
He has pledged to cooperate with investigators.
Before the resignation takes effect, it must first be accepted by parliament, the State Great Khural.
What are the accusations against Khurelsukh?
Nyambaatar Khishgee, the ex-mayor of Ulaanbaatar, the country's capital, on Saturday accused Khurelsukh of receiving $25 million (around €23 million) linked to the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway project.
The railway connects the Tavantolgoi coal mine with the Mongolian port of Gashuunsukhait on the Chinese border, a central hub for the export of coal from Mongolia to China.
The former mayor belongs to the president's party, but is part of a different faction within it.
The opposition Democratic Party picked up on the accusations and called on Khurelsukh to step down.
According to the allegations, Khurelsukh received the money in bribes from the conglomerate Bodi International LLC, which received the contract to construct the railway without a competitive tender.
Bodi on Monday denied having paid any cash bribes to obtain the contract.
Infighting in Khurelsukh's party
Khurelsukh, from the Mongolian People's Party, has been president since 2021.
But infighting has caused disruption in the party in recent years, with three prime ministers taking office in just nine months.
Khurelsukh paid a state visit to Germany from October 19 to 22 this year.

noticias.titulo: Japan scrambles jets to counter suspected Russian aircraft
noticias.resumen: Japan said it lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after two suspected Russian aircraft violated Japanese airspace.
noticias.texto:
Japan scrambles jets to counter suspected Russian aircraft
November 17, 2026
Japan scrambled fighter jets in its airspace after two suspected Russian aircraft entered its territory on Tuesday morning, an incident that could further strain ties between the two countries.
Tokyo said it had lodged a "very stern protest" with Moscow after the incident.
Japan lodges protest against Russia over alleged airspace violation
The aircraft entered Japan's airspace near Okinoshima in southwestern Japan shortly after 4:00 a.m. local time Tuesday (1900 GMT Monday), Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said.
"The violation of our national airspace by Russian aircraft is not only a grave infringement of our country's sovereignty, but also a threat to our security and is completely unacceptable," Kihara said.
"We lodged a very stern protest with Russia through diplomatic channels and strongly demanded measures to prevent any recurrence," he said.
Japan had lodged a similar protest with Russia in 2024 after a Russian patrol plane entered its airspace three times, marking the first confirmed incursion since 2019.
Kihara said the aircraft travelled through the Tsushima Strait and went between Yonaguni Island and Taiwan before heading to the Pacific.
Strains increasing in Japan-Russia ties
Japan's relations with Moscow have soured over the past weeks after a Japanese journalist was arrested on spying allegations and after Russia seized four of Japan Tobacco's Russian assets.
Russia and Japan share a decades-old dispute over the status of a number of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
However, relations especially deteriorated further after Tokyo joined global sanctions against Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
South Korea says Russian aircraft entered defense zone
Tuesday's reported violation comes soon after South Korea said it too had deployed fighter jets and conducted tactical maneuvers after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defense zone in the early hours of Tuesday.
An air defense zone is not sovereign airspace but a buffer area in which countries identify approaching aircraft for security purposes.
Military aircraft are generally expected to notify the relevant country before entering its air defense zone, though this is not legally required.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine updates: Key bridges in Kyiv, Crimea hit in strikes
noticias.resumen: Kyiv's mayor said Russian forces have hit bridges on the Dnipro River. Ukraine launched a massive attack on Russia earlier on Monday, hitting the Crimean Bridge. DW has the latest.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine updates: Key bridges in Kyiv, Crimea hit in strikes
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 17, 2026
What you need to know
- Russia struck two important bridges in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said
- Ukraine strike hits Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea to the Russian mainland, stopping traffic
- The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026:
Crimea strike kills 2, says Russia-installed governor
A drone strike on Crimea has killed two people, according to the Russia-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov.
He said on Telegram that the strike took place in the Leninsky district of Crimea, which was seized and annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
Earlier Aksyonov said that Ukraine had struck the Kerch bridge, causing traffic to be suspended.
Moscow built the Kerch Bridge to link the annexed Crimean Peninsula to the Russian region of Krasnodar Krai in the northern Caucasus.
The route is a major source of supplies for Russian forces in Ukraine's occupied Kherson region and is a strategically significant target for Ukrainian forces.
Kerch bridge partially destroyed, according to reports
The Kerch bridge, which links the occupied Crimean peninsula to mainland Russia, has been partially destroyed, according to unofficial reports.
Photos on various Telegram channels appear to show that one of the arches and part of the roadway have collapsed following a strike.
Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski shared a picture on his X account showing a single arch where there should be two, simply exclaiming "Wow."
Reports on the extent of damage have yet to be confirmed by official sources, but images and videos of the bridge are being widely circulated in the Ukrainian media space.
Russia's Transport Ministry said there had been an overnight drone strike on November 17 leading to a temporary suspension of traffic. It advised motorists not to travel towards the bridge and wait for further information.
Russian strike on aid distribution center earlier in the month killed 72, Ukrainian officials say
Ukraine's national police said late Monday that the death toll from a Russian strike on a village in the southern Ukrainian region of Zaporizhzhia earlier this month had risen to 72.
Four people were still missing after authorities concluded a two-week search operation on Monday.
Russia hit a former school that was used as an aid distribution center in Komyshuvakha on November 2 as people were collecting humanitarian supplies. The attack was one of the deadliest of the war.
The village is located close to the frontline.
Ukrainian police said Russia had attacked the search operation several times during the past two weeks.
"Unfortunately, the shelling of Komyshuvakha on November 2, 2026, became one of the most tragic attacks since the beginning of the full-scale war," Ukraine's national police said.
Ukraine holds new talks with US, European negotiators
Ukraine held fresh talks with US and European negotiators on ending the war with Russia on Monday evening, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian officials held online talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as representatives from Ukraine's European partners.
Kushner said progress had been made towards an agreement, although significant challenges remain to finding a path to peace.
The online talks come less than a week after delegations from the US, Ukraine and Russia met in Abu Dhabi for their first trilateral talks in nine months.
"Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain," Zelenskyy said. "Our team is working in the most constructive manner possible."
In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy also warned that Kyiv had intelligence that Russia would launch major strikes on targets across Ukraine on Monday evening and into Tuesday.
The Ukrainian leader warned that Russia "must know that for every act of evil they commit, there will be a just response from us."
In his remarks, Zelenskyy cited a Ukrainian intelligence report that said North Korea was supplying "dozens of ballistic missiles to Russia each month."
"This is extremely dangerous and not only for Ukraine," he said. "By using its ballistic missiles in this war, North Korea is making its weapons more effective. This creates additional challenges for the entire region around Korea."
Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge for second day in a row, Russian authorities say
Ukraine struck a bridge connecting the annexed Crimean peninsula and the Russian mainland late Monday.
The same bridge over the Kerch Strait was also struck a day earlier, Russian-installed authorities said.
"At the moment, traffic is suspended," Crimea's Moscow-installed governor, Sergey Aksyonov said Tuesday.
Russian officials also said Ukraine had struck oil refineries on Monday.
Monday's attack was the largest such assault on Russia since it launched itsfull-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia says it intercepted over 1,300 Ukrainian drones during the attack.
Overnight into Tuesday, Ukraine targeted Moscow with nearly 200 drones.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said early Tuesday morning that Russian air defenses had downed 20 drones heading towards the capital.
Russia hits two major bridges in Kyiv: What we know
Russia struck two bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv late Monday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
"According to preliminary information, there have been hits on the North and South bridges in the capital," Klitschko said on Telegram.
In a later post, Klitschko said the attack "caused damage to critical infrastructure," adding that there were "disruptions to water and heating supplies" because of strikes.
Earlier this month and in October, a series of Russian attacks hit several bridges in the Ukrainian capital, causing major disruption.
Earlier on Monday, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned Russia was planning strikes for Monday night and into Tuesday.
"Tonight, overnight, and throughout tomorrow, please pay attention to missile danger alerts," he said.
"And they there, in Russia, must know that for every one of their evils there will be our just response," Zelenskyy added.
Welcome to our coverage
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital were struck in an overnight Russian attack.
The strikes damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted water and heating in parts of the city, Klitschko said.
Ukraine on Monday attacked Russia, targeting Moscow with drones and striking an important rail bridge in the annexed Crimean peninsula.
The latest exchanges come as negotiators from Ukraine, Europe and the US discuss future talks with Russia on finding a path to peace.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest developments related to Russia's war in Ukraine.

noticias.titulo: Germany beat Netherlands 5-0 to win Nations League group
noticias.resumen: Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany cruised to a comfortable 5-0 win over the Netherlands to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals on Monday.
noticias.texto:
Germany beat Netherlands 5-0 to win Nations League group
November 17, 2026
Germany dominated neighbor and historic rival the Netherlands in their Nations League quarterfinal match-up at Berlin's Olympic Stadium on Monday evening.
It was the team's sixth game under head coach Jürgen Klopp and the 50th ever between the two sides.
Germany's 5-0 shellacking of the Oranje was their most lopsided victory since 1959, when they won 7-0. In all, Germany have now won 19 of those matches, the Netherlands have won 12, and 18 ended in a draw.
Speaking to German broadcaster ARD after the game, attacking midfielder Florian Wirtz — who scored twice in the fixture — said: "We hope that we can make it fun for the fans. It was definitely fun for us, especially in the second half."
Despite the loss, Xavi Hernandez's Dutch side will reach the final eight alongside Germany.
Prior to the match, Klopp had made it clear that he and his team were approaching Monday's showdown as a final after having lost to Greece 1-0 in his first home game in the job on September 27.
By night's end, Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck each scored once and Brajan Gruda scored once and added two assists on top of Wirtz's double.
Klopp has been high on Wirtz, who has come under fire for not delivering at Liverpool since his arrival there in June 2025, and his bet seems to be paying off with the 23-year-old now scoring four goals in his last four games for Germany.
"We don't care who we play. We want to play attacking football. We want to score goals and dominate the opponent. And I think we did that perfectly," said Wirtz on Monday evening before adding: "We want to keep going next year. We want to get better. I think we've taken some great steps in our development as a team."

noticias.titulo: United Airlines resolves tech outage that delayed flights
noticias.resumen: United Airlines said a system outage that delayed departures has been resolved. The disruption came on the heels of a stoppage that halted all flights to and across the US for five hours last week.
noticias.texto:
United Airlines resolves tech outage that delayed flights
November 17, 2026
United Airlines said it has resolved a "widespread system outage" that affected hundreds of departing flights on Monday.
Flight tracker FlightAware said 418 United flights were delayed on Monday afternoon.
The issue comes three days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network grounded flights across the US on Friday.
What did United Airlines say about Monday's tech issues?
United Airlines said there was "no indication" that Monday's outage was the result of a cyberattack.
There was also no indication that the issues affecting United Airlines on Monday were related to Friday's nationwide shutdown.
United Airlines said later on Monday that it had "resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures."
The airline added that airborne flights, as well as those operated by its regional brand United Express, were not affected.
The disruption on Friday and Monday highlights how vulnerable air travel is to tech failures.
Disruption follows other recent major tech meltdowns
United Airlines' computer problem comes amid other recent similar high-profile technology meltdowns, including Friday's nationwide grounding.
Thousands of people in the US said they were unable to access their online banking accounts at several large US banks after JPMorgan Chase reported a technical issue.
On Thursday, Microsoft saw a major disruption to its services, including its Outlook email and Teams messenger.
The tech company said Saturday that its services had been fully restored.

noticias.titulo: German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?
noticias.resumen: The German economy is growing again, albeit slightly. However, economists warn that without reforms, higher productivity and solid public finances, a loss of prosperity and growing debt threaten future generations.
noticias.texto:
German economy returns to growth, so why is the country still worried?
November 15, 2026
Is Germany's economy back on the up? The answer to that question depends on your perspective.
At the 2026 Mechanical Engineering Summit in Berlin this week, the mood was sullen. "A year ago, I said here: We are angry. Today I must say: We are stunned," Bertram Kawlath, president of the Mechanical Engineering Industry Association (VDMA), said in his opening remarks on Tuesday.
The mechanical and plant engineering sector was the backbone of German industry for decades. It once employed more than a million people; now 15,000 positions are being cut every month. Production has shrunk about 20% since 2018.
Kawlath criticized the federal government's infighting and lack of reform, as well as what the companies consider a continued high bureaucracy and tax burden.
"[We are] stunned by the whitewashing in so many government statements. Stunned by the increasingly visible decline of our country as a business location."
Germany's economy is growing again — a little
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz promised quick reforms and a rapidly noticeable economic upswing when he took office in May 2025. A year and a half later, reality has caught up with him.
Merz's coalition of his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), its Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union, (CSU), along with the center-left Social Democrats(SPD), keeps running into trouble. In addition, there are crises and wars. The German economy is facing more headwinds than seldom before, Merz said in October at the German Employers' Day conference in Berlin.
Given the circumstances, small successes are even more meaningful. "A heartfelt thanks for the good news you bring," Merz said when he received the autumn report of the Council of Economic Experts in Berlin, which predicted economic growth of 1.3% for 2026 and 1% for 2027.
The economic experts have a German government mandate to independently analyze business activity and make recommendations for economic policy. Earlier this year, they were much more pessimistic.
"The German economy has recovered quicker than expected from the energy price shock sparked by the war in Iran," said Monika Schnitzer, chair of the expert advisory board, explaining the prognosis. "We see a significant economic recovery, driven by surprisingly strong exports and high government spending."
The chancellor, who celebrated his 71st birthday on November 11, spoke of "encouraging signals" in his address. "The economy in Germany is slowly on the rise again. Considering the many crises in Germany, it was not totally expected that we would manage that."
Why 1% growth is not enough
But these improved prospects do not change the long-term problems. An ageing society means the bills for pensions, health and caregiving are constantly rising.
At the same time, the number of working-age people who finance these services is sinking. That puts increasing pressure on the public purse. According to Berlin's financial planning, social welfare costs, defense and interest on debt will account for 80% of the spending in the federal government's budget.
"We must realize that in the long term the expected revenues in the federal budget will not be enough to cover the planned expenses," Schnitzer warned. The growth rates are far below what is needed to secure the same level of prosperity as previous decades in the long term.
"To grow out of this budgetary predicament, we would need levels of economic growth which we haven't experienced in Germany for the past 50 years," she said.
The government is currently in final deliberations over its 2027 budget; spending upwards of €555 billion ($615 billion) is planned. Because revenue won't be enough to cover it, the government is planning to take on more than €118 billion in new debt. Adding the debt-financed special funds for infrastructure and the military, the new borrowing adds up to almost €204 billion.
Could Germany lose its top rating?
The economic experts have warned that if Germany continues with this path, the debt-to-GDP ratio could rise to 100% by 2040. This ratio indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output. At the end of 2025, it was 63.5%.
Germany is the only country of the world's leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) to still hold a AAA rating, the best possible credit rating in finance markets. It signals to investors the smallest possible default risk for German government bonds. "I want it to stay that way," Merz emphasized.
However, taking on less debt will not be simple. "A reduction in debt-based financing presents policymakers with a consolidation task of historic proportions and will require tough decisions," said Schnitzer. The belt-tightening must, however, be designed to enable growth. Some recommendations include reducing environmentally harmful tax benefits — like the energy tax breaks for diesel fuel.
The so-called "mothers' pension", a pension subsidy for older parents, should be revoked, said the experts. Tax increases could become necessary in the medium term, for example with value-added tax.
"The burden should be shared fairly between generations and societal groups," Schnitzer said.
Merz wants austerity throughout Europe
According to the chancellor, the experts' message has been received. Solid state finances are an issue in Germany but also throughout the European Union. Merz said there needs to be a consolidation course, adding that politicians have a duty to the younger generation. Reforms are needed, especially when it comes to social security systems.
Economic researchers are setting their hopes on increasing companies' productivity. Put simply, productivity describes how much a company can generate with its employees, machinery and resources in a set time.
According to the Council of Economic Experts, there is enormous variation even within the same industries. In Germany, the top companies are up to five times as productive as the weakest enterprises.
If the less productive companies caught up, economic growth could increase significantly, it said in the report. "New technologies and business models could drive peak productivity and allow new highly productive companies to develop."
Germany needs startups, venture capital
But innovations need capital. It's here that the Ifo Economic Research Institute sees considerable deficiencies.
New evaluations show that German universities produce significantly fewer successful business startups than their counterparts in the United Kingdom or United States. For example, for every 1,000 students, about 14 venture capital-backed founders emerge from the vicinity of Stanford University each year. In Cambridge, the European leader, it's 3.5. In Munich, by contrast, it's only 0.5.
There continues to be an abundance of inventors and tinkerers in Germany, especially in mechanical engineering. However, the message from the industry summit in Berlin was that for renewed success, labor costs must come down. Suggestions included longer working hours and more flexibility for employers around job protection.
The intention was not to cut employees' wages and salaries. However, a new study by the German Economic Institute commissioned for the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association showed that extending the working week by an hour alone would increase real gross domestic product by 1.5% in the coming five years.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Police raid Turkish pro-opposition broadcaster Sözcü TV, carry out arrests
noticias.resumen: It was the latest move against pro-opposition media, coming a month after police raided Turkey's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, where they shut down broadcasts and installed an administrator.
noticias.texto:
It was the latest move against pro-opposition media, coming a month after police raided Turkey's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, where they shut down broadcasts and installed an administrator.
Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sözcü TV and its media group early on Tuesday, conducting arrests and installing a government-appointed administrator, the group said on X.
It was the latest move against pro-opposition media, coming a month after police raided Turkey's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, where they shut down broadcasts and installed an administrator.
"Police are searching the Sözcü building under a court order. Police have cordoned off the building," its official X account said in a post just before 5:00 am local time (0300 CET).
"A trustee has been appointed to Sözcü! Police are searching the building...There have been detentions," it said, with one of its journalists saying staff were not being allowed inside.
"Outside Sözcü TV as of 06:00. We are not being allowed into the newsroom," Sezin Ceren Övüç wrote on X.
Among those detained were Funda Tuncer Sıdalı, who chairs the board, and Sözcü TV's former general manager Asım Akgül, Turkish media reports said.
According to its news website, police had raided both Sözcü TV and the offices of its group's online operations, appointing an administrator for both.
"In the early hours of the morning, the police carried out a raid on SÖZCÜ TV and Sözcü.com.tr. A search was launched in the SÖZCÜ TV building by counterterrorism teams. While some executives were detained, trustees were appointed to SÖZCÜ TV and Sözcü.com.tr," its website said.
"No trustees were appointed to SÖZCÜ newspaper, Tavır or Korkusuz," it said, referring to two other newspapers owned by the group.
Ersan Barkın, lawyer for the Sözcü Media Group, said the raids were based on a case that had previously been thrown out by the Supreme Court after finding no evidence that a crime had been committed.
"We're faced with a trustee decision arising from an investigation based on a case in which the Supreme Court, the highest judicial authority in Turkey, found no intent and no crime," he told KRT TV, referring to a case dating back to 2016.
"This trustee decision stems from a file in which no offence was established," he explained.
'Blatant coup against democracy'
Sözcü, which is close to Turkey's opposition, has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator as President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's government piles pressure on its opponents.
In July last year, it went dark for 10 days after being slapped with a ban by Turkey's RTUK broadcasting regulator over its coverage of the mass protests sparked by the jailing of Istanbul's powerful opposition mayor, Ekrem İmamoğlu on graft charges widely denounced as political.
The pre-dawn raids drew swift condemnation from Turkey's main opposition leader Özgür Özel, who heads the Yeni Parti.
"After Halk TV, now there are police and a government-appointed trustee at the doors of Sözcü TV as well! They no longer have any tolerance even for the slightest criticism," he wrote on X, referring to Erdoğan's government.
"They’re cornered; they’re mired in the swamp. That’s why they’re trying to choke out anything and anyone who isn’t one of them."
It also drew a sharp rebuke from the head of the nationalist opposition İYİ Party.
"The raid on SÖZCÜ TV and the attempt to effectively shut it down are a blatant coup against democracy, the rule of law, the sense of justice and the public’s freedom to access information, whatever justification is put forward," wrote Müsavat Dervişoğlu on X.

noticias.titulo: Nvidia board not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO as Trump backs return, reports
noticias.resumen: It comes as US President Donald Trump said he “wouldn’t mind” seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
noticias.texto:
It comes as US President Donald Trump said he “wouldn’t mind” seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO.
Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, according to sources familiar with the matter who spoke to multiple media outlets.
The board is focusing on the investigation into Huang, not discussions about reinstating him, the person told CNBC.
Huang resigned last week as CEO of Nvidia, the company he founded 33 years ago, following his admission to an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for an Nvidia customer and is alleged to have been a spy for China. Two other affairs with Nvidia employees were also reported.
Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.
The Financial Times had earlier reported that Huang discussed with confidants the possibility of returning to his post. A Huang ally also told the publication they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
Meanwhile, tech executives, including Elon Musk, have called for Huang's reinstatement in an online petition, which has gained more than 180,000 signatures.
US President Trump said on Monday he "wouldn't mind" Huang returning as CEO.
Huang and Trump had formed a close relationship, with Huang becoming a key voice for the US on artificial intelligence while he also lobbied for allowing chip exports to China.
Nvidia's vice president and chief financial officer, Colette Kress, is serving as interim CEO until a permanent successor has been named, the company said on Thursday.

noticias.titulo: Europe’s Sisyphean task: Staying ahead of Moscow's menace
noticias.resumen: Good morning. It’s Tuesday and my name is Angela Skujins. On today’s agenda: Defence ministers descend on Brussels to discuss hybrid threats and the China challenge, while the migration debate enters its second day from ice-cold Vienna.
noticias.texto:
Good morning. It’s Tuesday and my name is Angela Skujins. On today’s agenda: Defence ministers descend on Brussels to discuss hybrid threats and the China challenge, while the migration debate enters its second day from ice-cold Vienna.
Just in: As Europe weighs its role in potential Russia-Ukraine peace talks, the Kremlin launched strikes hitting two major bridges in Kyiv overnight. The attack damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted heating and water in parts of the capital, the city's mayor said.
“The 22nd package of sanctions, where is it? We are late.” That was the message from Lithuania’s Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys, who spoke to me on the sidelines of Monday’s Foreign Affairs Council meeting in Brussels, ahead of today’s gathering of EU defence ministers. He was pressed on how to respond to Russian aggression in Ukraine and Moscow's menace manifesting itself through hybrid warfare, impacting Europe.
On Monday, foreign ministers were tasked with putting flesh on the bones — or adding “substance”, as EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas put it — to discussions about how Europe should be represented in any potential Russia-Ukraine ceasefire negotiations.
Ceasefire first: From a Baltic perspective, Europe needs to take a tougher line with Russia. That starts with not falling for traps laid by Russian President Vladimir Putin and insisting that a ceasefire must come before discussions about what comes next.
This means proposals such as the four-pillar pitch outlined by Austria on Monday could prove harmful to Ukraine’s future. Budrys said Europe’s first and foremost responsibility is to look after Ukraine: accelerating its EU accession negotiations, discussing its NATO membership and strengthening its security through collective defence.
“So let's first decide on Ukraine: How will they be secure? We know how to strengthen ourselves. We should ask ourselves how Ukraine will fit into the Euro-Atlantic family,” he said, adding: “I think it is harmful to be fast with the ideas and propose something new.”
Actions have consequences: Pressure is also mounting for the EU to step up its sanctions regime against Russia, with work on the 22nd package looming. Defence ministers will also discuss how to respond to China’s role in Russia’s war effort, including its provision of dual-use technology found in Russian weapons, such as semiconductors used in lethal drones, and allegations that it has helped train Russian soldiers.
Europe also has skin in the game. Countries across the bloc, particularly those along its eastern flank, are experiencing the spillover effects of Russia’s invasion and its expanding hybrid campaign. Romania’s Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu struck a defiant tone ahead of Monday’s Brussels meeting, calling for closer NATO-EU coordination following an “unacceptable” escalation of incidents off Romania’s Black Sea coast.
“We have had four alerts in 24 hours, and we have had three ships hit over the weekend. This is unacceptable,” he said.
The warning was echoed by Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, who said Russian intelligence services had once again organised an attack against an Estonian defence company — an attempted arson attack that was thwarted. “Russia is attacking Europe,” he said. Estonia has announced plans to close all road border crossings with Russia from 1 December in response.
Back to Ukraine: Latvia’s Foreign Minister Baiba Braže told me that, whatever happens in the peace negotiations, strong sanctions remain essential. Europe must also ensure that: “Russia doesn't read our readiness to be at the table as a weakness, to give up something.”
European allies will also hear directly from Kyiv, with Ukraine’s Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara expected to brief ministers on the battlefield situation and Ukraine’s military needs. One issue to watch: Starlink satellite interruptions.
‘Super into NATO’: Another moment to watch comes over lunch, when EU defence ministers are due to meet US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby. The agenda lists transatlantic security and defence as the focus of their discussions.
One EU official described Colby as “super into NATO”, while another suggested there was little need for a crystal ball to predict that the Pentagon’s force posture review would feature in the conversation. The bigger question is what those discussions will reveal about the future shape of the transatlantic alliance.
Keeping the lights on: the EU has promised to ramp up humanitarian aid to help Ukraine make it through the harshest winter yet of the war. The new pledges include power generators, buses and floating bridges to prevent Russia from breaking the country in two parts along the Dnipro river.
“Russia is turning the winter into a weapon of war to plunge Ukrainians into the darkness and freeze them into submission but this is not going to happen because we’re there,” Hadja Lahbib, the European Commissioner for crisis management, told Jorge Liboreiro on Monday. “We have no choice, this is our security that’s at stake.”
Asked if the suffering inside Ukraine could trigger a new migratory wave to Europe, Lahbib said she’s “preparing for even the worst-case scenario” but expressed confidence that Ukraine will make it through the gruelling winter.
The big five: Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece have announced a partnership with Rwanda to establish the first-ever return hub outside the EU. The five countries aim to begin deporting rejected asylum seekers to the African country in 2027, although the final details of the deal are still being negotiated. The plan has also raised concerns over human rights and potential legal challenges.
The first facility is expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those sent there will be free to move around Rwanda and are expected to integrate into local society and the labour market, according to people familiar with the negotiations.
Going home?: After a period at the facility, the length of which has yet to be determined, migrants will be expected to rebuild their lives in Rwanda or voluntarily return to their countries of origin or another country where they have the right to reside.
What Rwanda will receive in return remains unclear. Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said his country's motivation for participating was a willingness to find solutions to migration management.
He is set to deliver a speech today at the Vienna Migration Conference, organised by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD), on his country's approach to migration and may provide further details about the partnership.
Vincenzo Genovese from Vienna has more.
After peace talks snub, Kallas faces reproach and uncertain future
Kaja Kallas is standing her ground after being dismissed by EU leaders as special envoy for talks with Russia. Asked whether she regretted making her pitch so forcefully last week in Dublin, Kallas remained defiant.
“I stand by my words and I’m ready to do this job,” Kallas said after chairing a meeting of foreign affairs ministers. She then admitted: “You know, it’s also some kind of relief that we don’t talk about who anymore, but we can focus really on the substance.”
In a tongue-in-cheek (yet scathing) remark, Kallas said that if leaders want to preach about the rule of law around the world, they should start by upholding the EU treaties, which leave foreign policy in the hands of the High Representative. The inference is that this means her.
The latest snub adds to an ever-growing list of missteps and setbacks that have plagued Kallas’ tenure. She’s now facing a difficult reality in which she, the High Representative, is excluded from the most consequential diplomatic process the continent has lived through since the end of the Cold War.
It’s a contradiction so glaring and profound that it challenges the very essence of her job, Jorge and Maïa De la Baume write in this must-read analysis.
More from our newsrooms
Serbia to accelerate work on EU accession, Student List representative says. Serbia’s Student List will speed up rule-of-law reforms needed for EU accession, MP Aleksandar Baucal said in the movement’s first international appearance. More on this story from Luca Bertuzzi.
Trump says he could meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in China. Trump is planning to discuss nuclear disarmament when he meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China this week. Nathan Rennolds has the details.
ECB warns AI share boom could end in 'abrupt repricing'. Eurozone funds have bought heavily into the technology, leaving European savers exposed if the boom turns to bust in the US. Simon Orminston has the story.
