noticias.titulo: After peace talks snub, Kallas faces reproach and uncertain future
noticias.resumen: The glaring exclusion of High Representative Kaja Kallas from the Ukraine-Russia peace talks has raised uncomfortable questions about the relevance of her job. Defiant but isolated, Kallas stands by her words.
noticias.texto:
The glaring exclusion of High Representative Kaja Kallas from the Ukraine-Russia peace talks has raised uncomfortable questions about the relevance of her job. Defiant but isolated, Kallas stands by her words.
Since taking on the job as the European Union's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas has dealt with her fair share of setbacks, rebuffs and snubs.
But this one particularly stung.
Last week, Kallas flew to Dublin to attend an informal summit of leaders and make a forceful pitch to become the special European envoy for the ongoing negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
She framed her argument to leaders as self-evident: you chose me for this.
"In June 2024, there was a decision by the leaders (on) who is representing (the EU) when it comes to security and foreign policy. And it was the discussion that in these five years there is going to be a negotiation with the Russians," she said, referring to the division of top jobs at the start of the legislature.
"If the leaders want to change that agreement, of course, they may, because it is the leaders' decision, but I think we should focus our energy actually on the substance."
But leaders were unmoved and dismissed her pitch outright. According to people familiar with the closed-door discussions, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni argued that Kallas lacked the institutional weight and discouraged her candidacy.
The summit concluded with an expanded joint European team for the negotiations with a grand total of seven representatives. None of them was Kallas.
Adding insult to injury, the EU seat is shared by the European Council and the European Commission, with senior officials from the cabinets of presidents António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen, respectively. The European External Action Service (EEAS), the institution that Kallas oversees, is out of the picture.
Asked about her absence, neither Costa nor von der Leyen spoke in her favour.
Snubbed and pushed aside, Kallas now stares down a political reality in which she, the High Representative, whom the treaties task with conducting the EU's common foreign and security policy, is excluded from the most consequential diplomatic process the continent has lived through since the end of the Cold War.
It is a contradiction so glaring and profound that it challenges the very essence of her job.
Some in Brussels believe what happened in Dublin is the natural consequence of the missteps and gaffes that have made Kallas an increasingly divisive – and increasingly isolated – figure in the big-power city.
Kallas has ruffled feathers by going off script on sensitive matters, such as China and Israel, and putting forward initiatives with little or no prior consultation with capitals, including a defence expert group whose launch was cancelled last minute in September after pushback from Italy, France and others.
The displeasure has fuelled calls to reform. Germany, for instance, has proposed to place Kallas under von der Leyen's supervision, mimicking the top-down hierarchy in national governments between a prime minister and a foreign minister.
A senior diplomat pointed out that Kallas spent this year opposing direct talks with Russia, only to then pitch herself as the special envoy to deal with Moscow.
"If she actually talked to people and consulted with them, she would have known where the dynamics would lead to," the diplomat said. "Now, events have overtaken her."
"On the merits she is not wrong," they admitted. "Nothing will come of these talks anyway. There's no way Russia will engage constructively."
A second diplomat was equally critical and said Kallas had been very "clumsy" in her intervention in Dublin, where she declared "Russians don't want me" as envoy.
This diplomat believes that Kallas still retains the way of working she had when she was Estonian prime minister. Back then, her outspoken, hawkish views made her a political star in Europe. In her current role, they can easily backfire.
"It was not the right approach. She put herself in a difficult position. She still has in mind the fact that she was prime minister, and forgets that her role is simply to coordinate the positions of the foreign affairs ministers," the diplomat said.
"Her job is to find the lowest common denominator among member states."
Doomed to fail
The High Representative's pitch was doomed to fail for reasons that go beyond personalities, management style and political background.
Russia's war on Ukraine has become the be-all, end-all subject on the political agenda. Defence, security, trade, energy, finance, technology, sanctions and accession are all at stake in Ukraine. Billions have been provided in budget, military and humanitarian aid. How the war ends is set to define Europe for generations to come.
This has compelled leaders to be extraordinarily involved in the conflict, with countless visits to Kyiv and high-profile meetings. The decision by the leaders of France and the UK to launch the Coalition of the Willing best encapsulates the personal commitment.
But their commitment has come to the detriment of their foreign ministers and eaten away at their portfolios. More often than not, foreign ministers find themselves bickering and haggling without making decisions, which are ultimately made by leaders.
In fact, for the peace talks, leaders have relied on their national security advisors, who are part of their tight-knit cabinet. Even US President Donald Trump has left the task on two hand-picked envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, rather than on Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who, compared to Witkoff and Kushner, is harder on Russia.
Kallas, whose title is equivalent to Rubio, has suffered a similar fate.
Earlier this year, Kallas promoted a list of maximalist demands that Europeans should press Russia to fulfil as part of the negotiations.
Though the document was confidential, the High Representative quoted it so many times, including in Dublin last week, that she effectively made it public. While foreign ministers debated the document at length, leaders never acknowledged it and proceeded with their deliberations unconcerned by its existence.
"The reality is that no foreign minister has an obvious leading role here. Not because foreign ministers are irrelevant, but because the decisions at stake go far beyond traditional foreign policy," a third diplomat said.
"This is, quite literally, a matter for heads of state and government. They are the ones who can ensure political coherence across different areas and ultimately take responsibility for the commitments involved."
A fourth diplomat put it more succinctly, saying Europe should focus its energy on establishing a "consistent, unified position" for the negotiations rather than getting caught up in "unproductive discussions" of names.
Admittedly, the demise of the High Representative is a story that has been written many times in the past and never proven correct – or at least not its entirety.
The prevailing opinion blames the byzantine architecture of the EU treaties, which envisions a high-ranking figure bound by the principle of unanimity and deprived of enforcement powers, as the root cause of the problem.
Still, most diplomats agree that the Estonian's way of working is an aggravating factor. The lack of backing from the Commission, where she serves as vice president, and member states, whose views she is meant to represent, leaves her vulnerable to attacks. When backlash erupts, she is left to fend for herself.
Outside Brussels, however, Kallas remains popular and her no-nonsense takes on Russia are frequently praised and go viral online. The fact that the Kremlin openly detests her is used by her defenders to argue she is doing a great job.
Asked by Euronews if she regretted pitching herself as special envoy so forcefully, Kallas remained defiant.
"I stand by my words and I'm ready to do this job," she said, calling on leaders to uphold the EU treaties the same way they uphold the rule of law.
But she added: "It's also some kind of relief that we don't take about who any more.'

noticias.titulo: Renault to create 2,000 jobs in France while cutting 1,000 others by 2028
noticias.resumen: French car maker Renault announced on Monday plans to create 2,000 jobs by 2028, mostly production roles, while cutting 1,000 mainly administrative staff as it seeks to hold off tough Chinese competition.
noticias.texto:
French car maker Renault announced on Monday plans to create 2,000 jobs by 2028, mostly production roles, while cutting 1,000 mainly administrative staff as it seeks to hold off tough Chinese competition.
French carmaker Renault announced on Monday plans to create 2,000 jobs by 2028, mostly in production, while cutting 1,000, mainly administrative, posts as it seeks to fend off tough competition from China.
The carmaker presented unions with its France Industrie FutuREady project, which aims to transform its industrial activities to respond to the growing challenge posed by Chinese carmakers to European vehicle manufacturers.
The reorganisation will involve the creation of 2,000 new jobs over two years, mainly "blue-collar" positions, Thierry Charvet, head of quality, manufacturing and supply chain, said during a call with journalists.
Renault has around 15,000 industrial jobs in France.
The plan will see 1,650 operators and production workers hired at its plants, along with 250 employees in indirect functions and 100 young graduates.
Renault also announced 1,000 voluntary departures among "white-collar" staff in indirect and administrative functions, under a scheme that still has to be negotiated with the unions.
The CFDT trade union criticised the pace of the planned changes as a "forced march schedule".
Certain jobs deemed strategic will be protected, including those in battery engineering, electronics and software, electric powertrains and industrial maintenance.
The company announced in September that it would invest €600 million ($660m) in Spain by 2030 to produce five new models.
Europe's car industry faces weak demand, excess production capacity and intensifying competition from Chinese manufacturers.

noticias.titulo: Is personalised medicine the future? EU-backed project to map 100,000 genomes
noticias.resumen: A massive European genome bank could pave the way for medicines tailored to each patient's DNA, faster diagnosis of rare diseases and new ways of prevention. Here's how it works.
noticias.texto:
A massive European genome bank could pave the way for medicines tailored to each patient's DNA, faster diagnosis of rare diseases and new ways of prevention. Here's how it works.
Could a medicine one day be designed on the basis of the genetic characteristics of the person who is going to take it?
Could doctors know in advance which patients are more likely to respond to a treatment or to develop side effects?
And could the genetic causes of diseases that are currently hard to diagnose be identified more easily?
Personalised medicine is no longer just a distant scientific vision. Some of its applications are already used in clinical practice, while wider deployment requires much more knowledge of the human genome.
The Genome of Europe programme is one of the largest European population genomics projects. In total, 49 partners from 27 European countries are working together to create a shared reference base of at least 100,000 human genomes, which will reflect the genetic diversity of European populations.
The programme has a budget of €45 million, of which €20 million come from the European Commission through the Digital Europe programme. The project officially started in the autumn of 2024 and is scheduled to run for 3.5 years.
Cyprus is taking part in this effort through the Centre of Excellence for Biobanking and Biomedical Research biobank.cy at the University of Cyprus. Its contribution includes sequencing the whole genome of at least 310 Cypriot volunteers, feeding into the European reference base.
Why Europe needs a genetic map
Human DNA is, to a large extent, shared by all of us. However, small genetic differences are important for understanding inheritance, predisposition to certain diseases and, in specific cases, how people respond to medicines.
These differences are not distributed in the same way across all populations. This means that a genetic database built mainly from specific population groups may not adequately capture the genetic diversity of others.
Genome of Europe aims to close this gap by creating a representative European dataset that can be used as a reference point for future research.
"Populations, such as that of Cyprus, have their own specific characteristics," explained Katerina Strati, an associate professor in the biological sciences department at the University of Cyprus.
She told Euronews that understanding the genome at the local level is essential, because the relevant information cannot simply be inferred from research in other populations.
For scientists, a reference genome acts as a yardstick. It allows them to examine the genetic variants they identify in a person and to assess how common or rare they are in the population to which that person belongs.
Cyprus maps its own DNA
Mapping the Cypriot genome in its current form began in 2019, Strati explains. The aim is to create a genetic reference background for the country’s population, which will support medical research and molecular diagnosis.
Under the Cypriot Human Genome Project (CYPROME), more than 1,000 exomes from Cypriot volunteers have already been analysed. The exome is the part of the genome that includes the protein-coding regions of genes. Its analysis differs from sequencing the whole genome, which examines a much larger section of DNA.
Apostolos Malatras, a senior bioinformatician at the Centre of Excellence biobank.cy, explained that creating a reference genome allows researchers to compare genetic findings against a common background.
Today, biobank.cy holds more than 123,000 biological samples, involves 12,257 volunteers and is active in 14 research programmes, according to the figures published on its website.
The samples do not correspond one to one to genomes or participants. A volunteer can provide more than one sample, and DNA sequencing is a separate process.
Studies carried out at the Cyprus Biobank focus on hereditary kidney diseases, heart conditions and other illnesses. Its research programmes also include efforts to develop preclinical models for rare kidney diseases such as Alport syndrome.
Mariel Voutounou, a project manager at the Centre of Excellence, described the search for a treatment as a long and demanding marathon.
"When a doctor or scientist is interested in starting research into a condition, we say that they are starting a time-consuming marathon. And that is because it takes a great deal of time and effort to collect all these data and samples," Voutounou said. "Someone who has a whole biobank and this wealth of information in their toolbox, we say that their starting line is 10 kilometres ahead of everyone else."
Who protects patients’ DNA?
DNA contains highly sensitive information, not only about a person’s health but also about their biological relatives. How is it ensured that the genetic data of thousands of volunteers will not be used without their knowledge or consent?
The Cyprus Biobank operates with the approval of the National Bioethics Committee of Cyprus and in accordance with the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). As Malatras explains, biobank.cy applies multiple layers of technical and organisational security, with restricted access to personal data.
Dr Georgia Charalambidou, who is responsible for ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) and education at the centre, explained that protection begins even before the first sample is collected.
"When a volunteer, an individual, comes here to the centre, the first thing we do is to provide them with sufficient information," Charalambidou said. "We try to make sure that they have understood it. We give them time to process it, to ask us questions and of course a consent form is always signed, in which all their rights are recorded."
Participation remains voluntary even after signing. "We always explain that they can withdraw their consent at any time, without any impact," Charalambidou stressed, clarifying that in the case of patients this decision does not affect their treatment or their relationship with their treating doctor.
The centre has also carried out a survey involving around 569 Cypriots, examining their views on genetic tests and taking part in genetic research.
According to Charalambidou, most participants were positive towards genetic research but want transparency and information about how their data are used. At the same time, they are interested in being able to receive results from the studies in which they take part.
"They want to know how we handle their data, what results exist. They also want to get something back," she said.
She noted that those who had been in contact with patients with diagnosed conditions were more positive about receiving genetic results back from specialist doctors. This finding, she added, highlights the need for better public information on genetic research.
Data work together without travelling
How can scientists in different countries use genetic data without putting their security at risk?
This is what the European Genomic Data Infrastructure (GDI) programme aims to ensure. It works alongside Genome of Europe, creating infrastructure for the secure interconnection of genetic data.
As Malatras explained, researchers will be able to carry out analyses on the systems where the data are stored, without the files themselves needing to be transferred from country to country.
This cooperation is particularly important for rare diseases, as it allows genetic findings from different populations to be compared.
Precision medicine is already used in some treatments, especially in oncology. However, the development of medicines tailored to the genetic characteristics of each patient remains a long-term prospect.
This is also the ambition behind the European collaboration: that the knowledge now being gathered from the DNA of thousands of volunteers will help deliver better diagnoses, more effective prevention and treatments tailored to patients’ needs.

noticias.titulo: US banking app users report widespread outages linked to software bugs
noticias.resumen: American users of several major banking apps and online portals reported outages on Monday, according to the monitoring site Downdetector.com, with one institution ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.
noticias.texto:
American users of several major banking apps and online portals reported outages on Monday, according to the monitoring site Downdetector.com, with one institution ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.
Among those affected by the outages were Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and the popular money transfer app Zelle.
Downdetector said outage reports peaked at around 2pm Eastern Standard Time (8pm CET) before subsiding.
JPMorgan Chase said in a statement posted on X that it "has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems", adding that "there is no evidence this is cyber-related".
"It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," the statement continued, with the banking giant vowing to restore service by the end of the day on Monday.
"Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue," JPMorgan Chase added.
The outage initially sparked concerns that it could be cyber-related.
Last month, cryptocurrency platform Binance was the victim of a hack involving $6.3 billion (€5.72bn) in stolen funds, the largest such incident ever in crypto.
More recently, French bank Credit Mutuel Arkea was the target of a cyberattack, losing around €100 million.
Was this related to the Microsoft and air traffic disruptions last week?
No. While the disruptions took place just days apart, government officials and company leaders have said they were unrelated.
The major outage at Microsoft on Thursday, which lasted for hours, severely affected services including Outlook, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot. It was due to a technical issue that arose during an upgrade. The tech giant has said there is "no indication" that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, such as a cyberattack, or by the actions of artificial intelligence agents.
Another outage that affected the nation's air traffic control system on Friday, grounding all US flights for several hours and disrupting domestic air travel over the weekend, was caused by a router that malfunctioned and overwhelmed the ageing air traffic control system.

noticias.titulo: What the EU can learn from Mark Carney on digital sovereignty
noticias.resumen: Building autonomy does not mean countries need to isolate.
noticias.texto: At Davos earlier this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney offered a compelling response to a world increasingly shaped by great-power rivalry. Middle powers need greater strategic autonomy, he argued, but they cannot secure it by retreating behind their borders. Instead, they need to build their own capabilities while working more closely with like-minded partners. On technology, he reasoned that countries should cooperate so they are not ultimately forced to choose between “hegemons and hyperscalers.” At the recent EU-Canada Summit, that philosophy began to translate into policy. Canada and the EU launched an “Alliance for the Future” based on closer economic, technological and strategic cooperation. They also concluded negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement designed to support a “secure, open and trusted digital environment”​ resilient economic relations​,​ and trusted cross-border data flows. That principle matters not only for Europe’s new relationship with Canada, but for its approach to other trusted partners. Sovereignty without isolation Like Canada, Europe has diagnosed its technology problem correctly. It depends too heavily on a handful of providers for the cloud, computing power, digital infrastructure and ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ models underpinning its economy and security. Reducing those dependencies will require Europe to put its money where its mouth is, including by unlocking more diversified private investment. Mario Draghi estimated that the EU needs an additional €750 billion to €800 billion of investment each year until 2030. The European Commission, meanwhile, wants to mobili​z​​​e €200 billion for AI and at least triple Europe’s data cent​er​​​ capacity within five to seven years. Europe cannot expect investment on an unprecedented scale while narrowing the field of companies able to provide it. But Europe’s approach risks moving in the opposite direction. ​ ​It could exclude some of the businesses investing most heavily in the continent and building European capabilities, while favo​ring others that remain dependent on non-European technology. That is the risk confronting policymakers as they shape the Cloud and AI Development Act. The legislation seeks to influence not only how Europe expands and secures its technological capabilities, but also which companies can take part. Herein lies the core trade-off.​ ​ Europe cannot expect investment on an unprecedented scale while narrowing the field of companies able to provide it. Whether it closes its technology gap will depend partly on its ability to draw on the capital and expertise of experienced, trusted partners. Look beyond ownership The debate over digital sovereignty therefore needs to move beyond the simplistic question of ownership or headquarters. A definition based principally on corporate nationality could exclude trusted companies with decades of investment, infrastructure and employment across Europe. It could also protect nominally European suppliers without necessarily making Europe more secure or resilient. Effective sovereignty should mean that Europe can keep essential services running during a crisis, protect critical systems and retain a choice of secure, trusted suppliers. Assessments should therefore examine who controls data, encryption, operations, security and continuity. Corporate nationality is relevant, but it cannot answer these questions on its own. A cloud provider may be EU-owned yet rely on processors, software and security tools developed elsewhere. Another may be headquartered outside the EU but operate European data cent​er​​​s, employ European engineers, place data and encryption keys under European control​,​ and comply with demanding European regulation. Any nationality test alone tells policymakers little about which arrangement provides greater sovereignty. ​​ ​In practice, sovereignty done right depends on who can access critical systems, where operational decisions are taken, whether data and encryption remain protected and, ultimately, whether services continue when normal arrangements fail. Nationality should carry the greatest weight where a provider is controlled from a country that presents a recognized security threat, or where the relevant jurisdiction has the capacity and record of exploiting technological dependencies. ​​The strictest restrictions are justified where foreign interference could threaten national security, including defense, law enforcement and the most essential public services. Countries such as Switzerland, Canada​ ​and the UK should not automatically fall into the same category as recognized security threats. Where the security conditions do not apply, nationality-based restrictions risk becoming protectionist rather than protective. Instead, Europe should apply three tests for trusted partners and domestic firms alike: whether operational control rests in Europe; whether the service can continue during a crisis; and whether the provider makes a substantial, long-term contribution to Europe’s technological capacity. ​​In practice, sovereignty done right depends on who can access critical systems, where operational decisions are taken, whether data and encryption remain protected and, ultimately, whether services continue when normal arrangements fail. Telecoms is a case in point. Regardless of where they are headquartered, operators must keep essential services running through cyberattacks, power failures and supply-chain disruption while protecting the confidentiality of EU data. A company’s registered address answers none of those operational questions. Build with trusted partners This matters beyond the Cloud and AI Development Act. The approach Europe takes to sovereignty could shape policy toward​ ​telecommunications, satellites, semiconductors and other strategic technologies. Rules that exclude trusted foreign investors primarily on the basis of nationality risk fragmenting the market and deterring some of the capital and experti​se Europe is trying to attract. They could also encourage reciprocal restrictions on European companies operating abroad. The better approach is the one Carney has begun to articulate: build domestic capability while deepening cooperation with countries that share your security interests and can contribute technology, infrastructure and investment. The EU should therefore provide a route for British companies that meet demanding security, control and resilience requirements to receive equivalent treatment as trusted providers. The EU’s developing relationship with Canada shows that this is possible. Its new Alliance for the Future explicitly combines closer economic integration with technological cooperation, security and resilience, while the Digital Trade Agreement seeks to remove unjustified barriers while maintaining strong safeguards. If deeper integration with Canada can strengthen European sovereignty, the same principle should apply to other trusted partners that meet equally demanding standards. The obvious next test is the UK. Britain sits outside the EU’s institutions but remains closely connected to Europe’s economy, technology sector and security. Infrastructure, investment and supply chains cross the Channel, while the UK and EU face many of the same cyber and geopolitical threats. ​​The EU should therefore provide a route for British companies that meet demanding security, control and resilience requirements to receive equivalent treatment as trusted providers, with reciprocal arrangements for qualifying European companies in the UK. Strategic autonomy does not require strategic isolation. The second UK-EU Summit on 20 November provides an opportunity to turn that principle into practice. Leaders should establish a UK-EU Digital Partnership, covering the mutual recognition of trusted providers, coordinating rules affecting cloud and AI infrastructure, and the removal of unnecessary procurement barriers before they become embedded. Such a partnership would support both sides’ sovereignty objectives by distinguishing genuine strategic dependencies from relationships that add to their resilience and security. Europe is right to seek greater control over its technological future. But ​​Carney has identified the crucial distinction:​ ​strategic autonomy does not require strategic isolation. Canada and the EU have begun to show what trusted partnership can look like. The UK should be next. Disclaimer POLITICAL ADVERTISEMENT The sponsor is Vodafone Group Services Limited . The political advertising is related to the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act and the development of EU-UK digital cooperation . More information here .

noticias.titulo: 5 takeaways from interview with Spanish election favorite Feijóo
noticias.resumen: The conservative leader discussed Trump, Morocco, Spain’s public finances and the relationship with far right
noticias.texto: MADRID — The man tipped to be Spain’s next prime minister, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative People’s Party, believes the current Socialist administration of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been fiddling the national accounts. In an in-depth interview with POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook , he explained that his concerns about Spain’s finances meant he was unable to make clear pledges on defense spending — and whether Madrid could reach its NATO target — until a full audit had taken place after the Nov. 29 election. Despite those doubts on cash flow, however, he still insisted he would fulfill his election promises on tax cuts, pensions and housing. POLITICO’s interview with Feijóo revealed a cautious leader who abides by his deals with the far-right Vox party, with which he is likely to form a coalition if he wins later this month. He signaled he would seek to repair the toxic relationship between Spain and Donald Trump under Sánchez — but was at pains not to appear too deferential to a U.S. president who is deeply unpopular in Spain. Here are the five key takeaways from the interview. Time to probe the national accounts Feijóo said he didn’t “believe the data” on public spending and pledged to conduct an audit of Spain’s accounts within his first 100 days in power. Referring to 2011, the last time the People’s Party succeeded the Socialist Party and had to revise the budget deficit upward, Feijóo said he would take “this history into account.” “I know full well that they lied to us in 2011,” he added. Since the pandemic, Spain’s economic growth has been one of the main success stories for Sánchez’s government. But now, his party is being dragged down in the polls by corruption investigations involving former close allies of the prime minister and by two train disasters this year that killed 115 people. Asked about the role of the audit office in the certification of accounts, he said that “you can choose not to record an expense.” “I know those tricks all too well,” Feijóo went on. “I’m not accusing anyone. I’m simply describing the facts.” Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez poses for selfies with supporters as he arrived to an election campaign rally in Alcorcon, near Madrid, on Nov. 15, 2026. | Oscar Del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images The Socialists reject Feijóo’s assertions and accuse the PP of incurring an EU sanction by concealing healthcare spending in the Valencia region. Pensions and tax cuts Feijóo’s doubts about Spain’s fiscal health aren’t leading him to question the sustainability of public pensions, even after the PP’s parliamentary spokesperson said the system, which is indexed to inflation, would “collapse” without changes . The PP has been walking back those remarks ever since. The Socialist Party has accused the conservative bloc of the PP and far-right Vox of being ready to cut pensions, but Feijóo replied that the retirement system was a “red line” and hit back at the Socialists for using the issue to scare pensioners. “I’m not going to debate pensions,” said Feijóo. “I’ve given my word, and my commitment in writing: adjusting pensions in line with the [consumer price index] is an absolute priority,” he said. He also pledged to go ahead with promised tax cuts and dismissed concerns that such measures could worsen Spain’s public finances. “I don’t believe that from the reduction in personal income tax revenue — where, theoretically, you’d lose, say, €10 billion — you wouldn’t recover 70% of it,” he said. He argued the tax reduction would “ultimately lead to increased consumption.” NATO 5% goal: We’ll see Feijóo knows that committing to NATO’s spending targets will put him on thin ice in Spain, and there’s little support for increasing defense spending if that means cutting public services . Feijóo has fiercely criticized Sánchez’s performance at the Hague summit in 2025 — where Madrid held out against a NATO spending hike — but has avoided clearly committing to invest 5% of GDP in defense. In his interview, Feijóo sheltered behind his skepticism about Spain’s books. “I don’t know if we’ll reach 3.5%, 3.1% or 3.8% of GDP, I just don’t know, because I don’t have a clear picture of the public finances,” the PP leader said. But he emphasized that “Spain is an Atlanticist country and, as such, it well understands that its commitment to NATO and its allies to guarantee the freedom and rights of more than a billion citizens must be a permanent and reaffirmed principle in our foreign policy.” Warm words for Vox It’s widely assumed that the PP will team up with the far-right Vox to govern if the numbers in parliament add up. People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo during the POLITICO interview. | Javier Goiri Basaldua/POLITICO After reaching a deal for the Senate ballot, Feijóo said he’d prefer to govern alone, but he’s convinced that he “knows what most PP voters think when faced with a choice between a one-off deal with Vox on the Senate ballot and handing Sánchez an absolute majority.” “The ballot box will decide the deals,” he added. The People’s Party leader also underlined that his relationship with Vox leader Santiago Abascal “has improved on a personal level” and that they agree that “ sanchismo is going to end in our country.” Asked to name Abascal’s greatest strength, Feijóo said he “has had the ability to recognize a shift to the right in Europe and to understand how that plays out in Spain.” It’s a cordial tone that opens the path to cooperation. Foreign policy: Trump, Morocco and China As PP leader, Feijóo has focused mainly on domestic issues; foreign policy has often been his weak spot, and he has tended to frame his strategy in opposition to Sánchez’s stance. On the U.S., the PP leader said he “respects President Trump.” But he added a caveat. “I don’t need to pay homage to any president of any other country however powerful it may be,” he added, knowing that Trump isn’t popular with Spanish public opinion beyond Vox voters. “I’ll protect Spain’s interests, and those are to have a good relationship with the White House, whoever the president is.” On Morocco, a thorny issue since this summer’s Ceuta crisis in which roughly 80,000 people entered the North African city from Moroccan territory, Feijóo said he wanted a “policy of good neighborliness and loyalty, but with reciprocity and firmness.” “That doesn’t mean not taking a firm stance when our country is invaded by citizens coming from Morocco,” he said. China is another foreign policy front that could see a shift between Sánchez’s government, which advocates for closer ties with Beijing, and one led by Feijóo. “China is one of the two global giants, and we’ll deal with it as such,” said the PP leader. He added he’d abide by any agreement at the European level to harden the EU’s stance towards China.

noticias.titulo: More than cash: EU defense spending push is ‘game-changer’ for industry, says arms boss
noticias.resumen: Panu Routila says the bloc's next seven-year budget would give the defense industry more planning and investment stability.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The EU’s next long-term budget could be a “game-changer” for Europe’s defense industry by giving companies predictable, longer-term funding, the head of Finnish defense firm Patria told POLITICO. EU member countries are still negotiating the size of the bloc’s next seven-year budget , with pressure to reach a deal by the end of the year before a series of national elections in key countries like France and Poland in 2027. The Commission has proposed allocating €131 billion of its nearly €2 trillion budget request to defense and space. Although the final amount is expected to be lower, as countries led by Germany and the Netherlands push for a smaller overall budget, it is likely to represent a huge increase from the roughly €25 billion in the current budget. That kind of money paid out over the next budget running from 2028 to 2034 would allow companies to make long-term investment plans — something that is riskier with current short-term EU programs — said Patria President and CEO Panu Routila. He called the next budget “totally a game-changer.” “Traditionally, the orders have been only for two years or so and not much more,” he said of current arms deals. As a result, “you cannot make really long-term investments even though the demand signals are there.” European defense industry groups have made a similar case. “Coordinated procurement, pooled demand, long-term contracts, greater regulatory predictability, and aligned priorities are essential to expand capacity, strengthen supply chains, and reduce duplication, making investments more effective,” the ASD defense lobby said after the NATO summit in July. So far, the EU’s efforts to boost its defense industry have been limited in duration. The €1.5 billion European Defence Industry Programme provides funding under the current EU budget through 2027 . The €150 billion Security Action for Europe rearmament scheme is a temporary five-year instrument, with disbursements and project completion deadlines extending through 2030 . Routila, who took over Patria in April, said it was extremely important that the EU’s next Multiannual Financial Framework “will lead to something. And something is not regulation only, something is clear products.” Like many other defense companies, the Finnish group has seen sales and profits soar following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. That war also saw Finland break with its past military nonalignment and join NATO in 2023. The need to continue supplying Ukraine and the uncertainty about the U.S. commitment to European security under President Donald Trump are adding to the pressure to rearm. A firefighter works to put out a fire at a residential building in Kyiv after a Russian attack, on Nov. 12, 2026. | Sergii Volskyi/AFP via Getty Images The scale of the European rearmament means there is a need to dramatically increase production. Routila argued that this would not be a major obstacle once companies receive more orders and greater long-term investment certainty. “It’s a problem that is solvable,” he said, comparing the scale of defense firms to the much larger vehicle industry. “The automotive companies, they make millions of vehicles a year. We make thousands of vehicles per year. So the magnitude of volume is different.” Patria has already increased its production, but “I would not say that we are yet working on top limit of our capacity. If there’s a good customer, we can still get orders,” he said. The Finnish state owns just over half of Patria, with Norwegian defense company Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace holding the rest. Patria, in turn, owns half of Nammo, a key manufacturer of 155-millimeter artillery ammunition. Patria is known for multinational projects such as the Common Armoured Vehicle System, a 6×6 armored vehicle developed through cooperation involving Finland, Latvia, Sweden, Germany, Denmark, Norway and the U.K. The company is also moving into drones, signing a letter of intent with Ukraine’s General Cherry in August on cooperation and planning to start drone production in Finland. In the first nine months of this year, the group’s net sales increased by 40% to €933.5 million, while operating profit more than doubled to €113.9 million.

noticias.titulo: I took the EU selection test. Here’s how it went.
noticias.resumen: With 175,000 applicants and just 1,490 jobs, the competition to clinch a dream job in the EU has never been tougher.
noticias.texto: For many aspiring Eurocrats, passing the European Union’s verbal, numerical and abstract reasoning tests is a dreaded rite of passage. From temporary to permanent contracts, anyone who dreams of working for the institutions must first pass these three tests, which form the first round of EU selection procedures — and are notoriously tricky. Earlier this year, the European Personnel Selection Office announced its first hiring contest for university graduates in seven years. Given the low bar for entry — anyone with EU citizenship and a bachelor’s degree could apply — almost 175,000 Europeans decided to give it a go. In 2019, there were just 22,000 candidates . With just 1,490 places on the final reserve list, competition has never been tougher. The cost is high: months, if not years, of studying and stress. But the payoff could be a job for life and a monthly starting salary of around €6,000, almost tax-free. Last week, I was one of hundreds of thousands of candidates from across the EU to sit the hour-long first round, hoping to advance in the so-called competition. Here’s how it went. The run-up Preparing for the reasoning tests involves navigating a hefty application manual, intense studying, and joining Facebook groups. Understanding the application process and how the tests work can feel like a test in itself. Candidates are expected to pore over the 24-page “Notice of Competition,” the subsequent “Notice amending the Notice of Competition” — yes, you read that right — and a 28-page document explaining how to take the online tests. And that’s all before you even start studying. Anyone hoping to pass knows they need to practice. With frequent flashbacks to my high-school years, I sat down to remind myself how to calculate percentages, interpret bar charts, and work out which shape comes next in a sequence. I’ll be honest: I took a fairly relaxed approach to preparing. But I did spend about 20 minutes a day practicing and revisited tips and tricks I’d learned in previous EU tests in the week leading up to the exam. Then there are the Facebook groups, where candidates unite in a strange but somehow comforting online community. Doomscrolling through hundreds of posts was entertaining: One candidate shared some sound advice from a testing platform telling them to talk to their pets before taking the exam to avoid being disturbed. Candidates resell practice books and compare paid practice services with the real test (several private companies have built their business around helping people prepare for EPSO competitions). D-day The days of imposing exam centers are thankfully long gone. Since Covid, EPSO has allowed candidates to sit the tests in the comfort of our own homes. But strict rules are in place to prevent cheating. I was scheduled to take the test on a Thursday afternoon, and a busy day at work left me little time to get nervous. But as I cycled home from the office about an hour before the test, the nerves started to creep in. When my allocated time slot began, I opened a link to enter the test environment. It hid all other tabs and apps, filmed me and recorded all sound throughout the exam. Before the test begins, you have to photograph your ID and record a video of your surroundings, including the top and underside of your desk — which was surprisingly awkward. Then the test began. First came verbal reasoning: 35 minutes to answer 20 questions. Short passages were followed by four statements, and I had to choose which statement was supported by the text — a harder task than it sounds when you’re short on time. The passages covered wildly different topics, some of which were very interesting. I learned that there are only three remaining species of elephant, discovered different types of shoelaces, and found out that the world’s largest rotating and revolving globe is in Maine. I was just over halfway through the test when, much to my dismay, my face started to itch. I’d heard horror stories of people being disqualified for touching their faces and the system flagging it as suspicious. In the end, I managed to answer 15 of the 20 questions, spending the last 14 seconds frantically clicking random answers in the hope I’d strike lucky. Next came numerical reasoning: 20 minutes to answer 10 questions, using tables of data and percentage calculations. I struggled with the time pressure here. While I found it relatively straightforward to work out how to approach each question, the calculations themselves often involved at least five or six steps. I also became somewhat obsessed with checking how much time I had left, and seeing the seconds tick by unsettled me. I managed to get through roughly half of the questions before having to resort to clicking at random again. The good news is that the test environment includes a pop-up writing pad and calculator. The bad news is that they take up almost the whole screen, making it difficult to keep track of the question, the answer choices and the data. The logistical challenge of using the tools was almost harder than calculating the difference in GDP per capita between France and the U.K. in 2003. As if an itchy face wasn’t bad enough, I started needing the toilet halfway through the numerical reasoning section. But leaving your desk during the exam is strictly off-limits and grounds for disqualification. So I unwillingly held on until the bitter end. Last but not least was abstract reasoning, my favorite. You get 10 minutes to answer 10 questions, each featuring a sequence of shapes,s and you have to work out which one comes next. Call me weird, but I find this part fun. There’s something satisfying about cracking the code. The aftermath And then, just like that, I was done, and the first round was over. The tests went by in a blur, and it’s hard to know how well I did. But I didn’t dwell on it: I went straight to a bar and ordered myself a well-deserved cold drink. Only time will tell if I advance to the next stage… Are you smart enough to work for the EU? Find out unofficially here .

noticias.titulo: EU’s Kallas fights to find a role in Ukraine peace talks
noticias.resumen: Bloc's top diplomat said foreign ministers want a more direct role in Ukraine peace talks after leaders selected a team of national security advisers for the job.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Kaja Kallas is scrambling to establish a role for herself in Ukraine peace talks after being excluded from the team negotiating on Europe’s behalf. The EU’s chief diplomat has repeatedly said she is the bloc’s top foreign policy official under EU treaties, while leading behind-the-scenes efforts to define the negotiators’ mandate — shaping what Europe should push for and where its red lines lie. “Take out the treaties and read the treaties,” she told reporters in Brussels when asked about her absence from the team negotiating the biggest security crisis Europe has faced in decades. “Who is dealing with the security and foreign policy issues? So, as we always say to our partners, rule of law actually in Europe is the treaties … So I stand by my words. And I’m ready to do this job [negotiating] as well.” After weeks of agonized debates over who should lead U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine, European Council President António Costa announced in Dublin last week that the team would include national security advisers from France, Germany, Poland, Italy and the U.K., plus representatives from the European Commission and Council. Kallas was not among them. The foreign ministers of Spain and Lithuania both criticized this approach as they arrived at a gathering in Brussels on Monday. “Europe needs one voice. We cannot speak with 27 microphones,” said Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys. “We need one and for that we need a clear mandate, clear procedures, [for] how we are agreeing on our joint position.” ‘Part of a mega-trend’ Some EU diplomats point to Kallas’s criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration as part of the reason she isn’t on the negotiation team. Others say the team is deliberately made up of national security officials who report directly to leaders, noting that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has not been involved in recent rounds of talks. While one national official involved in talks with Russia said Kallas was too divisive to be included, two EU diplomats argued the choice reflected a broader downgrading of foreign policy officials in global affairs. They were granted anonymity to speak frankly about the negotiating strategy, like others in the story. “This is part of a mega-trend that’s hard to fight,” said one of the diplomats. “More and more international questions that were once handled by foreign ministers are now being handled by prime ministers or presidents.” The key for Kallas and EU foreign ministers is to seek relevance by providing “geopolitical strategic perspective” on issues, even if they aren’t being directly consulted, the diplomat said. Envoys from the bloc’s 27 capitals had expressed a desire to play a more direct role in the Ukraine negotiations, Kallas said after her meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Brussels on Monday. “What many member states, ministers said, is that they don’t want to be debriefed about these things. They want to be, you know, involved in these talks.” “We have already prepared, with the foreign ministers, maximum demands,” she added, referring to a document laying out concessions for Russia to grant before talks could continue. Foreign ministers will work in coming weeks to refine these demands, drafting a negotiating mandate for Europe’s negotiating team in time for the next round of talks in Abu Dhabi, an EU official said. Yet other officials have said this job is likely to fall to EU ambassadors rather than foreign ministers, feeding into reports of a turf war between EU institutions over who controls foreign policy. In addition to leading the way on Ukraine, President Ursula von der Leyen’s Commission has also largely taken over managing relations between the EU and Israel, duplicating a department that previously handled relations with the Middle East and North Africa and sat within Kallas’ European External Action Service. Adding to the unease is a Franco-German effort to overhaul the EEAS by potentially integrating it more fully with the Commission in what some officials see as an attempt to bring the top diplomat job under control of the EU executive. For those involved in the talks, the explanation is simpler: They are happening at the level of national security advisers, not foreign policy heavyweights like Kallas. They point to Rubio’s absence from recent rounds, as well as that of Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov. While U.S. envoys said last week that Russia was open to letting Europeans join the peace negotiations, the Kremlin said Monday that no such agreement had been reached.

noticias.titulo: French presidential rivals take aim at Le Pen in debate
noticias.resumen: The far-right leader and four other candidates were quizzed on cost-of-living issues.
noticias.texto: PARIS — Four French presidential hopefuls took aim at Marine Le Pen in a live televised debate on Monday, challenging the far-right leader on her plans for the economy, public housing and her combative relationship with progressive nonprofits. The debate was centered around issues relating to the cost of living and saw candidates quizzed by voters struggling to make ends meet. Le Pen, who has a commanding lead in the polls , found herself on the receiving end of attacks from the other candidates on stage: far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, conservative leader Bruno Retailleau, the centrist Gabriel Attal and the center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann. “Your budget trajectory is a joke, it doesn’t add up,” Retailleau said to Le Pen, referencing Le Pen’s promise to save €140 billion by 2032 . The most heated moment came when Le Pen detailed her plans to require charities that receive public money to refrain from meddling with politics. “Your model is the same as that of your friends, Mr. Orbán and others, which is ultimately to shut up and stop those who do not think like you,” said Attal. “You’ve got a list,” retorted Mélenchon, when Le Pen said she would deliver a list of charities she believed were too political. Le Pen appeared to be playing it safe during the debate, trying to avoid being dragged into a damaging fight with her opponents. Her most pointed attacks targeted Attal, who is the leader of President Emmanuel Macron’s party Renaissance and was briefly prime minister in 2024. “I don’t have any lessons to learn from someone who spent 10 years creating the biggest debt in the history of this country,” Le Pen said to Attal. Le Pen and Mélenchon, who is polling in second place and could end up facing the far-right leader in the presidential runoff, avoided directly confronting each other during the debate. Mélenchon instead took the opportunity to hammer home his proposal to impose a 100% tax on inheritances beyond €12 million. “After 12 million, we take everything,” he said. There were some lighter moments when Mélenchon and Le Pen both agreed the set was too cold. Retailleau chuckled when the far-left leader said the pensions system was not in crisis. The center-right candidate Edouard Philippe, who is also the mayor of the port city of Le Havre, did not take part in the debate, as he had a conflict due to a municipal council meeting, according to his team. Philippe was once seen as the best-placed candidate to beat Le Pen in a runoff but has been struggling in the polls.

noticias.titulo: Brexit diminished us, Burnham says as he tees up closer EU ties
noticias.resumen: The British prime minister attacks Brexit — but hints at slower plan to lay out options for the U.K.'s future relationship.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Andy Burnham laid out his case for reigniting the decade-old Brexit debate at an opulent London banquet Monday, claiming Britain lost more than it gained by leaving the EU. Delivering his first major foreign policy speech at the Lord Mayor’s banquet in London, Burnham said he will sit down with EU leaders following Friday’s U.K.- EU reset summit — where the two sides are expected to sign an agri-food trade deal, link their emissions trading systems, and establish a new system of visas for young people— to work out “options for our long-term relationship.” But — in a sign of the balancing act he faces at home on the issue — the prime minister hinted at a new, slower timeline for outlining his next steps on Britain’s EU relationship after Friday’s tightly-focused summit. “After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship, recognizing that both Britain and the EU are very different to what they were,” he said.”This will take time and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next parliament. At every stage, the British people will be the boss.” Burnham had previously promised to lay out what he believes are the different options for Britain’s future relationship with the bloc “around” the time of the U.K.-EU summit. A government official, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said discussion is now likely to focus on early “next steps” for this process, rather than a menu of options for the public to consider. Burnham is treading a fine line with some members of his own Cabinet, who hold differing views on how far the U.K. should realign with the bloc and whether red lines — including attempting to rejoin the bloc’s single market or enter a customs union — should be crossed. “This is not about re-running the arguments of 2016,” the U.K. prime minister insisted Tuesday, while stressing any new arrangement in this parliament will not breach Labour’s 2024 manifesto, must improve the existing Brexit deal, and benefit working people struggling with the cost of living. Lamenting Brexit as “exactly what our enemies wanted,” the British prime minister said the U.K.’s withdrawal from the EU had been the “first domino to fall in a global move towards isolationism and protectionism.” “In the decade since Brexit, our standing in the world has diminished,” he said. “We treated both allies and institutions with insufficient care, and the effects went beyond Europe.” ‘He will impale himself’ Ahead of Monday’s speech, former Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson — who signed Britain’s post-Brexit settlement with Brussels in 2020 — warned Burnham against “wasting his premiership” relitigating the European question. “He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win — because the reality is that people are not fools,” Johnson said in an interview with the Telegraph newspaper published Monday . Burnham acknowledged it would “be easier to say nothing about the EU,” but said the Brexit deal Britain struck with the bloc ended with “Britain eventually leaving on bad terms, with bad feeling.” “To be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years,” he said, “The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.” Reform UK leader Nigel Farage — a key figure in the 2016 Brexit campaign — accused Burnham of a “total betrayal” in October when the prime minister prompted speculation he would open the door to restoring freedom of movement. Polling conducted by Ipsos in October found that 56% of Britons would vote to apply to join the EU and 51% said they would support a referendum after the next general election. This article has been updated with further reporting.

noticias.titulo: What Britain and the EU still don’t understand about each other
noticias.resumen: It's a crunch week for U.K. and EU relations — and a chance to fall for some decades-long misunderstandings.
noticias.texto: LONDON — They spent years locked in talks over Brexit — but Britain and the EU still sometimes manage to talk past each other. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham heads to Brussels for a much-hyped summit this Friday after promising a “new approach” to dealing with the European Union. “Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges. But being constructive and positive,” Burnham told an audience in the City of London Monday night. He’s already talked up a major revival of ties with the bloc — and even opened the door to British return to the EU, a decade after the U.K. public voted to leave. Yet there remain a host of things the two political bubbles still get fundamentally wrong about each other. POLITICO spoke to officials and experts on both sides to gauge the dynamic shaping Fridays’ “reset” summit — and beyond. Brussels isn’t thinking about the UK all the time Seven or eight years ago, Brexit was front-page news on both sides of the Channel. Now? Not so much. Policymakers in Brussels are grappling with the same thorny challenges that keep their counterparts in London up at night. Whether that’s Donald Trump, AI, climate change, or Chinese industrial capacity depends on what day of the week it is. “Less than 1 percent of my work is about the U.K.,” said an EU diplomat, granted anonymity like others in this article to discuss the relationship frankly. “A lot less, actually!” It’s important not to overstate this. EU officials point out that when called upon to engage with London, they have done so happily. There are entire teams of people in Brussels whose job it is to negotiate with the U.K. But there are also entire teams of people whose job it is to negotiate with the Philippines. Britain is still an important ally of the EU — hence Friday’s dedicated summit to hash out the finer points of the post-Brexit relationship. The door’s always open for more, but the bloc isn’t sitting by the phone waiting for a U.K. call. London’s budget is pretty tight As an EU member country, the U.K. was a big net contributor to the bloc’s budget. But it doesn’t exactly have cash to burn these days. “We need more money” was Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’ pithy response last month when asked whether Britain could rejoin the bloc. Since the global financial crisis, the U.K. public finances have been in a perpetually strained state. And the fraught politics of spending in Britain are not always understood abroad. As a result, EU negotiators have repeatedly misjudged their U.K. counterparts’ willingness to write checks for things. This led to a major failure of negotiations last year when talks on Britain joining the EU’s SAFE rearmament scheme unexpectedly collapsed over the question of money. “A lot of people think that was a huge screw-up,” a second EU diplomat said. Both sides had very different expectations about what a British financial contribution might look like. It’s also made things tricky in the run-up to this week’s summit. London has resisted a request to cut tuition fees for EU citizens studying in the U.K. on the basis that it would have to make up its universities’ budgets elsewhere. The European Commission isn’t all-powerful In 1988, Margaret Thatcher famously railed against a “European super-state exercising a new dominance from Brussels.” For some Brits decades later, leaving the EU was a rebellion against a controlling Brussels bureaucracy. But sometimes, seeing the European Commission as the EU’s central antagonist can make it difficult to understand where the power really lies. “The Commission calls the shots with third countries — until it doesn’t,” said David Henig, U.K. director at think tank the European Centre for International Political Economy. Henig said member countries tend to take charge “at the start and end of the negotiating process” — when they’re writing the Commission’s mandate, and then approving the final agreement. “We’re now at that latter point, when the dynamics change,” he said of the current EU-U.K. reset talks. The European Commission has a lot of responsibility and often has freedom of action. But if EU member countries want something, they tend to get it. Last week saw an obvious case in point: a compromise position on tuition fees was thrashed out by pragmatic EU officials, only for this to be toughened-up by member state ambassadors. It’s a dynamic that may have left some British observers scratching their heads — but it’s worth London getting used to it. Member countries will also be the ultimate arbiter should the U.K. eventually apply to rejoin the EU — even if the Commission would directly handle negotiations. Young people aren’t such a priority in Westminster When the EU first proposed a post-Brexit youth experience scheme — allowing young people to move between the U.K. and EU for limited time periods — back in 2024, both Labour and the Conservative dismissed the idea out of hand. Asked to choose between opportunities for young people and potentially angering euro-skeptic voters concerned about migration, for many in Westminster the answer was just common sense. When it became clear that setting up the scheme was a red line for Brussels, the reaction turned to one of puzzlement. Off-the-record, some British politicians and aides seemed genuinely perplexed: why would they care so much about this issue? “The U.K. only saw a youth mobility scheme as an EU ask because nobody was listening to young people,” Maurizio Cuttin, a board member at Youth Council UK, argued. “I remember officials telling me we didn’t need Erasmus+ or a youth mobility scheme.” For the EU, opening up opportunities for young people was a worthy objective in itself — but also had concrete advantages. It would maintain what officials euphemistically call “people-to-people contact” with post-Brexit Britain. The people staffing the EU institutions have themselves usually worked or studied abroad and see it as a force for soft power. That’s an argument less commonly heard in Westminster. Both sides remain traumatized by Brexit Here’s one point of agreement at least — both sides have scars on their back from the fraught Brexit process. “There’s a lot of traumatized people from Brexit here in the European Union,” EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier this month. She’s not the first to say it: Brexit as trauma has very much become a meme in Brussels. Partly it was a sheer political shock. But partly it was about having one topic dominate the political conversation for several years — to the exclusion of others. EU responses to any British overtures for a closer relationship should be read with Kallas’ summation in mind. Yet while Brits might not frame it quite the same way, it’s something both capitals have in common. For years, British politicians have stooped to avoid reopening the fundamental issue of Europe — even in the face of evidence it might be economically advantageous to do so. That’s something Burnham — Britain’s seventh prime minister since the Brexit vote — has set out to change. Pulling the U.K. out of its post-Brexit crouch will require convincing a bruised Brussels to trust again — and a weary electorate that reopening old wounds is worth the discomfort.

noticias.resumen: François Picard is pleased to welcome Phil Clark, professor of international politics at SOAS University of London. noticias.titulo: Only Stockholm, Helsinki and Copenhagen meet EU air pollution rules, as stricter enforcement looms
noticias.resumen: Apart from Copenhagen, Stockholm and Helsinki, no other major European city currently meets the revised EU limits for nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter - exposure to which caused a combined 216,000 excess deaths in 2023 alone.
noticias.texto: Only three cities are on track to reach EU pollution goals by the end of the year, a new study revealed on Tuesday (17 November), enforcing existing divisions between northern and south-eastern European cities. Copenhagen, Greater Stockholm and Greater Helsinki were the only major European cities or conurbations to have met new EU limits for pollution, while the vast majority of European cities are falling short of the new standards – expected to be transposed into member state law by December 2026. Despite progress noted across bustling cities such as Paris, Stuttgart, and Oslo, the Clean Cities report found no other major European city to currently meet the revised EU limits for nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, exposure to which caused a combined 216,000 excess deaths in 2023 alone. Clean Cities , a coalition of 150 NGOs and grassroots groups, found reductions in pollutants to mostly in cities that had implemented clean transport measures such as low-emission zones and electric buses, as well as changes in residential heating, improved cycling routes and school streets. Read more ‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal “The strong air quality performance of the Helsinki metropolitan area is above all the result of decades of consistent, long-term efforts,” said Antti Wemberg, senior specialist at the Finnish ministry of environment. “The city of Helsinki has been proactive in communicating air quality issues and providing practical guidance on how individuals can improve air quality through their own everyday decisions and activities,” Wemberg told EUobserver. The European Environment agency found that 9 out of 10 Europeans are still exposed to air pollution at concentrations unsafe for human health, and this is largely concentrated in areas in south, east and central Europe. Tuesday’s study found the most polluted urban centres to be in Zagreb, Bucharest, and worst-of-all, Athens. noticias.titulo: ‘Forever chemicals’ lobbyists met EU Commission 37 times in push to escape ban ahead of key decision
noticias.resumen: As the European Chemicals Agency finalises its conclusions on so-called 'forever chemicals', a new report reveals regular contact between senior European Commission officials and industry lobbyists.
noticias.texto: The EU’s attempt to restrict so-called “forever chemicals” (PFAS) is facing a coordinated industry push for exemptions that could leave the ban badly weakened, a report revealed on Tuesday (17 November). The findings by the watchdog Corporate Europe Observatory ( CEO ) come as the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) prepares its final assessment of the proposed ban, the last scientific step before the dossier lands on the European Commission’s desk for a decision. The commission has signalled that it favours banning PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) in some consumer products but may take a softer line on industrial uses, which it sees as vital to Europe’s competitiveness in sectors such as semiconductors, batteries and clean-tech manufacturing. With different parts of the industry each lobbying for their own exemptions or longer transition periods, campaigners fear the result could be a restriction full of loopholes. The fluoropolymer lobby, made up by companies and groups including Chemours, Daikin, Arkema and the trade association Plastics Europe, want fluoropolymers fully exempted from the PFAS ban. They say that they are essential to Europe’s green and digital transitions and that no viable alternatives exist. Since Ursula von der Leyen’s second term as commission president began, they have met the commission at least 37 times to discuss PFAS. That amounts to at least one meeting every third week, almost entirely with the most senior officials. But due to incomplete meeting records and vague descriptions of some meetings, the figure is likely to be higher, warned CEO. “It is a very damaging demand to make,” CEO researcher and campaigner Vicky Cann told EUobserver, referring to the full exemption. “It is very reckless, considering the health and environmental consequences of PFAS use”. Read more French kitchenware giant Tefal faces legal ultimatum over harmful chemicals, as Europeans’ health at stake A growing pollution crisis Over the past 10 years, the PFAS pollution crisis has got bigger. As its nickname implies, once created, they last forever in water, soil, and human bodies. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: EU flexes muscle on Russia sanctions, as Trump and Putin discuss Ukraine’s future in China
noticias.resumen: If new EU sanctions on Russia were meant to show strength at a delicate moment in Ukraine peace talks, they could have been stronger.
noticias.texto:
People watch as smoke rises above a Wildberries facility following a reported Ukrainian drone strike at the Koledino Industrial Park near Podolsk, Moscow Region, Russia, on 16 August 2026 (Source: EPA/STRINGER)
Russian elites are back on the menu in EU sanctions, but Ukraine peace talks seem to be headed toward another anticlimax.
Tatyana Kim, Russia’s richest woman and the CEO of online retailer Wildberries, is to face an EU visa-ban and asset-freeze in new sanctions to be agreed by foreign ministers in Brussels on Monday (16 November).
So is Russian gold-mining baron Ruslan Baysarov, Russian venture capitalist Alexander Chachava, and real-estate mogul Sergey Matvienko, according to a leaked EU proposal seen by EUobserver.
They are on a list of 137 individuals and entities to be added to an existing EU blacklist of over 4,600 names.

noticias.titulo: ‘Not apathy but disconnection’: We asked Europe’s youngest MEPs what they thought of the continent-wide Gen Z protests
noticias.resumen: From Porto to Athens, Europe was taken by surprise by the mass youth protests for better education, an affordable cost of living, and political accountability. EUobserver spoke to 12 of the youngest MEPs in the European Parliament to understand the issues at the heart of Gen Z unrest.
noticias.texto: From Porto to Athens, Europe was taken by surprise by the mass youth protests for better education, an affordable cost of living, and political accountability. EUobserver spoke to 12 of the youngest MEPs in the European Parliament to understand the issues at the heart of Gen Z unrest. One topic that has been largely misunderstood is political engagement. “It is not the apathy some attribute to Gen Z, but a disconnection from the political establishment, because it is not delivering for them,” said Lena Schilling, a 25 year-old Austrian MEP for the Greens. For instance, an EU study from October found that 55 percent of young Europeans had participated in at least one social initiative. The issue is that “fewer political candidates take an interest in young people,” 34-year old German Socialist & Democrat (S&D) MEP Delara Burkhardt told EUobserver. The average age of MEPs is 50, with the largest demographic in the parliament being men in their forties. Older people also make up an increasing proportion of those voting in Europe. Read more Listen: Is the right to protest under threat in Europe? It’s a “huge structural shift, [meaning] young people don’t feel listened to or represented,” said French S&D MEP Chloé Ridel, aged 34. The very few elected to speak on behalf of young people have “to elbow our way through our own committee.” Europe has seen wave after wave of youth-led protests in the last two months, starting with French high-school students demanding better education, bringing up to 600,000 people to the streets and continuous protests since 17 September. The French were followed by the Spanish housing movement, culminating in the first general strike in 14 years, counting some four million workers and close to 200,000 protesters across the country. The movement spread from Madrid to squares in Rome, Lisbon and beyond, as students and neighbours hoisted tents in central areas to protest the cost of living. The discrepancy between those elected and those electing , has resulted in a vast chasm in priorities – and language. The weekly protests erupting from every corner of the continent received responses of “warning of chaos and disruptions to public order, instead of addressing the legitimate reasons behind people’s dissatisfaction,” said 33-year old Czech Green MEP Markéta Gregorová.
