noticias.titulo: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
noticias.resumen: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
noticias.texto:
Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
- Published
Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.
This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".
US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.
But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.
Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.
BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.
The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.
This calls into question claims that Republican voters may have been confused about which Sullivan they were voting for.
How did two Dan Sullivans end up in the race?
Republican Dan S Sullivan has held the US Senate seat in Alaska since 2015 and was running for his third term.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr - a retired school teacher from a remote fishing village in Alaska - entered the race in May and has run a low-key campaign.
A New York Times story, external published the week before Election Day claimed that Democratic operatives with links to the Peltola campaign had tried to recruit "spoiler" candidates in the Senate race, including Daniel J Sullivan Jr.
The report said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team also tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.
Peltola has denied all knowledge of the alleged "scheme" and Sullivan Jr has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.
President Trump has posted multiple times on Truth Social since the election, claiming that the race has been "rigged".
But experts note it's not an illegal tactic, if it was employed.
"There is nothing to prevent a campaign from recruiting someone else to run, even if for political reasons," said Joshua Douglas, an election law expert at the University of Kentucky.
How does voting work in Alaska?
Voters in Alaska select their first choice candidate, followed by options to rank up to four other candidates in order of preference.
"There is no specific law preventing people with the same name running, but many states have laws or regulations about how names appear on the ballot. One of those regulations was used in Alaska" said Ruth Greenwood, director of the election law clinic at Harvard Law School.
On Alaskans' ballots the two Sullivans were listed as:
- Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.
- Sullivan, Dan S. (Registered Republican) Incumbent
There was a second registered Republican candidate, Gerald Heikes - who was also allegedly recruited into the race according to The New York Times.
As of Tuesday, Peltola holds 49.98% of the vote.
In the event that Peltola were not to clear 50%, officials eliminate the candidate in last place and reallocate those ballots to the voters' next choices. This process continues until two candidates remain, with one clearing the 50% hurdle.
Daniel J Sullivan Jr is the listed candidate in last place with 1.65% of the vote.
What does ranked-choice voting data show so far?
Senator Dan S Sullivan and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Trump said last week: "Anybody that voted for that second Dan Sullivan, the fake Dan Sullivan, was supposed to be a vote for the real Dan Sullivan".
Of the ballots analysed by BBC Verify that ranked Daniel J Sullivan Jr first, 38% of them recorded no valid second choice.
We do not know how many of these voters may have thought they had voted for the Senator Dan S Sullivan and then not ranked any other candidates.
A further 29% of Daniel J Sullivan Jr voters ranked the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola second, almost double the 15% that ranked the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan as second.
"In Alaska the likelihood that any confusion might play a significant role is diminished," Richard Pildes, a professor of constitutional law at New York University, argues, "because any voter who was unsure which Dan Sullivan candidate they meant to vote for could rank them first and second."
Additional reporting by Daniel Wainwright

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang to testify before US House committees next month
noticias.resumen: Huang said he is ready to return as Nvidia CEO if the company's board would like him back at the helm.
noticias.texto:
Jensen Huang agrees to testify before US House, says can resume CEO role
Huang said he is ready to return as Nvidia CEO if the company’s board would like him back at the helm.
Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, has agreed to appear in transcribed interviews with several United States House committees on December 1, even as he has said he would be “honored” to resume his job if the company’s board would like him to.
On Tuesday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee announced the upcoming interviews, which will also include the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee.
The US tech giant’s General Counsel Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on December 2 . It was not immediately clear whether the men would attend in person or speak remotely.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Republican chairmen of the committees, Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said in a statement.
“The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, raised questions over exports of the company’s advanced AI chips to China.
The lawmakers first called on Huang on November 5 to appear before the committees. That came amid initial reports from The New York Times that US authorities had started investigating Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys artificial intelligence (AI) chips from Nvidia, and with whom Huang has admitted to having an affair.
US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China.
Push to return
The announcement comes as Huang has expressed a willingness to return to the company since resigning last Thursday.
“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a post on the social media platform X.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Huang’s comments come amid reports that tech industry insiders were pushing for his return to the company, alongside a petition with more than 177,000 people calling for his return.
“The board’s decision now sits between a founder who has publicly asked for his job back, a shareholder base with the means to force the question, and an administration split between a president open to his return and a Treasury secretary demanding an outsider,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said in a note provided to Al Jazeera.
At the same time, Nvidia has announced a board-level committee to oversee national security and export controls, marking the first major governance move since Huang resigned.
The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman Sachs vice chair, Nvidia said. Directors Stephen Neal, former CEO of law firm Cooley, and John Dabiri, a Caltech professor, will also serve on the committee.
US President Donald Trump welcomed the move, calling the launch of a national security initiative a good idea.
Nvidia stock tumbled in midday trading on Tuesday. It was down more than 1.6 percent for the day, 11 percent over the previous five days and 29.2 percent over the previous month.

noticias.titulo: Iraqi PM heads to Lebanon amid push to explore oil routes beyond Hormuz
noticias.resumen: Ali al-Zaidi's talks expected to include proposed project linking Tripoli in Lebanon to Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline.
noticias.texto:
Iraqi PM heads to Lebanon amid push to explore oil routes beyond Hormuz
Ali al-Zaidi’s talks expected to include proposed project linking Tripoli in Lebanon to Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline.
Beirut, Lebanon – Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is set to visit Lebanon on his latest regional visit aimed at boosting economic cooperation amid the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.
Al-Zaidi will hold a series of high-level meetings in Beirut, including with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri.
High on the agenda of Wednesday’s talks will be strengthening bilateral trade, customs exemption deals and coordination on security and countering drug trafficking.
Diversifying oil export routes via a pipeline linking the Iraqi city of Kirkuk, through Syria’s Mediterranean port of Baniyas, to Tripoli in northern Lebanon, is also expected to be discussed. The proposed project is aimed at potentially bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, a key energy waterway that has been severely disrupted since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.
“After the war in Iran and the story of Hormuz and exports in the Gulf, [Iraq] is looking for alternative routes to diversify their export routes,” Walid Marrouch, professor of economics at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
Iraq’s crude oil exports were badly hit following the start of the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s energy passes in peacetime.
Last month, Iraq’s Ministry of Oil said crude oil exports reached about 2.7 million barrels per day (bpd), up from some 200,000 bpd in May. Before the war, Iraq was exporting about 3.5 million bpd. The increase has been boosted by the resumption of oil pumping this week through the Iraqi-Turkish pipeline at an initial capacity of 120,000 bpd.
Still, Iraq has been looking for alternatives to export its crude oil, primarily through Syria, which was previously difficult due to international sanctions under the leadership of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in late 2024.
Tamer Badawi, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute, said al-Zaidi’s visit to Lebanon was likely to be informed by US envoy Tom Barrack’s “efforts to diversify Iraq’s oil export routes across the region, particularly through Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Lebanon”.
He added: “The broader ambition is to develop alternative export corridors connecting Iraq’s oil infrastructure to regional networks.”
‘Lebanon can benefit’
One of the potential proposed alternatives is Tripoli, in northern Lebanon.
The impoverished city has emerged as an option because of the long-defunct pipeline from Kirkuk and a local refinery that in 1940 filtered 21,000 bpd of crude oil from Iraq, according to the Lebanese Directorate General of Oil. The refinery shut down in 1992, shortly after the end of the 15-year Lebanese Civil War in 1990.
Industry insiders say Tripoli’s oil infrastructure has three legacy lines with a historical peak capacity of 900,000 bpd.
While it would need to be repaired and renovated, a report this year by the Basil Fuleihan Institute of Finance (BFIF), an autonomous agency under the tutelage of Lebanon’s Finance Ministry, said “the terminal infrastructure remains a goldmine of latent capacity” with a moderate flow scenario of 300,000 to 500,000 bpd that could gain Lebanon annual revenues in the region of $80m to $275m.
The revenues could be a boon to the Lebanese economy, which has been beset by a complex economic and banking crisis since 2019 that has seen its currency lose more than 90 percent of its value and the majority of its population living in poverty.
Al-Zaidi’s trip to Beirut comes weeks after he met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus. During the visit, the two countries signed a cooperation agreement to rehabilitate the pipeline running from Kirkuk to Baniyas, in a project to be carried out by US energy giant Chevron.
“Upon rehabilitation, this groundbreaking project will have an initial transport capacity of 2 million barrels per day of crude oil,” the US Department of State said in a statement at the time.
Experts said al-Zaidi’s visit on Wednesday was a big opportunity for Lebanon to ensure its place in a prospective tripartite agreement with Syria and Iraq – but warned that if Lebanese officials failed to act, the country could be left behind.
“Lebanon can benefit, but if Lebanon does not get a seat at the table, it [could be circumvented] because Iraq can already reach the sea from Syria,” said Marrouch.
Before reaching Tripoli, Iraqi crude oil would have to pass through some 250km (155 miles) of Syrian territory.
Syria also has its own ports in Tartous and Latakia, with a smaller port in Banias. According to BFIF, Syria is set up to handle about 350,000 to 500,000 bpd, between refineries at Banias and Homs, “a direct Mediterranean outlet that circumvents both the Suez Canal and the Strait of Hormuz”.
The flow of crude oil through Syria would also be a boost for the country, where domestic oil production is currently insufficient and energy costs have spurred protests. Syrian officials have also warned about attacks on the Homs refinery.
But experts believe including Lebanon in the deal could still be beneficial for all parties.
Tripoli’s deepwater quays allow it to handle larger vessels, reducing freight costs per barrel for Iraqi crude and making the oil competitive in European and North American markets, said the BFIF report, adding that Tripoli’s coastline is “naturally shielded from harsh southern winds and rough swells,” unlike in Banias in Syria.
“This makes the port accessible year-round, even during severe Mediterranean winter storms that frequently force the closure of offshore loading operations in Banias,” the report said.

noticias.titulo: Religious ruling revives memories in Israel of Rabin assassination
noticias.resumen: Hostility towards Palestinian participation in Israel's government fuels fears of far-right political violence.
noticias.texto:
Religious ruling revives memories in Israel of Rabin assassination
Hostility towards Palestinian participation in Israel’s government fuels fears of far-right political violence.
As negotiations to form Israel’s next government continue, tensions across Israel have risen to an unprecedented high, evoking memories of the period leading up to the 1995 assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.
In a letter published last week, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, invoked a principle in Jewish religious law known as din rodef, issuing a religious ruling that could be used to justify the killing of politicians accused of facilitating a government backed by Arab-led parties. The same principle was invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of Rabin because he had signed the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians.
“The Torah obliges me,” Axelrod later told the Israeli news website Walla. “I knew it was not easy, but if the Torah obliges, then we go. We are Jews, we make sacrifices.”
Axelrod’s ruling has prompted widespread condemnation and demands for a criminal investigation. The Chabad Hasidic movement that Axelrod belongs to has also distanced itself from his remarks.
Twenty former senior Israeli security, military and public figures, including former heads of the country’s intelligence agencies, have called on the authorities to investigate Axelrod. Separately, left-wing member of parliament Ofer Cassif and his fellow lawmaker Michal Rozin have also demanded an investigation, warning of the growing risk of political violence taking hold across Israel.
The controversy comes after Israel’s parliamentary election in late October, in which parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel won 19 of the parliament’s 120 seats. Parties opposed to caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hold a majority in parliament, but several members of the opposition have refused to cooperate with the Arab parties.
History doesn’t repeat, it rhymes
For many in Israel, mention of din rodef, or the “law of the pursuer”, immediately evokes memories of the tensions and incitement that led up to Rabin’s killing on November 4, 1995.
Rabin’s widow, Leah, directly accused Netanyahu – who was then the leader of the opposition – of helping to foster that climate of hostility. She pointed to his presence at a rally a month before the assassination, at which protesters displayed an effigy of her husband dressed in a Nazi uniform.
Amir justified his assassination of Rabin by arguing that the prime minister’s pursuit of the Oslo Accords endangered Jewish lives, echoing the reasoning now employed by Rabbi Axelrod, who claims that an alliance with an Arab-led party would place Jewish lives at risk.
This conflation of politics and religion, while hardly unique to Israel, amounted to “political theology”, Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani explained.
“By political theology, I mean the way ideas about God, sacred authority and the chosen people shape political life,” he said of the rules governing who is entitled to rule, who is allowed to belong and whose life must be protected. “Sometimes these ideas are explicit, as in a rabbi invoking divine law against an elected politician. But they can also survive in apparently secular ideas about the nation, sovereignty and historical destiny.”
“Someone who accepts Arab participation in government can then be portrayed as betraying a sacred community, and violence against them can become, in the eyes of a believer, a religious duty,” he said of the rationale behind Axelrod’s ruling.
A real threat
“The threat of political violence is really high,” Cassif told Al Jazeera. “We all remember what happened in 1995 and the atmosphere that preceded Rabin’s assassination. This time it’s worse. Then it was just a few extremists on the fringe; now it’s the mainstream. They’re being openly encouraged by a prime minister who, I think, is ready to consider or do anything to hold on to power.”
Cassif also pointed to far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s own role in the atmosphere of incitement before Rabin’s killing. In October 1995, the month before the assassination, Ben-Gvir was filmed brandishing the hood ornament torn from the prime minister’s car, telling journalists, “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him, too.”
Fears of far-right violence have grown as coalition negotiations have dragged on. Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party have repeatedly sought to vilify Arab-led parties, both in their campaign ahead of the October 27 election and in their statements since.
Netanyahu has accused the parties of allying with foreign and hostile powers. And he used the swearing-in of the new parliament on November 10, anticipated to be largely ceremonial, to brand the incoming Palestinian politicians “terror supporters, haters of Israel” and denounce opposition politicians considering working with them.
Days earlier, right-wing protesters gathered outside the Herzliya home of Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader now tasked with forming a government, accusing the former general and chief of staff of being a traitor. One protester accused Eisenkot of having murdered his own son, Gal, who was killed in Gaza in December 2023. Turning his attention to Eisenkot’s wife, Hannah, the protester told her she would be joining her son.
“Obviously, this is a tense time,” said political psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal of Tel Aviv University, who has made a study of political violence.
“The ultra-rightists will try to stop the process of changing regimes,” he said, drawing parallels with the January 6, 2021, attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of President Donald Trump. “Thus, it is a dangerous situation.”
“What Netanyahu is doing now is what he’s been doing for years: taking the Arabs, [and] the democratic Jews who work with them, and presenting them to the Israeli public as an overwhelming threat,” Cassif said. “Using minorities and their supporters as a scapegoat has always been a cornerstone of nationalist right-wing policy, and so it is in present-day Israel.”

noticias.titulo: CAIR defends civil rights work against Trump’s ‘smear’
noticias.resumen: The country's largest Muslim advocacy group urges Trump to address rising hate crimes against Muslims.
noticias.texto:
CAIR defends civil rights work against Trump’s ‘smear’
The country’s largest Muslim advocacy group urges Trump to address rising hate crimes against Muslims instead of attacking its efforts.
The largest Muslim civil liberties organisation in the United States has condemned suggestions by President Donald Trump that it could face a blanket designation as a “terrorist” group.
The Council on American–Islamic Relations (CAIR) said the White House should be addressing violence against American Muslims, rather than attacking the rights group.
“The Trump administration should focus on addressing this surge in violent hate, not entertaining smears against the civil rights organisation that counters such hate,” CAIR said in a statement to Al Jazeera on Tuesday.
On Monday, Trump said he was considering giving a blanket “terrorist” designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and that his administration was also looking at CAIR, which is already classified as a “terrorist” group in Texas and Florida.
“CAIR is another one we are watching,” he said of the organisation.
When asked if he was considering naming CAIR as a foreign “terrorist” group, he responded: “I’m not going to say that yet, but it could happen.”
In its statement, CAIR said that it was “fully prepared to defend our civil rights work and the broader American Muslim community from any new attempts to censor free speech, punish dissent or otherwise undermine the rule of law”.
“Our advocacy for justice here and abroad is the real reason that anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian extremists spend so much time obsessing over our work,” it said.
‘Clamping down’
Trump’s comments on Monday came during an exchange with reporters outside the White House, following a question about Egypt’s crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood and whether Washington would consider a broader designation of the group.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration designated the Muslim Brotherhood chapters in Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt as foreign “terrorist” organisations.
Trump praised Egypt, where the Muslim Brotherhood originated, for cracking down on the group, indicating it did so at his request.
“Egypt has clamped down very hard on the Muslim Brotherhood, at my request,” he told reporters as he left the White House on Monday.
“Egypt did a great job,” Trump said.

noticias.titulo: Yemeni parliament approves law designating Houthis as ‘terrorists’
noticias.resumen: The law targets the group's financing and activities as Houthis make advances in southwestern Yemen.
noticias.texto:
Yemeni parliament approves law designating Houthis as ‘terrorists’
The law targets the group’s financing and activities as renewed fighting threatens to derail efforts to end Yemen’s war.
Yemen’s parliament has unanimously approved a law designating the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising the group’s activities and financing, as fighting intensifies between the group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government.
The vote, held over two sessions by videolink on Monday, comes seven years after the measure was first proposed. Parliament said it had deferred the bill, first tabled at a session in the city of Seiyun in April 2019, to give peace efforts a chance.
It noted that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, had attacked government-held areas of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and accused the Iranian-backed group of brushing aside “all options for peace”.
Yemen’s cabinet approved the draft law on October 11. The country’s National Defence Council had designated the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation by executive decision in October 2022. The United States also lists the group as a “terrorist” organisation, and Saudi Arabia treats it as one.
What does the law say?
According to the state-run Saba news agency, the legislation was formally submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, on Tuesday to be signed into law.
It runs to 55 articles and designates the group – including all of its political, military and civilian formations – “a terrorist organisation” and a “rebellious faction”.
It also toughens penalties for offences including seizing state authority, besieging cities, attacking civilians, laying landmines and attacking international shipping. Certain offences would carry the death penalty.
The law also sets out procedures to identify, trace, freeze and confiscate assets linked to the group and its affiliated entities.
Renewed fighting
The vote comes amid months of renewed hostilities after several years of relative calm on Yemen’s front lines. In late June, the Houthis announced an escalation against government forces and Saudi Arabia, saying the move was aimed at lifting what the group describes as a “blockade”.
In early September, a Houthi ground offensive on the western coast gave the group control of parts of Taiz and Hodeidah governorates after government forces withdrew from the port city of Mocha and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area.
Government forces launched an operation called “Dawn of Yemen” in early October to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. It initially made limited gains in recapturing territory lost on the Red Sea coast, but on Sunday, pro-government forces withdrew from those areas, allowing the Houthis to advance further.
Heavy fighting continues in Marib, al-Jawf and Lahij governorates, and the Houthis are pressing to take the city of Taiz, which the government and rights groups say is under a tight siege. The Houthis have also stepped up attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition says it is striking facilities that fund the group’s war effort.
The Houthis seized Sanaa in September 2014. United Nations-sponsored talks and regional mediation have failed to end the war since then.
Implications for peace and aid
Ismail al-Suhaili, a political science professor and senior researcher at the Mokha Center for Strategic Studies, said the law marks a shift towards a tougher government position after the failure of peace efforts. Moving the designation from an executive decision to parliamentary legislation gives it wider legal force, he said.
He said it could complicate future negotiations by shifting their focus from power-sharing towards restoring state institutions, disarmament and UN Security Council Resolution 2216.
Al-Suhaili warned that the law could put additional pressure on banks, traders and companies operating between government- and Houthi-controlled areas and deepen Yemen’s financial split. Donors and aid organisations could also become reluctant to work in Houthi-held areas, which could disrupt the delivery of essential supplies to civilians. The Houthis, he said, could respond with further military escalation or with countermeasures targeting government leaders.
Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, told Al Jazeera the law was “a late step” but provides a legal basis for holding those responsible for abuses to account and compensating victims.
While the law narrows the space for political negotiations in favour of military action, al-Hamidi said, it does not entirely rule out a future settlement.

noticias.titulo: Photos: Tens of thousands rally in France over living standards and wages
noticias.resumen: France witnesses its third major public sector strike since September, as protests highlight wage and service concerns.
noticias.texto:
In Pictures
Photos: Tens of thousands rally in France over living standards and wages
France witnesses its third major public sector strike since September, as protests highlight wage and service concerns.
Demonstrators have gathered across France after unions called a nationwide strike by public sector workers in a bid to secure pay rises, as protests over living standards and squeezed public services continue to roil the country.
France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were urged to mobilise on Tuesday after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands for across-the-board pay rises, following last week’s minimum wage boost for private-sector workers.
It is the third united day of strikes and protests in the public sector since September, after a previous mobilisation earlier this month drew hundreds of thousands of workers and saw police fire tear gas as clashes broke out in several cities.
More unions joined the call to strike after Lecornu’s meeting, saying the government’s proposed measures did not address what they describe as an urgent pay and cost-of-living crisis. In Paris, a major rally was taking place in the east of the city, with dozens of other demonstrations planned nationwide.
Police sources told AFP that between 40,000 and 80,000 people were expected to demonstrate in the capital, and up to 300,000 across France. In Paris, university professor Nicolas Prevot said he was marching to defend human rights, protect public services and keep the far right from power in next year’s presidential election.

noticias.titulo: Thousands demand cancellation of Nathan Cofnas talk at Oxford University
noticias.resumen: Online petition with more than 32,000 signatures demands the university 'cancel Nathan Cofnas's invitation to speak'.
noticias.texto:
Thousands demand cancellation of Nathan Cofnas talk at Oxford University
Online petition with more than 32,000 signatures demands the university ‘cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak’.
Thousands of people have signed a petition and protests are planned at the University of Oxford against the appearance of Nathan Cofnas, an American academic and self-described “race realist” accused of racism.
Cofnas, who had accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism last July, is due to give a talk at Oxford’s Oriel College on Tuesday evening at an event organised by the Oxford Reform student society, which is linked to the far-right Reform UK party.
Cofnas has drawn controversy for years with his eugenics-linked views tying race to intelligence, writing that Black people were less intelligent than others in an article which led to his dismissal from his position at a college at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.
He was suspended as a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University in Belgium in August after making plagiarism allegations against Arday, a Black Cambridge professor. Arday consistently denied allegations of plagiarism but acknowledged errors in his work.
Arday was later found dead in his home after resigning his post amid the ballooning scandal.
Cofnas was later allowed to resume some academic work at Ghent remotely, without teaching, while an investigation continued.
The Oxford Reform student society defended its event – titled “Is DEI Undermining Higher Education?”, referring to diversity, equity and inclusion – and said it is “committed to broadening participation in university life”.
In a statement, Oxford University said the event being hosted on its grounds “does not imply endorsement by the College of the views of its speakers”.
An online petition demanding the university “cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak” has more than 32,000 signatures.
“Ideas platformed at Oxford do not stay in the lecture theatre”, the petition said.

noticias.titulo: Election-winning student movement enters Serbia’s new parliament
noticias.resumen: Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time.
noticias.texto:
Election-winning student movement enters Serbia’s new parliament
Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time.
Following the October 25 vote that upended Serbia’s political landscape, the new parliament is meeting for the first time in Belgrade.
The vote redrew Serbia’s parliamentary map as a grassroots, student-led movement won the largest single share, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).
The Student List group was backed by 2.3 million citizens, altering the previous parliamentary arithmetic and balance of power. It holds a majority with 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with the Serbian Progressive Party’s 104.
Tuesday’s session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, assisted by the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly. The new speaker could be announced later on Tuesday.
The formal agenda follows a clear legal framework: verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies.
But beyond legal formalities, the political atmosphere is complex and large sections of the public have high expectations.
A new balance of power
Political analyst Djordje Vukadinovic told Al Jazeera, “Everyone is eagerly awaiting it. I would avoid making any predictions, because with the current opposition structure, you never know what might happen or what stance they will take.”
He added, “What I do know is that this is only the beginning of establishing a new government, and I believe not everything will be wrapped up today.”
Ahead of the session, a group of students wrote to the new lawmakers, reminding them of their “serious” responsibilities.
“All of you are becoming members of parliament in the highest legislative body of the Republic of Serbia for the first time. And only that. Nothing more. The fact that the highest state offices have for decades been presented as ‘comfortable armchairs’ is a systemic flaw. The people elected you. We are the people. You are the people. Act accordingly,” warned the Student Plenum of the Higher School of Civil Engineering and Geodesy in Belgrade in an open letter.
Aleksandar Cupic, an incoming Student List MP and an assistant professor in engineering, said new lawmakers must demonstrate institutional maturity.
“We do not plan to speak about our candidate for five or 10 hours, because that is neither in the spirit of the values we will represent nor is it rational. We owe it to the citizens to proceed with electing the speaker of parliament,” Cupic told reporters ahead of the session.
He said political groups had been consulting one another in a more moderate atmosphere than reports have suggested.
But on Tuesday, tensions were seen outside parliament.
A woman threw yoghurt over Lidija Vukicevic, a well known actress who supports the SNS, outside parliament and the crowd booed Vucic as he walked in.
The Serbian actress and former MP Lidija Vukicevic, who is backing the ruling SNS party, had yoghurt poured over her as she arrived at Serbia’s National Assembly for its first session following elections won by a student-led opposition movement.
The swearing-in session marks the start of a critical political countdown – a 90-day constitutional deadline to elect a new government.
Should that expire without parliament voting in a new cabinet, Serbia’s constitution mandates the dissolution of the National Assembly and the calling of snap parliamentary elections.
The developments are being watched across the region, as well as in European and global political circles.
Observers say the new political leaders will have to govern the state and rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbouring countries and the European Union – ties that have been strained in recent years.
Echoing that point, Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal told the international EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels that a peaceful transfer of power is only the start of a complex array of work.
“Changing power through non-violent and democratic means is only the first step,” Baucal said in Brussels. “Serbia now faces the task of rebuilding institutions that will prevent the personalisation of power and serve all citizens, regardless of who they voted for. I am convinced that from now on, the news coming out of Serbia will be largely positive.”
In a similar vein, the European Democratic Party (EDP) weighed in on the eve of the parliamentary session.
“Serbia must now heal the wounds of recent years through truth, justice and accountability … we sincerely hope a new chapter of freedom, democracy and reconciliation will begin,” the EDP said, adding that the session will test whether Serbia is ready for institutional reform.

noticias.titulo: US officially loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setback
noticias.resumen: A major health organisation declared measles endemic in US for first time since 2000, reversing decades of progress.
noticias.texto:
US officially loses measles-free status after 26 years in historic setback
A major health organisation declares measles endemic in US for first time since 2000, reversing decades of progress.
The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, reversing a public health achievement maintained for 26 years, as the country grapples with its largest outbreak in more than three decades.
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the Americas branch of the World Health Organization (WHO), declared measles endemic in the US, Bolivia, and Mexico on Tuesday after determining that the same strain of the virus had circulated continuously in each respective country for at least 12 months.
An international panel of experts that advises PAHO on the prevalence of measles and rubella “recommended that the measles elimination status be withdrawn,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, “a recommendation which I have accepted.”
Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000.
Countries that lost their measles-elimination status are required to submit a corrective action plan to PAHO in the coming weeks. PAHO said it will submit its recommendations to the countries in the next few days.
PAHO’s announcement follows a review of epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In a joint statement issued on Tuesday, the CDC said it remained committed to stopping measles outbreaks and regaining the country’s elimination status.
“The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Erica Schwartz said, adding that the agency would continue working to contain outbreaks.
The CDC said it has provided approximately $100m in additional funding to state and local health departments since August to strengthen vaccination efforts, surveillance and outbreak response.
The US has recorded approximately 7,700 measles infections since the beginning of 2025, according to CDC figures.
It is the highest number of cases the country has seen in more than 30 years. The climbing numbers come as vaccine hesitancy has grown under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has repeatedly cast doubt on the safety of vaccines despite scientific evidence to the contrary.
Before taking office, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.
To protect against illness, children are commonly given the measles vaccine in a combined shot with mumps and rubella vaccines, known by the acronym MMR.
But the vaccination rate among preschoolers in the US has fallen to about 92 percent, below the level experts say is needed to prevent major outbreaks.
As health secretary under US President Donald Trump, Kennedy has questioned the MMR vaccine’s ability to protect children.
He has suggested that the MMR’s effectiveness wanes by about 4.5 percent a year and said it contains “aborted fetus debris”, a claim experts have rejected as false.
The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths this year, but state health officials in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York have reported 10 deaths combined, a discrepancy that has fuelled tensions between federal and state health authorities over how measles fatalities are classified and counted.
Measles is considered highly infectious, and the WHO credits the virus with 95,000 deaths worldwide in 2024, mostly among children.
A reversal of decades of progress
Matt Ferrari, a biology professor and director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, believes the loss of the US’s measles elimination status can serve as a wake-up call for public health officials.
“This should be a humbling statement for the United States,” Ferrari told Al Jazeera.
For much of his career, Ferrari has studied strategies to control measles in countries around the world. The US was previously seen as a model.
“It was a motivating achievement that we use to drive support for measles elimination programmes all around the world,” said Ferrari. “Now we need to be looking for expertise elsewhere because we haven’t been pulling our weight.”
Edwin Asturias, a professor of paediatrics, infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, described the loss of status as a “stain” on the country’s public health programme.
“Measles cases are a signal that your immunisation programme and other systems within your public health services are having problems,” he told Al Jazeera.
Asturias said the US had the resources and experience to prevent the resurgence of the virus, pointing to its success in eliminating local measles transmission for more than a quarter of a century.
About 40 percent of current US measles cases are among adults older than 20, he said, highlighting the need to expand vaccination efforts.
Reaching these populations will require making vaccines available in workplaces, places of worship and other community settings, rather than relying solely on paediatricians and family doctors, Asturias explained.
The loss of elimination status also has implications beyond US borders, as measles can spread through international travel and migration.
“The United States is not, anymore, a place where you’re safe from measles,” Asturias told Al Jazeera. “If you’re a common person walking around with your children, you need to know now that measles has come to the country to stay unless something else is done.”
The risk is particularly concerning for unvaccinated people and those who cannot receive the vaccine, including those with weakened immune systems or undergoing cancer treatment.
What happens next?
Public health experts say the announcement should serve as a catalyst for a more extensive vaccination response.
While they do not expect PAHO’s announcement to prompt a significant change in federal policy, some hope it will spur action among state and local health departments.
Ferrari argued that the US should look to countries with experience containing measles outbreaks, including India, where community health workers visit households to identify children who may have missed vaccinations or whose families may be reluctant to vaccinate.
He also suggested that states may need to reconsider vaccination strategies, including whether to offer an earlier first or second dose to protect young children in areas where measles is circulating.
In the US, children are routinely given two doses of the MMR vaccine. The first dose is typically administered to children at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at four to six years, before they start school. Two doses are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles.
In countries where measles transmission is more widespread, the second MMR dose is often given between the ages of 18 and 24 months.
In June, Pennsylvania began recommending an additional early dose, called a “dose zero”, for infants aged six months and older in areas with sustained measles transmission. Ferrari said this is a perfect example of how states could adapt their approaches locally.
But the prospect of a broader shift in the federal response remains unlikely.
CDC Director Schwartz said last week the agency would continue “doing the same exact thing” in terms of its measles response, if the US lost its elimination status.
For Asturias, the federal response so far raises concerns about whether the country has the public health leadership needed to reverse the outbreak.
“This is hard to see happen,” he said. “But at the same time it is predictable when you don’t have experts running a public healthcare system.”

noticias.titulo: Trump announces critical minerals agreements at Quad meeting in Manila
noticias.resumen: US President Trump says the deals will prevent 'coercion by any single foreign supplier'.
noticias.texto:
Trump announces critical minerals agreements at Quad meeting in Manila
US President Trump said the deals would prevent ‘coercion by any single foreign supplier’.
United States President Donald Trump says that members of the Quad, a security grouping of the US and three Indo-Pacific countries, have reached agreements aimed at securing supply chains of critical minerals.
Trump met India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi – the other Quad leaders – in the Philippines on Thursday.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in remarks ahead of the meeting in Manila.
During the meeting, Trump said the agreements on critical minerals aimed to prevent “coercion by any single foreign supplier”. He did not single out China, which dominates global rare earth supplies.
Trump later said the US would have “everything we need” on rare earths in 10 months.
“We are making rare earth at a level that we’ve never made before. We’re going to catch them [China] within 10 months,” he said.
China last year imposed restrictions on exports of rare earths amid a trade dispute with the US. In June, the two sides agreed a deal aimed at restoring the US’s access to China’s rare earth supplies.
In a statement after the leaders’ meeting, the Quad expressed “grave concerns” about “economic coercion”, including through arbitrary export restrictions.
While the statement did not name any country, the US and Japan have complained about China’s restrictions on exports of rare earths vital to the manufacturing of everything from electric cars to mobile phones.
China has effectively shut off exports of key critical minerals to Japan for nearly a year as relations between Asia’s two largest economies have nosedived.
It was Trump’s first meeting of the Quad grouping – which his predecessor US President Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the meeting suggested the Quad grouping had a “functioning relationship”.
“Given the damage to the Quad during the Trump administration, including the instability caused by Trump’s tariffs on India, and India’s response by diversifying, the Quad meeting and statements like this give reassurance that there is still a functioning relationship,” Lucas said. “I’m not sure I’d call it an alliance, as I don’t think the Trump folks believe in alliances.”
Trump also joined a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila on the first day of a three-day trip to Asia.
After the Philippines, Trump will travel to China and attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, where he is expected to hold a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs says the talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.
Asked by reporters about a CNN report which claimed that US intelligence had determined Tehran was developing plans to use a so-called “dirty bomb” to target officials in the Trump administration, Trump said he was “looking into it”.
He said that if Iran posed an “imminent threat” to Washington, “they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before”.
He added that he “hoped” Iran did not pose a threat, but that he took such a scenario “very seriously” because “they happen to be crazy”.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghei said in a post on X that “Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations, including the recent claims published by The New York Times and the fabricated media narrative surrounding an alleged ‘dirty bomb’ propagated by CNN.”

noticias.titulo: Houthi advance on Aden may spur resurgence of Yemen’s southern separatists
noticias.resumen: Southern separatists try to regain power to defend Aden as Saudi Arabia reshuffles its military command against Houthis.
noticias.texto:
Houthi advance on Aden may spur resurgence of Yemen’s southern separatists
The Southern Transitional Council is trying to capitalise on recent Houthi military gains, emerging as a force to defend Yemen’s temporary capital, Aden.
A looming Houthi military threat to the Yemeni government’s de facto capital of Aden has increased the importance of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a southern secessionist movement, analysts have said.
The STC, which is believed to be supported by the United Arab Emirates, seeks an independent state for southern Yemen. An announcement that it had disbanded was made at the start of the year, following a Saudi-backed military campaign by Yemeni government forces against it. Other STC senior members declared the dissolution “null and void”, but the group had remained weakened in the months since.
However, following the sudden withdrawal of forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government from key positions on Yemen’s Red Sea coast this week, southern separatists now appear poised to gain more influence in the south.
With the Houthi group, also known as Ansar Allah, now 60km (37 miles) from the southern city, factions linked to the STC have stepped up to defend Aden from the Houthi advance.
Amr al-Bidh, a special representative for the STC president, has blamed the collapse of government forces on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September, as well as recent Houthi gains, on the government campaign against the southern separatists earlier this year.
“In January, the most effective anti-Houthi force in Yemen was taken apart by decisions in Riyadh, not by the Houthis,” al-Bidh told Al Jazeera.
STC leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi, who is believed to be based in the UAE and has maintained his distance from the Yemeni government, recently launched a mobilisation campaign across the south to prepare for the defence of Aden, Lahij and al-Dhalea.
Al-Bidh said that for the STC to stop the Houthi advance, it would require autonomy on the battlefield for its units.
“No front can be held for long when the people defending it have no say in how it is defended. What’s missing is a political decision to let southerners lead their own defence. We’re ready to put every capacity we have towards defending Aden,” al-Bidh said.
“We’ve always said the war will only end with a political solution that deals with the root of the conflict. That includes the right of the southern people to decide their own future. What won’t work is a deal made over the heads of southerners and signed by people who don’t represent them.”
Abdy Yeganeh, policy director for Independent Diplomat, said the STC could serve as a major bulwark against the Houthis during their current offensive.
“As a result of the January fallout between Saudi Arabia and the STC, the STC forces were weakened and undermined,” Yeganeh told Al Jazeera.
“Events in recent weeks have shown that despite attempts of marginalising the STC, they remain a credible local entity with significant popular support, with tens of thousands marching weekly across the south in their favour and with a capable military.”
Still divided
But military and strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab said that the STC remains politically divided and sections have become highly dependent on Saudi financial support.
“Without the support of the government and the support of Saudi Arabia, it cannot [repel the Houthis],” al-Dahab told Al Jazeera. “The capabilities of the Houthis have exceeded the combined capabilities of the government, let alone the [Southern] Transitional Council.”
The STC and Yemeni government forces have fought together against the Houthis, who captured Sanaa in September 2014. But relations between the two sides have also been fraught with differences, including clashes for control of positions and facilities in Aden and southern Yemen.
Following STC advances in southern Yemen in December 2025, the Saudi-led coalition, which has militarily supported the Yemeni government since March 2015, launched air strikes on an alleged UAE-linked weapons shipment to southern separatists. Al-Zubaidi fled Yemen, and some STC units came under the command of Saudi-backed forces. One of the most powerful forces affiliated with it, the Southern Giants Brigades, is now aligned with Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia’s King Salman issued a royal decree on Monday replacing Lieutenant General Fahd bin Hamad al-Salman with General Fayyad al-Ruwaili as the commander of its forces fighting the Houthis.
Al-Dahab said that appointing al-Ruwaili, Saudi Arabia’s chief of the general staff, to this role centralises decision-making in the face of a Houthi offensive.
“It gives the position greater power because whoever will assume command of the joint forces is the Saudi Chief of Staff,” al-Dahab said.
