noticias.titulo: Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know
noticias.resumen: A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington.
noticias.texto:
Is Iran plotting a ‘dirty bomb’ attack in the US? What we know
A CNN report quoting unnamed US officials alleges Tehran is developing plans for an attack on officials in Washington, DC.
CNN has reported that United States intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to target senior officials in President Donald Trump’s administration with a “dirty bomb” or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC. The broadcaster quotes seven unnamed US officials.
However, the report sets out no evidence to support the claims.
According to CNN, its sources described the planning as an effort by Tehran to give itself options, not as an imminent attack. One source said US intelligence had picked up Iranian “chatter” indicating that bomb-making materials had been stashed inside the US. That claim has not been independently verified.
The White House said it was “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time, there are no credible threats to the homeland”. Iran’s mission to the United Nations said Tehran “categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations”.
The report was released as talks to end the US-Israel war on Iran have stalled and Trump said last week that Washington does not “need” a deal. The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt has just arrived in the region, bringing the number of US carriers there to three and adding to fears of a renewed escalation.
So what is a dirty bomb? Could Iran build one? And how seriously should the latest claims be taken?
What is a ‘dirty bomb’?
A dirty bomb, technically known as a radiological dispersal device, combines conventional explosives, such as dynamite, with radioactive material. When the bomb explodes, the resulting blast scatters the radioactive material into the surrounding area.
Unlike a nuclear weapon, a dirty bomb does not need enriched uranium or a nuclear chain reaction. The radioactive material can come from medical or industrial equipment, such as machines used in hospitals and research facilities. That makes a dirty bomb far cheaper and easier to build than a nuclear device. It is also far less destructive.
The main health risk comes from breathing in contaminated dust near the blast. As the material spreads, it becomes less concentrated and less harmful. The damage depends on the size of the explosive charge, the type and amount of radioactive material and the weather, especially the wind.
According to the US National Academy of Sciences, most dirty bombs would immediately contaminate an area of one or two city blocks although wind could carry radioactive particles over a few square miles.
Experts said dirty bombs are unlikely to cause mass casualties. In testimony to the US Senate in 2002, Richard Meserve, then-chairman of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, estimated that deaths in most scenarios would be in the tens, not the hundreds or thousands.
“It’s important to understand that a dirty bomb isn’t an off-the-shelf nuclear bomb. There aren’t any mushroom clouds and massive shockwaves tearing down buildings and killing hundreds of thousands of people in the blink of an eye,” Talha Abdulrazaq, a researcher at the University of Exeter’s Strategy and Security Institute told Al Jazeera. “Instead, its primary effect would be psychological panic and hysteria in the target state alongside radioactive contamination, turning the area hit into a no-go zone.”
That is why experts call dirty bombs “weapons of mass disruption” rather than weapons of mass destruction.
Does Iran have the ability to build one?
In theory, yes. But so do many states and armed groups.
A dirty bomb is “really easy to make”, Scott Roecker, vice president for nuclear materials security at the Nuclear Threat Initiative, told Al Jazeera in 2022. Radioactive sources used in medicine and industry can be found in many countries and building a crude device does not require advanced technical knowledge.
Iran has a large civilian nuclear programme. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s last assessment, it held about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent as of June 2025.
In an April analysis for the European Council on Foreign Relations, Jacek Siewiera, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, wrote that although the stockpile falls short of what is needed for a nuclear weapon, it “could be extraordinarily dangerous from a radiological and sabotage perspective”. He warned that a dirty bomb could be “either a deliberate element of escalation or an unintended consequence of weakened central control” because international institutions no longer know who controls Iran’s nuclear storage sites.
But even enriched uranium is only weakly radioactive, which makes it a poor choice for a dirty bomb. Many analysts also argued that Tehran would be unlikely to waste material it spent decades producing.
A June 2025 analysis by Chris Kremidas-Courtney for the Euro-Atlantic Resilience Centre, a Bucharest-based think tank, reached a similar conclusion.
Iran is “widely believed to have access to sufficient radioactive material for use in dirty bombs, particularly from civilian nuclear and industrial sources”, he wrote. He pointed to isotopes such as caesium-137, used in cancer treatment, and cobalt-60, used in industrial radiography.
Kremidas-Courtney, however, described a dirty bomb as a possible “tool of last resort under extreme circumstances”. He also judged that the US “poses a high bar for direct infiltration” and ports and maritime chokepoints, such as the Strait of Hormuz, were more plausible targets.
Building a dirty bomb “is actually far easier than a conventional nuclear weapon” and does not require highly enriched uranium, Abdulrazaq said. Even after US strikes on the Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities, “a degraded capability doesn’t mean a destroyed capability,” he told Al Jazeera. “Iran certainly has access to all the components and expertise required to construct something as rudimentary as a dirty bomb.”
Iran “doesn’t have the missile or drone capability to strike US targets 10,000km [6,200 miles] and more away”, Abdulrazaq said. Therefore, any attack on Washington, DC, would almost certainly rely on clandestine smuggling networks or links to organised crime.
Even if Iran has the technical means, there is little public evidence that it has any ambition to build a dirty bomb, let alone set one off on US soil. Abdulrazaq said using a radiological weapon “would instantly destroy Iran’s remaining diplomatic credit” and would likely lead to an invasion and the collapse of its government.
“I highly doubt Iranian strategists are unaware of this reality, so the likelihood of a dirty bomb remains infinitesimally remote.”
How real is the threat?
According to CNN’s sources, US officials are divided on this point. One source said officials were debating whether Iran even had the personnel in place to carry out such an attack. The report also said there is no evidence that Tehran has decided to go ahead.
Iran does have a record of plotting against US officials. US prosecutors charged an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative in 2024 over an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Trump. But CNN noted that such plotting has mostly focused on opportunities to target officials while they travel abroad.
The latest report followed a series of US media stories about alleged Iranian plots. In October, the Axios news website and The New York Times reported on a memo from the director of national intelligence warning that Iranian plots against US personnel abroad had reached “advanced stages”. One official said some Iranian operatives may already be active inside the US. The memo did not identify specific targets or methods.
Critics said such reports, which often quote anonymous officials, risk building public support for escalation at a time when the war is deeply unpopular. In October, a Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey found that nearly 70 percent of respondents said the war was not worth fighting.
Iranian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei dismissed the CNN report as baseless. In a post on X, he suggested the claims were meant to frighten the public and build support for further hostile action against Iran.
Abdulrazaq noted that the claims came from “a US intelligence assessment rather than a direct threat made by Tehran”. “The Iraq war in 2003 and the lies surrounding Iraqi WMDs [weapons of mass destruction] is sufficient enough to doubt publicly communicated intelligence assessments in a wartime information environment,” he said.
He added that a dirty bomb attack would “hand-deliver the political rationale” for a major US war on Iran, including a ground invasion, with bipartisan support even after Democrats take control of Congress in January. “Iranian strategists aren’t stupid, and if I’m telling you this, they surely have made similar assessments, so I highly doubt the veracity of these intelligence reports,” he said.
Has the US gone to war on faulty intelligence before?
Yes. One example is Iraq.
Before the 2003 invasion, President George W Bush’s administration argued that Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction and links to al-Qaeda. In February 2003, Secretary of State Colin Powell made the US government’s case to the United Nations Security Council, including claims that Iraq had mobile biological weapons laboratories.
No stockpiles were found after the US-led invasion was carried out. In 2005, a presidential commission concluded that US intelligence on Iraq’s weapons had been “dead wrong”. Much of the case rested on unreliable sources, including an Iraqi defector codenamed “Curveball”, whose claims about mobile labs proved to be fabricated.
The media also came under scrutiny. In 2004, The New York Times published an editors’ note acknowledging that some of its pre-war coverage, much of it based on unnamed officials and Iraqi exiles, had not been as rigorous as it should have been.
Four decades earlier, two reported attacks on US destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin that the US government had said were unprovoked were used to justify a major US escalation in Vietnam. However, North Vietnam carried out the first attack in 1964 after US raids on its coast, and later evidence showed the second reported North Vietnamese attack two days later most likely never happened.
Have dirty bombs ever been used?
No successful dirty bomb attack has ever been recorded.
In 1995, Chechen fighters planted a container of radioactive caesium in Moscow’s Izmailovsky Park, but it never detonated. In 1998, a container of radioactive material rigged with explosives was discovered and defused near a railway line in Chechnya.
There have been other scares. In 2002, US authorities arrested Jose Padilla, an American accused of plotting a dirty bomb attack though he was never charged. In 2013, a truck carrying radioactive cobalt-60 from a hospital was stolen in Mexico, prompting UN warnings that the material could be used in a dirty bomb.
In 2022, Russia accused Ukraine of preparing to set off a dirty bomb and blame Moscow. Western governments dismissed the claim as “transparently false”.

noticias.titulo: US senators demand FAA pause upgrades linked to nationwide ground stop
noticias.resumen: Thousands of routers used in communications systems are slated to be replaced, raising the risk of more problems.
noticias.texto:
US senators demand FAA pause upgrades linked to nationwide ground stop
Thousands of routers used in communications systems are slated to be replaced, raising the risk of more problems.
A group of Democratic Senators has asked the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to pause its plan to replace thousands of routers until an investigation is completed into why one such upgrade caused a national ground stop last week.
“With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” the 13 senators wrote in a letter to the agency on Tuesday.
The FAA ordered all flights to remain grounded on Friday for about four hours, causing more than 10,000 flights to be cancelled and prompting ripple effects that continue to disrupt air travel in the US. It was only the second time the agency had issued such a sweeping order since the September 11, 2001 attacks.
The FAA said in a statement on Sunday that its initial investigation pointed to upgrades at two locations – a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas – as being the cause of the problem.
L3Harris, the agency’s network service provider, had been working to replace old copper wires with fibre-optic lines and to replace old routers with new ones made by Juniper Networks.
The FBI said on Tuesday that it was working with the Department of Transportation, the FAA, and L3Harris to investigate the incident, but had not taken possession of any equipment itself.
In their letter to the FAA, the group of senators asked the agency to halt plans to replace more than 3,000 additional routers.
“Based on information provided to our offices from L3Harris, the copper-to-fibre transition involves converting 3,648 routers to Juniper devices. To date, it is our understanding that 400 devices have been installed, and 69 are operational,” wrote the lawmakers from the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Maria Cantwell.
On Sunday, the FAA said the upgrades had started a long time ago.
“This type of work has been going on for years to transition from old copper wires that are being disconnected due to their obsolescence,” the FAA said on Sunday. The network became unstable, and data began flooding other equipment, causing problems with aircraft communications and radar feeds, leading the agency to order a halt to flights.
“I want the American people to know my number one job is to keep them safe,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy told ABC on Sunday. “So if we see these inconsistencies in the network, whether it’s communication with air traffic controllers and pilots, or with data feeds, we’re going to keep you safe.”
The White House has asked Congress for $50bn to complete an overhaul of the FAA’s technical infrastructure. Democratic lawmakers have said the administration was already authorised to use $12.5bn last year, but had only used a fraction of that so far.

noticias.titulo: Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate?
noticias.resumen: A rift has emerged in Trump’s cabinet over China’s access to advanced AI chips as export controls tighten.
noticias.texto:
Bessent vs Lutnick: Who is winning the China chip debate?
Trump avoids picking sides between feuding cabinet members, but US tightens chip restrictions on Beijing days before his summit with Xi.
A rift between United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over sales of advanced computer chips to China has spilled into public view.
On Monday, the administration of President Donald Trump introduced new rules requiring licences to sell advanced chips to buyers in named third countries suspected of being conduits to China. The new restrictions were written by Bessent’s Department of the Treasury and the White House – not Lutnick’s Department of Commerce, which usually oversees chip exports.
Trump, who is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, has so far not taken a side.
As the US reels from the resignation of chip maker Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang last week over revelations that he had an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, here’s what this all means.
What is this dispute about?
The two cabinet members, who are both veteran investors, disagree over how strictly the US should limit China’s access to the advanced chips that power artificial intelligence (AI).
The US restricts exports of certain advanced AI chips to China. In December 2025, Trump announced that Nvidia could sell its H200 chip to approved Chinese customers, on condition that 25 percent of the revenue would go to the US government. In January, the administration relaxed licensing rules for the H200 and similar chips.
On Monday, new controls were issued to monitor access to US chips in Southeast Asia and Brazil – penned by Bessent with the backing of the National Security Council, not by Lutnick.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick oversees these export controls and is charged with determining which critical technologies US companies can sell abroad, with an eye towards national security.
He has been one of the administration’s most vocal supporters of allowing Nvidia, the world’s dominant maker of AI super chips, to sell to China, despite the fact that it is racing against the US to dominate development of the AI industry.
“You want to sell the Chinese enough that their developers get addicted to the American technology stack,” Lutnick said in July 2025.
But US rules still bar the most advanced chips from being sold to China, and reports of restricted Nvidia chips allegedly being smuggled into the country through unofficial routes have put Lutnick’s role under the microscope.
Lutnick’s department was accused of turning a blind eye to such smuggling and stalling a planned crackdown on actors thought to be involved.
Fellow cabinet members and lawmakers have questioned his department’s handling of the issue, and some lawmakers say it has undermined US national security.
Bessent has pressed for tougher enforcement of existing export rules.
“We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented,” he said on Friday.
The two men have been rivals for some time. In 2024, Elon Musk and other Trump allies lobbied for Lutnick to get the Treasury job, but it ultimately went to Bessent.
What happened at Nvidia?
Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for the most advanced chips used for AI. Worth trillions of dollars, it is among the world’s most valuable companies, and its customers include tech giants Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta.
Nvidia’s cofounder and chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, whom some US officials have suspected of working for Chinese intelligence – a claim denied by China.
Alice Huang is a former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that builds data centres in Southeast Asia which cater for Chinese clients.
Megaspeed bought more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips in about two years, but US authorities suspect that many of these chips were then smuggled into China rather than used in Megaspeed’s data centres, a charge it denies.
On Friday, Bessent said four government agencies, including the Treasury, had pushed for months to put Megaspeed on a US trade blacklist, but Lutnick’s Commerce Department had not acted.
“Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
He also questioned whether Nvidia had properly vetted its customers.
“The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said.
What are the new rules?
The new rules require companies to obtain a US licence before shipping advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries Washington suspects of acting as conduit routes for chips to reach China.
It also requires any data centre in the world using Nvidia chips to obtain Washington’s permission before it can “rent” computer power to Chinese customers. This closes a loophole that previously allowed Chinese companies to “rent” the use of advanced chips without purchasing them outright.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the restrictions as “economic coercion” and said Beijing would take “necessary measures” in response.
In Washington, the new restrictions were welcomed by John Moolenaar, the Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China.
The committee, a panel of lawmakers focused on competition with China’s ruling Communist Party, is one of the most hawkish voices on Beijing in Congress. Moolenaar criticised the administration’s decision last year to ease curbs on Nvidia’s chip sales to China.
“Our most advanced AI chips are simply not for sale to our foremost enemy,” he said.
Who else has weighed in on the row?
Senior officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have argued for keeping the most advanced chips out of China, while lawmakers from both parties have criticised Lutnick.
“It would be dumb and stupid for us to sell that to anybody, especially a country that’s going to reverse-engineer it and leapfrog us,” Rubio said in May.
Greer made a similar case last week, saying that US “crown jewels” should remain in US hands or in the hands of allies.
David Sacks, Trump’s former AI adviser, however, defended selling chips to China and dismissed those pushing for tighter controls.
“The policy of the China hawks is effectively the policy of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party]. Neither one wants American chips in China,” he said in a podcast appearance on Saturday.
On the other side of the political aisle, some Democrats have called for Lutnick to step down from his position for his failure to police chip smuggling.
“Making powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security and economic competitiveness,” Senator Richard Blumenthal said in a post on X.
Both Lutnick and Jensen Huang have been summoned to testify before the Senate on December 3.
Where does Trump stand?
Trump has swung between restricting and allowing Nvidia’s sales to China. In April 2025, the White House curbed sales of the H20, a chip Nvidia made for the Chinese market – only to agree to allow them three months later.
His later decision in December to permit sales of the more powerful H200 marked a further easing of those restrictions.
Trump has stood by Lutnick, saying on Monday that he was not planning to remove him, days after the Reuters news agency reported that top White House aides had debated whether he should go.
Trump has acknowledged that the issue is splitting his cabinet, without explicitly taking sides.
“It’s a different viewpoint. One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Trump said. “They both are acceptable, but they are different views.”
Trump has also said it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia.
Trump and Xi are due to meet in Shenzhen on Thursday, during this week’s APEC summit. Ahead of their last meeting, when Xi visited the US in September, Washington banned imports of Chinese-made humanoid robots and threatened to sanction Chinese AI firms.

noticias.titulo: Ghost Towns of Afghanistan: The Environmental Toll of Decades of War
noticias.resumen: A father confronts the aftermath of environmental damage from years of war in Afghanistan.
noticias.texto:
Witness
Ghost Towns of Afghanistan: The Environmental Toll of Decades of War
A father confronts the aftermath of environmental damage from years of war in Afghanistan.
Ibrahim, a father living in Kabul, returns to his home in Nangarhar province on Afghanistan’s eastern border with Pakistan to revisit a place transformed by war, displacement and environmental damage. The village where he grew up now lies in ruins while the families who remain there face health problems they believe are linked to contamination from decades of conflict.
As Ibrahim explores the destruction and meets affected families, he reflects on his own family, the life they might have had if he had stayed and whether they could ever return home.
Ghost Towns of Afghanistan is a documentary film by Matty Feurtado and Ibrahim Sulemen Khel.
Published On 17 Nov 2026

noticias.titulo: UK sanctions eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements
noticias.resumen: Settler group also sanctioned for blocking Gaza aid as foreign secretary calls for 'protecting the two-state solution'.
noticias.texto:
UK sanctions eight Israeli construction firms over West Bank settlements
Settler group also sanctioned for blocking Gaza aid as foreign secretary calls for ‘protecting the two-state solution’.
The government of the United Kingdom has imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and a settler group blocking aid to Gaza.
The companies affected in Tuesday’s asset freezes include Har Hevron Development Company Ltd, Hemdat Shomron Ltd and SAG (Velvel) Construction and Development Ltd, which construct and develop homes in West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.
The measures were announced shortly before the final deadlines for the tenders for E1, a settlement project that would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from occupied East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of an independent state.
“Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this Government’s approach,” British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement. “That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.”
The government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, a group it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks from delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.
Reporting from London, Al Jazeera’s Jonah Hull said the sanctions on Tzav 9 come after the UK’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office has noted that thousands of families in Gaza are in dire need of aid after “catastrophic” floods.
Britain’s relationship with Israel has deteriorated significantly over the past three years because of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza as well as the Israeli government’s plans to expand settlements in the West Bank.
Israel in September threatened to close the British consulate building in East Jerusalem in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements.
British and Israeli diplomats last month reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure.
Attacks in West Bank continue
Meanwhile on Tuesday, Israeli forces carried out a series of raids and arrests in the West Bank, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
A Palestinian woman was killed in an attack on Monday night by Israeli settlers firing live ammunition at Palestinians in the area of the village of Ein ad-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho governorate, according to medical sources.
The Jericho Governmental Hospital reported that 10 Palestinians were injured by the settlers’ gunfire, including an elderly man.
Israeli soldiers also raided the Jalazone refugee camp and arrested two people in addition to arresting another person from el-Bireh after searching a home.
Troops also stormed Nablus, Tubas and the villages of Khallet al-Louza and Beit Falouh in Bethlehem governorate, raiding homes and shops and firing tear gas.

noticias.titulo: At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
noticias.resumen: Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs as students and teachers say little has improved.
noticias.texto:
At the origin of France’s education protests, students refuse to give up
Blockades continue at some schools in the Parisian suburbs, as students and teachers say little has improved in their classrooms.
Paris, France – On a cold, rainy morning in early November, students and teachers met outside the locked gates of Paul Eluard, a high school in Saint-Denis north of Paris. Some were wearing costumes. For 17-year-old Kamelia, dressing as a dinosaur helped her to maintain the joy and hope that coexisted with the anger driving the student movement in mid-September.
“Costumes are the fun part. They show that it’s not all about violence. There’s also good cheer and fun in all of this,” Kamelia told Al Jazeera. “Today there are huge protests all over France, and it’s very important. I got up early, and even though I’m a little tired, I came anyway.”
Four days after students at Paul Eluard returned from a mid-term break, they joined a national strike on November 5. Nearby, students from the trade school Bartholdi had blockaded the gates of their school. Although the size of the student protests peaked in early October, many young people, especially in the suburbs, are refusing to return to the classroom until some of their demands are met.
“Sometimes, we see rats in the courtyard and in the restrooms. The restrooms are a mess. We don’t have enough water; it flows very slowly. We don’t have enough to drink, and the restrooms are dirty. The hallways are dirty, the classrooms are dirty, and there are cockroaches,” 17-year-old Nohlan, a student at Bartholdi, told Al Jazeera outside the school’s blockade.
The movement started at a high school in Creteil, a suburb southeast of Paris in the Val-de-Marne region, on September 17, and rapidly spread to Saint-Denis, then the rest of France. Students blocked the entrances to their schools to protest poor classroom conditions and took to the streets.
“The movement started in the suburbs, then Paris followed suit. Now the whole world is watching us,” Kamelia said. “[In Saint-Denis], we’re basically ignored, even though we’re part of this country. But we’re here, and we are the future of this country.”
By the end of September, an estimated 400 schools across France, including some universities, had joined the student movement. Protests on October 17 in Paris saw an estimated 550,000 participants, according to the interior minister, while organisers put the number at 800,000.
Although this is not the first time in recent years that students in working-class suburbs have protested against school conditions, the scale of this year’s movement has been remarkable.
“It really started to gain momentum, and when everyone started to get involved, it was incredible. It really moved me because last year, we set up a few blockades, but no one heard about them,” Kamelia said.
Although students are at the heart of the movement, many teachers have since joined, expressing solidarity with their students and deploring the conditions under which they have to teach.
High school students are setting the pace for the movement, said Lucie Sabze, an English teacher at Paul Eluard.
“I’m impressed by the students, their demands and their political discourse, which is very lucid and very clear,” she told Al Jazeera. “I think the scale of the movement can be explained by a growing frustration.”
Teachers at Eluard are celebrating one “victory”. They had been calling for the resignation of the head teacher, who they accused of letting an officer from France’s notoriously violent motorised antiterrorism brigade into the school to arrest a student.
On Sunday, a government agency announced Xavier Artaud had stepped down “as a safety precaution”.
“Given the unacceptable public accusations made against the high school principal by name, he requested protective measures requiring his removal from the Saint-Denis area,” said the Academic Director of National Education Services.
Bruno Gbalou, an English teacher at neighbouring Bartholdi, noted that conditions have only deteriorated in recent years.
“It’s been about 15 years since I came back from England and started teaching here, and things have only gotten worse. So there are more students, but we have fewer resources,” Bruno Gbalou told Al Jazeera. “It’s not fair to the students, and it’s not fair to us, and that’s one of the reasons why we’re going on strike.”
In a statement to the media in early October, President Emmanuel Macron said the government planned to respond to students’ demands “in the most concrete way possible”.
“I understand the anxieties, sometimes the anger, that our youth can have, whether about the climate, technological changes or geopolitical situations,” Macron said.
But the students who spoke to Al Jazeera said they do not believe the government has offered them real solutions. The November blockade at Bartholdi in Saint-Denis was in response to a lack of solutions, said student Nohlan.
“There’s still no change. We’re hoping for change, but we’re waiting, and waiting,” he said.
Louis Boyard, a member of the French National Assembly for Val-de-Marne, the administrative area where the protest movement started, explained that the government’s policies have significantly reduced educational resources.
“Macron pursued a policy of austerity, and as a result, he gradually dismantled public education while providing massive subsidies to the private sector because he supports private education over public education,” Boyard told Al Jazeera. “Macron thinks that by sweeping the problem under the rug, people will just go home. That’s not true. The people speaking out can’t really afford to eat any more. One in three French people are skipping meals. People – young people – have gone too far in this movement to back down now.”
The left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, whose leader Jean-Luc Melenchon is currently polling about 20 percent in France’s upcoming presidential elections, has been accused of weaponising the student movement for political gain. But Boyard insisted that the movement was organic, and that LFI had simply followed because the party is “always on the side of those who fight”.
“Whenever there’s a struggle led by young people, I participate because I believe that young people have every right to get involved and fight,” Boyard said. “The movement took off because all the high school students looked at each other and said: ‘We’re not being respected. So we’re going to make sure we’re respected’.”
When he was a high school student, Boyard participated in a blockade, prompted by an asbestos problem, in 2018. Thanks to the protests, the students were able to get the school rebuilt.
“I’ve already won a victory this way, and we were justified in doing it. [The current students], too, are justified in doing it,” Boyard said.
As she inflated her dinosaur costume to join the protests in the centre of Paris, Kamelia wanted to send a message of hope.
“Everyone is rising up – all the young people. We’re a generation who’s truly awakened. It makes me so happy,” she said.

noticias.titulo: Infantino’s FIFA challenger Diallo claims to have support beyond Europe
noticias.resumen: French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received 'spontaneous signs of strong support' against Infantino.
noticias.texto:
Infantino’s FIFA challenger Diallo claims to have support beyond Europe
French football chief Philippe Diallo says he has received ‘spontaneous signs of strong support’ against Infantino.
French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo says he has the backing of countries beyond Europe in his bid to depose Gianni Infantino in the upcoming FIFA presidential election.
“To beat him you need 106 votes, which is a majority,” Diallo said on Tuesday following his nomination as the European governing body UEFA’s representative.
“It is now up to me and my team to go and convince those on other continents, but already since yesterday I have received spontaneous signs of strong support which will be revealed in the coming days.”
Diallo was speaking in Paris the day after accepting an invitation from UEFA to stand against Infantino in the election to be held next March.
UEFA, which has 55 member associations, said that European nations had “unanimously pledged their full support” to Diallo, ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for candidates to declare themselves.
Under its Slovenian president Aleksander Ceferin, UEFA has led the opposition to Infantino since his plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors was revealed in July.
Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of widespread uproar, but UEFA has since gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the current FIFA president in Switzerland.
Diallo announced in September that the French Football Federation (FFF) was withdrawing its backing for Infantino in the election, following similar announcements from other European associations. At the time he said that “the trust placed in the FIFA president has been betrayed”.
‘Open governance’
“There can no longer be a type of single-handed governance where the biggest issues in football are decided behind the scenes, without any transparency and without anyone being consulted, without going through the executive committee,” Diallo, 63, said on Tuesday.
“My vision will be one of open, collegiate governance, in which the different bodies really play their part.”
Diallo, the 63-year-old son of a Senegalese boxing champion, has been president of the FFF since January 2023.
UEFA had been struggling to find a credible candidate to stand against Infantino in the election, which will take place at the FIFA Congress on March 18 next year in the Moroccan capital, Rabat.
Arsene Wenger, the French former Arsenal manager and FIFA’s current chief of global football development, had at one point been seen as a potential candidate who could get Europe’s backing, but he will not stand.
FIFA has a total of 211 member associations, with each having one vote in the presidential election. A majority is needed for a candidate to win.

noticias.titulo: Costa Rican journalist shot dead in first such killing in 25 years
noticias.resumen: Camilo Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said. The first known killing of a journalist ⁠in Costa Rica in ⁠25 years, ​Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long ⁠being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodriguez, who gained prominence for publishing allegations against suspected drug traffickers and politicians, was shot dead on Monday, authorities said.
The first known killing of a journalist in Costa Rica in 25 years, Rodriguez’s death comes as the country grapples with a surge in drug violence driven by international trafficking groups, despite long being regarded as one of Central America’s most peaceful and stable democracies.
Rodriguez, 51, was attacked at about 3.20pm local time amid heavy traffic on a main highway on the outskirts of the capital San Jose, the Red Cross reported.
President Laura Fernandez condemned the attack in a video message.
“I am filled with indignation and outrage over the cowardly murder of communicator Camilo Rodriguez. Regardless of the content of his communications, what happened today in our country is a stain on freedom of expression,” Fernandez said.
Attorney general Carlo Diaz told local news outlet Extra Noticias that investigators found multiple bullet impacts and a crime scene resembling a contract killing, likely linked to the allegations Rodriguez had published. He gave no further evidence and did not name suspects.
“We know he was a communicator who publicly identified people for alleged links to drug trafficking,” Diaz said, adding that Rodriguez had previously reported threats but had declined protection.
“Silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society.“
Diaz pledged efforts to hold those responsible for the murder accountable.
The last such attack on a media worker happened in July 2001 when radio producer Parmenio Medina was gunned down on a Santo Domingo highway, in roughly the same area as Rodriguez’s attack took place.
Costa Rica’s homicide rate doubled between 2013 and 2023 and has only eased slightly since then.

Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang will testify before several congressional committees on 1 December, setting the stage for a high-stakes hearing in the wake of his resignation following an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, has also agreed to appear for a closed-door transcribed interview the following day, 2 December.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” Congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, who chair the committees, said in a press release. “The American people need answers on Mr Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous [People’s Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal.”
The three congressmen chair the foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the intelligence committee of the House of Representatives, respectively. On 12 November, they had signed a letter warning Huang that he could face a subpoena if he did not agree to the closed-door meeting.
Nvidia chips are key to powering the artificial intelligence boom. The Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO after allegations of extramarital relationships with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees surfaced.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been Megaspeed International’s executive director. The Singapore-based cloud computing company has bought nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. The company said Alice Huang stepped down in 2025.
Megaspeed ultimately facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of US export controls. On Friday, Malaysia stated that they were investigating whether the company diverted advanced AI ships to other countries.
A recent joint Department of Commerce and Department of Justice letter, stated that the Department of Commerce, under Secretary Howard Lutnick, first started an investigation in Megaspeed on 2024 for potential export control violations. The justice department, led by Attorney General Todd Blanche, took over in 2025.
In his first remarks since his resignation, Jensen Huang said on Thursday he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO. Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley tech giants, along with 165,000 signatories to an open letter, have called for his reinstatement. Trump has also signaled his openness for the disgraced tech CEO’s return.

noticias.titulo: Hi-tech Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit
noticias.resumen: Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
In a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit, meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

noticias.titulo: Paul Kelly pleads for Albanese to ‘show some backbone’ over AI as creatives campaign for copyright protections
noticias.resumen: Music legend is joined by Jimmy Barnes and Peter Garrett in backing Not AI’s To Take campaign ahead of Aria awards Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s creative community has launched a major campaign pleading with the Albanese government not to water down copyright law amid furious lobbying from AI companies, ahead of Wednesday night’s Aria awards. noticias.texto:
Australia’s creative community has launched a major campaign pleading with the Albanese government not to water down copyright law amid furious lobbying from AI companies, ahead of Wednesday night’s Aria awards.
Music legends Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly and Peter Garrett are among those backing the Not AI’s To Take campaign, supported by dozens of creative groups representing the recording, writing, publishing, film, television and media industries.
While the government maintains it will not undermine copyright law, the industry minister, Tim Ayres, said on Tuesday “the status quo is no good” for the creative sector, ahead of a package of AI legislation expected by early 2027.
But creatives have pushed back on such claims, arguing copyright law doesn’t need updating – just better enforcement, and that changes could put the $70bn creative industry and its 600,000 workers at risk.
“[AI platforms] haven’t made one phone call yet. They haven’t called us. They haven’t called anybody,” said Dean Ormston, CEO of music rights organisation Apra Amcos.
“There’s nothing wrong with the copyright framework. The problem is getting somebody to sit at the table and have a discussion with us.”
Not AI’s To Take is backed by the likes of Aria, the Copyright Agency, the Australian Directors’ Guild, Screen Producers Australia, the Australian Society of Authors, the Australian Writers’ Guild, and media organisations including Foxtel, Free TV, Nine, Seven and Guardian Australia.
Australian musicians including Montaigne and KLP have backed the campaign online, while Guardian Australia understands Barnes, Kelly and Garrett – some of Anthony Albanese’s favourite musicians – will also feature.
“Our government has been a huge supporter of Australian music and creativity, and now we’re asking them to continue that support by standing firm on copyright and making sure big tech doesn’t get to rewrite the rules at the expense of creators,” said KLP, real name Kristy Lee Peters.
In quotes shared on the campaign’s website, Barnes said: “I think that these companies should go and f..k themselves.”
Kelly is quoted as saying: “Australia has had some of the best copyright laws, something to be proud of. Now is the time for our government to show some backbone.”
Although Albanese has declared it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, some AI companies have argued it is too difficult to make individual licensing deals under existing copyright law. AI companies have said they need legal certainty on the copyright issue before investing and training models in Australia, with Anthropic putting forward an “opt-out” model to scrape creative works unless a rightsholder objected.
However Anthropic told a Senate committee it would “provide ongoing access to frontier models to eligible Australian entities, regardless of whether training is permitted.”
The government is expected to unveil a long-awaited legislative package on AI in late 2026 or early 2027, with proposals around datacentres, online safety, productivity and copyright. Albanese said last week that artists “need to be compensated if their work is used”. But the creative community is concerned that lobbying from big tech may sway government decisions.
“This isn’t a smear campaign. We’re just making some noise out in the open, where tech companies are doing it in the shadows,” said Patrizia Di Biase-Dyson, CEO of the Australian Publishers Association.
“Everything is at stake. We have to do as much as possible to educate everyone.”
Ormston said creative industries welcomed the investment and opportunities of AI, and had applauded both Labor’s rebuffing of a text and data mining exemption and Albanese’s public support. But he said artists were worried about potential changes.
“Our very clear message to the government has been: hold firm. You are absolutely saying the right thing. You are absolutely right in the fact that while we want AI in this country, we want it on Australia’s terms,” Ormston said.
Asked about the campaign on Tuesday, Ayres said “nothing has changed in terms of the government’s approach” to copyright.
“I understand the anxiety, though. For those workers, the status quo is no good for them. Their work is currently being appropriated, today, offshore. We have set out a program for a scheme of legislation that would protect those rights, make sure that artificial intelligence investment in Australia is on Australia’s terms.
“We’re not about undermining copyright here. That commitment has been made so many times now.”
A spokesperson for the attorney general, Michelle Rowland, said the government was “committed to supporting” creatives, and pledged any copyright changes would “deliver meaningful control and fair compensation”.
But independent senator David Pocock urged caution around any moves, warning that copyright changes could create a legal “loophole” to make Australia a global “data laundering hotspot”.
“There are more than 100 court cases on foot involving copyright and AI training in the US and we should wait for these to play out before making any changes given the risks of getting it wrong are so high,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Chris Minns’ backflips are adding up. Is he ‘clearing the runway’ or panicking?

noticias.texto:
If recent coverage is to be believed, the New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, is a talented gymnast. A last-minute intervention by the premier on Monday afternoon, the day before a suite of reforms on underquoting were due to take effect, marks a quadruple or quintuple policy “backflip” by Minns in recent weeks, depending on who you ask.
The laws banning real estate agents from lowering the advertised price of a property beneath a previously rejected written offer have been shelved for up to a year, after the premier flagged on Monday morning he had received concerns from estate agents in his own electorate about their effect amid a housing market downturn.
The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said the move was “government by 2GB”, referencing the Sydney talkback radio station which had also raised the issue on Monday morning.
“But this isn’t the first time” she told presenter Ben Fordham on Tuesday.
First, the government backed down last month from implementing changes to several local and regional rail line timetables after criticism from commuters.
Next, after a social media post by Sloane, it changed gender-neutral language of “carer” and “lactating parents” in a new parliamentary breastfeeding policy to reflect what Minns said was “commonsense language like ‘mother’ and ‘breastfeeding’”.
After the Daily Telegraph ran a “Nup to the Cup” campaign against plastics legislation, which included requiring cafes to offer dine-in customers mugs and glasses instead of takeaway cups, the government dropped the changes, which would not have been implemented until 2028.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
This weekend, it made an election promise of a two-year funding guarantee for community preschools after the opposition had warned the sector was facing a $150m annual cut from January.
But Eamonn Fitzpatrick, a lobbyist and former communications and campaign advisor to federal and state Labor governments, says the reversals are more about “clear air” than pre-campaign jitters as the government enters the final sitting days before the March election.
“That is the job of this final sitting week, let’s not forget you go into summer. It’s a dead period,” says Fitzpatrick, who worked alongside Minns in the office of former Labor premier Morris Iemma.
“What you’re seeking to do, actually, in either putting things on hold, changing your minds, revising policies, you’re actually just minimising distraction … clearing the runway.”
Fitzpatrick says interventions are part of Minns’ brand as a strong leader, but insists his style is no more top-down than previous premiers.
Minns has consistently polled ahead of Sloane as preferred premier but he has made no secret about the threat from One Nation, whom he and his ministers have started to refer to as the state’s unofficial opposition.
Peter Lewis, the non-executive chair of strategic communications company Essential, which undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election, said recent polling suggested voting intention in November in NSW was at 27% for Labor, 26% for One Nation and 23% for the Coalition.
Lewis says he thinks the threat of One Nation in NSW is being “used to push the political debate towards the right and could be used as an excuse for the government not to embrace more progressive policies”.
“I wonder if there is a bit of a mistake in that. One Nation voters are being driven by dissatisfaction with the status quo and so governments that are seen as actually addressing issues probably have a better case to answer.”
Defending its underquoting backflip, Labor has said it is protecting buyers from being shut out of sales at lower prices amid a downturn which has seen home values in Sydney drop by 10.1% from their 2026 peak, according to data from Cotality.
In question time, the fair trading minister, Anoulack Chanthivong, whose department was responsible for the reforms and who has now been overruled for a third time by Minns on policy, said the market had changed and the government had responded.
Both he and Minns pointed out that Sloane and the opposition had supported the underquoting laws at the time, which were conceived for a “rising hot market”.
But, Lewis says “there is a cost in being seen to change a position” – and points to Peter Dutton’s 2025 federal election campaign as an example.
“Maybe Minns has done this early enough in the cycle for it not to be an issue, but as you get close to the election it changes, particularly when they’re walking back commitments that have been made to benefit people.
“It can be read as panic.”

noticias.titulo: Australia’s gender pay gap falls below 20% for first time
noticias.resumen: Men still dominate top-paid positions but businesses’ ‘deliberate’ decisions have narrowed gap, workplace gender equality agency report finds Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian women earn 80c for every $1 men earn, on average, after Australia’s gender pay gap fell below 20% for the first time in 2025-26. The workplace gender equality agency’s (WGEA) report on Wednesday showed men still dominated top-paid positions but businesses’ decisions have narrowed the gap. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Australian women earn 80c for every $1 men earn, on average, after Australia’s gender pay gap fell below 20% for the first time in 2025-26.
The workplace gender equality agency’s (WGEA) report on Wednesday showed men still dominated top-paid positions but businesses’ decisions have narrowed the gap.
WGEA chief Christine Castley said most Australian employers were ignoring backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and improving their hiring and promotion to ensure women reached senior positions.
“Employers are actually thinking in a very deliberate way about what’s going on with workplace gender equality and then taking action,” Castley told Guardian Australia.
The overall WGEA pay gap was 19.7% for the year, with the 2025-26 survey including federal government public sector employers for the first time.
The figure has improved significantly in the last decade, from 26.3% in 2015-16. Coverage has also increased, now covering more than 6m employees across 9,096 employers.
The private sector’s pay gap fell from 21.1% last year to 20.3% this year, as women accounted for a growing share of full-time management and leadership roles.
Bigger pay rises in female-dominated industries, including retail, aged care and childcare, also helped narrow the gap.
However, women-dominated industries and occupations were still typically paid less than those dominated by men. The average woman still earned $27,467 less per year than the average man, WGEA found.
The survey accounted not only for wages but all earnings, including penalty rates, superannuation, bonuses and overtime. Average total remuneration in the survey was $125,568.
The overall distribution of pay did not improve from 2024-25. Women make up about half of Australia’s workforce but men remained overrepresented in the highest-paid positions.
Every level of management was dominated by men, WGEA found. The disparity was greatest at the chief executive level, where three in four CEOs were men and the gender pay gap widened to 27.6%.
Women accounted for just 36% of employees in the top pay quartile in the private sector. In the commonwealth public sector, women’s representation in the top quartile was 46% and the gender pay gap was just 7.8%.
Promotion rates are similar between genders but women are less represented at higher levels, likely because they resign or take time off for care and domestic responsibilities, previous WGEA work has found.
Wednesday’s report found just 7% of manager roles are part-time, but 29% of women work part-time compared with 12% of men. WGEA called for workplaces to redesign roles to allow more part-time work.
In the financial services sector, which has the worst pay gap at 26.7%, men would be more likely to be promoted or get bonuses as they took on more visible work, Castley said.
“[It’s] the person who can attend the client functions [and] can be available 24/7, the person who’s most visible to the leadership of the organisation, versus, perhaps, the person [doing] the work that’s behind the scenes,” Castley said.
Superannuation provider Rest was an outlier in the finance industry. Its pay gap has fallen to 9.4%, from 20.1% in 2022.
Rest’s chief people officer, Amy Murrell, said the improvements had been helped by extending paid parental leave to all permanent staff, regardless of gender, time of arrival or primary or secondary carer classification.
“It’s not going to happen naturally,” Murrell said. “I think you have to prioritise it for it to make sense.”
The firm had also increased representation after setting targets for at least 40% of employees to be women and 40% men at every level of its business, from its board to its investment team.
Castley said some Australian business leaders had taken on an “anti-DEI” narrative, amid global backlash to diversity, equity and inclusion measures, but most businesses were “getting on with the job”.
WGEA asked businesses to set new targets for the first time in 2026. The most popular goals included improving gender balance at junior and managerial levels and consulting employees on gender equality efforts.
“These are the real issues that need to be tackled … and it’s actually very reassuring that those are the targets that employers have picked because it demonstrates, I think, a very real commitment to actually taking action,” Castley said.

noticias.titulo: Voldemort, Gotham City and the Greens: Victorian election gets a jolt of life as leaders face off in sole debate
noticias.resumen: Ben Carroll, Jess Wilson, Ellen Sandell and Warren Pickering grilled by undecided voters – and each other – as state prepares to head to the polls For a brief moment on Tuesday night, the Victorian election looked like it might actually get interesting. Two weeks into the offical campaign, with early voting opening on Wednesday, the contest has been pretty short on excitement. The Labor government has continued to slide in the polls , while the Coalition opposition has largely been focused on not getting in its own way for long enough to cruise to victory. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
For a brief moment on Tuesday night, the Victorian election looked like it might actually get interesting.
Two weeks into the offical campaign, with early voting opening on Wednesday, the contest has been pretty short on excitement. The Labor government has continued to slide in the polls, while the Coalition opposition has largely been focused on not getting in its own way for long enough to cruise to victory.
But the only debate of the campaign offered a welcome jolt of life. Dubbed the “People’s Forum” by hosts News24 and the Herald Sun, Tuesday evening’s showdown delivered a few moments of political theatre.
There was the moment the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, mocked the premier, Ben Carroll, for refusing to say the names of his predecessors, Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, telling the Labor leader they’re “not Voldemort”.
“I can say their name just as you can say Jeff Kennett’s name,” Carroll responded.
“Jeff Kennett,” Wilson immediately retorted.
(For all the back-and-forth, Carroll never did say their names).
Or Wilson’s apparent “Julia Gillard moment”, according to the Herald Sun, when she told Carroll she “would not be lectured” by him on the costings of her policies. The premier had claimed the Liberal plans didn’t “stack up” and would require cuts to healthcare funding to pay down debt.
“I like to see these scare campaigns that you run,” Wilson said. “But Ben, I won’t be lectured by you or your government on costings when you have racked up $200bn worth of debt in this state.”
Then there was One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, who said the state resembled “Gotham City” because of rising crime and vowed to lock up more offenders – even if that meant sending them interstate.
“I don’t give a damn if our prisons are full. You’ve broken the law. You’re going to jail. They’re bringing in a supermax in New South Wales. That’s where you’re bloody going,” he said.
The only person to receive rousing applause was Billy, a bearded schoolteacher who asked how the leaders planned to rebuild trust in politics when, as he put it: “Nobody believes a word you say any more – and it’s fundamental. No fun, and mostly mental.”
But many of the night’s most memorable moments came courtesy of Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, whose late inclusion on the panel followed a stoush between Carroll and Wilson over whether Pickering should be invited.
“Having four of us on the stage tonight tells you everything about how politics is changing,” Sandell told the 100 undecided voters gathered at the Sofitel in Melbourne.
In her green blazer, and unmistakably in enemy territory, Sandell spoke authentically and was the only leader willing to take all three other parties to task: Labor over donations from the gambling industry, the Liberals over money from property developers and One Nation for its links to billionaire Gina Rinehart, who she said is “writing [their] policy”.
“If you’re wondering why you can’t afford your groceries or your rent or to buy a home, just look at who is funding these three other parties,” Sandell said.
When offered the opportunity to ask any other leader a question, Sandell asked Carroll how he can claim to fight for working people given cuts to the public sector and fights with health workers, teachers, council workers and firefighters over wages.
She also engaged in a back and forth with Wilson on several issues. Asked whether she would possibly support the Liberals with confidence and supply in the event of a hung parliament, she said the Greens values were “quite far apart” from the Coalition’s: “Jess Wilson wants to rip up treaty. She wants to rip up renewable energy. She wants to make sigfniciant cuts to public service.”
Wilson relied on an often repeated line that treaty “goes far further than what the voice [to parliament] ever did” and “undermines our parliament”.
Sandell’s response: “You know that’s not true though, you can’t lie to the Victorian people like that.”
The pair also clashed over pro-Palestinian protests in Melbourne’s CBD, with Sandell defending the right to “peaceful protest”.
“There is a very clear difference between antisemitism, which is unacceptable, and actually standing up and calling out war crimes that are happening by the government of Israel,” she said.
Wilson responded: “At these protests, we have seen people throw rocks at police officers. That is not a peaceful protest.
Sandell responded that existing laws already dealt with such incidents and argued that protest permits were not the answer.
“Politicians shouldn’t be the ones deciding who gets to protest,” she said. “That is an authoritarian government move, and we do not want that.”
Pickering agreed with Sandell and said politicians should not be deciding who gets to protest. He described One Nation as a “flagbearer” for the principles of democracy, including freedom of speech.
“I don’t necessarily think the permits are the way to go,” he said.
Wilson, who holds a comfortable lead in the polls, arguably had the most to lose from the debate but held her own. She largely avoided taking the bait from the other leaders, including Pickering, who during his turn to ask a question, tried to pressure her on the Coalition’s position on legislated net zero targets. Wilson stuck to her line that she was governed by “practicality” and “not ideology”.
She was less definitive on the Suburban Rail Loop, leaving open the possibility of scrapping the multibillion-dollar project once the Coalition had “visibility” of the contracts that have been signed.
Asked by moderator Kieran Gilbert if the Coalition would be willing to scrap the project and move on, Wilson said: “That’s exactly what the review is for.”
Carroll, meanwhile, acknowledged that Labor had made mistakes during its 12 years in government but leaned heavily on its record, including 121 new schools, record NAPLAN results, the highest-paid teachers in the country and 17,000 nurses.
He also repeatedly referred to his decision to call a royal commission into allegations of corruption on government construction sites, describing it as one of the “hardest” things he had done.
Victoria will not get another leaders debate, after Carroll and Wilson failed to agree on terms for one on free-to-air television.
The audience members were polled as they left the Sofitel, with 39% saying Wilson had won the debate, followed by Sandell on 25% and Pickering on 16%. Just 13% were undecided at the end of the night and only 7% picked Carroll.
It appears no matter what the premier has to say, many Victorians have stopped listening.
- Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

noticias.titulo: ‘Line their own coffers’: independent MPs lambast Labor’s last-minute changes to election funding laws
noticias.resumen: Crossbenchers say the proposals could allow an ‘uncapped amount of money’ to flow to major parties through investment funds Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Independent MPs say the government’s last-minute changes to controversial election funding laws would allow “an uncapped amount of money” to flow to the major parties through investment funds. The amendments to the incoming federal electoral laws , which the government describes as “technical”, were introduced on Tuesday afternoon and come weeks before they are set to begin operating. Sign up for Guardian Aust
noticias.texto:
Independent MPs say the government’s last-minute changes to controversial election funding laws would allow “an uncapped amount of money” to flow to the major parties through investment funds.
The amendments to the incoming federal electoral laws, which the government describes as “technical”, were introduced on Tuesday afternoon and come weeks before they are set to begin operating.
From January, political parties and candidates will face campaign spending limits and donation caps during federal elections. Disclosure thresholds for political gifts and donations will be lowered to $5,000, and public funding per vote received will be increased from $3.35 to $5.
But crossbenchers, who have long criticised the changes as favouring major parties and incumbents, say the latest tweaks further enable a lop-sided system.
They take particular aim at changes to allow political parties to invest and grow their funds without the interest earned contributing to donation ceilings.
“The amendments would enable a federal account holder to continue to grow their capital in a competitive manner and when the federal account funds are not required for incurring electoral expenditure,” the bill’s explanatory statement said.
“This would allow federal account holders a greater degree of flexibility to administer their financial assets as they wish, protecting the right to take part in the conduct of public affairs directly.”
Major parties often set up investment arms to grow funds in time for election cycles. The Cormack Foundation in Victoria serves as a major financial backer for the Liberals, while Labor Services and Holding and Pilliwinks are Labor’s and the Nationals’ equivalents, respectively.
In 2024-25, Cormack donated $4.7m to the Liberals, while Labor Services and Holding donated $598,00.
The federal government intends to pass the eleventh-hour changes in both houses this sitting fortnight ahead of the electoral laws coming into effect from 1 January 2027.
The independent ACT senator, David Pocock, said the bill continues the “major party stitch-up” and enabled “an uncapped amount of money to flow from their huge investment vehicles into their political accounts”.
“They like to talk about taking money out of politics but they legislate to drive more in,” Pocock said.
“And while the government is prioritising law changes that will line their own coffers, they’re failing to bring forward the overdue measures to strengthen our democracy like banning deepfakes in elections or legislating truth in political advertising.”
Independent Curtin MP, Kate Chaney, said the changes didn’t address the bill’s serious flaws, and instead included tweaks to protect the existing investment vehicles and assets of major parties.
“Rather than being a new act of bastardry, this bill tweaks the act of bastardry performed on Australian democracy last year,” Chaney said.
“We don’t let Coles and Woolies make laws about supermarket competition, but this is what it looks like when major parties make laws about who can compete with them.”
The electoral laws overhaul is already being challenged in the high court by former parliamentarians, Zoe Daniel and Rex Patrick, on three grounds.
The two are arguing the $800,000 cap on spending in each electorate impinges on the implied right of political communication.
While the expenditure cap applies to all candidates, the former independents argue newcomers are at disadvantage because major parties can also tap into their national campaign budget, which is capped at $90m.
They also argue two other changes unfairly disadvantage candidates without political parties: the $50,000 cap on individual donations, aimed at preventing Clive Palmer-sized campaigns, and rules stopping a single donor, such as Climate 200, from giving to more than five candidates in a state or territory.
Daniel and Patrick said the latest amendments were not about getting big money out of politics but stopping competitive newcomers.
“Rather than trying to make this flawed law fair, the government is doing the opposite by introducing amendments that would entrench access to wealth for the ALP and the LNP through the enormous investment vehicles that only they have,” they said.
“No new entrant could amass such wealth under the new laws. They are pulling up the drawbridge, and it is transparent to anyone who cares to look.
“It is classic cartel behaviour akin to Coles and Woolies land-banking to prevent competition from newcomers.”

noticias.titulo: Andy Burnham delays taking stock of UK’s relationship with EU
noticias.resumen: PM to wait until after Brussels summit at which he hopes for agreements on food, farming and emissions UK politics live – latest updates Andy Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he comes under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink. The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he hopes to secure agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
