noticias.texto:
Andy Burnham has said there is “no rush” to decide on the UK’s longer term relationship with the EU, as he comes under pressure from his own party to press the brakes on the pace of the rethink.
The prime minister said he would “take stock” of the wider relationship after Friday’s summit in Brussels at which he hopes to secure agreements on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
In an interview with Sky News, Burnham admitted that he would now not set out the full options for a closer EU relationship until December – but denied he was “stepping back” from his previous commitments to pursue ties.
The prime minister had been expected to give a speech or deliver a statement setting out options for a closer relationship early next week, probably Monday, and to argue that it would be in the UK’s long-term interest.
While he may still address MPs, he is now likely to focus on the details of the deal secured at the summit, delaying his bigger plans to around the same time as his 10-year plan for the country, No 10 sources said, adding that the two were linked.
No 10 insiders told the Guardian that Burnham wants to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion, with even some Remain-minded MPs acknowledging there is more work to be done.
These will include discussions with European counterparts to establish what the EU is willing to negotiate and whether it might be possible to get a better bespoke deal, or what the terms of rejoining the single market or customs union might be.
Since Burnham announced in September that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he has reiterated that the existing deal is not good enough, and that he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship this autumn.
In addition to the customs union or single market, these could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, reversing Brexit in its entirety, or no change at all.
But after revealing his personal preference would be to fully rejoin the bloc, Burnham has encountered some resistance, including from within the cabinet, with some MPs with Leave-voting seats anxious about reopening the debate.
Senior government figures say that Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be confirmatory after MPs had endorsed a deal.
In his interview, Burnham said: “All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available. And so that people can see the pros and cons, we’ll set those out in due course. There’s no rush to do that. The British public will be in charge of whatever comes next.
“We’ll see how [Friday’s summit] goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.”
The prime minister denied that he was “jumping the gun” or “making any assumptions” about where the UK would end up – but pointed to polling which shows the public wants closer ties with the bloc.
Some Labour MPs, however, are concerned about the impact of freedom of movement in particular, as the debate around immigration in the UK has grown with the rise of Reform UK.
“I won’t get ahead of public opinion. I will listen to what the public feel is the right long term solution,” Burnham added.
While much of the deal expected to be agreed in Brussels on Friday is over the line, there are still tensions over the level of the cap on the youth mobility scheme cap, as well as over tuition fees.
Officials are also expected to discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €50bn (£40bn) safe defence fund, collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

noticias.titulo: How Ukraine struck the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule

noticias.texto:
At 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces. Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018, driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine, by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph). SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue. On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight, with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Spared a lot’: Kessler twins explained assisted dying decision in final letter
noticias.resumen: Pop-singing sisters, who died aged 89 last year, described their declining health and desire to depart life together Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing twins who chose to jointly end their lives through assisted dying last year, said they had “reached rock bottom” due to health problems and had been relieved to be able to die together. The German sisters, who became huge television stars in the 1960s and 70s, especially in Italy and the US, said a catalogue of health conditions had left them with no desire to carry on living. noticias.texto:
Alice and Ellen Kessler, the identical pop-singing twins who chose to jointly end their lives through assisted dying last year, said they had “reached rock bottom” due to health problems and had been relieved to be able to die together.
The German sisters, who became huge television stars in the 1960s and 70s, especially in Italy and the US, said a catalogue of health conditions had left them with no desire to carry on living.
In a letter released by a friend, the 89-year-olds wrote: “Dear friends, we’re sorry that we’ve chosen to go this way, but due to our medical conditions we had no quality of life any more.
“Apart from our heart problems, we no longer have our senses of taste and smell. On top of that Ellen has suffered a brain stem stroke, and as a result we’ve reached rock bottom.”
Because they had “entered the world together”, they wished “to depart it together the same way”, they added, concluding: “Don’t be sad; we’re happy that assisted dying exists, because certainly as a result we will have been spared a lot.”
They signed off: “Wishing you all the very best. We’ll see you on Cloud 9.”
The sisters died on 18 November last year , assisted by a doctor and a lawyer, in the villa they shared in the Grünwald district of Munich in Germany, which was divided into two mirrored halves, one for each.
They had planned the process together, working with an assisted dying organisation, but had kept this from their friends.
The letters were posted into the letter boxes of people close to them on the evening before their deaths, with a handwritten instruction on the envelope: “Don’t open until 17 November.” Inside each envelope they had placed the gift of a piece of their jewellery.
Bibi Johns, a 97-year-old actor and the singers’ closest friend, the three having met on the set of the 1959 film La Paloma, said she heard of their deaths on the radio before she had had the chance to open the letter from them.
“It was a shock,” she told the newspaper Bild. “Alice and Ellen were like sisters to me. For me it feels as if they have merely gone on a long journey. I’m still waiting for them to call me up.”
They bequeathed to her a gold pendant depicting the heads of two signs of the zodiac, a gift in 1968 from the French singer Marcel Amont to his then-partner Alice.
The year before their deaths, in an interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera, the sisters said their wish was “to leave together, on the same day … the idea that one of the two will go first is very difficult to bear”. In their lifetimes they had also made a pact that neither would marry.

In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

noticias.titulo: ‘They were keeping it for a rainy day’: Ukraine’s Kerch bridge attack is proof Kyiv still has cards to play
noticias.resumen: Partial demolition of bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea is obvious embarrassment to Putin days before meeting with Xi and Trump Europe live – latest updates Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones. The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing , one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due
noticias.texto:
Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch road bridge overnight is the culmination of weeks, and perhaps months, of military operations plus years of industrial development, during which Kyiv has developed its own cruise missiles and long-range drones.
The demolition is not quite total, because the rail bridge is still standing, one line in operation – but the attack is an obvious embarrassment to Russia two days before Vladimir Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
The collapse of a span of the roadway and the loss of its supporting arch above appears to be a level of damage that “cannot be repaired any time soon”, says Ben Hodges, a former commanding general of the US army in Europe.
The 19km (12-mile), $3.6bn (£2.7bn) road bridge connecting Russia to the east of Crimea was completed in 2018, a project closely associated with Putin and his efforts to secure the 2014 annexation of Crimea by opening up a supply route to the peninsula.
The Russian leader was filmed driving an orange truck into Crimea, greeted by cheering workers once the construction was complete. “Putin initiated this project himself,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said at the time.
That was four years before Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which has, if anything, made Russia’s position in Crimea more precarious, though the change in the balance of power is a while coming.
Russia was able to bomb anywhere in Ukraine in 2022, while Kyiv was denied long-range western missiles, particularly those powerful enough to strike such a politically sensitive and strategic target.
Instead, Ukraine tried to blow the bridge up with a truck bomb in 2022 and a sea drone attack a year later. Neither did much long-term damage. It was only as Ukraine’s own long-range drones and cruise missiles came to fruition near the beginning of 2026 that a knockout strike became possible.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that the culminating attacks on the bridge, the end of two days of strikes, involved Ukrainian-made Neptune and Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles, Palianytsia rocket drones plus Ruta cruise missiles from the Dutch manufacturer Destinus, the only foreign arms company confirmed as involved.
It was, the Ukrainian president said, the “seventh stage” in an operation “carried out over several weeks”. Radars, jamming equipment and air defence systems were progressively neutralised, opening up corridors of attack.
Meanwhile, Russia had already started what is becoming a battle of the bridges. Moscow attacked Kyiv’s busy Northern and Southern bridges in early October, part of its scaled-up campaign against the capital and the country’s other large cities.
Russia is struggling to make progress on the frontline, and a record 50,000 troops were killed or seriously wounded in October, according to the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte. Its efforts are focused on knocking out Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water supplies, though attacking bridges show its target list is expanding in grim desperation.
Yet the Kremlin has chosen this expansion at a time when Ukraine can strike back. The pro-war Russian military blogger Military Informant notes that Ukraine has a “parity in firepower”, having downed the Kerch road bridge in two days of air raids. “It cannot be ruled out that the railway section will be destroyed next,” the blogger adds.
If anything, further attacks on the bridge are almost certain both to prevent its repair and to make resupplying Crimea more difficult. Cutting the bridge entirely, rail and road, would leave Moscow with only the R-280 land highway from Rostov to Crimea, already the subject of months of Ukrainian drone attacks.
Hodges has long argued that Crimea could be a defining theatre of the war, because “of what Crimea represents to Putin”. Ukraine should try to make “Russian occupation untenable” by destroying the bridge and asserting fire control over the R-280, he adds.
A supply squeeze, however, is a slow process, though its political benefits may be felt more quickly. Bringing down the road bridge “further kills the narrative that Russian victory is inevitable or that Crimea is theirs”, Hodges says, although Trump may not bring up the episode in his meeting with Putin and Xi on Thursday.
The danger is that both sides, in their desperation to end a deadlocked war, will escalate further. However, cut out of the talks in Shenzen, Zelenskyy had little choice but to remind Trump as well as Putin that Ukraine still has cards to play.
Emily Ferris, a Russia expert with the Rusi thinktank, says Ukraine’s military-industrial complex was ready for some months, meaning the timing of the attack on the Kerch bridge can be interpreted only as political.
“They were keeping it for a rainy day, and that day has come,” she said.

noticias.texto:
Zelenskyy urges partners to send air defence deliveries without delay as Russia intensifies attacks
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to send deliveries of air defence missiles to Kyiv without delay, as he addressed ministers during the Ukraine Defence Support Group in Brussels.
“Russia keeps attacking us with jet-powered Shaheed drones, cruise missiles, and, most dangerously, ballistic missiles, and we need to defend against all of this,” he said.
“The world has enough [of air defence missiles] and America has them, some European countries have them, and some of our other partners around the world have them, too. These interceptors should not be sitting in warehouses. They should be in air defence batteries, protecting our cities, towns and villages from Russian strikes and saving lives, of course.”
“We all understand that there are long waiting lists for new interceptors, but we need them here and now,” he added.
Zelenskyy warned that “every successful Russian strike makes Russia more aggressive, more demanding, and less willing to compromise.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to send deliveries of air defence missiles to Kyiv without delay, as he dialled into a meeting of Ukraine’s key allies at a high-level meeting in Brussels (17:07).
The renewed request came hours after Ukraine critically damaged the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia, in what Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation which drew comments from allies (10:32, 14:55, 15:01, 17:34).
Several European partners, including Denmark, Germany, Sweden and the UK, declared their plans to further support Ukraine amid growing concerns about a particularly difficult winter ahead (9:55, 9:58, 16:01, 17:11).
On Thursday, top EU leaders are going to meet in Berlin for latest talks on Ukraine within the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb saying the meeting will be “very important” to help influence the structure of any peace talks with Russia (13:03).
In other news,
46 people were injured, including four seriously, after two commuter trains collided near the main railway station in Prague (10:09).
Candidates for Serbia’s Student List, the grassroots movement of political outsiders that pulled off a spectacular victory in last month’s elections over the party of the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić, have been sworn in as MPs as they begin the process of forming a government. (13:46).
Former US president Joe Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, got published today, with some of his unfiltered views on Ukraine’s Zelenskyy, Ukraine, France’s Emmanuel Macron and Brexit (13:41).
After 65 days without a government, the Swedish outgoing prime minister and Moderates leader Ulf Kristersson has asked for more time before parliament votes on whether they want him as prime minister (15:50, 16:29).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Collapsed part of the Kerch Bridge was once described as technically most challenging part of structure - snap analysis
Pjotr Sauer
The section of the Crimean Bridge that appears to have collapsed in Tuesday’s attack was described by Russian engineers at the time of its construction as the most technically challenging part of the entire project.
Dmitry Kondakov, a senior executive at the company building the bridge, said in 2016 that shipping arches were “the most difficult thing we have to do”, noting that Russia had little experience constructing such complex structures.
Another senior official described the operation to install the arches as the “pinnacle of the entire construction project”, calling it the most technically demanding stage of building the bridge.
Their comments highlight the complexity of the rebuild operation planned by Russia (11:12).
The US undersecretary of defence Elbridge Colby has praised Europe for stepping up to take more responsibility for Ukraine’s defence, helping mount the Ukrainian forces mount “a resilient denial defence.”
Colby said Europe and the US “have made tremendous progress in making Nato 3.0 a reality,” while continuing to support Ukraine.
But he said more needs to be done, urging Europe “to focus its defence industrial-based efforts on military efficacy and battlefield utility, rather than ancillary domestic or industrial policy objectives” and continue its spending on Ukraine-related schemes.
Turning to Ukraine, he said:
“In October, for the second consecutive month, Ukraine gained more territory than Russia and Russian forces suffered their highest monthly casualty toll of the war.”
But in a rather curious part of his statement, Colby appeared to distance the US from some of the recent deep strikesin Russia.
He argued:
“It is our view that focusing on support, our support on the frontlines and on associated mid-range strikes is the most effective way to enable Ukraine’s defence, and thus to set the conditions for an end to the war. …
While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the frontline.
Moreover, such strikes as especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate. Moreover, it is important to note that the balance of advantage in deep strikes may well favour Moscow.”
He added:
“This is not to say that Ukraine should be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back. Rather, that we should be clear about is that the focus of our support should be on enabling and advancing Ukraine’s ability to hold the line of battle and, where possible, make gains.
Strikes focused on the frontline and direct support to that battle area, of course, fall into this category, but consistent with this approach, strikes that target Russia’s war making machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advances on the frontlines.”
Colby also said the US administration “remain firmly committed to bringing this conflict to an end on terms that secure a durable peace,” even as it appears that Russia wants to continue the war.
Russia could 'try to cause humanitarian emergencies' in large cities to break Ukraine's resolve, German minister warns
Germany’s defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that “the fifth war winter … threatens to be harder than the ones before,” as Russia “has further expanded its arsenal of attack drones and ballistic missiles.”
“With daily airstrikes, Russia is trying to take out Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and water supply. It is terrorising Ukraine from the air because it cannot achieve military success on the ground,” he said.
Pistorius warned that Russia “may intentionally try to cause humanitarian emergencies in Kyiv, Odesa and other large cities to break the Ukrainian people’s resistance.”
“If Russia were to succeed, the consequence would be dramatic, both for Ukraine and for Europe,” he said.
Earlier, UK’s Wes Streeting said the aim of the meeting is to discuss how to “put Ukraine in the best possible position for future negotiations.”
Zelenskyy urges partners to send air defence deliveries without delay as Russia intensifies attacks
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged allies to send deliveries of air defence missiles to Kyiv without delay, as he addressed ministers during the Ukraine Defence Support Group in Brussels.
“Russia keeps attacking us with jet-powered Shaheed drones, cruise missiles, and, most dangerously, ballistic missiles, and we need to defend against all of this,” he said.
“The world has enough [of air defence missiles] and America has them, some European countries have them, and some of our other partners around the world have them, too. These interceptors should not be sitting in warehouses. They should be in air defence batteries, protecting our cities, towns and villages from Russian strikes and saving lives, of course.”
“We all understand that there are long waiting lists for new interceptors, but we need them here and now,” he added.
Zelenskyy warned that “every successful Russian strike makes Russia more aggressive, more demanding, and less willing to compromise.”
Swedish parliament speaker wants to see new government or snap poll called by Christmas
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
The Speaker of the Riksdag, Andreas Norlén, has said granted Ulf Kristersson’s request for more time for coalition talks (15:50) but that he wants to have clarity for the Swedish public by Christmas.
He said he would give parties one more week before he calls in the party leaders to decide what will happen next, but that he is determined to get to the end of this process soon so that by Christmas, Sweden will either have a new government or can prepare to go back to the polls with a second election.
He said:
“My opinion is that this formation of government needs to come to an end in good time before Christmas. I want that when the Swedish people celebrate Christmas they will know that Sweden either has a new government or are preparing themselves for another election.”
Swedish minister says he has 'not seen any serious intent' from Russia to negotiate Ukraine peace
Sticking to the Swedish theme for a moment, Sweden’s defence minister Pål Jonson is the latest leader to stop by the journalists upon his arrival at today’s Ukraine Defence Contact Group in Brussels.
In his comments, he said the meeting was “timely” as “the situation in Ukraine is very challenging due to the fact that Russia scaled up its production, both of ballistic missiles and also drones and glide bombs.”
Sweden will spend €4bn on helping Ukraine in 2027, Jonson said, noting cross-party backing across the parliament.
The minister also said that Sweden signed a letter of intent with Ukraine and the UK on the upcoming delivery of Gripen fighter jets for Ukraine.
Responding to questions from reporters, Jonson also said that the US undersecretary of defence Colby did not say “specific” information on the ongoing review of the US posture in Europe.
“We are expecting it to come by the end of the year,” he said, adding that “the message is clear that Europe is going to shouldering the lion’s share of conventional deterrence by 2028.”
Asked about the peace negotiations with Russia, the Swedish minister said he “has not seen any serious intent from the Russian side” on ending the war in Ukraine, stressing the need to keep supporting Kyiv in the meantime.
Jonson pointedly disagreed with Finland’s president, Alexander Stubb, who has repeatedly called for direct talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Asked if he sees any merit in that approach, he said:“Not quite, because we do not see any serious commitment from the Russian side to making any kind of compromise.”
“I know there’s all kinds of ideas drifting around that we should also have a discussion about the European security architecture. We do not welcome that.”
Sweden's Kristersson asks parliament speaker for more time to form new government
Miranda Bryant
Nordic correspondent
In other news, after 65 days without a government, Moderates leader Ulf Kristersson has asked for more time before parliament votes on whether they want him as prime minister.
Two weeks after he was given the task to attempt to form a “middle” coalition government by the Speaker, he said on Tuesday afternoon that he had requested a few more days.
The Speaker will hold a press conference later this afternoon when he is expected to respond to the former prime minister’s request.
His announcement comes after the Centre party leader, Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist, asked Kristersson and the Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson to present a “total package” for her party to choose between after talks between the left-leaning parties failed to produce a result.
She has already said yes to Andersson’s proposal of a coalition between the Social Democrats, Green party and the Centre party with cooperation with the Left party. But the Left party has since continued to demand ministerial posts, which the Centre party has refused to accept.
Kristersson said:
“A majority government that cannot agree does not work, so nothing would get done. A few more days are needed before a vote takes place, so that the Centre party can have a complete basis for decision making which is needed to take a position.”
If the vote on Kristersson does not lead to a government, parties have just one more attempt before another election will be automatically called.
Kristersson said he does not want another election, but is “totally prepared” for one and already has a team of people preparing in case.
Ukraine preparing for prisoner of war exchange with Russia, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv is working on a prisoner of war exchange with Russia, “one of the most important agreements reached at the trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi.”
He said Ukraine would submit its proposals to the US, and could “deliver results in the coming weeks.”
“The timeline for implementing this agreement depends on how quickly the Russian side acts and on the American team’s communication with them,” he said.
Acting on the success of the humanitarian operations in Oleshky, Ukraine will also propose 10 other areas in the occupied parts of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions where similar actions are needed, Zelenskyy said.
Kerch Bridge strike shows Ukraine's 'ingenuity and absolute determination to defend itself,' UK's Streeting says
Arriving earlier, UK defence secretary Wes Streeting – who co-chairs the group - said the meeting comes “at a critical time for the war in Ukraine” in what he argued “has been a terrible year for Vladimir Putin.”
“Russian casualties are [at] intolerably high levels as a direct result of his illegal and unnecessary war. The economic costs on his economy and his own people have been catastrophic. And all of those lives and all of those, economic costs are coming with little to no gain. The frontline isn’t moving, and Ukraine continues to show extraordinary resilience, courage and ingenuity.”
Streeting said the meeting was focused on “mobilising the support for allies … to see Ukraine through what will inevitably be a challenging winter.”
“We’re all invested in the, attempt to negotiate a peace, and an end to this conflict that has to be on terms that are acceptable to Ukraine. There can be no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine.”
On the Kerch Bridge strike, he said:
“I think we’ve just seen another example of Ukrainian ingenuity and Ukraine’s absolute determination to defend itself against Russian aggression. We stand with Ukraine, as they do that.”
Just like Rutte, he said he expected “a number” of announcements from Ukraine’s allies to help Kyiv in the coming months today.
Ukraine's Kerch bridge strike 'unavoidable' as Ukraine defends itself from aggression, Nato's Rutte says
Over in Brussels, the Ukraine Defence Contact Group is about to meet for their latest talks on Ukraine, including the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge A. Colby.
Nato’s secretary general Mark Rutte just arrived and chatted with reporters, telling them he is “relatively optimistic” ahead of the meeting, hoping for “some good announcements this afternoon.”
“A lot of people are working very hard to bring peace to Ukraine. But in the meantime, we have to make sure that they have what they need to get through winter, that they have what they need to be as strong as possible in the peace negotiations.”
On the Kerch Bridge, Rutte said that “it’s important that Ukraine defends itself.”
“And that means also hitting out at logistical nodes; it’s unavoidable that they do that. … We have to see, of course, what exactly happened but at least [from] the media footage, it seems that they were successful.”
Rutte declined to comment on the peace negotiations, saying merely that “the US is playing a crucial part here.”
“I think it’s good that Europe is now at a table – that was one of the outcomes of Abu Dhabi – I think the Europeans have organised themselves now quite well.”
Asked about the renewed Starshield restrictions affecting Ukraine, he said that “relevant parties are working very hard to make sure that as soon as possible, things are back to normal.”
“I know that anyone who can be helpful here is working on this.”

noticias.titulo: Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media during Israel’s election, report finds
noticias.resumen: Digital monitors recorded 400% rise in posts attacking Arab Israelis, including Netanyahu’s disproven fraud allegations Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud. A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 Octobe
noticias.texto:
Anti-Arab hate speech surged on social media in Israel around the country’s general election last month, digital monitors have said, as politicians including Benjamin Netanyahu levelled disproven allegations against Arab Israeli parties of election fraud.
A new report by the Israel-based Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter recorded a deluge of anti-Arab discourse across social media platforms such as X, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok in the days surrounding Israel’s 27 October election.
According to FakeReporter’s analysis, anti-Arab sentiment on X rose by more than 400% from election day on 27 October to 29 October. Similar content also spread across Facebook and other platforms.
Arab-majority parties won 19 seats in the Israeli Knesset in last month’s election, potentially putting them in a kingmaker position. The opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been invited to try to put together a coalition to replace Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist government.
The posts mainly pushed three messages, the first of which was the allegation that “the Arabs stole the election” via fraud, vote buying and foreign interference, according to the report. Israel’s electoral commission had already publicly refuted such claims.
Posts also depicted Arab citizens of Israel as a security threat and called for them to have their right to vote restricted.
Some of the most-viewed posts also came from top Israeli officials and Netanyahu’s post “They stole the election in Israel!” was viewed 1.2m times. A post by the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, calling for heads of Arab political parties was also viewed more than 350,000 times.
FakeReporter said much of the anti-Arab hate speech was fuelled by politicians from Netanyahu’s political bloc. “It can be said that they were a major factor in spreading hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel following the election,” its analysis said.
Arab citizens of Israel, the majority of whom are Palestinians, make up 21% of the population of Israel. Since the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack and Israel’s subsequent war in Gaza, Arab political leaders have faced increasingly inflammatory attacks and accusations of dual loyalties.
In the run-up to the election, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar the country’s two main Arab majority political lists from running – a move later struck down by the Israeli supreme court.
Eisenkot last week condemned what he called a “racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation” against the country’s Arab citizens.
The Brandeis Institute and FakeReporter sent letters to Google, Meta, TikTok and X on 4 November calling on them to take steps to stop the proliferation of hate speech against Arab citizens of Israel on their platforms.
Only Google responded, saying that Israel’s election is a “Priority 0” for the company and that it has dedicated resources to monitoring traffic around the election, but that the Central Elections Committee had made no requests for extra moderation procedures.

noticias.titulo: Trump claims US is ‘looking into’ Iranian bomb plot in Washington despite ‘no credible threats’
noticias.resumen: US officials ‘continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute’ plot to detonate a ‘dirty bomb’, report says Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there are “no credible threats” at this time. Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously” Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Donald Trump has claimed the US is “looking into” whether Iran is developing plans to detonate a so-called “dirty bomb” in Washington, even as the White House said there are “no credible threats” at this time.
Trump said his administration takes the idea “very seriously”
After a CNN report, citing seven unnamed US officials, that new US intelligence suggested Iran was working on plans that would use a dirty bomb, which combines conventional explosives with radioactive material, or a chemical weapon against senior Trump administration officials.
The report noted, however, that US officials “continue to debate whether Iran can or will attempt to execute such a plot”.
The US president’s war on Iran is deeply unpopular among Americans. His Republican party was widely rejected by voters in the midterm elections, in which the GOP lost control of the Senate and House of Representatives.
Asked in the Philippines on Tuesday if there was reason to believe that such an Iranian attack was imminent, Trump said: “If there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before. I hope it’s not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy.”
Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement: “We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
CNN cited the unnamed officials as saying that Tehran’s planning was an effort by Iran to “give itself options rather than an indicator of an imminent attack”, but the plans include specific locations and targets.
While the plans would signify that Iran is willing to escalate its tactics against the US, there is no evidence to suggest they will go ahead with them.
The US and Israel went to war with Iran starting in February, with early airstrikes killing Iranian officials, including supreme leader Ali Khamenei. Trump has repeatedly claimed the war will be over soon, but it has continued.
The US president has argued that US involvement in the war is necessary so that the country doesn’t build nuclear weapons. Iran has blocked trade through the strait of Hormuz, creating rising fuel costs – and rattling the global economy.

noticias.titulo: Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank
noticias.resumen: Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’ UK politics live – latest updates Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution. The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.
The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month.
Miliband announced the measures just before tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement were due to be allocated by the Israeli government, while saying he wanted to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way.
Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot has said that, if appointed, he will take a tougher approach than Benjamin Netanyahu to settler violence.
The sanctions are designed to stop the flow of finance to eight identified construction firms, although in practice the extent to which any of the firms are dependent on British finance is yet to be tested.
On 8 September, Miliband announced an expansion of its Global Human Rights sanctions regime, as well as a complex set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. The Foreign Office said that it welcomed and encouraged trade with “green line Israel” and firmly distinguished this with activity in settlements.
The Foreign Office said the current Israeli government had “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them”. More settlements had been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years.
The entities targeted by sanctions are Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Miliband – who was criticised by some for broadening the sanctions criteria and planning a ban on trade with illegal settlement – said: “Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.
“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.”
But he added in a potential olive branch: “We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”
Miliband and his Middle East minister, Stephen Doughty, have repeatedly highlighted the Israeli government’s refusal to let a variety of dual-use goods into Gaza. The Foreign Office said civilians in Gaza were in desperate need of winter supplies, with catastrophic floods leaving nearly 4,000 households without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters.
According to the UN, more than 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins bought by humanitarian partners and donors are outside Gaza ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities. The Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.
The Israeli government claims the blockage of some goods is necessary to prevent Hamas obtaining items that could be used to attack Israel. The dispute over dual-use goods and closed entry points into Gaza has lasted for more than two years.

noticias.titulo: Burnham delays announcement about options for closer relationship with EU until next month – as it happened
noticias.resumen: The prime minister earlier said he wanted to open a national debate on Britain’s relationship with the bloc This chart, from the Milburn report, shows what is likely to happen to the Neet rate, with or without the Milburn policies. The Alan Milburn report has now formally been published. It should be online here very soon. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
This is in effect the creation of a two-tier welfare state, where the help you receive isn’t determined by your health but the date on your birth certificate. The £3.6bn in cutswould sever the link between need and entitlement that sits at the heart of the safety net – potentially leading to the perverse situation where two people with the same disability get unequal support simply because they’re a different age.
After months of stories inflaming the narrative that feckless youngsters are feigning disability for cash, as a fashion statement or because of “social contagion”, Milburn will have felt under immense pressure to curb the youth benefits bill as a trade-off for his other large-scale spending plans. That pensioners receive roughly 55% of the welfare budget and young people (excluding children) just 2.5% is conveniently ignored.
Andy Burnham has delayed his announcement about the possible future options for Britain forming a closer relationship with the EU until next month. (See 5.07pm.)
For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.
Liberal Democrats have today been paying tribute to John Pardoe, the former Liberal deputy leader, who has died. Ed Daveydescribed him as “one of that small band of MPs who kept the Liberal flame burning brightly in the 1960s and 70s”. Paul Walter has more in a post at Liberal Democrat Voice.
What disability and health charities are saying about Milburn report
Here is some reaction to the Milburn report from disability and health charities.
From Ross Barrett, senior policy manager at the MS Society
Proposals to create a new youth welfare system in place of personal independence payment (Pip) and the universal credit (UC) health element would likely mean some young people with MS losing financial support. This could be dangerous and ultimately counter-productive.
Without Pip, young people will struggle to manage the overwhelming extra costs of the condition, face worsening health, and may find it harder to stay in work.
From a National Autistic Society spokesperson
We welcome the report’s calls for significant investment in earlier employment support and that there should be no changes to financial entitlements until that support is place. We also welcome the focus on driving down the disability employment gap, something we have been demanding for years.
For Alan Milburn’s proposed system to be effective for autistic people, it will require a very high level of autism training and understanding for anyone supporting autistic young people or deciding what they are entitled to.
FromDr Sarah Hughes, CEO of Mind,
Employment support on its own isn’t enough - it needs to go hand in hand with an overhaul of mental health support. It’s hugely promising to see such a clear ambition to better tailor mental health support through an open access approach that Mind has been calling for. This means that young people will be able to get support they need, on the day they need it, enabling them to get into work.
“But building a bridge to employment won’t work without an adequate benefits safety net. We’re concerned that young people with mental health problems could be left scrambling desperately to make ends meet, so we must see clear evidence that benefits will meet their essential costs. Without this, these changes could worsen mental health, make it harder to engage with support and push our young people further into the cold.
From Simon Antrobus, CEO at the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB)
Young people with visual impairment are twice as likely to be NEET than their peers. There is clear ambition to raise the bar of opportunity for disabled young people to pursue the careers they want. But we will only achieve the seismic change we all want to see if support is shaped by specialists who understand the unique needs and societal barriers faced by disabled young people, including those with vision impairment.
Burnham delays announcement about options for closer relationship with EU until next month
Andy Burnham has delayed his announcement about the possible options for Britain forming a closer relationship with the EU after the next election.
At Labour conference in September, Burnham said that he wanted to open a national debate on this topic, indicating that joining the customs union or the single market, or even rejoining in full, were all potential options that could be put to the public in Labour’s next manifesto.
In recent weeks, No 10 has been saying that Burnham would do this around the time of the UK-EU summit taking place that is taking place on Friday – implying soon afterwards. Whether his intervention would take the form of a speech, or a statement to MPs, or the publication of a document has not been specified.
But, in his interview with Sky’s Beth Rigby, Burnham said he was now planning to set this all out alongside his 10-year plan, “next month”. He has said the 10-year plan will be published before the Commons rises for the Christmas recess on Thursday 17 December.
Burnham told Rigby:
I’m in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal. That’s what I’m doing this week [at the summit]. We’ll see how it goes.
And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. And I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.
Burnham also insisted there was no rush.
All I’m going to do is look at what options might be available, so that people can see the pros and cons, but [I] will set those out, in due course. There’s no rush to do that.
When it was put to him that Boris Johnson said it would be madness to reopen the debate about the UK being a member of the EU, Burnham replied:
I’m afraid I’m not going to listen to Boris Johnson on this particular matter. He burnt bridges and created a lot of bad feeling. And consequently Britain has suffered as a result of that.
Burnham says government departments will have to find savings to fund new Youth Opportunity Service
Andy Burnham has recorded an interview with Beth Rigby from Sky News to mark the publication of the Alan Milburn review. Here are the top lines on this topic.
Burnham described the publication of the Milburn report as a “watershed moment” for Britain. He said:
Let’s first be clear what this is. It’s a watershed moment. I said to the cabinet this morning, I don’t think a British cabinet has sat around that table in 50 years or more and talked about a vision for young people, support from the very early years all the way through school and then into opportunity beyond school. And that’s what this is about.
He did not rule out implementing the Milburn recommendation to cut employer national insurance for young people. (See 3.38pm.) Asked if he would accept this idea, he replied:
We’re going to look at the whole of the report in the round. Some of the implications of those proposals are for the budget, and they’ll have to be considered as part of that. But we’re not ruling anything out at this point in time. We’ll look at everything in the round.
He confirmed that government departments will be asked to make cuts in some areas to free up funds for the Youth Opportunity Service being set up. (See 1.33pm.) Asked if benefits were being cut to fund better employment support, Burnham said:
No. That’s not the approach that we’ll be taking. I am asking the cabinet to reprioritise. That’s the discussion that I’ve been having. So Department for Education, Work and Pensions, Health and Social Care – finding money now, to put in place the first budget for the Youth Opportunity Service next year.
This is what the Milburn report says about what the new Youth Opportunity Service should do.
A new Youth Opportunity Service (YOS) should operate in every part of England as the delivery mechanism for these Guarantees. Its purpose should be to make sure that a young person who is outside education or work, or at serious risk of becoming so, has somewhere to go and somebody responsible for helping them move forward. Access to the YOS should depend on a young person’s need for help, not on whether they happen to be claiming benefits. It should be easy to find, welcoming and non-stigmatising, whether a young person reaches it online, through a physical service or through an organisation they already know and trust. It should identify young people before detachment becomes entrenched, help them find jobs, apprenticeships, courses, work experience and other opportunities, understand what is getting in the way and, where more sustained help is needed, bring together one Participation Plan and one named relationship around the young person. It should operationalise the new welfare and benefits system for young people.
Milburn said an initial £500m should be spent setting up the service in 2027.
Bev Craig says she wants to see Manchester implementing Milburn's plans for tackling Neets within 12 months
Josh Halliday
Josh Halliday is the Guardian’s North of England editor.
Andy Burnham’s successor as Greater Manchester mayor, Bev Craig, said she wants to implement Alan Milburn’s model for tackling the Neets crisis “within 12 months,” describing the current system as “simply not acceptable”.
England’s mayors would be responsible for huge parts of the proposals to get hundreds of thousands of young people earning or learning under plans set out by Milburn on Tuesday.
Among sweeping changes to health and skills programmes, the mayors of strategic authorities would be responsible for getting young people into work or education up to the age of 24 – which Milburn’s report describes as a “fundamental change” from the current system where teenagers hit a “cliff edge” of state support as soon as they reach 19.
A new funding settlement would see the more established authorities - like Greater London, Greater Manchester and South Yorkshire - given committed pots of cash for at least three years to replace the rolling annual grants they receive from central government.
Mayors whose areas underperform in getting young people into work would face financial penalties as part of this model.
Speaking to the Guardian, Craig said her predecessor Burnham now had a “moral imperative in acting fast” on Milburn’s recommendations – and said Greater Manchester should be at the front of the queue for these new responsibilities.
Asked whether she was concerned about Milburn’s proposed cuts to disability benefits for young people, which by 2036/7 would amount to £3.6bn a year, Craig said that was “not my reading of the 278-page report”.
She added:
There naturally will be a debate on social security that will move through parliament, but my takeaway from this report is that we’ve got a generation of young people who want to work and want to get into education, who currently aren’t supported to be able to do that.
Craig said the status quo was “simply not acceptable” and that nearly 40,000 young people in Greater Manchester were neither earning or learning. According to the Centre for Cities thinktank, Manchester has the third highest number of young Neets in England behind London and Birmingham - although this is not particularly surprising given the size of these cities.
Here are comments on the Milburn report from education unions.
From Matt Wrack, general secretary of the NASUWT, a teachers’ union
We reject any approach to getting young people into employment, education and training which is based on punitive cuts to welfare or which seeks to blame schools or teachers.
Young people should not be penalised for the wider and prolonged failures of successive governments to create high quality training opportunities, invest in decent jobs and to create the social conditions in which young people can thrive and feel hope for the future.
From Paul Whiteman, general secretary at the school leaders’ union NAHT
We welcome the recognition that young people should have an education system which prepares them not only for exams, but for adult life, further study and employment. NAHT has long supported a broad and balanced curriculum, alongside greater parity of esteem between academic, vocational and technical pathways, so that every young person can pursue a route that reflects their talents, strengths and aspirations.
From Jo Grady, general secretary of the UCU, which represents academics
Creating tens of thousands of new jobs in further education would be a welcome step towards tackling youth unemployment. But the government cannot expect colleges to deliver this ambition while presiding over a further education workforce crisis.
Scottish government says it's doing 'many' of ideas Milburn recommends already
The Scottish government has said that “many” of the reforms proposed by Alan Milburn are already being implemented north of the border. In a statement, the Scottish government’s education secretary, Màiri McAllan, said:
We will take time to consider Alan Milburn’s report in detail. We are so ambitious for our young people, who face unique challenges in today’s economy, having grown up in the nearly 20 years since the global financial crash, through years of Westminster austerity and the economic and social catastrophe of Brexit.
Where there is opportunity to collaborate with the UK Government and others for the benefit of young people in Scotland, we will take it. However, many of the reforms it recommends for England – including stronger vocational curriculum and qualifications, tracking of young people’s activity and joined up support wrapped around them to help them participate – reflect approaches Scotland has already embedded over many years …
Alan Milburn’s interim report notes there are around 40% of 16 to 19-year olds starting an apprenticeship, compared with around 20% of 16 to 18-year olds in England. In Scotland, 95.7% of school leavers are in a positive destination three months after leaving school, the joint second highest on record. For 16-24 year olds, the employment rate is higher in Scotland than in England, and the majority of our economically inactive young people are students.
Funding tax cuts 'difficult', says McFadden, when asked about Milburn's national insurance proposals
In the Commons, Pat McFadden sidestepped a question from Oliver Dowden about whether the government would implement Alan Milburn’s recommendation for a cut in employer national insurance for young people. (See 2.06pm.) But, when the Labour MP Jonathan Brash asked if ministers would accept this proposals, McFadden gave a more direct reply. Arguing that tax was a matter for the chancellor, he said:
There is already a break in the system for employers with regard to employees under the age of 21.
I’m sure the chancellor listens to all representations about tax but he has the difficult job of netting off all these representations whenever there is a fiscal event.
This is what the Milburn report says about cutting national insurance.
While structural reductions in employment taxation cannot be delivered immediately, that should not prevent government from setting a clear direction towards lower payroll taxes. Rather than across the board, poorly targeted and unaffordable cuts in employer national insurance, I propose a different course: targeted support now, followed by a 5-year glide path to lower national insurance costs for workers aged 21 to 24. Businesses need confidence that government’s ambition is to reduce, not continually increase, the cost of employing a young person.
A start should be made with the 2 sectors which provide the most entry level jobs for young people: retail and hospitality. When fiscal conditions allow, the point at which employers in those sectors pay employer national insurance for 21 to 24 year-olds should double and rise progressively from the current £5,000 threshold to a new one of £10,000. Before the 2025 changes that threshold was £9,100. Unlike a full or partial employer national insurance exemption for 21 to 24 year-olds, increasing the threshold would have the biggest impact on the costs of recruiting low paid young workers and those who work fewer hours. It would especially help employers recruit young people doing ‘Saturday jobs’ as once the threshold reaches £10,000, a 21 year-old could work 15 hours a week at current minimum wage rates without the employer paying any employer national insurance. Over time the government should consider how to extend this new employer national insurance relief to other sectors in the economy, focusing on those with the biggest potential to create more entry level jobs for the young.

noticias.titulo: ‘They learn the job doing the job’: the project helping UK’s Neets into work
noticias.resumen: Labour’s plan to get young unemployed people into work involves overhaul of welfare support, but for those with disabilities, specialist help is crucial When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country. The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
When Rory Bowman finished school he joined the cohort of almost a million Neets – young people not in education, employment or training – around the country.
The 21-year-old has autism and said he was exhausted after struggling for support in mainstream education for years. He didn’t think he could manage university, but couldn’t find a job or training that would accommodate his neurodivergence.
Then he came across Project Search, a nationwide year-long transition-to-work programme that helps young people with learning disabilities or autism move into permanent paid employment.
It changed his life and now Bowman is thriving in his work as a personal trainer at Pure Gym.
“Getting actual experience in workplaces, understanding how they function, what would be expected of me and how to interact with people, it was exactly what I needed,” he said. “And having a job coach who does half the jump with you.”
Alan Milburn’s report on how to get the UK’s Neets into work has recommended an overhaul of welfare support for young people, including moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits and on to a new “youth allowance”.
In return, eligible 18-to-24-year-olds will be guaranteed a fully funded, six-month job if they have been claiming universal credit for 12 months. Milburn said this was about prioritising “their longer-term life chances” over “immediate shorter-term finances”.
Interns and staff at the Project Search course run by Phoenix College in Tower Hamlets welcomed the bold commitment to get more young people into work, but there were concerns about cutting support and the quality of job opportunities being offered.
Bowman said he disagreed with the proposal to cut benefits like the personal independence payment (Pip) for young people to help push them into work.
“I think alongside any workplace initiatives, Pip is still absolutely a must-have. I would argue it’s more important to have if you’re going to be engaging in a structured programme – for me, things like noise-cancelling headphones are essential,” he said.
“I need that funding more to enter the world of work than I did when I was sat at home playing video games.”
Staff said getting young people, especially those with extra needs, into a long-term sustainable job wasn’t as simple as filling a vacancy – many students need holistic support and extra help even once they’re in work.
“We’ve been noticing a lot more interns coming in with serious mental health conditions and that requires extra help,” said Renato Marques, principal of Phoenix College. “But here, even for our very high-needs students, everything is geared towards getting them into a workplace.
“They learn the job doing the job. A lot of courses say they are preparing students for work, but they are not taking them into work.”
Rather than studying at a traditional campus, their interns learn in classrooms hosted in partner businesses – including a global law firm, a large distribution company and Queen Mary University of London – and they rotate through daily 9am to 3pm work placements.
Over the past six years, 68% of students ended up in employment at the end of the course – four times higher than the national average rate of disabled young people who are Neet.
All graduates also have access to a follow-on service they can use for advice in the first few years of their career.
For students with higher levels of need, the college developed a pre-supported internship combining two days of workplace experience – supported by an on-hand job coach – with extra training in social skills and independent travel.
Osman Osman, assistant principal for Project Search, said Milburn’s plan would only work with better paid and resourced careers advisers in schools, and high-quality work experience and job offers.
“You see careers advisers managing schools with a thousand kids, and they’re expected to meet with every single one, and it’s a very, very hard job to actually get those young people work-ready,” he said. “We spend a long time building our young people’s confidence and skillset in the field they’re interested in.
“And any job offer has to be meaningful placements because inset days, taster sessions or a week’s work experience often lead to no actual outcomes for young people.”
Tawhid Ahmed, 21, said finding work or apprenticeships after finishing school had been overwhelming – he now works at Phoenix College after building confidence and social skills on the course.
“I have a learning disability, and it was hard because I’ve been rejected for so many jobs. The fact that I was able to find Project Search really was a blessing,” he said. “Now I do admin and I have really good colleagues who help and support me. I want to help students face challenges that I’ve faced as well.”
Businesses are also a key part of the puzzle – Milburn’s proposals included a raft of incentives to encourage employers to take on more young people, including tax breaks.
“Employers might scoff at the review because there’s a lot of expectations placed on them,” said Cigdem Yilmaz, supported employment lead on the course. “We need an army of people, maybe that’s people like us, to be working with employers until we can get more young people on to the ground. Otherwise it’s just going to be more of the same.”
Max, a 22-year-old with autism, is being supported by the Youth Environmental Service (Yes), which works with environmental organisations to create accessible and entry-level employment in the west of England.
The organisation, which targets young people from diverse backgrounds and those with disabilities, provides access to paid work as well as peer support networks, a transferable skills programme and one-to-one coaching.
“That was really beneficial, especially for neurodivergent people, because it’s really nice to be put on a level playing field with everyone,” said Max, who is employed part-time by Bristol-based Make a Film.
The 22-year-old, who has a degree in plant science, said the traditional way to apply for jobs was not accessible for all and called for more opportunities that offered young people a clear career development.
“I really strongly believe that there are lots of young people who are really passionate, who really hold skills, really great valuable skills for the workplace. But there aren’t enough jobs that are entry level, which give opportunities for training to actually get into something that will set them off into a future career that they are passionate about,” he said.
Prof Neil Greenberg, the president of the Society of Occupational Medicine (SOM), which works to protect people in the workplace, emphasised the value of work in building self-esteem, routine and social support, for all young people.
“We shouldn’t be waiting until people are completely ready to put them into work. They need to get a flicker of work as soon as they can, because once people try it out and they get success, that builds more success,” he said.
Chris Goulden, the interim deputy chief executive of the Youth Futures Foundation, which supports young people into work – particularly those from diverse and marginalised backgrounds – said stereotypes of young people being lazy or unwilling to work were “untrue” and “unhelpful”.
“The number of jobs that most young people are applying for are in the hundreds, so I think it is an unhelpful stereotype and not born out of evidence that we have experienced,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Ministers vow to create new welfare system for young people as they back Milburn report
noticias.resumen: Government promises spending cuts to pay for the proposals, described by prime minister as ‘watershed moment’ UK politics live – latest updates Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report? Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report , promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through. Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told his cabinet colleagues on Tuesday morning the report was a “watershed moment” and offered a “comprehensive vision
noticias.texto:
Ministers have promised to create an entirely new welfare system for young people as they gave their backing to Alan Milburn’s 278-page report, promising spending cuts next year to help pay for his proposals and giving him a government role to push them through.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, told his cabinet colleagues on Tuesday morning the report was a “watershed moment” and offered a “comprehensive vision” as he invited its author to address the meeting.
He then sat in the Commons in a public display of support as his work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, backed Milburn’s vision of a youth employment system with much more employment support but significantly lower benefit payments.
“We need a new settlement for young people,” McFadden said. “This new settlement must give people the best chance of higher living standards for the whole of their lives. It must change the equation that sees us spend £25 on the consequences of inactivity for every pound to be spent on opportunity.”
He added that the search for departmental cuts to help pay for the proposals would begin almost immediately.
“I have no doubt it will also be an issue in the spending review, but the first thing we should do is reprioritise spending to get more support to young people,” he told MPs. “And I’m happy to do that from my department.”
As he was speaking, the government announced Milburn would be given a role as chair of a new youth opportunities unit, monitoring the implementation of his proposals across government.
Milburn’s plans would involve a new youth employment system based on major state intervention to help young people into work, to be paid for in the long term by cuts to disability and sickness payments for under-25s.
The job support schemes were likely to prove so expensive, Milburn said, that the entire package would only save the government £200m a year.
“I know that much of the public debate about this issue centres on welfare reform,” he told a press conference in London. “For some people, the only exam question they’re trying to answer is how to cut the benefits bill. That is important, and it does need to be done. But the primary question for me is not about saving cash, it’s about improving lives.”
Under Milburn’s plan the government would spend nearly £2bn a year on a youth opportunity service, which would provide support and advice to give every young person a guaranteed route into education, training or work.
It would involve spending just over £2bn to create more vocational training courses and apprenticeships, and a further £1bn in direct payments and tax breaks for companies that hire young people.
The tax breaks would include national insurance cuts for businesses that hire young people, starting with the hospitality sector.
This was one proposal that McFadden refused to back explicitly on Wednesday, saying: “We know that employment costs matter and we will consider all these things as we move forward.”
The new system would be paid for largely by taking disability and sickness benefits away from young people and replacing them with a single youth allowance, which would be considerably below what some people can claim currently.
People aged 18 to 24 would no longer be able to claim personal independence payments, which would be replaced by a new allowance available only to those whose conditions are “well established, significant and ongoing”.
The benefit cuts would be expected to save £3.6bn by 2036-37, with an additional £2.4bn being generated by higher tax receipts. That money would be almost entirely swallowed by the £5.8bn cost of the new system, Milburn said.
Milburn began his review last year amid concern at the top of government over the rising numbers of young Neets. That figure reached 1 million earlier this year, equating to 13% of young people – a higher rate than in any European country except Romania.
“Britain is at risk of losing a generation of young people,” he warned.
Ministers and Milburn himself have worked hard to avoid the response which greeted Keir Starmer’s attempts last year to cut the benefits bill by £5bn by restricting access to disability payments.
The former prime minister backed down in the face of opposition from his own MPs, in a humiliating retreat that arguably began his long departure from office.
As well as addressing the cabinet, Milburn spoke to Labour MPs on Monday night, while Burnham spoke at a second parliamentary meeting on Tuesday morning.
Milburn criticised Starmer’s approach during his press conference on Tuesday, calling it a “fiscal grab”, adding: “I do not think that’s the way to do it.”
Early signs suggest the outreach efforts have been successful, with several of the architects of last year’s rebellion speaking in favour of the proposals.
Debbie Abrahams, the chair of the work and pensions select committee, called the review “an opportunity of a generation”, adding: “We must change the status quo.”
Marie Tidball, one of the few visibly disabled MPs in the Commons, said: “I welcome the government’s significant shift in approach and the Milburn review’s emphasis that there won’t be crude cuts to benefits and instead reforms to fundamentally change our welfare system.”
However, some Labour MPs and charities have criticised the proposed cuts to disability benefits.
John McDonnell, a former shadow chancellor, said: “The question does remain why is it that young people, if benefit cuts go ahead, are forced to pay for the new system, and we’re not taxing wealth?”
Katie Schmuecker, a principal policy adviser at the Joseph Rowntree Foundation, said: “Cutting sick and disabled young people’s benefits should not be part of this package.
“Financial support is part of what helps young people take up earning or learning. The wider support offer won’t succeed if the young people it is meant to help are also struggling to afford food or the bus to college.”

noticias.titulo: Ikea ditches plans for new UK stores, blaming high business taxes
noticias.resumen: Retailer’s British boss says John Healey ‘missed opportunity to back retailers’ in October’s budget Business live – latest updates Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes , which it said were the highest in Europe. As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Ikea has ditched some planned store openings in the UK blaming the cost of business taxes, which it said were the highest in Europe.
