As its annual UK sales little more than flatlined at the Swedish flatpack furniture retailer, its UK boss, David McCabe, said: “There are locations where we were planning to open a new unit, and those plans have been abandoned due to the cost that we experience and the complexity within the market.
“I would hope that we’re able to bring those projects back to life,” he added. “But it’s a very real impact here in the UK, when those investments will go to other countries in Europe.”
The planned investments were smaller UK stores, but the retailer declined to comment on exact locations. Ikea has been pushing further into smaller high street shops, rather than its traditional out-of-town outlets.
Ikea’s UK arm pays the most business taxes of its operations in Europe, and the third highest in the world, after the US and China, he said.
The retailer’s UK sales edged 0.5% higher to £2.26bn in the year to the end of August. Sales rose 4.7% in the first four months of the year but fell in the second half as weak confidence and “sustained pressure” on household budgets led consumers to pull back on big purchases.
McCabe said he had talked to customers in stores in recent weeks who were planning to replace an entire bedroom, but then decided to just buy one or two smaller pieces of furniture and a refresh with new textiles to save money.
“We are seeing a change in the way that customers shop and we do anticipate a difficult period going forward,” he said. “We don’t think that there’s going to be a sudden, miraculous turnaround in confidence.”
McCabe described John Healey’s recent budget as a “missed opportunity to back retailers under real pressure”, but said Ikea continued to talk to the government.
The company has spent £54m on reducing prices by an average of 20% on 425 products, including its popular Billy bookcase, Hemnes daybed and the cantilever Poäng armchair.
Ikea is using seasonal offers to pull in customers, for example discounts on extendable dining tables, folding chairs and soft toys in the run-up to Christmas.
McCabe said smaller stores, between 1,000 and 2,000 sq metres, had been popular with customers, in sites such as Oxford Street in London and retail parks.
As well as the Oxford Street shop which opened within the former Topshop flagship site, Ikea opened stores in Brighton, Norwich and York last year, followed by a small store in Chester. It also opened a “plan and order” site – dedicated to kitchen, bedroom, and living room planning – in Dundee, and one in Aberdeen last month.

noticias.titulo: Scammed migrant workers in UK to be considered possible victims of modern slavery
noticias.resumen: Home Office changes policy after legal challenge over case of care worker scammed out of £22,000 Migrant workers who are financially exploited can now be considered victims of modern slavery, after a legal challenge by a care worker who was scammed out of £22,000 to pay an agent for a job in the UK that did not exist. The care worker, Ali*, from Pakistan, was put in contact with an agent who told him he could organise a certificate of sponsorship for him to work in a UK care home. The agent was recommended by a friend who said he had been helped to secure a UK care job. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Migrant workers who are financially exploited can now be considered victims of modern slavery, after a legal challenge by a care worker who was scammed out of £22,000 to pay an agent for a job in the UK that did not exist.
The care worker, Ali*, from Pakistan, was put in contact with an agent who told him he could organise a certificate of sponsorship for him to work in a UK care home. The agent was recommended by a friend who said he had been helped to secure a UK care job.
After handing over £22,000 and obtaining what he thought was a genuine certificate of sponsorship and a health and care skilled worker visa from the Home Office, he, his wife and their two young children moved to the UK in October 2023, excited about their new start.
He was keen to begin work as soon as possible as he had incurred heavy debts owed to family members from whom he had borrowed money to cover the cost of obtaining the documents.
After he arrived in the UK, he kept calling the number he had been given to find out when he could start work. Eventually, he was told to go to a car showroom where he met a man who told him he had been scammed, as he had encountered others in a similar situation who had been sent to him too.
Ali was devastated to learn he had lost all the money to a scam. The friend who had recommended the agent told him no job had been forthcoming for him either and so he had returned to Pakistan.
“At that moment I felt like my whole life had just started to cave in,” Ali said in a witness statement about his case. “We had invested everything we had and got into very heavy debts on the basis of this care worker job. I feel trapped by my debts and my family’s needs.”
He and his family were left destitute as a result of the scam. He said that as a result of the extreme stress, his hair turned white and he lost two stone in weight.
Luke Piper, the head of immigration at Work Rights Centre, said the charity had come across many other cases of migrant workers being subjected to financial exploitation. In a recent survey of more than 100 migrant care workers conducted by the charity, nearly three-quarters (74%) had experienced some form of financial exploitation.
“There is a worrying disconnect between those experiencing modern slavery and those getting help,” Piper said.
Ali was referred to the national referral mechanism for potential victims of trafficking and modern slavery and was initially found not to qualify as a potential victim of modern slavery. Supported by Work Rights Centre and Central England Law Centre, he challenged the home secretary for not including financial exploitation in the list of forms of modern slavery.
A judicial review was issued earlier this year and the decision was then reversed so that the Home Office will consider his case as one of potential human trafficking.
The Home Office has admitted in a court order that it previously “adopted an unduly narrow approach to the concept of exploitation” and said it would recognise financial exploitation as a form of modern slavery and trafficking.
Tessa Burwood, the solicitor at Central England Law Centre who represented Ali, said: “Home Office compliance checks for the health and care visa scheme are meant to ensure that vulnerable migrant care workers are only employed by genuine agencies and to prevent the forms of exploitation that are so commonplace in the sector. Something has gone seriously wrong here.
“The fact that financial exploitation will hopefully now be recognised as a form of modern slavery is a small step in the right direction but it is not the end of the nightmare for migrant care workers, who may still face years of uncertainty and instability due to the impact of this poorly conceived visa scheme.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on operational matters, the financial exploitation of visa applicants and visa holders is completely unacceptable. Where evidence of abuse is identified, we work closely with enforcement and safeguarding partners to protect vulnerable people and take action against those responsible.”
*Name has been changed.

noticias.titulo: Democrat Mary Peltola closes in on victory in closely watched US Senate race in Alaska – live
noticias.resumen: Challenger nears 50% of the ballot to secure victory in final midterms contest Protests greet Trump on Asia visit – follow live Sign up for US Breaking News email Abdul El-Sayed , the Democratic-Senator elect from Michigan, said today that he would be happy to work with the Trump administration to pass one of his tentpole policy agenda items – Medicare For All. “Everybody’s like, ‘ah well, you’d work with Donald Trump to get Medicare For All?’. I’m like hell yeah, because the point for me is Medicare For All. I don’t care who puts their name on it. I need to go back and talk to Michiganders, a
noticias.texto:
The final Senate race of this year’s midterm elections could be resolved tomorrow if Alaska election officials run the state’s ranked choice voting system to determine the result.
With 98% of ballots counted, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is out in front with 49.98% of the vote. By contrast, incumbent Republican senator Dan S Sullivan has a 45.93% share, according to the latest Associated Press figures.
In terms of actual voting numbers, Peltola is ahead by just over 11,000, with 141,637 compared to Sullivan’s 130,162. All eyes will be on Peltola to see if she can keep the pace to achieve 50% of the ballot, two weeks on from the election.
If not, then voters’ second choice votes will be counted. The outcome will determine the final balance of power in the chamber for the next two years, with Democrats already holding a 55-44 majority.
It comes in a turbulent Alaska race, which has seen president Trump demand that Peltola be removed from the ballot and prosecuted. Piling on, Alaska’s Republican governor has since ordered an investigation into Peltola’s campaign.
A New York Times investigation reported that operatives working with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit another Dan Sullivan – Dan J Sullivan – a retired teacher from Petersburg, to split the incumbent’s vote. Peltola and her campaign have denied this.
The ‘other’ Sullivan, who stood as an independent candidate, has only received 4,684 votes – a 1.65% share – and is looking unlikely to be the cause of the Republican senator’s failure should he not retain his seat.
Elsewhere, president Trump has arrived in Manila, the capital of the Philippines, for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, where he is due to meet south east Asian leaders and take part in the first leaders’ meeting of the Quad partnership – consisting of the US, Japan, India and Australia – since he returned to the White House in January 2025.
You can follow that here:
In other developments:
Donald Trump defended his commerce secretary Howard Lutnick after he came under fire for allegedly slow-walking export restrictions on Nvidia chips to China. This comes after treasury secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC last week that he has been pushing “for months” to add Megaspeed, the data center company led by an alleged Chinese spy who was reportedly in a relationship with ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, to the US trade blacklist.
Trump blasted the new leadership of CBS News’ 60 Minutes, which was overhauled under the network’s conservative editor-in-chief Bari Weiss. In a social media post, the president was particularly critical of a report on the more than 800 American service members wounded and 23 killed in the war in Iran that 60 Minutes aired on Sunday.
Trump also said that he would “not mind” seeing Jensen Huang reinstated as the chief executive officer of Nvidia. The president says the ex-CEO has learned a lesson, and denied that national security has been put at risk.
The president also continued to shift responsibility to the Biden administration for the nationwide ground stop over the weekend. Trump said that he needed more funding to overhaul the outdated telecommunication system responsible for the disruptions.
The Trump administration has warned Elizabeth Warren, the senior Democratic senator expected to chair the powerful Senate banking committee, that she could face “significant legal consequences” if she fails to preserve records related to investigations into Donald Trump. The warning mirrors other letters justice department officials have sent to Democratic lawmakers who have indicated they will investigate the Trump administration when the party becomes the majority in Congress next year.
A federal appeals court heard arguments in Donald Trump’s hush money case, as the president tries to see the case shifted to federal court where he could have it dismissed on grounds of immunity. The hearing concerned a May 2024 ruling that found Trump guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
In a new memoir, Joe Biden offers harsh criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has led Ukraine through four-and-a-half years of war against Russia. According to Biden, the Ukrainian president was “difficult to work with”, “moody and stubborn in our private conversations”, and “not as grateful as I expected” for US diplomatic support and military aid.
Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, was published on Tuesday, shortly before his 84th birthday and as he battles advanced prostate cancer. Largely a trumpeting of achievements in office, with scant admission of failings ultimately crowned by his own party deeming him unfit for office and forcing his withdrawal from the 2024 campaign against Donald Trump, the book has not been well reviewed.
The war in Ukraine takes up much of the middle of the book. Detailing frustrating talks with Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, Biden describes the buildup to war and US-Ukraine co-operation from the invasion of February 2022 until Biden left office in January 2025.
His portrait of Zelenskyy is not entirely negative.
“I had worried that President Zelenskyy, who had come from such an unlikely background [as a comedian and actor] might not have the right stuff for a crisis like this one,” Biden writes. “This was no TV comedy.” But, the former president adds, he found himself impressed by Zelenskyy’s fortitude, and “delighted that my worries proved to be unfounded”.
At a press conference earlier, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the next House speaker, pledged to extend Affordable Care Act tax credits, restore Medicaid cuts, expand Medicare eligibility, end “the reckless and costly war of choice” on Iran, end tariffs, and end Citizens United.
“Folks are drowning in this Republican economy, and House Democrats are committed to turning that situation around, beginning on day one,” he said.
He also called for banning members of Congress from trading stocks, saying: “That will be a high priority. This is what the American people are demanding that we do, and we are going to execute on that mission.”
Jeffries was speaking ahead of the vote tomorrow to elect the next House speaker, which he is expected to win. Asked about progressive resistance to making him speaker, Jeffries replied: “You’ll have to ask, you know, those individuals that you believe are resistant to voting for me in caucus tomorrow.”
Can Chris Van Hollen really beat Chuck Schumer? – podcast
The blue wave has hit Washington, and with the flood of new Democratic lawmakers comes a debate over who should lead the party. Yesterday, Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen said his campaign to unseat Chuck Schumer as Senate majority leader is gathering momentum. He has painted himself as the underdog candidate to Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade. What does this leadership battle tell us about the kind of party Democrats want to be?
In today’s episode of our Stateside podcast, Kai Wright speaks to the Guardian’s senior politics reporter Chris Steinabout Van Hollen’s chances, and hears from the Guardian’s midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang about why new senators in her region are having doubts about Schumer.
Senators set to vote on controversial nominee to lead FDA
Lawmakers in the Senate health, labor and pensions committee are set to vote on Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the body that oversees approvals for prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs and vaccines, as well as much of the country’s food supply.
Overton has received bipartisan pushback to take over the agency, which sits in the Department of Health and Human Services. During a confirmation hearing in September, she faced questions from Republican and Democratic lawmakers about her stance on vaccines. While she said that “every vaccine on the US market right now is safe and effective”, Overton gave evasive answers about how she would push back against Donald Trump and his administration when they undermine trust in vaccines at a time when the US is experiencing the highest number of measles cases in decades (the US has since lost its measles elimination status).
Overton also did not correct the president’s statement that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) could be “quite lethal” during an executive order announcement about revisions to the childhood vaccine schedule. This despite the scientific consensus that inoculation is the best method of prevention for all three viruses.
At the time, Senator Bill Cassidy, the health committee’s Republican chair, said Overton’s “active role” in the directive was “almost disqualifying”.
On Sunday, Cassidy told CBS News that he remained uncertain about Overton’s path to confirmation. “I still have questions. And so, I cannot tell you the outcome of that vote right now,” the outgoing senator said.
“We’re not going to have perfection,” Cassidy added. “The question is, do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody’s mind but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence,”
If confirmed, Overton, 37, would be the youngest ever FDA commissioner. A former physician, she is now deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy, and served as a White House fellow during Trump’s first term.
Hung Cao faces lawmakers to become permanent Navy secretary as Iran war continues
Hung Cao, who currently serves as the acting Navy secretary, is facing lawmakers on the Senate armed services committee to be confirmed as the permanent top official.
However, in order to be confirmed Cao will need 60 votes for a congressional waiver to exempt him from the federal law that requires former military officers to have been retired from active-duty service for at least seven years before they are eligible to take top civilian Pentagon positions.
Since Cao only retired as a Navy captain in 2021, he’ll need at least seven Democrats to cross the aisle and confirm him, compared to the usual simple majority required for a presidential nomination.
Jensen Huang agrees to appear before House lawmakers in wake of Nvidia scandal
Jensen Huang, the embattled former CEO of Nvidia, will appear before House lawmakers on the House foreign affairs committee, the select committee on the Chinese Communist party, and the House intelligence committee for transcribed interviews on 1 December.
Huang will appear alongside Nvidia’s general counsel Tim Teter.
“We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security,” said Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, the Republican chairs of the respective committees. Huang’s testimony will come after he resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia last week following revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Her company, Megaspeed, was under investigation for purchasing Nvidia’s advanced chips and allegedly diverting them to China.
While the battle between Democrats Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer continues for Senate majority leader in the new Congress, in the House Hakeem Jeffries is still poised to clinch role of Speaker, making history as the first Black member to lead the lower chamber.
As of now, there doesn’t seem to be any clear opposition to Jeffries’ bid. Last week, the long-serving Democratic congressman Glenn Ivey told me on the phone that Jeffries is “a shoo-in”.
“I don’t even know if he’ll have any competition. It could well be done by acclamation [voice vote]. I guess we’ll just have to see,” he added.
Today, however, Punchbowl News reported that Jeffries instead plans to ask for a recorded vote in the Democratic caucus meeting on Wednesday, as a sign that he is not worried about the numbers he has to win.
A reminder that while the election for Senate leadership happens in a closed-door, secret ballot, the House Speaker is elected by the entire chamber in the new year. As of now, Democrats have an 85-seat majority in the House, with 18 races yet to be called.
National Security Agency highly classified network goes down - report
The highly classified network that the national security agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to a report by CNN, citing six people familiar with the matter.
NSA Net, the network, allows the agency’s employees to send classified information internally. According to CNN’s sources, there is no evidence of a cyber-attack, but the NSA has now launched staggered arrivals of their staff.
In lighter news today, new members in the US House are all taking part in the time honored tradition of the suite selection lottery, where every incoming representative has the chance to snag one of the available offices for the new Congress.
El-Sayed: 'It does not matter that you win elections if you don't do anything with the seat'
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic-Senator elect from Michigan, said today that he would be happy to work with the Trump administration to pass one of his tentpole policy agenda items – Medicare For All.
“Everybody’s like, ‘ah well, you’d work with Donald Trump to get Medicare For All?’. I’m like hell yeah, because the point for me is Medicare For All. I don’t care who puts their name on it. I need to go back and talk to Michiganders, and I need to know that our service made their lives easier,” he said at the Atlantic Summit in Washington DC.
Earlier, when asked by interviewer Jonathan Lemire whether El-Sayed would prefer for Democrats to elect more progressive members, or grow a broader electoral map with more diverse ideologies, the incoming lawmaker said that he was less concerned about his colleagues’ politics, as opposed to their ability to unite and pass legislation.
“I don’t need everybody in my caucus to agree with me on everything, but I do need us to get into the business of legislating in ways that protect our rights and provide better, more durable public goods and protect us from the exceeding power of a few very, very large financially oriented organizations in our lives,” El-Sayed said. “It does not matter that you win elections if you don’t do anything with the seat.”
As Republicans scramble to shift blame for the recent chaotic FAA flight stoppage, JD Vance took a new tact, claiming a Democratic focus on transgender sports issues were to blame.
During an interview on Fox News on Monday, host Laura Ingraham pressed Vance on why his fellow Republicans had not been able to fix issues with air traffic control even though they had controlled the White House and Congress for the last two years.
“A lot of the stuff that needed to get fixed, we have been working on and we have been patching that stuff, Laura. But in terms of rebuilding the infrastructure using 21st-century technology, that is something that Congress needs to reinvest, give us the resources to do, and we will absolutely get it done,” Vance said.
Acknowledging that the Democratic party had taken back control of both the US House and the Senate after the 3 November midterms, Vance continued: “We could absolutely do this with Democrats in the new Congress if they set to side the ridiculous obsession with men in women’s sports and did what they said they would do, which was focus on affordability and focus on rebuilding our infrastructure.”
The comment sparked immediate outrage days after a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage on Friday that appears to have been caused by a transition from old copper telecommunication lines to fiber optic cable. The stoppage resulted in thousands of US flights being delayed or canceled, leaving passengers stranded or forcing them to resort to alternate travel methods to try to keep their weekend plans.
“What is this idiot talking about?” Fred Wellman, an incoming Democratic congressman from Missouri, posted on X.
“HE’S SO BAD AT THIS,” posted Pod Save America host Jon Favreau.
“Whatever consultant keeps telling him to randomly connect any issue to trans people is just stealing money,” journalist Jemele Hill posted on X. “The only person who is obsessed with this issue is JD Vance, and he’s not self-aware enough to realize how positively clueless this discourse makes him look.”
And one quick note about the US Senate race in Alaska. If Mary Peltola wins, she will be the first Democrat from the state to be elected to the Senate since 2009.
News of the rule commerce department rule comes at an inopportune time for Donald Trump, who is set to meet with China’s Xi Jinping this week at a trilateral summit alongside Russian president Vladimir Putin.
As my colleague Graeme Wearden notes at our designated business blog, China’s foreign ministry spokesperson GuoJiakun said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, noting that the US has “repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries”.
Trump administration announces ongoing investigation into China-linked data center company Megaspeed
Graeme Wearden
Two departments have confirmed they are investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia’s chips to China.
A joint statement issued by the Department of Commerce and the Department of Justice explains that Megaspeed has been under investigation since 2024, for “potential export control violations.”
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list, they explain.
And they also state that commerce department agents conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.
The Department of Justice then took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
Touting their own work, the departments added:
This investigation is the result of the excellent work of the Department of Commerce under Secretary Howard Lutnick and the law enforcement efforts of the Department of Justice under Attorney General Todd Blanche.
That, presumably, is a response to suggestions that Lutnick could be fired following accusations that he had shielded Nvidia from federal oversight, and had failed to blacklist Megaspeed.
The news of this investigation comes after the commerce department announced an interim final rule on Monday, written by and at the direction of the treasury department and the National Security Council, which curbs remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips by third countries. This includes Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil.
Notably, it addresses the concern that China has been able to use third countries to access advanced chips in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. The involvement of the US treasury department is particularly striking given secretary Scott Bessent’s jabs in an interview with CNBC last week that he has been pushing “for months” for greater exports controls to China on advanced chips, but Howard Lutnick’s commerce department ultimately “has the pen”, when it comes to regulation.
Trump announces deal with Thailand he says will remove tariffs on US exports
Yohannes Lowe
Donald Trump is meeting with Thailand’s prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul to sign what the White House has described as a “trade deal”.
The US president said Thailand will eliminate all tariffs on US exports and remove substantial non-tariff barriers as part of a trade agreement Trump has hailed as “historic”.
“Today’s deal lays the foundation for much stronger trading relationship that will bring the United States and Thailand closer than ever before,”

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO

noticias.texto:
Jensen Huang said he would be willing to return to Nvidia as CEO in his first remarks since resigning from the company Thursday.
“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a statement published in the Wall Street Journal and CNBC.
Nvidia’s board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang, according to reports from the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. However, the company expects to report its quarterly earnings after market close Tuesday , after which it may face questions from analysts and investors about Huang’s future there.
The CEO founded Nvidia in 1993 and ran the company until last week, when he resigned over affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple employees who reported to him.
Huang and Nvidia initially said the executive’s dealings with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean datacenter firm Megaspeed and a suspected spy, were a routine customer relationship. However, Huang disclosed the affair in an email to employees, and the board announced an investigation into its national security implications .
Nvidia’s board has also created a committee to oversee exports and national security issues.
The US government confirmed on Tuesday morning that the commerce and justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024. Though the government has never officially restricted sales and exports to Megaspeed, Nvidia put Megaspeed on an internal “no sell” list in June 2025 after the commerce department requested its records of any sales to Megaspeed, according to a statement from the department. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting US advanced AI chips to Chinese firms in potential violation of export restrictions.
Huang’s full statement is published below.
 Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.
I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.
I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.
Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.
Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

noticias.titulo: Three people killed in plane crash in Arizona’s Grand Canyon national park
noticias.resumen: Wreckage of Piper Comanche aircraft was found on Monday after going missing in park’s North Rim area Three people were killed in a plane crash near the northern rim of Grand Canyon national park in Arizona , the federal park service said on Monday. The Grand Canyon regional communications center received a report of a missing Piper Comanche aircraft at about 11.30pm on Sunday, a statement from officials said . The plane was last known to be in the Basin area of the park’s North Rim, a higher-elevation and less-visited section of the park. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Three people were killed in a plane crash near the northern rim of Grand Canyon national park in Arizona, the federal park service said on Monday.
The Grand Canyon regional communications center received a report of a missing Piper Comanche aircraft at about 11.30pm on Sunday, a statement from officials said. The plane was last known to be in the Basin area of the park’s North Rim, a higher-elevation and less-visited section of the park.
Search crews began looking for the aircraft in the early morning hours on Monday. Officials said they located the wreckage and a debris field in the Basin area at about 10.15am on Monday. All three people onboard the aircraft were killed.
The National Park Service (NPS) has not released the victims’ identities, saying that was out of respect for their families.
According to officials, the crashed aircraft was found after the Arizona department of public safety conducted an aerial search using night vision and forward-looking infrared technology. Coconino county search and rescue, Kane county search and rescue, and the air force rescue coordination center also assisted with the operation.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will investigate the cause of the crash with assistance from the NPS, officials added.
The area where the crash occurred sits between 8,000 and 8,800 feet (2.4 and 2.7km) above sea level, about 1,000 feet (305 meters) higher than the South Rim.

noticias.titulo: US loses measles elimination status amid worst outbreak since 1991
noticias.resumen: Infectious disease is now continually spreading after being eliminated for 26 years, with more than 5,400 US cases The US lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years. The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The US lost its measles elimination status, global health authorities announced, an official recognition that the infectious disease is endemic in the US after being eliminated for 26 years.
The announcement comes as the US endures the worst measles outbreak since 1991, with more than 5,400 cases and eight deaths in 2026.
“Measles is resurging globally amid the persistent gaps in vaccination coverage, and this global trend is also affecting the Americas,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa da Silva Jr, the director of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional branch of the World Health Organization. “The endemic measles transmission has now been re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and United States.” Silva made the final decision on US elimination status.
Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to medicine and requires 95% of the community to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks. The measles vaccine is safe and highly effective. However, pockets of low vaccination have grown in the US following pandemic-era disruptions and widespread misinformation.
The nation’s largest doctors group, the American Medical Association, described loss of measles elimination status as a “deeply troubling and entirely preventable setback for our nation”.
The loss of measles-free status comes after Donald Trump and his health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, spent nearly two years sowing confusion about the safety of vaccines. In just one recent example, Trump called for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combination vaccine to be split into separate shots, arguing without evidence that “together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal”.
“As a pediatrician, I saw firsthand how decisions made in Washington hurt our children and families,” said Dr Annie Andrews, a Democratic senator-elect. “Nothing makes that clearer than the loss of our measles elimination status.” The loss of elimination status has already heightened criticism of Kennedy. High-profile epidemiologists called Kennedy’s work at the health department “malpractice” and equivalent to a “crime scene”.
Barbosa called the role of misinformation in measles transmission “dynamic” and urged health departments to develop bespoke campaigns tailored to under-vaccinated communities.
Experts caution against piling blame for measles outbreaks solely on the Trump administration. The MMR vaccine has been the target of misinformation for more than two decades, including work by Kennedy before his White House role.
“There is a profound problem with measles in all three North American countries,” said Noel Brewer, a behavioral scientist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who studies vaccination behaviors, and specifically measles. He chairs a committee that considers evidence on US measles elimination status, and contributed to the scientific work that underpinned Pan American Health Organization (Paho)’s decision.“The US has had large outbreaks and exported those to Canada and Mexico, and those cases have come back again to the US,” said Brewer.
Canada lost its measles-free status in 2025, but Barbosa said the country now represented the “good news” in the region. The nation stopped measles transmission for 60 days. This is the first step on the way to regaining measles elimination status. The UK and several European nations have also recently lost elimination status.
“What we’re experiencing is not a United States specific thing,” said David Margolius of the Big Cities Health Coalition. Instead, there is a, “global surge in cases, global decline in vaccination rate”.
Public health leaders with the Big Cities Health Coalition (BHC), which leads health departments that serve 47 million Americans, described the announcement as a “profoundly sad moment for our country”.
“Recent declines in measles vaccination rates have opened the door to outbreaks across the country, resulting in preventable illness, hospitalizations, and tragic loss of life,” BHC members said in a statement. “These outcomes are especially heartbreaking because measles is a disease that we know how to prevent. Yet too many voices spreading fear and false information are exacerbating the problem.”
Expert epidemiologists recommended US measles status change during a closed-door meeting in Washington DC. A range of evidence would have been presented, including interviews with positive patients collected by local US health authorities and whole genome sequencing that can provide a fingerprint of the virus’s origin.
Although measles elimination status is an official designation, it carries real consequences for Americans. Where measles cases were once typically imported by international travelers, endemic measles transmission means Americans face new risks of infection, and are being asked to dig up decades-old vaccination certificates and possibly quarantine for 21 days.
“Now is the time to go and find that evidence, because now this is a real day-to-day life thing that could happen to you,” Margolius said earlier in November.
Re-establishing elimination status will require “a national plan to eliminate measles again”, said Brewer, “an integrated plan that’s publicly communicated with specific tasks assigned to named parties”. He added that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the president should speak out “forcefully” in favor of vaccination, and Congress should allocate more funding.

noticias.titulo: US Pentagon fails ninth straight audit despite progress in organizing finances
noticias.resumen: The audits check whether financial statements ​are fairly presented and financial systems ‌and processes are sound The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general ⁠report released on Monday – but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time. The US defense department chief financial officer, Jules Hurst, told ⁠Reuters an independent auditor ⁠found that ​financial statements for 14 of the Pentagon’s 25 standalone reporting entities passed in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September, up from ⁠11 the prior year. noticias.texto:
The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general report released on Monday – but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.
The US defense department chief financial officer, Jules Hurst, told Reuters an independent auditor found that financial statements for 14 of the Pentagon’s 25 standalone reporting entities passed in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended in September, up from 11 the prior year. Those entities account for 56% of the department’s assets – and 86% of its liabilities.
“For the first time ever, a majority of assets from the department are on clean opinions,” Hurst said. The audits check whether financial statements are fairly presented and whether financial systems and processes are sound.
The Pentagon is a vast bureaucracy that has struggled with some 149 financial management systems, many of which are inadequate and outdated. They include technology built on 50-year-old computer code.
As the administration seeks a record $1.5tn in national defense spending from Congress, modernizing those systems has become a priority as the Pentagon strives to show lawmakers it can be trusted.
The Pentagon as a whole was first audited in 2018 and has consistently failed to pass annual audits because of its system and accounting problems. Congress gave it 10 years to pass, which falls in the fiscal year starting in October 2027.
Among the entities passing an audit for the first time in the 2026 fiscal year was the Pentagon’s Medicare-Eligible Retiree Health Care Fund.
To complete an audit without relying on the antiquated systems, officials drew from 61 core systems in the Pentagon’s more modern cloud-based war data platform. They obtained statistically significant data samples that were used for the audit.
The department is also using artificial intelligence tools from Palantir and xAI, alongside in-house applications, to automate financial reconciliations and documentation.
“Passing the audit is ultimately a time problem,” Hurst said, adding that AI allows auditors to test more data.
Beginning this year, the Pentagon plans to consolidate 25 separate audit opinions into eight, ahead of seeking a full department-wide opinion in fiscal 2028.
Congress phased in audit requirements for federal agencies over decades, and most major agencies must have their financial statements audited annually.

noticias.titulo: Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public
noticias.resumen: A cache of internal records outlines the bank's dealings with Jeffrey Epstein, Donald Trump and Russian oligarchs. The German lender has sought to deflect criticism by claiming its bad behavior is a thing of the past.
noticias.texto:
Deutsche Bank under fire after internal documents made public
November 17, 2026
Deutsche Bank is in damage control mode again after an international consortium of more than 200 investigative journalists published internal documents from the global lender on Tuesday under the name "Inside Deutsche Bank."
The documents, published in Der Spiegel, Financial Times, Le Monde and The New York Times, among others, cover Deutsche Bank's business dealings with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, now US President Donald Trump, and a host of Russian oligarchs.
Gleaned from nearly 15 million documents leaked to a journalist from India and another from South Africa, the e-mails and meeting minutes trace the bank's aggressive pursuit of business deals in Russia, and with high-profile Russian oligarchs, right up until Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 — despite risk warnings from numerous managers.
Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing was among the executives who took part in the bank's Russia strategy working group. The bank also still employs more than 160 people in Russia and generated 2025 pre-tax profits of €61 million ($67 million) there through a local subsidiary.
Not just about Deutsche Bank's business with Trump, Epstein and Russians
In all, the documents cover the past 20 years of the German lender's business dealings and raise questions about the efficacy of internal controls by showing that Deutsche Bank had repeatedly put financial interests before international sanctions compliance and anti-money laundering rules.
Other red flags raised in Tuesday's reports suggest that Deutsche Bank sought to set up tax-optimization schemes for wealthy clients, that criminal networks may have been able to move illicit cash through the institution, that it helped facilitate arms deals, that it helped companies in environmentally damaging industries and that it held funds for the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Has Deutsche Bank really changed its ways?
Beyond more recent negative headlines involving alleged anti-money laundering and compliance failures, Deutsche Bank has been trying to restore its public image ever since its involvement in the US subprime mortgage rate scandal helped trigger the 2008 global financial crisis — a fiasco that ultimately cost the bank more than €20 billion in penalties and settlements.
When Sewing later took over in 2018, he promised to turn the institution around. Although he has made Deutsche Bank profitable once again, he did so at the cost of massive job cuts, and some compliance failings have continued.
As its shares fell by up to 6% in Tuesday trading.
Deutsche Bank issued a statement claiming that the reports were old news and that the institution had long ago turned over a new leaf.
In an e-mailed statement to the press, Deutsche Bank Supervisory Board Chairman Alexander Wynaendts wrote, "During my tenure I haven't seen a single decision from Christian Sewing that I was not comfortable with."
A Tuesday statement from the bank described the revelations as "legacy" matters and claimed they would have no lasting negative financial impact on the institution.
Nevertheless, German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Tuesday called on Deutsche Bank to "provide full transparency regarding how it has addressed past failures and internal control deficiencies and how it will effectively prevent these in the future."
Further, Klingbeil said authorities must investigate and "take necessary action" where appropriate.

noticias.titulo: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
noticias.resumen: Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?
noticias.texto:
Saudi Arabia: Crackdown on dissent intensifies amid Iran war
November 17, 2026
Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.
The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.
The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.
In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.
"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.
According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM, the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.
Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?
Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.
"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Lea Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.
This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.
"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.
Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority
Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST, echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.
Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.
However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.
"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.
DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

noticias.titulo: US and Mexico lose measles-free status
noticias.resumen: The United States lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization has said. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status.
noticias.texto:
US and Mexico lose measles-free status
November 17, 2026
The United States is experiencing its highest number of cases in more than three decades. Some 7,700 people in the country have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.
As of November 12, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. US states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the highly contagious virus this year.
Pennsylvania has been the worst-hit state, reporting seven measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases.
Why are measles caseloads rising despite readily available vaccines?
Tuesday's declaration by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but is the latest sign of measles' avoidable resurgence.
"Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said.
Thanks to a series of functioning vaccines, measles had been virtually eradicated throughout most of the developed world for decades.
Vaccine hesitancy and disinformation has risen in recent years in the US, seemingly fueled at least in part by the COVID pandemic.
The rising influence of renowned vaccine critic Robert F. Kennedy Jr., now the US Health Secretary — who dropped out of the 2024 presidential election campaign to form an alliance with Donald Trump — was one of the clearest indicators of this.
"This is a serious warning for our region, but it is not an irreversible setback," PAHO Director Barbosa said. "We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again."
Bolivia, Mexico, US and Canada no longer designated measles-free
As of November 13, PAHO said that the Americas region had reported 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year.
The organization considers endemic transmission to be re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country.
Canada had reached this status in November 2025, with Bolivia, Mexico and the US now deemed to have joined it.
The PAHO said that Canda had "interrupted the chain of transmission" that led to its designation and was working to regain elimination status.
Meanwhile, it said the other three countries "are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response."

noticias.titulo: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
noticias.resumen: The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.
noticias.texto:
Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
November 17, 2026
During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.
Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
What does Russia mean by 1997?
The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.
According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.
What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?
A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.
In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.
"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."
The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.
Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?
In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.
For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.
Who decides which alliances a country can join?
As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.
Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.
Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?
During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.
Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.
In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.
In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.
Why is the demand back on the table?
Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.
Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.
So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.
This article was originally published in German.

noticias.titulo: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
noticias.resumen: The European Court of Human Rights has called for the release of imprisoned elected lawmaker Can Atalay. Atalay has been in prison for almost five years despite rulings from the Turkish Constitutional Court.
noticias.texto:
Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
November 17, 2026
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.
The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.
The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.
It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.
The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.
Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.
From leading activist to a jailed member of parliament
As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.
He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.
Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."
Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.
A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.
His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.
Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.
After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

noticias.titulo: Fresh clashes at the Eritrean border — is Ethiopia sliding into a regional war?
noticias.resumen: As Ethiopian troops push Tigrayan forces toward the Eritrean border, fears of a new regional war are growing. With tensions rising between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, the Horn of Africa faces uncertain times ahead.
noticias.texto:
Ethiopia-Eritrea border clashes raise fears of regional war
November 17, 2026
After a few weeks of relative stability, fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border areahave raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudanhave hit new lows.
Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23. It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia.
According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme.
While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War.
The war ended with theAlgiers Agreement, in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea, a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles.
"It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said.
He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region.
The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea
"The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time", Abdurahman Sayed said.
Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forcesduring the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties. At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray.
Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces.
"So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW.
However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time."
Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab, by force.
Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads
At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further.
Sudan and Egypt, both downstream the river Nile, have been on edge for years because of Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (GERD). The massive GERD, built on the Blue Nile just kilometers from Ethiopia's border with Sudan, gives Addis Ababa significant leverage over the timing and regulation of water flows downstream, raising concerns in Sudan and Egypt over water security and dam operations. The Ethiopian government has rejected claims that the dam could be used as a means to pressure Sudan and Egypt.
Since 2023, Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war between two rival military forces: the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. In mid-November, both sides accused the other of direct participation in each other's internal conflicts.
Two countries with severe internal conflicts and mirroring alliances: Could the situation deteriorate further into potential direct fights between the two armies? ICG's Magnus Taylor believes there is a risk, but at least not for now.
"The most likely scenario is we just get a continuation of this kind of proxy style of involvement with each other's opposition groups rather than formal direct involvement on the ground in the conflict," Taylor said.
Sayed also believes that, at the moment, there is no need for direct confrontation.
"The RSF can do the job that Ethiopia and any other country backing them wants them to do," Sayed said. "But if there is a need and the RSF are failing, the Ethiopian army could be pushed to get involved."

noticias.titulo: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
noticias.resumen: Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.
noticias.texto:
Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
November 17, 2026
Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.
This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.
The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.
What are Nvidia's plans for the new oversight committee?
Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.
Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).
The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.
Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.
"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.
The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.
The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month. 
How has the scandal highlighted the question of US-China chip trade?
US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.
"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."
Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.
Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.
That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.
The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

noticias.titulo: Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington
noticias.resumen: Iran has said CNN's claim that Tehran would attack Washington with a "dirty bomb" was an attempt to manufacture further legitimacy to continue the war. Trump has said his administration takes the claim "very seriously."
noticias.texto:
Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington
November 17, 2026
Iran on Tuesday dismissed a CNN report that Tehran was preparing a so-called "dirty bomb plot."
US President Donald Trump said his administration was taking the report "very seriously."
What did reports say about an Iranian attack on Washington?
Tehran's dismissal came after CNN reported on Tuesday that "Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC," citing multiple US intelligence sources.
The article also reported that "US intelligence has picked up Iranian chatter claiming that it has stashed bomb-making materials inside the country" and that "many national security officials assume that pre-positioned nuclear materials have already been in the US for years," citing, again, multiple US intelligence sources.
When asked about the story during his visit to the Philippines, Trump said that if there was such a threat, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."
"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.
Iran decries 'fabrication'
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei slammed the report, calling it "a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda."
"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations," he said on X.
"Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," he said, naming CNN's reporting on the alleged "dirty bomb plot" and The New York Times without specifying any of its reporting.
Baghaei also said the US and Israel hit water storage reservoirs "during the recent acts of aggression."
Where does the Iran war stand?
The Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, continues as negotiations to bring an end to the fighting stall.
Both US and Israel have been holding off from major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.
Tehran has said it is in control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway. There are near-daily reports of ships hitting mines in parts of the strait Tehran says are unauthorized for transit.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait.
Before the midterm elections, Trump said, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes that started the war, though he did not provide any timeframe.
Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of an APEC leaders' summit in China on Thursday and discuss ending the war in Iran.
Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.
Qatar, another mediator in the war, on Tuesday called for restraint "to avoid any escalation that could undermine negotiation efforts."

noticias.titulo: APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
