noticias.resumen: Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?
noticias.texto:
APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
November 17, 2026
The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.
Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.
Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.
Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."
Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.
"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.
"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."
Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.
Contentious issues may be left for later
Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.
She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.
Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."
She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.
With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.
China, the US and Russia: three leaders, three agendas
Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.
Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine.
"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."
Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.
"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."
Ukraine: why Beijing is reluctant to mediate
Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.
Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.
An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.
Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."
The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.
He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."
He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.
"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.
"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."
Iran: little sign of substantive cooperation
W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran.
The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."
Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.
"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

noticias.titulo: EU, ASEAN pursue deeper trade ties, but hurdles remain as businesses struggle with informal barriers
noticias.resumen: 2027 could be a landmark year for EU–Southeast Asia trade, with several deals nearing completion. But the harder task will be to ensure that businesses actually use them.
noticias.texto:
EU, ASEAN pursue deeper trade ties, but hurdles remain
November 17, 2026
The European Union and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could be heading for a breakthrough year in 2027, when the two sides mark 50 years of diplomatic ties.
A long-awaited trade agreement with Indonesia is expected to take effect, while a deal with the Philippines is nearing completion and negotiations with Thailand and Malaysia are making progress. By the end of next year, the EU could have trade deals in place with six Southeast Asian states, up from just two today.
The anniversary could also revive the long-standing ambition of a broader trade agreement between the EU and ASEAN.
On November 17, the European Commission hosted a dialogue in Brussels to discuss trade relations with Southeast Asia, including progress on existing and pending free trade agreements (FTAs).
But attention is turning to what comes next. "Finalizing FTAs is only the beginning, not the end," Chris Humphrey, executive director of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, told DW.
FTAs can reduce tariffs and remove trade restrictions, but that is of little use if businesses don't know how to use them, he added.
"Unfortunately, in many cases, this is where there is a failure. Communication and training are key," Humphrey said.
The hard work begins after signing
For Brussels, the priority should now be to tackle the less conspicuous obstacles to trade, he stressed.
Cutting customs delays, simplifying regulations, and helping smaller European businesses enter unfamiliar Southeast Asian markets will determine whether an FTA succeeds.
"European companies with little or no experience in Southeast Asia would benefit from greater on-the-ground support, particularly practical, firsthand guidance on informal business practices and the unwritten local rules," Alfred Gerstl, an associate professor at Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic, told DW.
One option is to expand the assistance offered by European chambers of commerce, trade delegations, and EU offices in Southeast Asia. This could range from helping firms find distributors to explaining local licensing requirements and how to qualify for preferential tariffs.
In Vietnam, for instance, sustained pressure from Brussels has helped improve market access for European pharmaceutical firms. In Indonesia, the EU has worked on trade facilitation while pressing Jakarta over import restrictions and halal certification requirements, said Camille Nessel, a researcher at the Universite Libre de Bruxelles.
Regular consultations with businesses on both sides could also help Brussels spot problems before they become trade disputes.
Trade policy has also acquired a geopolitical purpose in Brussels. "If trade policy is expected to reduce strategic dependencies, we are asking it to deliver on objectives that remain insufficiently defined, let alone demonstrating how to achieve them," Nessel told DW.
Diversifying trade and reducing dependencies
The EU wants to reduce its dependence on a handful of suppliers for the minerals needed for batteries and other clean technologies, while Southeast Asian producers, particularly Indonesia, want foreign investors to help develop domestic processing industries rather than merely buy raw materials.
The EU and Indonesia have already clashed over Jakarta's restrictions on nickel exports.
European investment in processing facilities, agreements on environmental standards, and greater regulatory certainty would give both sides concrete gains, said Nessel. "The real value of an FTA is not just opening a market but giving the EU the leverage to keep it open," she added.
Pasha Hsieh, Lee Kong Chian Professor of Law and Jean Monnet Chair at Singapore Management University, said Brussels should prioritize ratifying its investment protection agreements with Singapore and Vietnam.
Signed in 2018 and 2019, respectively, the agreements still require ratification by all EU member states before entering into force. "These delays underline the need to follow through on negotiated commitments," Hsieh said.
The issue is particularly relevant as the EU looks to develop investment protocols in other Southeast Asian states where investors have sometimes faced uncertainty over legal protections. Indonesia, for instance, has terminated numerous bilateral investment treaties, including agreements with the Netherlands and Spain.
Towards an EU-ASEAN trade agreement?
A larger question is whether the EU should continue pursuing bilateral deals with Southeast Asian countries or revive its original ambition of a region-to-region agreement with ASEAN.
The EU and ASEAN launched negotiations for a region-wide FTA in 2007 but suspended them two years later amid disagreements over wide economic disparities among ASEAN members and political concerns. Technical discussions resumed in 2017, but little has come of them.
ASEAN already has regional agreements with China and several other economies. Beijing upgraded its free trade agreement with ASEAN in October 2025.
Region-to-region frameworks extend beyond trade. Humphrey, of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, called for negotiations to begin on a region-to-region Digital Trade Agreement and Investment Protection Agreement.
The EU-Singapore Digital Trade Agreement, which entered into force in February 2026, offers a possible model for wider cooperation, he noted, adding that common approaches to customs procedures, supply-chain standards, and green technologies could create greater alignment with ASEAN members that are not yet ready for full FTAs.
"European businesses have long complained of operating at a disadvantage due to the lack of a region-to-region deal. It is high time that both sides elevated their ambitions and embraced the idea of working towards such an agreement," Humphrey said.
The 2027 anniversary would be a convenient deadline for agreeing on what comes next, but Gerstl warned against mistaking another round of diplomatic ceremony for progress.
"There is a risk that attention will focus almost exclusively on the 2027 summit in Singapore and that the group photo will become the defining image of the event, only for momentum to fade in the years that follow," he added.

noticias.titulo: Guinea jails 200 in wildcat gold mining crackdown
noticias.resumen: A Conakry court has jailed 22 former local officials from the gold-rich northeastern Siguiri region, as well as 200 people accused of illegal mining. It's part of a wider crackdown that sent thousands fleeing into Mali.
noticias.texto:
Guinea jails 200 in wildcat gold mining crackdown
November 17, 2026
Guinea on Tuesday jailed 22 former regional administrators and 202 others accused of illegal gold mining in the northeastern Siguiri region near the border to Mali.
According to the UN Environment Program, unauthorized gold mining is a source of income for more than 300,000 people in Guinea. The country's rich gold mines pull in workers from across West Africa.
What happened in the gold mining trial in Conakry?
Conakry's Court for the Repression of Economic and Financial Offenses sentenced 22 former officials from Siguiri to two years each in prison for complicity in environmental degradation, destruction and water pollution. They were each fined 10 million Guinean francs (around €1,025 or $1,125).
The court also sentenced 202 alleged illegal miners — several of them foreign nationals — to three-year prison sentences. They faced the same charges plus an additional count of mining illegally.
They were ordered to pay a combined fine of 10 billion Guinean francs.
Beyond that, the foreign nationals were banned from Guinean territory for a period of 10 years.
Why is Guinea cracking down on illegal mining?
Guinea's government announced a bid to stamp out illegal gold mining earlier this month, saying it wanted to prevent damages to farmland and rivers and other environmental destruction.
These efforts turned violent last week as protesters and security forces clashed in the northeast, with 10 people killed and 13 injured.
More than 1,200 artisanal miners were arrested in Siguiri in November.
Many more fled across the border to nearby Mali, often then having to await transportation to their homes in Burkina Faso.

noticias.titulo: US flexes climate action muscle at COP31 despite Trump no-show
noticias.resumen: The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show climate action in the US is alive and well.
noticias.texto:
US flexes climate action muscle at COP31 despite Trump no-show
November 17, 2026
The United States, isn't at the table at the UN climate conference in the Turkish coastal city of Antalya. It's the second consecutive year that President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly said he believes climate change is a hoax, has not sent a federal delegation to the annual summit.
But that doesn't mean the US is totally absent. Far from it, since more than 120 state and local leaders from across the country are attending as part of the "America Is All In" coalition.
"We understand the importance of showing up. And if others refuse to do so, we will," said Chris Wheat, executive director of the coalition.
It's crucial, he added, to show the world that "millions of Americans are continuing to press forward on climate action" — even if the message from Washington, D.C., is a different one.
Historically, the US has released more emissions than any other country, and it is currently the world's second-biggest emitter of planet-warming greenhouse gases after China. Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has actively promoted the use of oil, coal and gas, the fossil fuels that are heating the planet and contributing to an increase in extreme weather events.
The president has also cut funds for clean energy projects and rolled back some of the climate policies of his predecessors, such as rules limiting power plant emissions.
Momentum beyond White House
The unofficial US delegation of mainly Democrat lawmakers, mayors, governors and ex-officials — including former Secretary of State John Kerry, former Vice President Al Gore and California Governor Gavin Newsom — are not taking part in the climate negotiations. But they have been holding discussions at events on the conference sidelines.
They are keen to send a message to the international community that, despite their government's absence, efforts to transition to clean energy are gathering pace at the state level.
Mike Williams, a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, an independent liberal public policy research institute based in Washington D.C., said the presence of US lawmakers in Antalya sends an important signal that "there's quite a lot of us in the US that are still deeply invested in this. It's not just the person sitting in the White House."
Nearly half of US states, representing about 60% of the US economy, are committed to reducing emissions in line with the Paris Agreement — the 2015 global pact to limit global warming. Many have implemented initiatives such as tax incentives for renewables and other policies designed to curb emissions.
A report by America Is All In and the University of Maryland's Center for Global Sustainability found that current state policies, combined with market trends and falling technology costs, could slash US carbon emissions by up to 46% below 2005 levels by 2035.
States tout climate action
"Even if we find a hostile federal government, they're not going to be able to stop the momentum," Minnesota Governor and Kamala Harris' running mate during the 2024 presidential election Tim Walz told a crowd at the summit in Turkey, adding that his state was on track to have a "100% carbon free" grid by 2037, earlier than their target of 2040.
Walz said the state was also producing sustainable aviation fuel to reduce flight emissions, manufacturing green steel and increasing the share of electric vehicles. "It's all moving forward," he said. "So this false choice that we need to choose the economy over clean energy — that has been totally rejected."
New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham said her state — the second-largest oil and gas producer in the US — had significantly cut emissions from the potent greenhouse gas methane through stricter regulations. She also touted measures such as shutting down coal power plants and expanding wind and solar energy.
"The largest wind farm in North America is in New Mexico," she said. "We're going to show the federal government, I am undaunted by their lack of responsibility and effort in cleaning up fossil fuels."
What's next for US climate policy after midterms?
The climate conference comes shortly after the US midterm elections, in which Trump's Republicans suffered a significant defeat. Democrats in Antalya have been keen to reassure the international community that the US would return to the COP table in the event of a change of government in two years.
Jorge Gastelumendi, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Climate Resilience Center, noted that US credibility around climate change and foreign policy in general had been "badly damaged" under Trump. "And so it's going to be a matter of how that could be built back up."
Meanwhile, Governor Newsom of California, a state of around 40 million people that plans to get 100% of its energy from renewables by 2045, said the US administration's climate withdrawal was also hurting the country's competitiveness.
"We need to reengage in these international agreements, and we need to recognize that China is outpacing us in many critical areas," such as solar power and electric cars, he told reporters in Antalya. "There is no substitute for national leadership."
Williams from the Center for American Progress said he wouldn't hold it against any countries wary about the US returning to the climate negotiations after two exits under Trump.
"Nobody should be under any perception that the US would be welcomed back with open arms," he said. "I think there needs to be an effort to show a willingness to collaborate […] That's another reason why it's important we're here now to show that there is this very large undercurrent of support within the US in spite of what's happening."

noticias.titulo: Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens
noticias.resumen: Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.
noticias.texto:
Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens
November 17, 2026
Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.
The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.
The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.
Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.
Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.
According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.
90 days to form a government
The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.
The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.
They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.
The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.
A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.
Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

noticias.titulo: Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future
noticias.resumen: Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.
noticias.texto:
Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future
November 17, 2026
"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.
Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.
"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.
"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."
The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.
Klopp hallmarks starting to emerge
It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.
The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.
"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.
"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."
That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.
Scherhant, Gruda and Wirtz make their cases
But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.
"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.
Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.
"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.
"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."
Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."
Germany need to change perceptions
While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.
"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."
Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.
"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.
In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine updates: Russia-Crimea bridge appears destroyed after strike
noticias.resumen: Zelenskyy said a strike on the Kerch bridge in Crimea was in response to continued Russian attacks targeting his country's infrastructure. Meanwhile, two bridges were hit in Russian attacks on Kyiv. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine updates: Russia-Crimea bridge appears destroyed after strike
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 17, 2026
What you need to know
- Ukraine strike hits Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea to the Russian mainland, stopping traffic
- Images show part of the bridge destroyed
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the strike on Kerch bridge an 'unprecedented operation'
- Russia also struck two important bridges in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said
- The attacks come as Ukrainian, European and US negotiators discuss future talks with Russia on ending the war
These are the main developments from Russia's war in Ukraine on November 17, 2026:
Germany's Pistorius defends Ukraine after bridge strike
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.
Pistorius said criticism of Ukraine's deep strikes in Russia was misplaced. He added that the focus should be on Russia's repeated attacks on Ukraine's energy, water and heating infrastructure.
He added that attacks inside Russia against non-civilian targets and sites used by the military are legal and legitimate targets.
Moldova says Russian drone flew over its capital
The government of Moldova said it had temporarily closed its airspace for security reasons after authorities detected a Shahed-type drone.
"For security reasons, the authorities have closed down the entire airspace of the Republic of Moldova," the country's Defense Ministry said in a statement.
Moldovan police said they received several reports from Chisinau residents who heard explosions.
The drone incursions into Moldova involved one drone reportedly flying over the country's eastern regions, while a second one entered the southern part of the country and flew towards Chisinau.
Moldovans were urged not to approach suspicious flying objects or touch any drone debris found, as it could contain "explosive elements."
Moldova, which borders Ukraine, has reported several fallen drones on its territory since the beginning of Russia's invasion of Ukraine. But none of them had reached the capital.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu rejected what she called "the boundless cynicism of Moscow's leaders" and vowed to continue supporting Kyiv in the war.
"This evening several Russian drones violated our airspace, one of them over Chisinau, alarming residents," Sandu wrote on X.
"Russia's war threatens all of Europe," she said. "Moldova stands for peace. We'll keep pushing for sanctions on Moscow, standing with Ukraine and building our defence with partners."
US criticizes Ukraine for Crimea bridge strike
A top US official criticized Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, saying it could provoke Russia into further escalation.
US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war" or, Colby added, in blunting Russia's advances.
"Such strikes, especially those that target civilian infrastructure such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public's resolve and the Kremlin's own willingness to escalate," Colby told a gathering of Ukraine's backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
Wildberries is a Russian e-commerce giant targeted by Kyiv. Its CEO, Tatyana Kim, was added to the list of EU sanctions Monday.
It all comes as Trump said he may discuss the Ukraine war during a highly anticipated meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday.
WATCH — Ukraine hits strategic Russian bridge to Crimea
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed the partial destruction of Russia's strategic Kerch bridge, which connects occupied Crimea with Russia proper.
Biresh Banerjee speaks to Ukrainian lawmaker Lesia Vasylenko and DW's Kyiv correspondent Nick Connolly about the attack and the overall situation in Ukraine.
France rejects claims its troops are fighting in Ukraine
France on Tuesday rejected Russian claims that French troops deployed in Ukraine were directly involved in fighting against Russian troops.
"Not only French ones, we know this. We have conveyed our concern... this is no longer support for Ukraine, but direct participation in the war," Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told reporters.
The French government said the accusation was "absurd."
Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo told parliament that a "very limited" deployment of French troops is in Ukraine for training and equipment maintenance.
"There is the absence of any intention to fight, contrary to what the Russian foreign minister said this morning, which is absurd," she added.
Germany reacts to Crimean bridge attack
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul urgently called for a negotiated settlement to the war in Ukraine, after a Ukrainian airstrike partially destroyed a bridge to the Crimean Peninsula.
"The last thing we need before this winter is another escalation," Wadephul said during a visit to Azerbaijan. "What is needed now are bold steps towards a negotiated settlement. And I hope there is now the necessary resolve for this everywhere."
He described the attack that damaged the bridge as difficult for Russia, underlining the need to step up efforts to find a negotiated settlement.
"Russia started this war in violation of international law. And it must live with the consequences," Wadephul said.
IN PICTURES: The Kerch bridge before and after Tuesday's strike
WATCH: Could attacks on Ukraine's power grid trigger a nuclear disaster?
European regulators warn that a nationwide blackout could create cooling problems at several Ukrainian reactors simultaneously. How realistic is that scenario, and how well prepared are the plants?
Hungary suspends Ukraine rail traffic after Russian drone attack
Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said that rail traffic was being suspended to and from Ukraine on Tuesday and Wednesday, after a Russian drone came down in Western Ukraine.
"A Russian drone recently crashed in Zakarpattia, 300 metres from the Mukachevo railway station. The Hungarian crew of a train arriving from Hungary was ordered to disembark," Magyar said in a Facebook post.
"We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for today and tomorrow," Magyar said.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban had earlier said that Russian drones had attacked Zakarpattia, targeting areas near Mukachevo and Uzhhorod, not far from the border area with Hungary.
"As Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukraine's civilian population, similar operations against Zakarpattia, which until now has been relatively protected due to its geographical location, can also be expected in the future," she said.
IN PICTURES: Kerch bridge strike
Vladimir Putin briefed on Kerch bridge strike — Russian media
Russia state media has reported that President Vladimir Putin has been briefed by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin "on the situation around the Crimean Bridge," citing Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov.
"Following the government commission meeting, Marat Khusnullin reported to President Putin on the situation surrounding the Crimean Bridge," Peskov told reporters.
"According to the Investigative Committee, on November 16 and 17, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the Crimean Bridge using unmanned aerial vehicle, resulting in damage to the structure," TASS reported.
Russian media also quoted Peskov as saying that the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia would be "even better" after it was restored, giving an indication as to the extent of the damage caused.
"There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before," Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.
Ukraine's Zelenskyy confirms strike on Kerch bridge
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that the Kerch bridge was targeted by Ukrainian forces, describing it as "an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure."
"Today, everyone can see the consequences for the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea," Zelenskyy said in a lengthy post on social media platform X.
The Ukrainian leader said the strike was a culmination of an operation "carried out over several weeks" by his country's military and involved destroying air defense systems, radar systems and electronic warfare equipment in the lead up to the attack.
Zelenskyy said that the road section of the bridge was hit by "Palianytsia" drones and while the railway section was targeted by "Neptune" missiles and "Ruta" drones.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," Zelenskyy said and pointed to continued Russian strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure.
His post was accompanied by footage appearing to show the moment the bridge was struck and then the subsequent aftermath with one part of the bridge collapsed.
Germany and Norway to purchase more air defenses for Ukraine
Germany and Norway will fund a new US air defense package for Ukraine's defensive needs, according to Germany's defense chief.
"Russia is intensifying its air attacks because it is not making progress on the battlefield," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said at an EU meeting in Brussels.
Pistorius said that Germany would contribute $300 million (€272 million) towards the weapons package that would include Patriot interceptor missiles.
The package will also include previously announced IRIS-T systems, as well as new radars and ammunition for F-16 fighter jets and drones.
The announcement comes ahead of a meeting of Ukraine's military backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels later today.
Germany has, since the start of Russia's invasion, provided civilian aid totalling more than €45.7 billion and provided or earmarked military aid of around €57.8 billion, according to the German government.
Power outages in 9 Ukrainian regions after Russian strikes — energy official
Ukraine's Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov, said that Russian strikes on energy infrastructure had caused power outages in nine Ukrainian regions.
"As a result of the strikes, some consumers have been left without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Rivne, Sumy, Chernihiv and Chernivtsi regions," Nekrasov said.
"The situation is extremely difficult in the Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Since last week, Russia has been continuously attacking energy facilities in the Dnipro region," Nekrasov said.
Russian government talks to be held after Kerch strike — Russian media
A government meeting is expected to take place soon following the strike on the Kerch bridge, Russian state media agency TASS reported.
"A meeting of the government commission on the aftermath of the attack on the Crimean Bridge, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, will be held soon at Government House," TASS quoted the Russian government as saying.
"The meeting will address issues related to the restoration of the Crimean Bridge and the organization of transport links," TASS reported.
The extent of the damage caused is not yet known and Russian officials have only confirmed that a strike had taken place and that traffic has been disrupted.

noticias.titulo: Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
noticias.resumen: The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.
noticias.texto:
Could the Airbus' €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?
November 17, 2026
A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.
The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.
"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."
He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.
An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."
A thorn in the side of EU-US trade relations
Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.
The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.
A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.
The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.
"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.
She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.
Does the €3 billion Airbus loan amount to state support?
At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.
"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."
A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.
A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."
Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.
Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.
Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.
"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."
In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.
"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."
He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.
"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."
It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants.
Why the Airbus-Boeing subsidy dispute keeps resurfacing
Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."
She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.
"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."
Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.
"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

noticias.titulo: Turkish authorities raid opposition Sozcu news channel, appoint new management
noticias.resumen: Turkish authorities have raided the Istanbul offices of Sozcu TV, halting broadcasts, appointing a trustee and opening an investigation. This marks another crackdown on pro-opposition television channels in Turkey.
noticias.texto:
Turkish authorities raid opposition Sozcu news channel
November 17, 2026
Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of the pro-opposition Sozcu TV early on Tuesday, arresting admins and installing a government trustee as the head, the group said on X.
The channel announced in a predawn post that police were searching the building under a court order.
What did Sozcu say about the raid by Turkish police?
"Police are searching the Sozcu building under a court order. Police have cordoned off the building," its official X account said in just before 5 a.m. (0200 GMT).
"A trustee has been appointed to Sozcu! Police are searching the building... There have been detentions," it said, with its journalists saying staff were not being allowed inside.
According to the media group, the trustee took control of the television channel and the news website but not the print newspaper.
After the raid, regular news broadcasts were stopped and a documentary was shown instead.
At noon, the channel resumed its regular coverage, mentioning the raids only at the beginning of the broadcast. One of the channel's news presenters, Damla Dogan Tuncel, said on X that the channel had challenged the decision and was awaiting a court ruling.
"In the meantime, the broadcast would continue with normal news bulletins," she said.
'Terrorism' charges
The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said the action against Sozcu TV was part of an investigation into alleged breaches of Turkey's "anti-terror financing laws."
The prosecutor's office claimed that the channel had suspected links to a network that was led by US-based cleric Fethullah Gulen. The cleric, who died in 2024, was accused by Turkey of orchestrating a failed military coup in 2016.
Sozcu Media Group lawyer Ersan Barkin said the raids stemmed from a 2016 case that Turkey's Supreme Court had previously dismissed, finding no evidence of criminal intent or wrongdoing.
"This trustee decision stems from a file in which no offence was established," he told KRT TV.
Government silences last critical news channels
The move is the latest suppression of critical linear media in Turkey, coming a month after the police raided the country's most-watched news channel, Halk TV, and installed an administrator.
Since then, news broadcasts on the channel have remained on pause.
Another pro-opposition news channel TELE1 was also raided and seized by the government, while its owner Merdan Yanardag was jailed on espionage charges.
Over the last decade, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government has seized control of most of the media landscape, particularly television broadcasters.
While the critical voices were pushed onto the online space, Halk TV and Sozcu TV were prominent pro-opposition voices in TV.
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index, Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Deutsche Welle correspondent Alican Uludag was also jailed and released this year on charges including insulting President Erdogan.
Opposition lashes out at the government
Opposition leader Ozgur Ozel, whose party was also raided and seized by a trustee, said "the government no longer has any tolerance left for even the slightest criticism."
"May our hearts wither if we surrender to these would-be dictators," he said on X.
Istanbul Mayor and Erdogan's jailed rival Ekrem Imamoglu said "the government's election fear is growing and growing."
"With courage, perseverance, and determination, people will continue the struggle," he said, from his blocked X account.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire
noticias.resumen: Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire
Published November 17, 2026last updated November 17, 2026
What you need to know
- German human rights group Pro Asyl has said plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected migrants to Rwanda will be a "shipwreck"
- Germany expects to see the highest number of new businesses opening in 2026 in more than a decade
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finnish President Alexander Stubb for talks expected to focus on security policy and Russia's invasion of Ukraine
- A massive leak of internal documents from Deutsche Bank has exposed misconduct and incompetence at the lender, media say
Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:
German universities draw in largest number of foreign students in EU
New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.
Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.
France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.
The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.
Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%) had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.
Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.
UN rights chief voices concerns over Rwanda deportation plans
The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers to a deportation hub in Rwanda.
Türk said he had not yet seen the draft proposal but that his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by the proposed transfer of people from five European Union countries to Rwanda, where they have no genuine connection and which has its own set of human rights challenges."
Instead, he called for a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."
Lufthansa and VC pilots' union negotiations end without breakthrough
Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.
The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.
VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.
"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.
Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.
VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.
The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.
Berlin bans association accused of supporting Hezbollah
The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.
Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.
The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.
The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.
The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.
Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.
Rwanda migrant deportation hub scheme condemned by rights groups
A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.
The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.
The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."
Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.
"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.
"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."
In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.
"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.
"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.
Criticism from within the coalition
The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.
"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.
"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."
Rwanda deportation hub planned for 2027
The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.
According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.
Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.
German government at odds over Rwanda plan
The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.
Germany funding $300 million more US arms supplies for Ukraine — Pistorius
Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.
He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.
Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.
He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.
He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.
Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.
He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.
Wadephul wants closer ties with Azerbaijan, Armenia to counter Russia
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.
"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.
He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.
Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.
German foreign minister in the Caucasus
Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.
He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.
In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.
This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.
Deutsche Bank shares plummet after reports on incriminating documents leak
Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.
The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.
The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.
Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.
Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."
It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."
European Commission doubles growth forecast for Germany
The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.
The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.
The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.
Number of start-ups set to reach highest level since 2015
Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).
The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.
However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.
In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.
The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.
The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.
Welcome to our coverage
DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!
Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.
Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."
Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.
And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.
Read on here for more on these and other German stories!

noticias.titulo: What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
noticias.resumen: When "GTA VI" is released on November 19, millions of people worldwide will rush to their consoles to play it. How has this video game created such a cross-generational buzz?
noticias.texto:
What makes 'Grand Theft Auto VI' more than just a game?
November 17, 2026
"Oh, it's so on now!" is the tagline in the latest trailer for the video game "Grand Theft Auto VI," or "GTA VI" for short.
"GTA VI" is a game of superlatives that's been crashing through records. The hype around it is unparalleled. No game in history has clocked so many pre-orders. It's thought that around 10 million people have already purchased it. There's no denying it: "GTA VI" is a global cultural phenomenon.
A few days before its release on November 19, fans can already start downloading the game. The file is so large that downloading it can take several days, depending on the internet connection. Providers have already registered a significant spike in data traffic.
As soon as the game is unlocked, players can start speeding through the fictional US metropolis of Vice City in a stylish sports car with criminal couple Jason and Lucia.
Miami gets cast as Vice City
To mark the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," its real-life inspiration — Miami — is getting a full-scale "Vice City" makeover. This promotional push includes the Miami Heat basketball team stepping onto the hardwood in custom "Vice City" jerseys for a home game, a local festival featuring artists from the game's official soundtrack, and roadside "Vice City" signage installed across the area.
Expectations for "GTA VI" are sky-high. Nearly 5,000 people have been working on the game for more than 10 years. Development costs are estimated at around $1 billion (€900 million).
"Based on those figures alone — as well as the series' extremely successful and popular track record — this can certainly be described as a truly exceptional release," says Rudolf Thomas Inderst, cultural studies scholar and professor of Game Design and Game Studies at Germany's Neu-Ulm University of Applied Sciences.
When such an effort is put into a product, it's only natural for people to expect great things, he adds. Inderst is expecting "GTA VI" to showcase the absolute best of what modern gaming can do across gameplay, storytelling, visuals and tech.
Social satire and gameplay freedom
This video game series has been around for almost three decades, setting new standards through its different versions. A biting satire on US society and the American dream, "GTA" parodies politics, culture and the media.
The game is also renowned for its gameplay freedom and spectacularly staged chaos in a crazy world where players can do whatever they please. Shoot down helicopters with a bazooka, go to the hairdresser's, take a stroll on the beach, go to a nightclub, take part in car races and much more.
What makes it a standout among video games is how its NPCs — non-player characters, those not being controlled by a human player — are brought to life. They respond based on a player's interactions with them, displaying individualized behaviors and traits ranging from fear to hostility. "GTA VI" has an estimated 600,000 animations for the civilians in the fictional state of Leonida.
'Grand Theft Auto,' a long-running hit
"GTA VI" is essentially a huge adult playground, striking a chord across several generations. Millennials grew up with "Grand Theft Auto III," "Grand Theft Auto: Vice City," "Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas," and "Grand Theft Auto IV," while Gen Z grew up with "Grand Theft Auto V." Generation Alpha might still be too young for the latest edition, but will likely find ways to play it anyway.
Social media has certainly played a part in the series' ongoing success, particularly "GTA V" and its multiplayer spin-off, "GTA Online." Numerous content creators stream gameplay sessions on Twitch or YouTube, and particularly funny or crazy gameplay moments end up on TikTok.
At the same time, a dedicated role-play community has grown around the game. Players gather inside the world of "GTA" to act out specific characters, such as taxi drivers, judges or small-time criminals. They invent realistic backstories for their personas, and many even use accents to stay in character.
Perfectionism has its downsides
The hype surrounding "GTA VI" is not only good news for the game itself but could also boost the entire games industry by drawing more people back to their consoles. This is because the boom triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic was followed by studio closures and redundancies. Worldwide, it's estimated that 50,000 people in the games industry have lost their jobs since 2022.
But while publisher Rockstar Games is well-known for the meticulous polish of its titles and attention to detail, the perfectionism so prized by fans also has its drawbacks, especially for those working on the game. Rockstar, like many other game developers, has frequently faced major criticism regarding its labor practices.
Former developers report extremely long working hours and a heavy workload that resulted in health issues. Trade unions accuse company managers of employee surveillance, resulting in a culture of workplace stress and low morale.
Coinciding with the launch of Rockstar's largest game to date, the developers behind it are pushing for trade union recognition. That move would give them a collective voice to address working hours, pay, pensions and parental leave. If successful, their campaign could set a major precedent for the wider video game industry, which continues to face challenges around fair labor practices.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
noticias.resumen: Research suggests that students who aren't careful about how they use ChatGPT and other AI tools risk poorer academic outcomes. It's a huge challenge for teachers.
noticias.texto:
AI in the classroom: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'
November 16, 2026
Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.
"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.
Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
How AI enables 'cognitive outsourcing'
In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.
There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.
Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.
Franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.
"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.
Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.
Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.
How AI use is linked to lower test scores
Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.
That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.
"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."
With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.
"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.
Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.
Should schoolsl restrict AI in class?
US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.
Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.
But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.
Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.
Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.
Ninety-one percent of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.
The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.
German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.
The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.
Students should question AI, too
Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.
"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.
Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."
That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.
In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.
