noticias.titulo: North Macedonia prevents 'terrorist' assassination plot targeting person in Greece
noticias.resumen: Guns and sketches marking specific locations were reportedly seized as part of the operation, which was carried out in cooperation with Greece's national intelligence agency.
noticias.texto:
Guns and sketches marking specific locations were reportedly seized as part of the operation, which was carried out in cooperation with Greece's national intelligence agency.
North Macedonia's National Security Agency (ANB) announced on Tuesday that it had prevented a "terrorist" assassination plot targeting a person in Greece and that it had dismantled an Iranian-linked network.
The ANB said it had brought down "a wide network of proxy actors" linked to Iranian Edris Jahangiri Mavaneh, who it described as a "collaborator of the Iranian security and intelligence services".
The agency said the network "undertook preparatory logistical activities to carry out a terrorist act/assassination against a person in Greece" while "under the direct instructions of the Iranian national."
Guns and sketches marking specific locations were reportedly seized as part of the operation, which was carried out in cooperation with Greece's national intelligence agency.
An anti-terrorist force also took part, police said. Raids were carried out at four locations.
The operation began in early 2026, the security agency's head, Bojan Hristovski, said, adding that the group had held "conspiratorial meetings on the territory of third countries, including Iran."
"As for the Macedonian network, it involves individuals embedded within criminal structures in the country," Hristovski told a press conference.
Four suspects have been taken into custody, while another has been placed under house arrest, an official said.
One person was detained in Greece and transferred to authorities in North Macedonia.
A sixth suspect was still being sought.

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang breaks silence says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia's CEO
noticias.resumen: Jensen Huang says he’s open to returning in his first statement since resignation.
noticias.texto:
Jensen Huang says he’s open to returning in his first statement since resignation.
Jensen Huang has said he is prepared to return to chip giant Nvidia as its chief executive in his first statement since resigning last Thursday over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in a statement to US media.
"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO."
A campaign to reinstate Huang, the co-founder who led Nvidia for 33 years, gained steam over the weekend, with President Donald Trump on Monday adding that he was open to Huang returning.
But Nvidia's board has since said it is considering both internal and external candidates and said on Monday that it had no intention of reinstating Huang.
Huang will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on 1 December before the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will then sit for a closed-door transcribed interview a day later on 2 December.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said Republican representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence Committees, in a press release.

noticias.titulo: Hormone-disrupting chemicals pose growing health threat, UN warns
noticias.resumen: Hormone-disrupting chemicals found in everyday products pose growing risks to human health and the environment, while regulations remain insufficient to tackle them, warns the UN.
noticias.texto:
Hormone-disrupting chemicals found in everyday products pose growing risks to human health and the environment, while regulations remain insufficient to tackle them, warns the UN.
Chemicals in many everyday items that interfere with the body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and scientists now have a better understanding of the harm they can cause, the United Nations said on Tuesday.
These substances, which can interfere with the body's hormonal systems, have been detected in breast milk and umbilical cord blood. Early exposure, sometimes before babies are born, can disrupt hormone activity and have lasting effects on brain development, growth and reproductive health, the UN warned.
In a new report, two UN bodies called for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment, warning that policies and regulations aimed at transforming the products and sectors responsible for widespread exposure remain “fragmented and insufficient”.
“What makes [endocrine-disrupting chemicals] particularly concerning is that they can disrupt hormones that regulate many essential functions in both humans and wildlife, from development and reproduction to metabolism and behaviour. These effects can be long-lasting, and in some cases, irreversible,” said Sheila Aggarwal-Khan, director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Industry and Economy Division.
Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics and pesticides.
They have been linked to problems affecting fertility and reproductive development, brain development and neurological function, thyroid and other hormone regulation, metabolism, the immune system and cardiovascular health.
“This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs,” the two UN bodies wrote.
“Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed – to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year.”
While scientific evidence has advanced considerably since the previous assessment from 2012, experts warn that regulation has been slower to translate that knowledge into action.
How are endocrine-disrupting chemicals regulated in Europe?
In the European Union, endocrine disruptors are regulated through several pieces of legislation, including general chemicals legislation and sector-specific rules covering areas such as packaging, pesticides and biocidal products.
However, critics say the current legislative framework is failing to adequately protect people and the environment from exposure.
“Despite some progress in the EU, such as the introduction of new hazard classes to identify EDCs, EU citizens and wildlife continue to be exposed to a cocktail of these harmful chemicals,” said Michael Warhurst, executive director at the environmental non-profit CHEM Trust.
In the EU, 231 substances have been officially identified as EDCs, while an additional 121 substances are currently under evaluation.
The challenge extends beyond Europe. More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report warned.
There have been greater efforts in recent years to develop testing programmes. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, said Laura Vandenberg, one of the lead authors of the report.
Chemicals have been removed from products when people became aware and stopped buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A, which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said.
But this can lead to a “whack-a-mole problem”, where one chemical is replaced by another that is structurally similar or has not been sufficiently tested, she added.
What are the next steps?
The UN said regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations.
“This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted,” said Bethanie Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden’s University of Gothenburg and the UN Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights.
“We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact,” she added.
Olwenn Martin, a chapter author, said that scientific understanding of how these chemicals disrupt the endocrine system is growing, and that they appear to be implicated in a wider range of diseases than previously thought.
“What concerns me most is that regulation still assesses most substances one at a time. That is like tackling climate change one greenhouse gas at a time, ignoring their combined effect,” Martin said.

noticias.titulo: Brazilian chicken ban: EU delays decision despite positive audit
noticias.resumen: Mercosur meat imports remain a contentious issue among EU countries, amid divisions over a deal liberalising trade between the two blocs.
noticias.texto:
Mercosur meat imports remain a contentious issue among EU countries, amid divisions over a deal liberalising trade between the two blocs.
The 27 EU member states postponed a vote on Tuesday to lift the ban on Brazilian chicken imports after several countries asked for further clarification from the European Commission regarding Brazil’s compliance with EU antimicrobial regulations.
The vote was scheduled after the EU banned imports of Brazilian meat in September over Brazil’s use of antimicrobials to stimulate animal growth.
The ban angered Brasilia, as it came only a few months after the contentious Mercosur trade deal with Latin American countries provisionally entered into force, opening up trade in agricultural products, including Brazilian meat.
“A number of Member States requested further clarifications on the system put in place by Brazil,” Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said. She added that the Commission would now “take the time to address these comments and questions” before a new meeting takes place in early December.
The ban, which followed a vote by national experts in May, covers beef, poultry, eggs and honey. However, an EU audit found in early September that Brazil’s poultry control system was operating effectively.
Heated topic between EU countries
Imports of Brazilian meat remain a divisive issue among EU countries, with several countries, led by France, strongly opposed to the Mercosur agreement signed in January this year.
EU farmers fear being exposed to dumping due to lower production standards in the countries that signed the deal — Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay — particularly regarding health and phytosanitary rules.
To address farmers’ concerns, the deal includes quotas capping tariff-free access for sensitive agricultural products. Annual beef imports are limited to 99,000 tonnes at a reduced tariff of 7.5%, equivalent to 1.5% of EU production, while poultry imports are capped at 180,000 tonnes a year, or 1.3% of EU output.
However, ratification of the deal has been delayed since the European Parliament referred the agreement to the Court of Justice of the European Union, questioning its legality.
Facing pressure from Mercosur countries and EU member states backing the deal, notably Spain and Germany, the European Commission eventually decided in May to provisionally implement the agreement pending a ruling by EU judges on its legality.

noticias.titulo: Trump warns Iran over allegations of dirty bomb threat to Washington
noticias.resumen: Iran denied media reports based on US intelligence that it may be planning a dirty bomb attack in the US capital, with questions swirling about its actual intentions or real capabilities for such an act, but Trump issued a strong warning against Tehran "because they happen to be crazy."
noticias.texto:
Iran denied media reports based on US intelligence that it may be planning a dirty bomb attack in the US capital, with questions swirling about its actual intentions or real capabilities for such an act, but Trump issued a strong warning against Tehran "because they happen to be crazy."
US president Donald Trump issued a stern warning to Iran on Tuesday about the possibility that Tehran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington DC, as reported by US broadcaster CNN citing what it called "sources familiar with the latest intelligence."
When asked whether the threat was imminent, Trump told reporters in Manila that "well, if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before."
Asked again whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent, the US president replied that "I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," adding that "we are looking into it."
While Iran continues its fiery rethoric threatening with devastating consequences if attacked again, CNN reported that new US intelligence indicated that Tehran was developing plans to potentially detonate a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in the US capital. However, according to the report, US officials were still divided over whether Iran has the capability to carry out such a plan or would actually move to execute it, and that officials were divided over the credibility of the intelligence.
The CNN report said that, according to its sources, the plans the United States has learned about were very specific and included locations and targets, prompting contingency planning, but CNN quoted one source as saying that "there is disagreement over whether they actually have the personnel in place to execute the plan." According to CNN's sources, Iran's capability to launch this kind of an attack has not grown, but what has changed is the Iranian incentive and that there was no evidence that Iran decided to move forward with its plans.
A dirty bomb is a weapon made of conventional explosives packaged with radioactive material that contaminates the environment through a non-nuclear explosion, affecting several city blocks or several kilometres.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis downplayed the concerns by issuing a statement saying that the United States is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”
CNN's published its report the day after Israel's Mossad chief Roman Gofman returned from Washington where he reportedly met senior US officials, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, to share Israel's latest intelligence on Iran. Israel's prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been insisting that the US and Iran must carry on the military campaign against the Iranian regime.
According to multiple US media reports, senior members of the US administrations have reportedly been moved over time to military compounds or protected government residences due to potential security threats.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei called the allegations "baseless".
In a statement on X, Baghaei said that the dirty bomb plans allegations are a "contrived" media narrative "designed to justify attacks on Iran's vital infrastructure."
The Iranian diplomat said that Tehran "considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be completely illegitimate and firmly rejects and explicitly denies the false and fabricated allegations made in this regard."
He warned that "Iran knows very well how to respond to any act of aggression and assures that this response will not be forgotten."
Tehran has been threatening the United States and Israel as well as any country supporting new military actions against Iran with a fiery response, including on their home territories.
These mounting threats come as the United States and Iran remain locked in an ongoing confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz with both sides increasing pressure to force concessions towards most favourable terms in case of a peace deal.

noticias.titulo: ‘Change is possible’: Danish offshore wind giant wins Earthshot Prize after quitting oil and gas
noticias.resumen: Inspired by John F. Kennedy’s Moonshot, which united millions around the goal of reaching the moon, Prince William’s Earthshot Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious environmental awards.
noticias.texto:
Inspired by John F. Kennedy’s Moonshot, which united millions around the goal of reaching the moon, Prince William’s Earthshot Prize is one of the world’s most prestigious environmental awards.
A people-powered movement to ban forever chemicals, a coal-powered company that pivoted to renewables and even an entire country are among this year’s Earthshot Prize winning solutions.
Crowning the five winners in Mumbai today (17 November), the UK’s Prince William hailed young innovators as “torchbearers of a global movement” as world leaders clash over climate action at COP31.
The British prince’s Royal Foundation charity launched the 10-year award programme in 2020, with the aim of finding new solutions and technologies to tackle the planet’s greatest environmental perils.
Each winner receives £1 million (€1.2 million) as well as the backing of businesses and funders to help grow their solutions further and faster.
There are five ‘Earthshots’ - or goals: Protect and Restore Nature; Clean Our Air; Revive Our Oceans; Build a Waste-free World; and Fix Our Climate.
The winners were chosen from 15 finalists at the sixth Earthshot Prize awards ceremony.
Who are the Earthshot Prize 2026 winners?
The Prize’s biggest awards night yet in Mumbai was a celebration of optimism that saw the Prince and Princess of Wales joined by sports, Bollywood and film stars. Earthshot Ambassadors Robert Irwin, the Australian conservationist and TV presenter, and Nomzamo Mbatha, the South African actor and humanitarian, also took to the stage.
The winners were selected by Prince William as well as heavyweights from the climate world: Paris Agreement architect Christiana Figueres was on the panel alongside German climate activist Luisa Neubauer and Kenyan environmentalist Wanjira Mathai.
Along with £1 million (€1.2 million) prizes for each of the winners, all 15 Earthshot Prize finalists get the support of powerful investors, philanthropists and environmental organisations, helping them to access funding and expertise to accelerate their growth.
Fix Our Climate winner: Ørsted
Ørsted is a shining example of how quitting fossil fuels can lead to becoming a profitable company in Europe’s clean energy transition.
20 years ago the company was known as DONG Energy - one of Europe’s most coal-intensive utilities. Then it sold its oil and gas business and pioneered offshore wind, cutting its direct carbon emissions by more than 98 per cent. Since 1991, Ørsted has installed more than 11 gigawatts of offshore wind, enough to meet the needs of 22 million people, and has a further 7.2 GW under construction across three continents
Speaking about their transformation, Rasmus Errboe, Group President and CEO of Ørsted, said: “It surely hasn’t been easy, and we still have to work hard every day to deliver secure, affordable and clean energy - and provide even more jobs to our communities. But this is what the world needs, and I hope our work can serve as inspiration for others.”
Earlier this year Ørsted took on the Trump administration, mounting a legal challenge when it tried to suspend leases on all large US offshore wind projects. Shares in Ørsted rose by about 4 per cent when the news broke.
By 2030, Ørsted aims to build 8.1 GW of new offshore wind, including Hornsea 3 in the UK, which will be the world’s largest single offshore wind farm once it’s running. Together, these projects are expected to power around 17 million more homes and avoid more than 28 million tonnes of CO₂ every year.
By winning The Earthshot Prize, Ørsted aims to set a new standard for the industry and inspire other renewable energy developers to follow.
Build a Waste-Free World winner: PFAS-Free France
PFAS-Free France built a people-powered movement that led to France’s landmark 2025 law to phase out many uses of PFAS - toxic “forever chemicals” found in thousands of everyday products - and make polluters pay for the clean-up.
More than 140,000 French citizens supported PFAS-Free France’s campaign, showing how ordinary people can force industry to make better products, clean up our environment and protect the health of people for generations to come.
By 2030, PFAS-Free France aims to see France’s law fully put into practice and help to achieve similar bans in five other major countries or regions.
Winning The Earthshot Prize will support scientific research, public campaigns and international partnerships to speed up the adoption of stronger laws, protecting millions more people from these harmful chemicals.
Protect and Restore Nature winner: Bhutan
For the first-time ever, an entire country has won the Earthshot Prize.
Bhutan has taken the pioneering step of writing the protection of nature into its national constitution. Its forests protect Himalayan water systems that help sustain 1.6 billion people downstream across South Asia. A country of just 800,000 people is helping to protect the water security of nearly a fifth of humanity.
Winning The Earthshot Prize will help Bhutan reach its 2030 ambitions. Through Restore Bhutan, its national nature coalition, it aims to restore 50,000 hectares of damaged land, reviving forests and rivers, delivering nearly 2 million tonnes of CO₂ savings and securing 133 billion litres of water.
Clean Our Air winner: Mahindra Last Mile Mobility
Mahindra Last Mile Mobility is rapidly putting one of the world’s largest sources of on-road air pollution on the path to electric in India. With more than 400,000 of its electric rickshaws already sold, and by making electric vehicles affordable for the drivers who own and run them, Mahindra is powering one of the fastest and most consequential green transitions the planet has ever seen.
By 2030, it aims to put one million electric vehicles on India’s roads and make electric the first choice for short city journeys. Winning The Earthshot Prize will help speed up the rollout of electric rickshaws in major cities including Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Bengaluru and Delhi, tackling challenges around parking, charging points and policy to bring cleaner transport to India’s busiest urban centres.
Revive Our Oceans winner: Niue Ocean Wide Trust
The Pacific island nation of Niue has a population of just 1,700 people, yet its Ocean Wide Trust is protecting an area of ocean larger than the United Kingdom. Through a pioneering way of investing in conservation, Niue is funding the long-term protection of its waters, safeguarding marine life while supporting the communities that depend on it. The groundbreaking scheme has already helped boost fish numbers by 60 per cent.
Winning The Earthshot Prize will help Niue Ocean Wide Trust attract the investment and partners it needs to raise a further US$10 million (€9.09 million) by 2028. That will bring it closer to its US$18 million (€16.3 million) goal for a permanent fund to protect Niue’s ocean for generations to come. The Prize will also help Niue share its model with other Pacific island nations, with the aim of at least one more country adopting it by 2028.
What has happened to previous Earthshot Prize winners?
The 2026 finalists and winners join an existing community of 75 finalists supported since 2020, whose work has collectively avoided or captured more than 18 million tonnes of CO₂, protected or restored 58 million hectares of land and 85 million hectares of ocean and coastline, removed or avoided 465,000 tonnes of waste, saved 21 million tonnes of water and improved air quality in regions home to 600 million people.

noticias.titulo: Apple to face landmark trial in France over alleged planned obsolescence of iPhones
noticias.resumen: If found guilty, the US tech firm could face fines of up to 5% of its annual revenue, equal to roughly €21.7 billion.
noticias.texto:
If found guilty, the US tech firm could face fines of up to 5% of its annual revenue, equal to roughly €21.7 billion.
Apple will stand trial in Paris in June next year on suspicion of having organised the planned obsolescence of several iPhone models by preventing repairs outside official outlets, a source close to the case told AFP on Tuesday.
The case brought by French prosecutors against the US tech giant on charges of "obstructing repair and refurbishment" is a first, the campaign group Stop Planned Obsolescence said, welcoming the move after filing a complaint in December 2022.
"We strongly contest these unfounded allegations," Apple said when contacted by AFP.
Planned obsolescence refers to techniques used by manufacturers to deliberately shorten the lifespan of their products, generally electronic devices, thereby encouraging consumers to replace them more frequently.
If found guilty, Apple could be fined up to €300,000 plus, an additional fine of up to 5% of its annual revenue — which would roughly be €21.7 billion as of publication — and could face compensation claims from clients.
According to the source close to the case, Apple Distribution International and its parent company Apple Inc are to appear in court for a four-day trial starting on June 17.
They are accused of obstructing repairs to a range of iPhone models for more than two and a half years, from November 2021 to July 2024.
Affected models range from the iPhone XS and the iPhone 12, 13, 14 and 15 series to the iPhone SE released in 2022.
Apple is accused of configuring its software to "make it impossible to repair or refurbish" the phones outside its authorised network, the source added.
For example, the Face ID feature might be disabled if the camera were replaced by an unauthorised repair shop, or the "battery health" feature could stop working.
The alleged aim was to boost sales of Apple's flagship product and increase the revenue of the multinational, which now generates more than $400 billion a year, with roughly half coming from iPhone sales.
It is not the first case brought against the US tech giant by the Stop Planned Obsolescence group.
In February 2021 it agreed to pay €25 million for failing to tell iPhone users that software updates could slow down older devices.
That settlement was one of several around the world after Apple admitted in December 2017 that its latest iOS operating software was slowing the performance of older telephones whose battery life was deteriorating.

noticias.titulo: Jensen Huang to face US Congress interviews on Nvidia’s sales to China on 1 December
noticias.resumen: Huang is set to appear before the United States' House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee on 1 December.
noticias.texto:
Huang is set to appear before the United States' House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee on 1 December.
Nvidia's cofounder Jensen Huang will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on 1 December before the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
It comes after he resigned as CEO of the chip giant following reported extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will then sit for a closed-door transcribed interview a day later on 2 December.
"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said Republican representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawfor, the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence Committees in a press release.
"The American people need answers on Mr. Huang and Nvidia’s role in allowing dangerous PRC actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal," they said.
The US bans the sale of the most advanced chips to China as part of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to lead AI. This measure came under former President Joe Biden, who signed the CHIPS Act into law.
Under the Trump administration, Huang lobbied the US to relax its export controls on chips to China, with several meetings with President Donald Trump.
Trump eventually allowed the export of its H200 chips, which are more powerful, to China in exchange for 25% of the revenue.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department unveiled new restrictions that will make it harder for some countries, such as China, Russia and Iran, to access the most advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centres located in other countries.

noticias.titulo: UK urged to overhaul youth benefits as one million young people drift out of work and study
noticias.resumen: The review’s author says only Romania fares worse in Europe on youth inactivity, even though young Britons are less likely to be unemployed than their peers in France, Spain or Italy.
noticias.texto:
The review’s author says only Romania fares worse in Europe on youth inactivity, even though young Britons are less likely to be unemployed than their peers in France, Spain or Italy.
A government-commissioned review has called for a separate welfare system for young people in the United Kingdom, cutting back some cash payments in favour of work placements and paying employers to hire those left out of the labour market.
The 267-page report, led by former Labour minister Alan Milburn, demands a “complete system reset” in how the state treats 16- to 24-year-olds who are Not in Employment, Education or Training, known as NEETs.
Their number passed one million earlier this year. The review warns it could reach 1.27 million by 2031 without action.
"A lost generation is not a fact of life... it’s a moral crisis," Milburn told reporters at the launch on Tuesday.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government will publish its full response next year, followed by draft legislation. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called the report "a radical blueprint for a new settlement with young people". He said ministers had already agreed to some measures, including more tailored help for young jobseekers.
Out of work, or out of reach?
The review aims to cut the NEET rate from 13% to about 5% by 2036, close to the level in the Netherlands.
“Across Europe, only Romania had a higher NEET rate than the UK in 2025,” Milburn wrote.
The headline jobless figures tell a different story. Office for National Statistics data published on Tuesday showed UK youth unemployment fell to 15.1% in the three months to September, though that remains more than three times the overall rate of 4.6%.
That puts the UK slightly below the EU average of 15.5% for under-25s in September, according to Eurostat. Young people fare far worse in Spain (22.8%), France (21.9%) and Italy (19.9%). Germany (7.5%) and the Netherlands (8.8%) are well ahead.
The gap between the two measures points to the problem Milburn’s review is trying to tackle. Many young Britons are not counted as unemployed because they have stopped looking for work altogether.
Across the EU, Eurostat puts the NEET rate for 15- to 29-year-olds at 11% in 2025, down from 15.2% a decade earlier. Italy has made the biggest gains, cutting its rate from 25.7% to 13.3%.
Less cash, more support
The report’s main proposal is a dedicated welfare system for the young that puts placements and support ahead of payments. It admits this could mean that “some people get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system”.
Milburn argued that the present system can be “detrimental to their longer term life chances” by allowing young people to stay out of work.
Young people would face a “duty to engage”, meaning those who turn down offers of work could lose some benefits. Each would be given a dedicated adviser and a personalised route into employment. A national network of local services combining careers advice, job support, health care and practical help would be in place by 2029.
The proposals are likely to be politically sensitive. Former prime minister Keir Starmer was forced to water down his own welfare reforms after a revolt within the Labour Party.
To encourage hiring, the review suggests raising the earnings threshold at which employers start paying tax on wages for workers aged 21 to 24. It also proposes a £3,000 (€3,400) payment to firms that take on someone who has been NEET for six months, with extra help for small businesses and for hiring young people with disabilities.
“Rather than simply writing young people a short-term check, we have to build them a long-term future,” Milburn said.
‘Easy to get burnout’
Milburn described the UK jobs market as “very fragile”, and young jobseekers say the competition is fierce.
Abigail Gomes, 21, has been looking for work for seven months since graduating from university. “There are just too many young people applying for one job,” she told AFP.
She said the constant cycle of applications and rejections “can create anxiety and depression among young people”, and that “it’s easy to get burnout”. Gomes has recently been offered a temporary retail job over Christmas.

noticias.titulo: Russia plays for time as Europe and US push for direct peace talks
noticias.resumen: The next phase of the peace talks remains uncertain as Russia continues to play down the possibility of face-to-face talks with Europe, despite mounting pressure from Washington to make it happen.
noticias.texto:
The next phase of the peace talks remains uncertain as Russia continues to play down the possibility of face-to-face talks with Europe, despite mounting pressure from Washington to make it happen.
Europe has finally settled on a joint team to speak on the continent's behalf in the negotiations to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Yet, despite this diplomatic breakthrough, uncertainty remains over what comes next.
Russia has again cast doubt on the possibility of holding face-to-face talks with the European delegation, which now comprises France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, the EU institutions (Council and Commission) and NATO.
European, US and Ukrainian officials all agree that the only way to move the process forward is to start a multilateral format with the Russians.
But Moscow seems to be in no hurry.
"The date has not yet been agreed and the expansion of the format – some people are talking about it – but it has not been agreed with us," Yury Ushakov, a close aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin, said on Monday.
Adding to the confusion, Ushakov suggested that "it may be necessary to hold another round, or perhaps more than one round, of trilateral talks" with the US and Ukraine before sitting down with the Europeans.
After speaking with Ushakov, US special envoy Jared Kushner sounded cautiously optimistic, saying preparations were underway for a multilateral meeting that should take place "in the near future".
"We discussed how to facilitate direct engagement between Europe and Russia, which has been largely absent over the past four years," Kushner said on social media.
"It is important that both sides hear each other's concerns and proposals directly as we work toward a more stable and secure future for Europe."
So far, the peace talks have proceeded in two parallel tracks: Ukraine, Russia and the US, on the one hand, and Ukraine, Europe and the US, on the other.
In practice, this has left Europe in the room next door, trying to catch up with what is discussed in the main room, as it happened in Abu Dhabi.
The US side has concluded the two-track configuration has reached its limit and the time has come for Europe and Russia to sit at the same table, at the same time.
Europe, long opposed to this direct engagement, is now on board.
"We are absolutely ready to engage at the multilateral level," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said.
Privately, European officials and diplomats say that expectations should remain low because, when it comes to Russia, nothing can be guaranteed, particularly given the volatility of the negotiations, which have gone through multiple ups and downs – and a protracted pause – in the past year alone.
Moscow'scontinued delays reinforce the widespread belief that Putin is playing lip service to the White House and has no intention of treating diplomacy seriously. The brutal attacks against Ukraine ahead of the winter bear witness to that.
The fact that Moscow talks about Europe's security architecture but refuses to talk with Europeans is cited as further reason to be wary.
The topic is seen as a ploy to divert attention from Ukraine, regurgitate old grievances and reassert Russia's long-lost sphere of influence. According to the New York Times, the Russian demands presented to the US were that NATO stop expanding, withdraw its troops to 1997 borders and halt military support for Ukraine.
"It's absurd. Russia misbehaves, and then they want to be rewarded for it," a senior diplomat snapped. "I don't see how it could fly at all."
Despite the daunting odds, Europeans are keen to show their readiness and availability, while preparing new sanctions on Russia and support for Ukraine.
Senior officials from the joint European team will meet with their US and Ukrainian counterparts on Thursday to work out the next steps in the process. The meeting will take place on the sidelines of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.
Brussels, meanwhile, has begun drafting a common mandate in case the multilateral format happens. The mandate is meant to compile the principles that Ukraine's allies have followed since the start of the war.
Austria, one of the first member states to publicly call for direct talks with Russia, has circulated a two-page document, seen by Euronews, to structure the negotiations built around four key pillars: political, security, humanitarian and economic.
The paper calls on the EU to maximise its "sanction leverage", prepare a special mission to monitor an eventual ceasefire and develop a strategy for the use of the immobilised Russian assets. It also floats a "division of labour" among the EU, NATO, the United Nations, the OSCE and the Coalition of the Willing to safeguard a future peace.
"Europe finally has a negotiating team that is expected to join the next round of talks. Now the focus must shift from the 'who' to the 'what'. This team urgently needs a mandate on substance," Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said.
"What is at stake is nothing less than Europe's own security."

noticias.titulo: Egypt pitches reforms and energy plans at World Economic Forum meeting
noticias.resumen: At a World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi pledged to simplify business procedures and outlined plans for industry, energy and AI. The government is preparing a 2027–2030 economic programme to boost productivity and give private businesses a larger role.
noticias.texto:
At a World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi pledged to simplify business procedures and outlined plans for industry, energy and AI. The government is preparing a 2027–2030 economic programme to boost productivity and give private businesses a larger role.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi called for more foreign investment on Tuesday, outlining business reforms at a World Economic Forum meeting in Cairo.
He said Egypt would announce an economic programme in December covering 2027–2030, aimed at increasing productivity and giving private businesses a larger role.
Reforms had cut the average time for goods to clear customs to two days, he said.
He also said Egypt’s shift to a flexible exchange rate had helped foreign investors transfer their profits abroad. Knowing they can bring their earnings home could encourage companies to invest in Egypt, where their projects can create jobs, generate business for local suppliers and bring in tax revenue.
Representatives of around 80 organisations, including major companies and international financial institutions, attended Tuesday’s discussions, part of the two-day Country Strategy Meeting on Egypt, according to the presidency.
El-Sisi cited economic growth of 5.1% in the 2025–26 financial year and net foreign direct investment of $18 billion (€16.4bn).
The investment drive comes as Egypt faces pressure to reduce debt and open more of its economy to private businesses. In an August report, the International Monetary Fund warned that high debt and borrowing needs left the country exposed to economic shocks. The fund has also said sales of state assets have progressed more slowly than expected.
Industry and investment targets
As part of Egypt’s industrial strategy, el-Sisi highlighted the country's target for industry to account for 20% of economic output by 2030.
The government also wants private investment to reach 67% of total investment by 2030, according to a cabinet statement issued on Monday.
Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Mohamed Farid Saleh set out a foreign direct investment strategy developed with the World Bank in an article published by the World Economic Forum on Monday.
The initial priorities include IT services, solar and wind power, food processing, clothing and transport. Further reforms are planned for sectors including data centres and green hydrogen.
Farid wrote that simpler licensing and online government services would help businesses get projects running. Under Egypt’s existing Golden Licence scheme, eligible projects can receive a single cabinet approval to build and operate.
El-Sisi also discussed whether the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development could help establish new investment zones during talks with its president, Odile Renaud-Basso, on Tuesday. No funding agreement was announced in the presidency’s account.
Energy exports and AI ambitions
El-Sisi reiterated plans to bring Cypriot gas to Egypt’s Idku and Damietta liquefaction plants for export to Europe by 2028.
Egypt also aims to generate 45% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2028, he said, alongside plans to expand electricity connections with neighbouring countries and Europe.
Shipping through the Suez Canal was improving, the president said. He repeated his estimate that Egypt had lost about $20bn (€18.2bn) in canal revenue in recent years.
He also highlighted opportunities for investment in data centres, cloud computing and AI research as part of Egypt’s national AI strategy.

noticias.titulo: Computer love or hate: Charlotte de Witte's AI singer collaboration divides techno fans
noticias.resumen: The international DJ released the EP Azadi with NAVA, a virtual AI singer, to represent Iranian women banned from performing publicly, but techno star's choice has not gone down well with some of her fans.
noticias.texto:
The international DJ released the EP Azadi with NAVA, a virtual AI singer, to represent Iranian women banned from performing publicly, but techno star's choice has not gone down well with some of her fans.
What if the undisputed queen of global techno crossed over to the "dark side"? That is what many people thought when on Thursday 5 November (and even earlier, to be fair) Charlotte de Witte, the 34-year-old Belgian DJ and record producer who boasts 6.5 million Instagram followers, released her new EP.
Azadi (in Persian, "freedom", a word we came to know during the protests in Iran in 2022), released on her own label KNTXT, contains three tracks (Azadi itself, Omid, which means "hope", and Tales of the Desert) with the acid techno sound that has always set her apart, as do the 140 BPM, but this time with a rather unusual vocalist.
De Witte, voted the world’s No. 1 techno DJ for the seventh year in a row in the DJ Mag Top 100 DJs 2026 ranking, has in fact used an AI singer for the first time. This is NAVA, developed by British-Iranian artist Farbod Mehr.
In an official statement, the artist said that "NAVA represents Iranian women who are forbidden to perform in public" and that the EP is conceived as "a small act of resistance", with all proceeds donated to the NGO FEMENA, an organisation that supports women’s rights activists and feminist movements in the SWANA region and in Asia.
The EP is therefore not a record produced entirely by artificial intelligence, but a musical collaboration in which only the lead voice is that of a virtual singer.
Who is NAVA?
NAVA is a project created in 2025 by Farbod Mehr, a British digital artist of Iranian origin. The virtual singer was developed using artificial intelligence and her visual identity is inspired by Persian art and cultural tradition.
Mehr has said that his aim is to symbolically represent Iranian women, who cannot freely perform as solo singers in front of mixed audiences. One only has to think of the case of Parastoo Ahmadi, who in June was sentenced by a court in Qom to 74 lashes, a two-year travel ban and a two-year suspension from artistic activity. Her offence? Having posted a concert streamed on YouTube in December 2024, in which she performed without a headscarf and wearing a sleeveless dress.
Reactions from fans and experts
The intention is certainly good, but it has not been welcomed unanimously, as de Witte may have hoped. Her fan base has been extremely voiciferous with its criticisms. The decision to use an artificial voice to represent women who have been deprived of the possibility of expressing themselves through music has in fact raised numerous objections among electronic music fans.
Many are asking why the voice of a real person was not used. For instance, on Reddit one fan states: "I have completely stopped enjoying her music. There are other ways to give voice to Iranian women, without resorting to 'an artist' created by artificial intelligence". For another fan the initiative is to be praised, but they believe she could have chosen a different path: "Apparently, artificial intelligence is supposed to represent Iranian women living under oppression, but is it really possible that there were no Iranian artists in the flesh to sing on the track?"
Some users also fear that normalising AI-generated voices could reduce professional opportunities for singers, backing vocalists and musicians, replacing human artistic performances with artificial tools.
Criticism has also come from within the Iranian techno scene. AliPink, a DJ and producer, a pioneer of the country’s underground scene and founder of the label Techno Tehran Records, has challenged the decision to rely on an artificial singer to represent Iranian women.
In a comment posted on Instagram and later picked up by the platform Tehran Herald, AliPink described as "deeply questionable" the idea that an artificial voice is needed to represent these women, stressing that there are already Iranian artists in the flesh, with talent and stories to tell.
AliPink has also questioned the very value of the project, adding: "There is a fundamental difference between raising awareness of the difficulties faced by Iranian women and using their struggles as a concept to promote music generated by artificial intelligence".
There are, however, also those who defend the project, pointing out that if de Witte had used a real Iranian artist she would have put her at risk by having her sing those songs. One Instagram user commented under the post in which de Witte shared a preview of the EP before its official release: "Wow, as a Persian woman and artist, this really hits me deeply. People do not realise how much Iranian women have to fight, much harder, just to do what artists in other countries are free to do every day". Another Instagram user wrote: "I have been waiting for this release, thank you Charlotte, for highlighting the voices of Iranian women, who are repressed by their government and denied the chance to express themselves creatively".
The debate is therefore more complex than a simple clash between supporters and opponents of AI. For some, NAVA represents a missed opportunity to involve artists of flesh and blood directly, while for others it is a tool of expression and solidarity when there are no alternatives.
The thin line between creativity and copying
The story is part of a broader debate about the role of artificial intelligence in the music industry. In recent years, generative tools have become capable of creating voices, melodies and entire compositions, calling into question the relationship between human creativity, technology and intellectual property.
So far the music industry has mostly proceeded through self-imposed limits. For example, Spotify requires that every use of unauthorised voice cloning be explicitly flagged and is prohibited, while Bandcamp (a direct-sales platform for record producers) categorically bans music generated "entirely or largely" by AI. Since 2026, moreover, Beatport has refused to accept tracks for upload if they are deemed to be fully AI.
Charlotte de Witte’s decision to use an AI voice reignites a question that is now increasingly central in the music industry: whether, and what, space artificial intelligence should have in artistic creation? Above all, where does technological experimentation end and the replacement of human labour begin?
With Azadi, the Belgian DJ has taken this debate into a particularly sensitive area, that of freedom of expression and women’s rights. Whatever the intentions and the solidarity message behind the project, one crucial question remains: when we use artificial intelligence to give a voice to those who cannot speak freely, are we really giving their voice back to them or are we simply speaking in their place?

noticias.titulo: EU’s Rwanda migrant return plan faces backlash over human rights concerns rights record
noticias.resumen: Kigali’s human rights record is under scrutiny as it prepares to host the first EU return hubs outside the bloc. Rwanda’s Interior Minister rejected the criticism, pointing out to the country's experience in dealing with migrants.
noticias.texto:
Kigali’s human rights record is under scrutiny as it prepares to host the first EU return hubs outside the bloc. Rwanda’s Interior Minister rejected the criticism, pointing out to the country's experience in dealing with migrants.
The announcement of a partnership between five EU countries and Rwanda to set up the first return hub outside the bloc has sparked controversy across Europe.
Although the final deal is still under negotiation, growing criticism has emerged over Rwanda’s human rights record. Furthermore, the planned deportations from the five participating countries — Austria, Germany, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece — to Rwanda, which are expected to begin in 2027, could face legal challenges before European courts.
“I see neither future nor humanity in it,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said in an interview when asked about the initiative, in an indirect swipe at the five member states involved in the project.
The proposed partnership concluded in Vienna on Monday would establish the EU’s first return hub outside the bloc, with the facility expected to accommodate around 100 people at a time. Those transferred to Rwanda would be free to move around the country and would be expected to integrate into Rwandan society and the local labour market.
Many members of the European Parliament strongly condemned the political agreement, citing both the risk of abuses in Rwanda and the prospect of migrants being stranded in a country with which they have no ties.
“It is particularly disturbing that the fate of human beings is entrusted to a country burdened by documented allegations of serious violations of fundamental rights,” said Italian MEP Marco Tarquinio of the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) group.
Similar concerns were voiced by other MEPs, including Iraqi-born Swedish MEP Abir Al-Sahlani of Renew Europe, who questioned the rationale behind the agreement in an interview with Euronews’ flagship programme, Europe Tonight: “If we in Europe were not able to send them back to their countries, what makes us believe Rwanda will be able to?” Al-Sahlani asked.
The European Parliament has previously taken a hard line on Kigali. It called for the suspension of an EU-Rwanda memorandum of understanding on critical raw materials, over alleged war crimes and the occupation of territory in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo by Rwanda’s defence forces.
Humanitarian organisations also voiced their opposition. In a joint statement, a total of 45 NGOs described the partnership as a “cruel measure” that pushes migrants into further insecurity.
Rwanda's human rights record in question
Rwanda has sought to establish itself as a partner for Western countries looking to relocate migrants beyond their borders, although previous agreements of this kind have faced significant challenges.
In 2018, Kigali backed out of an agreement with Israel to accept refugees deported against their will, while a deal to transfer asylum seekers from the United Kingdom was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court because of Rwanda’s poor human rights record.
In 2025, Kigali agreed to accept 250 migrants from the US under a deal with President Donald Trump’s administration but has so far relocated only a few of them.
According to an Amnesty International report, in all these cases Rwanda failed to show it could guarantee fair procedures and adequate protection for people transferred from another jurisdiction.
Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta dismissed the criticism in response to a question from Euronews at the conference on Tuesday.
“Human rights in Rwanda are respected for everyone, and specifically for the migrants who choose to come to our country,” he said, describing his country’s integration policy as “one of the most progressive” because it allows refugees to work.
Biruta defended Rwanda’s long experience with migrants. He pointed out that Kigali currently hosts more than 140,000 refugees and asylum seekers and has run a transit centre for people evacuated from Libya since 2017.
“Which other country has come forward to propose a solution for those refugees? We were the only ones,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Uzbekistan’s mountain lakes and trails draw visitors in every season
noticias.resumen: Emerald lakes, mountain trails and boat trips offer different ways to experience the Tashkent region, where seasonal landscapes and growing tourism are bringing more visitors into the mountains.
noticias.texto:
Emerald lakes, mountain trails and boat trips offer different ways to experience the Tashkent region, where seasonal landscapes and growing tourism are bringing more visitors into the mountains.
In the mountains of the Tashkent region, the landscape changes with every turn. At Urungach, the lower lake takes on an emerald hue as water gathers in spring and recedes by summer. Further along, Chimgan draws hikers and skiers, while Charvak Reservoir offers boat trips beneath the surrounding ridgelines.
Together, these places offer different ways to explore the region’s mountains, from walking remote trails to spending time by the water.
Urungach’s changing emerald lake
Known for its jade-coloured water, Urungach attracts visitors looking for a distinctive mountain landscape. The smaller lake, also called Jade Lake, sits among rugged rock formations and steep terrain, with a larger lake above it.
According to Efrat Turaboyev, a representative of the tourism department, the smaller lake is around 180 metres long and reaches a depth of 16.5 metres at its deepest point. Water flows into it from the upper lake through underground channels, as well as from nearby mountain streams.
The water level changes throughout the year. It generally rises in April, reaching its highest point during spring, before receding around the middle of June. The cycle repeats the following year, giving the lake a different appearance depending on when visitors arrive.
The main visitor season runs from mid-April to June. Daily numbers can range from around 50 to 500 people, with weekends generally busier than weekdays.
For visitors from Germany, the scenery remains appealing even when the weather is cloudy or rainy.
Frank Karis says the changing weather gives the landscape a dramatic quality, while Simone Rode describes the mountains and natural surroundings as peaceful and relaxing.
Tourism and village life
Urungach’s growing popularity is creating opportunities for nearby communities, where livestock farming, agriculture and beekeeping remain important sources of income.
Residents also sell honey and other local products to visitors. Guesthouses are beginning to open in nearby villages, offering travellers a place to stay and meals prepared with local produce.
Most visitors currently travel by private car, often using four-wheel-drive UAZ or Niva vehicles suited to the mountain roads. Access is improving as roads are developed around the villages, although the journey to the lake still requires planning.
Tourism representatives are also considering camping areas and tent accommodation in lower parts of the mountains. Plans for 2027 include creating places where visitors can stay overnight before making the trip up to the lake.
For local communities, the lake has become a source of pride as well as a growing attraction. Its distinctive colour is the main reason many people make the journey.
Chimgan throughout the year
A journey from Urungach to Chimgan brings a different mountain experience. The area is known for its trails, broad views and access to outdoor activities in both summer and winter.
Shahzod Abduvaliyev of the Tashkent region tourism department says Chimgan has a long history as a recreational destination, dating back to the late 19th century. Its accommodation options now include hotels, hostels and family-run guesthouses.
During winter, visitors come for skiing and other snow-related activities. In warmer months, horseback riding, trekking and time by natural lakes and swimming pools are among the options.
The area also attracts travellers interested in village life. Some communities have retained traditional ways of living, and visitors can find local bread, honey and other regional products.
Tourism has become an important source of income for residents who provide accommodation, food and other services. According to Abduvaliyev, transport and visitor facilities have also improved, with connections from Tashkent and accommodation options ranging up to four-star hotels in the Bostanlyk district.
Safety measures are part of the area's tourism infrastructure. Warning signs identify places where swimming is prohibited and alert visitors to potential wildlife risks in forested areas.
A boat trip on Charvak Reservoir
Near Chimgan, Charvak Reservoir offers another way to experience the mountain scenery. Visitors can take boat trips across the blue water, with steep rocky slopes rising along the shoreline.
For tourist Ekaterina Sidorchuk, the colour of the reservoir and the surrounding rocks made a strong impression. She describes the boat ride, the movement of the waves and the traditional music on board as part of the experience.
She says she would like to return with her children to share the landscape with them.
Andrey Sidorchuk, who first visited the area 18 years ago, has returned with his wife to explore places she had not seen before. He says the trip has left them with many impressions and that they plan to continue travelling through Uzbekistan.
Different ways to experience the mountains
Urungach, Chimgan and Charvak each offer a different way to experience the Tashkent region. At Urungach, the lake’s emerald colour and changing water levels give the landscape a seasonal character. Chimgan draws visitors throughout the year for hiking and winter sports, while Charvak’s blue waters are best explored by boat, with mountain slopes rising along the shore.
Tourism is also creating new opportunities for people living in the surrounding villages, from guesthouses and local food to guiding and other visitor services.
As access improves and more travellers discover the area, the region’s mountain landscapes are becoming an increasingly important part of Uzbekistan’s outdoor tourism offer. The lakes, trails and villages each provide a different perspective on the same mountainous region.

noticias.titulo: Deutsche Bank shares fall as leak reveals Trump tax document error
noticias.resumen: Deutsche Bank shares fell more than 6% on Tuesday after reports based on 15 million leaked records shed light on its dealings with clients including Donald Trump.
noticias.texto:
Deutsche Bank shares fell more than 6% on Tuesday after reports based on 15 million leaked records shed light on its dealings with clients including Donald Trump.
Deutsche Bank shares fell more than 6% in Frankfurt on Tuesday before paring losses to 3.8% by early afternoon, after an international media investigation shed new light on the lender’s dealings with Russian oligarchs, convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and US President Donald Trump.
Germany’s largest bank said some of the cases dated back as much as two decades and that it had reviewed them at the time and worked with regulators where relevant.
It said it had spent €7 billion strengthening its internal controls between 2019 and 2025 and told Reuters news agency it expected no significant financial impact from the reports.
The investigation, dubbed Inside Deutsche Bank, drew on more than 15 million files supplied by two whistleblowers whose identities the consortium has kept confidential.
More than 200 journalists worked on the project, including reporters from the Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, The New York Times and German public broadcaster ZDF.
What the records revealed
The Financial Times reported that Deutsche Bank accidentally sent a Trump tax document to another client’s accountant in 2017, during his first term as president, and did not tell the White House.
Speaking to reporters in Manila on Tuesday, Trump called the disclosure “illegal”. The bank declined to comment on his reaction, Reuters reported.
The FT also reported that Deutsche Bank processed $582 million (€528 million) in payments linked to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein that it later flagged as suspicious.
Other reports described tax arrangements the bank set up for wealthy clients and suspected money laundering through services it provided to other banks.
The records show that Deutsche Bank sought to expand its Russian business shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, despite internal warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.
Chief executive Christian Sewing took part in the working group that prepared the strategy, according to reports based on the documents.
Deutsche Bank said in March 2022 that it would wind down its remaining business in Russia and take on no new business there. Its annual report shows that it still had 162 full-time equivalent staff in Russia at the end of 2025 and recorded a pre-tax profit of €61 million in the country that year.
German finance minister calls for answers
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil called for “full transparency” about how Deutsche Bank had addressed past failures and gaps in its internal controls, and how it would prevent them from recurring, according to AFP.
He also called for regulators and law enforcement authorities to scrutinise the bank.
Deutsche Bank chair Alexander Wynaendts backed Sewing in a statement emailed to Reuters, saying he had been comfortable with every decision Sewing had made during his tenure as chair.
Deutsche Bank said it had already taken steps to protect confidential information about clients, employees and others and would continue to do so. It gave no details of those steps in its public statement.

noticias.titulo: EU's 2040 climate target at risk as bloc waters down carbon market reform
noticias.resumen: A leaked compromise proposal seeks to shield European industry from rising carbon costs, but environmental groups warn that concessions on free emissions allowances and international carbon credits could undermine the bloc's 2040 climate ambitions.
noticias.texto:
A leaked compromise proposal seeks to shield European industry from rising carbon costs, but environmental groups warn that concessions on free emissions allowances and international carbon credits could undermine the bloc's 2040 climate ambitions.
The European Union's 2040 climate target risks being undermined by reforms to the bloc's carbon market, the Emissions Trading System (ETS), according to a leaked document seen by Euronews.
The Irish Presidency of the EU Council has softened a proposal, to be discussed by EU ambassadors on Wednesday, amid growing political pressure on the ETS as national governments struggle to reconcile emissions targets with industrial competitiveness and high energy costs.
The compromise text seeks to secure political support for the bloc's carbon market beyond 2030. However, climate advocates warn that concessions to protect European industry could weaken the system's contribution to the 2040 target, leaving other sectors of the economy to make up the shortfall.
The Council text retains the European Commission's July proposal to slow the decline in carbon allowances, extend free permits for industry and introduce international carbon credits into the EU carbon market, allowing emissions at home to be offset through projects abroad.
But negotiations are further reshaping the plan, especially around how much flexibility governments and industry will have to avoid domestic emissions cuts.
Free allowances and international credits
Under the Irish Presidency's proposal, industrial companies would retain 80% of their free allowances if they submit an investment plan, even if they subsequently fail to carry out the proposed decarbonisation investments. The remaining 20% would be conditional on starting construction of eligible projects.
Free allowances are permits that companies receive without having to buy them at auction. They are designed to protect EU producers against competition from countries with less stringent climate rules, such as China and the US.
The proposal marks a significant political concession to industries concerned about losing free allowances, raising questions about whether the ETS will provide sufficient incentives to cut emissions.
The compromise would shield industry from carbon costs for longer, while leaving governments to ensure that this protection translates into investment in European production and clean technologies.
On international carbon credits, the Council has retained the Commission's proposal to set aside allowances equivalent to 260 million tonnes of CO2 to finance their purchase. It also leaves open the possibility of a pilot phase between 2031 and 2035, allowing the EU to test the system before implementing it in full.
The Council has also maintained stringent quality and integrity requirements for international credits, making the ETS emissions reduction trajectory increasingly dependent on their availability.
However, if industries can't buy them, it could jeopardise the 2040 climate target, since it requires at least an 85% domestic net emissions reduction, with international credits accounting for the remaining 5%.
The Irish Presidency is seeking to build consensus among the 27 EU countries before negotiations turn to more politically sensitive questions of climate ambition and burden-sharing between member states.
It hopes to secure an agreement at the Environment Council on December 11. The European Parliament is expected to vote during its December 14-17 plenary session in Strasbourg.
Fragmentation at national level
The Irish Presidency faces an uphill battle given the depth of divisions among member states and the complexity of the negotiations.
EU countries are already divided over how quickly the supply of carbon permits should shrink, whether companies should be allowed to use international carbon credits to meet their obligations and how far industrial sectors should be shielded from rising carbon costs, according to a second document seen by Euronews.
Taken together, the demands risk diluting the ETS when it is expected to drive a large share of the bloc’s next phase of emissions cuts.
In general, governments want to preserve the ETS as a source of revenue for decarbonisation, but concerns are mounting about the costs it imposes on energy-intensive industries competing with manufacturers from China or the United States.
EU capitals are split over the total number of emissions permits available to companies — some argue they should decline to increase carbon pricing and encourage divestments in fossil fuels.
Others fear the impact of withdrawing free allowances on their struggling industries.
A slower reduction would ease the pressure on power plants and factories to cut emissions, potentially tempering carbon prices and giving companies more time to adapt. But it would also mean fewer emissions cuts in the sectors covered by the ETS, making the 2040 target harder to reach.
Environmental groups sound the alarm
A recent analysis by the Öko-Institut, commissioned by environmental campaign group WWF Germany, warned that the Commission's proposed ETS reform was "incompatible" with the EU's target of cutting net emissions by 90% by 2040.
“The Commission would rather gamble on climate protection than safeguard the future of European industry," said Lisa Okken, industrial policy expert at WWF Germany.
"Its proposed reform lacks the carbon price signal needed to incentivise the urgent modernisation of European industry. This gap is being filled with complicated accounting tricks and excessive flexibility.”
Another key concern cited by the environmentalists is the proposal to allow additional emissions beyond the existing emissions cap in exchange for future permanent carbon removals through expensive technologies designed to capture CO2 from the air.
"It remains unclear whether these removals can be delivered at the scale required, as the necessary capacity simply does not exist today," reads the study.

noticias.titulo: Fresh public sector strike in France under way over pay as government struggles to pass budget
noticias.resumen: Tuesday's demonstrations follow talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, which left unions dissatisfied, as they continue to push for across the board pay rises.
noticias.texto:
Tuesday's demonstrations follow talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, which left unions dissatisfied, as they continue to push for across the board pay rises.
Another major day of protests took place in France on Tuesday, as part of a nationwide strike led by public sector workers calling for pay increases, despite government efforts to ease tensions as demonstrations roil the country.
This come as France races to adopt a 2027 budget against a backdrop of strained finances, eight weeks after social unrest erupted in mid-September, amid student anger at school conditions.
The movement has since broadened in scope, taking aim at the cost of living crisis and rising fuel prices. Tuesday's demonstrations follow talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, which left unions dissatisfied, as they continue to push for across the board pay rises.
In an attempt to meet union demands, the government has announced eight additional index points for the lowest-paid public sector workers. It has also brought forward an increase in the national minimum wage from 1 December, in reaction to inflation.
Despite this, in its draft budget, the government has ruled out any general pay rise for the fourth consecutive year, citing the country's finances, amid a mounting public deficit and national debt.
This is unacceptable for the unions, which put the loss of purchasing power for public servants at 16 percent since 2017, leading to increasing numbers of public employees ending up on or close to the minimum wage against a backdrop of inflation.
Demonstrations have seen a decline in turn out in recent weeks, according to figures from France's Interior Ministry.
Sophie Binet, Secretary General of the General Confederation of Labour (CGT) trade union told Euronews that "records" couldn't be "broken everyday."
"This is the first time in social history that eleven days of national protests have occurred in under two months. So, yes, there have been ups and downs. We don't break records every day, but this is significant", she said.
"Everyday we are also learning about other protests across Europe. They have been inspired by France", she added.
Protests have been largely peaceful, however there have been instances of fringe violence, including attacks on journalists and police, public buildings, the use of firecrackers, as well as looting and attacks on 17 October.
Meanwhile, police forces have been accused of using disproportionate measures to clamp down on demonstrations, prompting a number of investigations into law alleged police misconduct.
France's protests erupted as the country nears elections in spring.
Manuel Bompard, deputy for the hard left France Unbowed party told Euronews that primary goal is to address the demands of young people and unions."
He added that "during the election campaign, all candidates present their own proposals. Our proposals align with the demands being voiced in the streets today. The primary goal is not the election campaign itself."

Heavy snow swept across the Yorkshire Dales in northern England on Tuesday, 17 November 2026, making driving treacherous.

noticias.titulo: Finland’s satellite provider Iceye bids €2 billion for Italian rocket maker Avio
noticias.resumen: The satellite firm is promising €1 billion of investment in Italy, but the deal is likely to face scrutiny in Rome, which has a say through its stake in Avio’s biggest shareholder.
noticias.texto:
The satellite firm is promising €1 billion of investment in Italy, but the deal is likely to face scrutiny in Rome, which has a say through its stake in Avio’s biggest shareholder.
Finnish satellite operator Iceye has made a €2 billion offer for Italian rocket maker Avio, aiming to create an “integrated European space and defence company”.
Iceye announced the bid on Tuesday, offering €41 per share for all of Avio’s ordinary shares. According to an AFP calculation, that values the company, which specialises in space propulsion and launch vehicles, at €2.05 billion.
Iceye provides satellite imaging to the defence and intelligence sectors and said that "Europe’s need for sovereign space and defence capabilities is growing."
"Governments need control of their critical space infrastructure, and Europe needs it most," chief executive Rafal Modrzewski said in a statement.
The company argued that combining the two businesses would give governments more confidence in their access to space.
"The combined group would be vertically integrated, bringing together satellite production, launch and mission operations in one company. That would give governments greater certainty over deployment and continuity of supply," Iceye said.
Under the plans, Avio’s launch and propulsion business would stay centred in Italy. Iceye said it would also invest €1 billion in the country over five years “on top of Avio’s existing plans”.
Any deal would need regulatory approval.
The bid is likely to be closely examined by the Italian government. Rome holds around 30% of defence contractor Leonardo, which is Avio’s largest shareholder with an 18% stake.

noticias.titulo: Qatar warns Gulf escalation poses 'grave danger' and announces new talks with Iran
noticias.resumen: Qatar warns the US and Iran to "avoid any escalation" as Iran's new attacks in Bahrain and its strikes on Gulf shipping are putting diplomacy under pressure. Qatar's foreign ministry announces new talks with Tehran, aiming to bridge the divide between US and Iran.
noticias.texto:
Qatar warns the US and Iran to "avoid any escalation" as Iran's new attacks in Bahrain and its strikes on Gulf shipping are putting diplomacy under pressure. Qatar's foreign ministry announces new talks with Tehran, aiming to bridge the divide between US and Iran.
Qatar warned on Tuesday that the ongoing escalation in the Gulf poses a “grave danger” to the chances of a deal between the US and Iran, as it announced a meeting with Iranian officials later in the day.
Dr. Majed Al Ansari, spokesperson for Qatar’s foreign ministry, said the risks extended “not only to freedom of navigation and the global economy, but also to the chances of reaching an agreement”.
Speaking at a weekly briefing in Doha, he urged all sides to exercise restraint and avoid further escalation that could undermine negotiations.
The meeting with Iranian officials would focus on proposals already under discussion, he said. He did not give a location or name the participants, describing it as part of regular contacts aimed at narrowing differences between Washington and Tehran.
“Today’s meeting with the Iranian side will take place as part of mediation efforts and an exchange of views on the current proposals,” the Qatari diplomat said, adding that Tuesday's meeting aims to bridge the divide between US and Iran.
His comments came after Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched drones at a US radar system at Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Airbase on Tuesday.
Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, and US' Central Command (CENTCOM) said that they intercepted the drones, without any damage.
Separately, Iran's attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz continued on Tuesday with a tanker’s crew being unaccounted for after the ship was struck for a second time north of Oman’s Khasab, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Tuesday. The second strike caused a fire on board.
US President Donald Trump has said he will maintain the naval blockade on Iran, while Tehran continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil and gas exports.
Cost of a prolonged stand-off
Al Ansari warned that the continuing stand-off was affecting global energy markets and food security, as well as the economies and security of Gulf states.
“It is in no one’s interest to remain in this situation and enter a stalemate,” he said.
Asked about Qatar’s contacts with its Gulf neighbours, he said coordination was continuing, pointing to recent meetings with Saudi and Emirati officials.
Diplomatic efforts were also under way in Oman, where Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, on Tuesday. Oman’s foreign ministry said they discussed ways to prevent further escalation and protect international shipping.
