noticias.titulo: Basel, Baia Mare and Omiš named Europe’s Christmas capitals for 2027
noticias.resumen: Basel in Switzerland, Baia Mare in Romania and Omiš in Croatia have been recognised as 2027’s Christmas capital, city and village, respectively.
noticias.texto:
Basel in Switzerland, Baia Mare in Romania and Omiš in Croatia have been recognised as 2027’s Christmas capital, city and village, respectively.
The 10th edition of the European Capital of Christmas awards has crowned Basel in Switzerland, Baia Mare in Romania and Omiš in Croatia as the continent’s go-to festive destinations for 2027.
Organised by the European Capital of Christmas initiative, this decision was reached by a majority vote among an international jury chaired by Danuta Hübner, the former EU Commissioner for Regional Policy.
Aside from the three winning destinations, special mention was also given to the “Spanish-Portuguese Christmas” spearheaded by the village of Fuentes de Oñoro in Spain and the town of Vilar Formoso in Portugal. This is being recognised for the “cross-border celebration that the two towns have organised since 2023 together with the Municipality of Almeida”, the organisation said.
This collaboration is marked by a 15-metre-tall pine tree that stands on the border line. The event includes a market that joins the two towns, as well as a Three Kings parade. There are also bilingual workshops for children, food from local producers as well as charity drives, such as a toy collection, charity walk and race between the two countries.
The three category winners
Basel, Switzerland: European Capital of Christmas
With a festive season marked by a Christmas market tradition that dates back to 1978, Basel was named the European Capital of Christmas for 2027, taking over from Barcelona.
Today, the Christmas market attracts more than one million visitors a year to Basel, who come to explore the stalls on Barfüsserplatz and around the Barfüsserkirche church.
Since 2023, Christmas in Basel has also featured “Zauberhöfe”, or magic courtyards, across the old town, which run from November to December – offering retreats away from the hustle and bustle of everyday life and imbued with the festive spirit.
While at Theater Basel, the Advent Days grant visitors free entry to performances every evening from 1-23 December.
The city’s application also highlighted the Harley Niggi-Näggi parade, where, since 1999, drivers dressed as Santa Claus ride Harley-Davidson motorcycles in the city centre to raise funds for charities.
Baia Mare, Romania: European City of Christmas
Baia Mare was named the European City of Christmas for an application that includes a range of events, featuring two ice rinks, a route of lights between the old town and Mara Park, as well as a village museum that will become a stage for local festive traditions. This will run from 26 November 2027 until 10 January 2028.
Liberty Square in the old town is where most festivities will take place, while Mara Park will host the traditional charity fair, run by the Social Assistance department. These two destinations will also be linked by a dedicated tourist train.
The northern Romanian’s diverse community also make it special, with residents hailing from Romania, Hungary, and Germany, as well as Jewish and Roma residents – a social facet that has been part of the city for centuries, with Baia Mare welcoming Ukrainian communities more recently.
The award organisers said: “The application sees that coexistence as the meaning of its Christmas, which, in the dossier’s words, aims to be ‘a work of the heart’.”
Omiš, Croatia: European Village of Christmas
At the centre of Omiš’s application was the Nart Christmas village. This small area is home to just 11 permanent residents – all of whom are members of the Lučić family.
What the population lacks in size, however, it makes up for in festive spirit; building a two-kilometre-long illuminated trail with more than five million LED lights.
This alone draws around 70,000 people during Advent, who are treated to klapa music, a living nativity scene, cooking from at least 10 family farms and a sanctuary of more than 150 animals. Klapa groups, folklore associations and theatre companies all take part in the programme.
The village itself sprawls over almost 40,000 square metres, with the array of lights following existing paths, native trees and dry-stone walls.
The European Capital of Christmas initiative also highlighted that most of the decorations are handmade from natural or recycled materials that are then stored, repaired and rearranged each year.

noticias.titulo: Second tanker in two days sinks off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast, search operation under way
noticias.resumen: The tanker had disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and by 8:02 am (07:02 CET) local time the emergency buoy was activated, emitting a signal for a sunken ship.
noticias.texto:
The tanker had disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and by 8:02 am (07:02 CET) local time the emergency buoy was activated, emitting a signal for a sunken ship.
A Liberia-flagged gas tanker sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea on Tuesday, according to the Defence Ministry.
Bulgarian military personnel and aircraft are involved in the search and rescue operation for the crew of 19 Filipino citizens of the gas carrier GAS HUSKY, which sank about 50 nautical miles (around 100 kilometres) off the coast, the ministry said in a statement.
It said that a Cougar chopper has been dispatched to the site where a life raft with people had been located. The rescue operation is ongoing.
The tanker had disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and by 8:02 am (07:02 CET) local time the emergency buoy was activated, emitting a signal for a sunken ship.
The tanker, en route from Alexandria, Egypt, to the Romanian port of Midia, is the second merchant ship to sink off Bulgaria’s coast in two days.
On Monday, a Somali-flagged cargo ship sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone not far away from the site of Tuesday’s incident.
All 12 crew members on board were saved in a rescue operation.
Investigations into the causes of the incidents are being launched. So far, there is no official information on whether the vessels were hit by drones.
There had been several deadly drone attacks against merchant ships off Bulgaria and Romania in recent weeks, widely blamed by analysts and political leaders on Russia’s war against Ukraine.
This is a developing story and our journalists are working on further updates.

noticias.titulo: EU preliminarily finds Temu broke rules on illegal and unsafe products
noticias.resumen: The preliminary findings point to weak product checks, content moderation and seller sanctions, potentially exposing the Chinese online marketplace to a fine of up to 6% of its global annual turnover.
noticias.texto:
The preliminary findings point to weak product checks, content moderation and seller sanctions, potentially exposing the Chinese online marketplace to a fine of up to 6% of its global annual turnover.
The European Commission has accused Temu of not doing enough to stop illegal and unsafe products from being sold on its platform, in preliminary findings that could see the Chinese online marketplace fined up to 6% of its global annual turnover.
The preliminary findings come months after Temu was fined €200 million by the Commission for allowing the sale of illegal products such as dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers on its platform, arguing that the Chinese retailer was not carrying out appropriate risk assessments.
Temu was then asked to come up with an action plan to address several breaches of its rules governing digital services known as the Digital Services Act, which was subsequently approved by the Commission in October.
But the Commission found that Temu was not doing enough.
Safety standards
Commission investigators cited several ongoing issues, including "ineffective controls to ensure safety standards", "weak content moderation" and an "ineffective sanction system".
On safety standards, investigators say Temu only requires sellers to provide test reports for only a handful of products and even then, these reports are often not checked by the company.
Temu’s safety checks of high-risk products such as electronics and cosmetics were also not prioritised by the company, nor were the results of spot checks followed up.
Content moderation
Temu’s moderation system was found to have not done enough to prevent the sale of illegal products. The report says the current moderation system appears to mainly look at the product’s own information rather than checking the safety of the product itself.
Investigators also found that the company’s comparison system does focus on product safety when looking at previously identified non-compliant goods, meaning consumers may find it harder to find safe products.
Investigators also found that the number of human moderators had not grown in line with the expanding range of products on the platform.
Sanctions
The Commission also found that the Chinese retailer’s sanction system was "fragmented" and "ineffective", arguing that it does not target traders effectively, nor does it act as a sufficient deterrent.
For example, investigators have said that sanctions are imposed on stores rather than the traders that operate them, meaning if a trader has one of their stores banned, they can simply keep selling through another store.
They also found that Temu was taking too long to act against traders who repeatedly violated the platform’s rules, such as suspending their stores.
Temu’s response
The Chinese retailer rejected the Commission’s findings.
"We respectfully disagree with the Commission's preliminary findings concerning our measures to mitigate risks related to the dissemination of illegal products," the company said in a statement.
Temu said it "invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise" and that it “implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products".
It added that they will "review and respond to the findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission".
"We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns."
Next steps
Temu can now review the Commission’s findings and prepare its defence.
However, if the Chinese retailer fails to convince the Commission that it is making enough of an effort to stamp out illegal trade on its marketplace, then it could face a fine of up to 6% of its annual global turnover.

noticias.titulo: EU readies fresh sanctions on Russia amid 'absurd' demands and winter strikes
noticias.resumen: A new round of EU sanctions against Russia is already in the works. Banks, crypto platforms and the "shadow fleet" are the likeliest targets.
noticias.texto:
A new round of EU sanctions against Russia is already in the works. Banks, crypto platforms and the "shadow fleet" are the likeliest targets.
The European Union is preparing a new round of economic sanctions against Russia as Moscow intensifies its airstrikes, seeking to make Ukraine's winter unbearable.
The Kremlin's demands to redesign Europe's security architecture, which High Representative Kaja Kallas slammed as "absurd", add further urgency to the matter.
The European Commission began consulting member states on Tuesday. The process, known as "confessionals", is meant to test the waters and avoid surprises.
The sanctions package is expected to target Russia's banking sector, the cryptocurrency channels it uses to skirt mainstream payment systems, and the decrepit "shadow fleet" it has deployed to bypass the oil price cap.
The Commission has set up a dedicated sanctions office to improve enforcement inside the bloc and crack down on countries that help Russia evade restrictions.
The fight against circumvention will feature prominently in the proposal.
Brussels is keen to prevent a repeat of the previous sanctions package, which saw various member states slap vetoes to water down, postpone or outright eliminate elements they resented. The chaotic negotiations left a bitter aftertaste among officials and diplomats and prompted a reckoning on working methods.
The bloc has recently turned to listings – individual sanctions on people, companies and organisations – that are presumably easier to agree. The thinking was upended in September after France shocked its peers by demanding the renewal of a high-profile oligarch to secure the release of two prisoners in Azerbaijan.
The focus now returns to the big-tent packages that have become a staple in the European strategy against Russia's war of aggression.
The proposal in the works will be the 22nd since February 2022 and will be formally presented before the end of the month.
No major or headline-grabbing measures are expected to be included to ensure the negotiations proceed smoothly and conclude in December.
The discussions will overlap with efforts to advance the peace negotiations into a multilateral format, with European and Russian representatives sitting at the negotiating table simultaneously. Despite US pressure, Moscow continues to resist this format, claiming that Europe should first present a "constructive, substantial contribution".
Russian officials could use the announcement of the sanctions as a pretext to continue refusing direct talks with the European delegation.
The prevailing opinion in Europe is that Russia does not take the peace talks seriously, as shown by the relentless attacks it is launching against Ukraine to impair the energy system and trigger widespread blackouts at sub-zero temperatures.
Kyiv has already asked Brussels to increase humanitarian aid to keep the lights on and the economy running during the war's harshest winter yet.
"I don't think the appetite for more sanctions is diminishing among member states," a senior diplomat said, dismissing the risk that the sanctions might derail diplomacy.
"With negotiations ongoing, it's important to show that European partners are steadfast in their support for Ukraine and their pressure on Russia."
On Wednesday, the Commission will present its proposal for a €45 billion support loan to cover Ukraine's 2027 financial shortfall.

noticias.titulo: ‘Time for action’: Germany and 10 other EU countries urge new copyright rules in the AI age
noticias.resumen: Germany and 10 other EU countries urge the Commission to propose new legislation protecting copyright in the age of AI, ahead of a Culture Ministers’ meeting on Thursday.
noticias.texto:
Germany and 10 other EU countries urge the Commission to propose new legislation protecting copyright in the age of AI, ahead of a Culture Ministers’ meeting on Thursday.
Germany and 10 other member states are urging the European Commission to table new legislation to safeguard copyrighted works in the age of artificial intelligence.
Germany, Spain, Poland, Austria, Cyprus, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Portugal, Slovakia and Slovenia have thrown their weight behind stronger protection for the cultural and creative sector as AI technologies advance.
“We call on the European Commission to present a corresponding legislative proposal as soon as possible,” reads a note the 11 countries submitted for the agenda of the Culture Ministers’ meeting on Thursday and Friday.
Advanced AI systems such as large language models are trained on trillions of data points, scraped from the open internet among other sources, often with little regard for whether the material is protected by copyright.
For the tech sector, restricting access to copyrighted material would leave Europe further behind the US and China in the AI race. For the creative and cultural industries, current practices amount to mass theft and undermine their livelihoods.
“Since AI has moved from pure research into broad practical application, it has led to profound upheavals in human creative processes and the perception and experience of art and culture. Its extent is becoming increasingly clear, and the need for action more urgent,” the document continues.
Balancing technological innovation with the protection of human-created content also divides national governments, where economy ministries tend to side with start-ups and culture ministries with creators.
The initiative is the latest push by the supporters’ culture ministries for a new legislative tool to shield copyright holders from the data scraping of AI developers. It follows a similar call in May by eight countries, showing the initiative is gaining support.
“The aim is to protect human creative work while enabling AI innovation in Europe. European innovation and AI development require fair competition and a level playing field with non-European providers, irrespective of where the AI was developed and, in particular, where it was trained,” the document states.
The Commission is due to present a legislative package on digital transformation, simplification and copyright in the second quarter of 2027, according to its work programme.
Earlier this month, the EU executive closed a public consultation on possible measures to strengthen copyright protection, including the use of protected content in AI.
The EU already has a Copyright Directive, which allows creators to opt out of having their work used to develop AI. In the note, the countries call for swift action to make that opt-out easier to enforce.

noticias.titulo: Nvidia sets up committee to oversee national security and export controls
noticias.resumen: “Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones said.
noticias.texto:
“Nvidia recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security,” Nvidia chairperson Harvey Jones said.
Nvidia's board has established a national security and export control oversight committee, which comes amid growing scrutiny from the United States over how the artificial intelligence giant handled exports of its chips to companies linked to China.
Nvidia's cofounder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after multiple extramarital affairs were revealed, including with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang and Trump had formed a close relationship, with Huang becoming a key voice for the US on artificial intelligence while he also lobbied for allowing chip exports to China.
“NVIDIA recognises that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security," said Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors.
He added the company "has both a responsibility and an opportunity to lead the industry in addressing these challenges," and that it was "committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation”.
The new committee will oversee the company's national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management, Nvidia said in a statement
The panel will meet quarterly, including with management and in executive session, and retain independent outside experts in law, national security and trade compliance, the company added.
Nvidia launched an investigation into Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy. The board said last week that it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised.
Meanwhile, on Monday, the US Commerce Department unveiled an interim final rule targeting remote access to advanced computing chips and servers through overseas data centres.

noticias.titulo: Serbia's new parliament meets for first time since student-led movement won election
noticias.resumen: The landslide result last month followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.
noticias.texto:
The landslide result last month followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.
Representatives of Serbia's student-backed movement were sworn in on Tuesday, in the first parliamentary sitting since last month's historic election victory ended 14 years of rule by Aleksandar Vučić's right-wing party.
The landslide result followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.
The disaster, widely blamed on corruption, triggered Serbia's largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milošević in 2000 and paved the way for victory on an anti-graft platform.
The inaugural parliamentary session, which saw the movement's 140 candidates officially take their seats, formally recognises the movement's majority and is the first step towards forming a government.
Political newcomers
Earlier hundreds of supporters gathered outside parliament to welcome the new lawmakers, chanting protest slogans and applauding.
Some held banners wishing the freshly elected MPs luck, while the arrival of Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) candidates drew jeers and boos.
One SNS member had yogurt poured on her head by a woman in the crowd as she walked up the steps of the parliament's entrance.
The Students' List secured 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, enough to govern alone, while Vučić's coalition won 103. Minority parties took the remaining seven seats.
Most of student-backed candidates are political newcomers from academic or arts backgrounds.
"We are preparing very seriously for everything ahead, studying the laws, parliamentary procedures and MPs' duties," prominent Student List candidate Mirjana Nikolic told the AFP news agency earlier this month.
The students' victory sparked days of raucous celebration in cities across the country and the highly anticipated session's broadcast is expected to draw viewers nationwide.
Challenges ahead
Once parliament is constituted, the new majority will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government.
The student movement has pledged wide-ranging reforms, including improving healthcare, boosting education and doubling the defence budget.
It will also have to balance the country's historically close ties with Russia with its long-stated goal of joining the European Union and manage relations with Kosovo, its former province whose 2008 declaration of independence Belgrade does not recognise.
The election of a parliamentary speaker will also bring a new acting president, a role the speaker has held since Vučić cut short his second presidential term in September to run for prime minister.
A snap presidential election must be called by 27 November and held by 27 December.
Both the student movement and Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party are expected to field presidential candidates, but Vučić is barred from running again under the constitution's two-term limit.
Instead, the former president took up his new place in parliament as the opposition leader.

noticias.titulo: Reporting a revolution: Anders Engman's 1956 Hungarian uprising photos on show in Budapest
noticias.resumen: At 23, Anders Engman entered the revolution as a reporter for a Swedish weekly. He worked in over 100 countries, but saw covering the 1956 Hungarian events as his key work.
noticias.texto:
At 23, Anders Engman entered the revolution as a reporter for a Swedish weekly. He worked in over 100 countries, but saw covering the 1956 Hungarian events as his key work.
An open-air photography exhibition has opened in the garden of Hungary's National Museum of work taken during the 1956 revolution by Swedish photojournalist Anders Engman.
Engman portrayed the historic days with exceptional sensitivity, and he also took one of the famous portraits of Erika Szeles, who was killed in the fighting at the age of 15.
"The images he shot in Budapest, in Győr, along the Hungarian-Austrian border and later in the refugee camp in Austria are today not only key documents of the revolution but also of the history of international press photography," said Zsuzsanna Szabados-Jámbor, deputy director-general of the Hungarian National Museum.
At the opening ceremony, Engman's widow said that he arrived in Hungary, almost like a child, at the age of 23; and although in the following decades he travelled the world and worked in more than 100 countries, the revolution remained his most important work.
"When he was asked what had influenced him the most and what was the most important thing he had ever done, he always immediately replied: Budapest, 1956," recalled Inga-Britt Liljeroth.
One of the most striking photographs in the exhibition shows artist Tibor András drawing on the shot-up Grand Boulevard.
The painter and war correspondent’s son recalled the events of 70 years ago as follows:
"My mother locks the door because my father wants to go out to draw, and she says, don’t go anywhere, you have two children, if you die, what will happen to us? My father was a hot-tempered man, he put on his spring shoes, look, these are spring shoes he is wearing, because my mother had hidden his clothes, he opened the window overlooking the small room corridor and jumped out of the window. This shook me terribly as a little boy, that my father ran off and went out because he felt that he had to be there."
Anders Engman’s widow still keeps several hundred more photographs taken of the revolution in Hungary, and the Committee of National Remembrance is already discussing with her their future presentation.

noticias.titulo: How Ukrainian forces struck Putin's prized and heavily defended Crimean bridge
noticias.resumen: Ukraine's unprecedented seven-stage operation reportedly partially destroyed one of Russia's most heavily defended infrastructure sites, a vital military supply route to occupied Crimea and the crown jewel of Vladimir Putin's occupation of the peninsula.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine's unprecedented seven-stage operation reportedly partially destroyed one of Russia's most heavily defended infrastructure sites, a vital military supply route to occupied Crimea and the crown jewel of Vladimir Putin's occupation of the peninsula.
Ukrainian forces used a combination of drones and missiles to strike the road and railway sections of the Crimean Bridge overnight into Tuesday, following weeks of coordinated attacks aimed at dismantling Russian air defences protecting the crossing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed details of the strike, which marked the culmination of a seven-stage operation developed and coordinated by Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) and the General Staff of the Armed Forces, involving 11 different weapons systems.
Images circulating after the attack appeared to show one of the bridge's main arches and part of its roadway collapsed into the sea, potentially dealing a major blow to the crossing linking Russia with occupied Crimea.
Russia's Transport Ministry confirmed that both road and rail traffic had been suspended following a second consecutive day of attacks, but did not confirm the reported collapse.
How Ukraine carried out the operation
In a detailed statement published on X, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had spent several weeks systematically targeting Russian military systems protecting the crossing.
"Our warriors gradually destroyed air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective," Zelenskyy said.
He identified eleven weapons systems used throughout the operation: Dovbush, Vendetta, Da Vinci, Sichen, Mich-2000, Ruta, Palianytsia, An-197, FP-1, FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptune.
At the final stage, Ukrainian forces used different weapons to target the bridge's two transport sections.
"Today, at the key stage, the 'Palianytsia' drones performed exceptionally well, striking the road section of the bridge, while 'Neptune' missiles, 'Ruta' drones, and FP-5 drones struck the railway section," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president also highlighted the use of the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile in a precision-guided strike.
"Using 'Flamingo,' our warriors carried out a precision-guided strike – and the communications uplink worked flawlessly until the very last seconds."
Robert Brovdi, known by his callsign "Magyar", commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, also commented on the attack, identifying several Ukrainian military units involved in the operation.
According to Brovdi, the strike was a joint operation involving deep-strike units of the Ukrainian Navy, the Rocket Forces and Artillery, the newly formed 7th Centre of the 414th "Magyar's Birds" Brigade, the 1st Centre of the Unmanned Systems Forces and Ukraine's Security Service (SBU).
"The sacred bridge is tired. It's time for rubber dinghies," Brovdi wrote.
He also suggested that the attack would have lasting consequences for Russian transport connections to the peninsula.
Fire Point, the Ukrainian manufacturer of the Flamingo cruise missile, reacted to the attack on X, posting a brief message: "Crimea is Ukraine btw."
"Crimean Bridge. Sanctioned," Ukraine's Presidential Sanctions Commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk wrote in a separate post on X.
Zelenskyy did not specify how many drones or missiles were launched, how many reached their targets, or which weapons were responsible for the reported collapse.
What happened to the bridge?
Images published by Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels, appear to show only one of the bridge's two arches remaining.
The channels reported that the other arch and part of the roadway had collapsed into the sea following the overnight attack.
Russia's Transport Ministry said the damage was being assessed but did not confirm the reported collapse.
The extent of the structural damage has not been independently verified.
Why the Crimean Bridge matters
The 19-kilometre Crimean Bridge connects Russia's Krasnodar Krai region with the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula across the Kerch Strait.
Constructed after Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014, the $4 billion project opened to road traffic in 2018, with passenger rail services beginning in 2019.
The bridge serves as a critical military supply and transport route for Russian forces operating in occupied territories in southern Ukraine, facilitating the movement of military equipment, supplies and personnel.
It also holds enormous symbolic significance for Vladimir Putin, who championed its construction as a way of cementing Russia's control over Crimea following the annexation, one of the defining moments of his presidency.
The bridge has repeatedly been targeted by Ukrainian forces, suffering significant damage in October 2022 and July 2023, although neither attack permanently put it out of commission.
Zelenskyy described the latest operation as a response to Russia's continued attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, including bridges in Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and the Odesa region.
"We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation – and every proposal has been met with loud rejection," he said.
"Ukraine’s defensive capabilities are strong and will remain so, and we will never leave terror against our cities and people unanswered."

noticias.titulo: Neanderthal gene variant linked to lower schizophrenia risk, study finds
noticias.resumen: Modern humans have Neanderthals to thank for a common genetic variant that affects the occipital lobe.
noticias.texto:
Modern humans have Neanderthals to thank for a common genetic variant that affects the occipital lobe.
A gene mutation inherited from Neanderthals may reduce the risk of schizophrenia by almost 10%, a new study has found.
Neanderthals were close evolutionary cousins of modern humans, but they went extinct about 40,000 years ago. Due to interbreeding between species, modern people outside of Africa have up to 1% to 4% Neanderthal DNA, while sub-Saharan Africans are thought to have far less Neanderthal DNA.
The study found that Neanderthals passed on a common genetic variant affecting the occipital lobe, which is found at the back of the brain. The occipital lobe is home to the brain’s visual cortex and plays a role in vision, mental imagery and reading.
Neanderthals are thought to have had larger occipital lobes than modern humans. Yet modern people with the genetic variant have smaller occipital lobes — a reduction of about 0.85 cubic centimeters per copy, according to the study, which was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The variant lies near DAAM1, a protein-coding gene involved in brain development.
In people with two copies of the gene variant, it is also linked to a nearly 10% lower risk of schizophrenia, but the variant does not seem to affect intelligence or other major psychiatric disorders.
“This Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability,” wrote study authors and evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo
“These findings caution against equating the size of a brain region with cognitive abilities,” they added.
Zeberg, of the Karolinska Institutet in Sweden, and Pääbo, a 2022 Nobel Prize winner from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, have worked together for years to identify how Neanderthal genes affect human health today.
They previously found that a major Neanderthal-inherited gene cluster on chromosome 3 raises the risk of severe COVID-19. Subsequent research found the same variant protects against HIV.
In 2021,another research teamfound that Neanderthal ancestry may alter the gene pool in a way that affects schizophrenia risk.
But according to Zeberg and Pääbo, any “protective effect” appears specific to the recently identified gene variant.

noticias.titulo: Germany and Norway to buy more US air defences for Ukraine, including Patriot missiles
noticias.resumen: Ukraine has desperately been urging its backers to help find more Patriots as they are the only system capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine has desperately been urging its backers to help find more Patriots as they are the only system capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
Germany and Norway will fund a new package of US Patriot air defences for Ukraine, Germany's defence minister said on Tuesday, as Kyiv struggles to defend against repeated Russian air strikes.
"Russia is intensifying its air attacks because it is not making progress on the battlefield," minister Boris Pistorius said at an EU meeting in Brussels.
Pistorius said that Berlin would contribute $300 million (€272 million) to buying the latest tranche of US weaponry, with the focus of the package on air defence, and in particular Patriot interceptor missiles.
Russia has stepped up its bombing campaign on cities and infrastructure around Ukraine in what Kyiv says is an attempt to freeze the country into submission this winter.
Ukraine has desperately been urging its backers to help find more Patriots as they are the only system capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles.
Kyiv has been facing a dire shortfall as US stockpiles have been drained by the war with Iran.
The announcement of fresh support comes ahead of a meeting of Ukraine's military backers at NATO headquarters in Brussels later on Tuesday.
The United States under Donald Trump has stopped giving weaponry to Kyiv but allows other countries to purchase American arms for Ukraine.
NATO says that Washington's allies have so far spent more than $10 billion (€9 billion) on US weaponry for Kyiv.
The push to shore up Ukraine's defences comes as there appears to be renewed momentum in US-led efforts to halt the fighting in Ukraine.
But Kyiv and its backers say Moscow continues to escalate its attacks and is showing little sign that it is genuinely interested in peace.

noticias.titulo: Kim Jong Un tours ski resort with wife and daughter
noticias.resumen: North Korea's Kim Jong Un tours a ski resort in Samjiyon with his family, smiling and smoking in photos.
noticias.texto:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a ski resort under development in Samjiyon, near the Chinese border, on Sunday and Monday.
Photos released by state media on Tuesday show him smiling in sunglasses and smoking a cigarette, with his wife Ri Sol Ju nearby. His daughter Ju Ae was also pictured skiing down a slope.
According to the Korean Central News Agency, Kim toured hotels and ski facilities and praised the construction and surrounding mountain scenery.
The visit came as US President Donald Trump suggested he might meet Kim during his trip to China.
Beijing said it had no information about such a meeting, while analysts saw no indication that the resort tour was linked to possible talks.
Trump and Kim met three times between 2018 and 2019, but no new meeting had been confirmed.

noticias.titulo: The 5 Labour groups that matter as Burnham shows his hand on welfare
noticias.resumen: The prime minister’s proposals to alter social security will need support across his parliamentary party to succeed.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Keir Starmer’s failed attempt at welfare reform was the beginning of the end of his premiership. Andy Burnham needs to avoid a similar fate. The new prime minister’s own effort to tackle a rapid surge in working-age sickness and disability benefit claims kicked off in earnest on Tuesday, when former Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn published a long-awaited review into youth unemployment — before being given a new post chairing a youth opportunities unit to help drive the reforms. He proposes changing the disability benefits young people are entitled to while giving them a legal right to education, employment or training. He also suggests that employers’ National Insurance contributions should be cut for 21-to-24-year-olds in the retail and hospitality sectors for five years. There’s a long way to go before MPs find out which of Milburn’s recommendations the government implements. A white paper and legislation are not due to be published until next year. Getting Labour MPs — many of whom are long-standing anti-poverty campaigners — to back plans which ultimately aim to cut Britain’s massive welfare bill will be no mean feat. Despite a huge majority in the House of Commons, Starmer was forced to roll back plans to reduce personal independence payments — which go to disabled people both in and out of work — after a well-organized campaign by senior Labour figures back in 2025. POLITICO runs through the key figures from the governing party whose views on the report — and critically Burnham’s eventual proposal — are worth paying attention to. 1) The committee chairs Treasury Committee Chair Meg Hillier and Work and Pensions Committee Chair Debbie Abrahams played a crucial role in halting some of Starmer’s welfare reforms. Hillier wrote an amendment to Starmer’s welfare plans which would have stopped the bill at its first hurdle. More than 100 Labour MPs from across the party signaled they would back it, forcing ministers to change course and promise any changes would only be made after a review by Disabilities Minister Stephen Timms, which is due later this month. Abrahams — who supported Hillier’s blocking amendment — was another key organizer of the welfare revolt under Starmer, and has repeatedly warned that reform should not take support away from those who need it most. Hillier said last week, after some of Milburn’s proposals were previewed in an interview in the Times newspaper, that he had “done some very good work on this” and she was “giving him a fair wind.” She said it was “quite radical and quite bold and quite right to be looking holistically at the person in the middle of this, not just about the money or the structure of the benefits.” On Tuesday, Abrahams described them as the “opportunity of a generation,” welcoming Milburn’s “rigorous analysis” on why young people become “NEETs” – not in education, employment or training. 2) The ministers Milburn’s proposals come with a price tag, making Chancellor John Healey a crucial figure to watch as Burnham finalizes his plans. The overall changes would cost £5.8 billion a year — offset by £6 billion in savings, Milburn suggests. Also sitting around the Cabinet table is Burnham’s de facto deputy, Louise Haigh, who helped organize the rebellion against Starmer’s welfare reforms. And Vicky Foxcroft, who quit as a government whip in June 2025, warning that cuts to PIP and Universal Credit should “not be part of the solution” to bringing down the welfare bill, is now a culture minister. All are now bound by collective responsibility, where ministers must not speak out openly against the government agenda. But every word they utter on welfare will be closely scrutinized for clues on exactly where the government might land. 3) The grandee Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown — who has long campaigned against poverty and inequality — is seen as an authority on welfare in the Labour Party. He parked the convention that ex-prime ministers try not to make life difficult for their successors in an interview with the New Statesman last year, reflecting on the “worrying issue” of reducing social security that left people “in poverty as a result.” He campaigned for — and lauded — the Starmer government’s move to abolish a two-child benefit cap. Any intervention by this ex-PM would be significant. 4) The wider rank and file The strength of feeling among other key backbench MPs who rebelled over Starmer’s plans will be an important barometer of how Burnham’s own reforms take shape. Marie Tidball — who has a congenital disability affecting all four of her limbs and strongly campaigned for changes to Starmer’s reforms behind the scenes — welcomed Milburn’s messaging that there “won’t be crude cuts to benefits.” Rachael Maskell, another vocal rebel, also welcomed the report, though warned employers should not “discriminate against young people being able to secure a job, not least if they experience severe anxiety or mental health challenges.” Mainstream — a soft left Labour faction of which Burnham was an early backer — said in a statement there is “much to welcome” in the review. However, the group’s interim council warned in its X post that the ambition “must not come at the expense of anyone already struggling to get by.” 5) The Starmerites Ministers who served under Starmer know just how hard welfare reform is — and their views on Burnham’s plans will grab attention. Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves is yet to comment on Milburn’s costly suggestions, but was busy defending her own record by highlighting a new report showing reduced levels of child poverty after she scrapped the two-child benefit cap. Liz Kendall — who was work and pensions secretary under Starmer —was keen to raise a lack of AI skills and experience that could affect NEETs.

noticias.titulo: Uganda in talks to host EU migration hub
noticias.resumen: ”The discussion is at a stage of a cup of coffee,” the foreign ministry’s permanent secretary said.
noticias.texto: VIENNA — Uganda is in talks with European Union countries about hosting a hub for rejected asylum-seekers, a senior official from the African nation told POLITICO. On Monday, five EU countries — Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands — announced plans to start deportations to a center in Rwanda from next year. On Tuesday, Vincent Waiswa Bagiire, permanent secretary to Uganda’s foreign affairs ministry, confirmed that his country was interested in hosting a return hub. Bagiire said Uganda had a “discussion” with the Netherlands but “we haven’t got far.” He didn’t say which other countries Uganda had been speaking with but said the talks were not that advanced: “Let me say that the discussion is at a stage of a cup of coffee.” In June, European diplomats said Uganda and Uzbekistan were being discussed as potential locations for EU migration centers. However, Uganda has three criteria that need to be met before it can host a hub, Bagiire said on the sidelines of a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. “If we are to establish a hub, it will be strictly for people of African origin; they should not have a criminal record; [and] no unaccompanied minors,” he said. He added that the discussions involve “no more than 50” people, who would be sent to open facilities. “No detention, they’re not prisons — at all. People can integrate within the communities … they’re free to do whatever they need to do. The same way we treat our refugees,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Russia’s Lavrov says French troops in Ukraine amount to ‘direct participation’ in war
noticias.resumen: The Kremlin's foreign minister seized on a French media report to warn Europe against deploying troops to Ukraine.
noticias.texto: Russia’s top diplomat accused Paris of directly taking part in the Ukraine war following a report that French troops are in the eastern European country carrying out noncombatant operations. “We conveyed our concern through available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer support for Ukraine, but direct participation in the war,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters Tuesday at the East Asia Summit in Manila, adding that French troops were also “assisting in goal setting, providing satellite data and much more.” Lavrov’s comments come a day after Radio France Internationale revealed Paris had kept troops in Ukraine for several months to provide training and equipment maintenance under the “Volia mission.” The troops, who are in the French military detachment in Poland, have been involved in the operation in Ukraine since at least summer 2026, RFI reported. Since the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russian officials have periodically warned Europe against putting troops into the country, as Moscow looks to deter the continent from participating in Ukraine’s resistance with active soldiers. The Elysée Palace did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot pledged to fight “tooth and nail” for European security during Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, following the announcement that Paris would represent Europe in Ukraine peace talks as part of the “E5,” alongside Germany, Italy, Poland and the U.K. In Manila, Lavrov declined to expand on the upcoming trilateral meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, taking place in Shenzhen in southeastern China on Thursday. “It is broadly clear what the leaders will discuss. They will have an opportunity for a free exchange of views. Be patient. There is very little time left to wait,” Lavrov told reporters.

noticias.titulo: Brussels signals unwillingness to be Burnham’s EU sounding board
noticias.resumen: The British prime minister wants to gauge what's possible with the bloc before laying out options to voters back home. EU diplomats say it may not be so straightforward.
noticias.texto: LONDON — Andy Burnham wants to sound out options with the EU in his quest to ease Brexit. But Brussels is signaling that the U.K. prime minister needs to get his own plan together first. The PM used a major foreign affairs speech Monday night to slow the timeline of his ambitions for bringing Britain closer to the bloc. Instead of setting out “different options” for future relations around the time of Friday’s upcoming EU-U.K. summit, as he promised in September, he now wants to first fish for options with European allies. But that timeline isn’t being welcomed with open arms in Brussels. A senior EU diplomat with knowledge of the European Commission’s desired process made clear to POLITICO that the first step is for Britain to decide what changes it is considering. “On the next steps, it should be about the U.K. first assessing its options and then engaging with the EU, rather than the other way around,” said the official, granted anonymity to discuss internal thinking. Britain’s PM may, however, find more sympathetic ears among member states than in the European Commission. A second EU diplomat said Burnham’s suggestion that he would sound out Brussels about different options “makes sense,” adding there is a “need to be pragmatic.” “There are very real mutual benefits to be unlocked,” they said. “Rather than getting lost in abstract debates about the ultimate destination, perhaps the more useful question is where we can make co-operation work better, here and now?” A third EU diplomat said there could be a “gray area” in which both things are true. While Britain can’t do “substantial negotiations” with the EU until there’s a “consensus” in the U.K., the same diplomat said it would be right for “some level of conversation with Brussels to see what’s sensible” so that realistic options can then be discussed with the British public. But others agreed that the U.K. must provide sharper definition. A fourth EU diplomat said: “I think the next step in this process is that the EU needs a little more clarity on where the U.K. stands.” A fifth said Burnham must first “include in his vision something that is realistic” which can then “be worked on together with the EU.” Anand Menon, the director of the UK in a Changing Europe think tank, said a timeline where Brussels wants firmer proposals first should come as no surprise to Britain. “The EU wants Britain to come to them and say this is the kind of relationship they want,” he said. “They want us to do that with a relationship that’s on offer rather than make up something that they are not willing to give.” Two U.K. government officials suggested that Burnham will still address future relations with Europe after the summit — but that this would be more limited to the “next steps” for the process. Later on Tuesday, Burnham seemed to soften his language again, telling Sky News he will consider “whether there are options” to deepen Britain’s relationship with the EU. He said he would set them out alongside a government-wide 10-year plan due later this year. That would appear to fall short of what Burnham billed back in September, when addressing supporters in his first Labour Party conference speech as leader. Back then, the U.K. prime minister promised “to lay out to the country what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners” at some point “around the summit” in Brussels on Friday. He left a full-blown push to rejoin the EU open as one of the possibilities. Since then, however, there has been a wave of hesitancy coming from within Burnham’s own Cabinet about the ramifications of reopening the fraught Brexit debate. British public opinion may have changed greatly since the 2016 referendum, but U.K. politics remains scarred by the rancorous debates it produced. Burnham used a Lord Mayor’s banquet speech in London on Monday evening to try cool off the timeline of his new approach. “After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship, recognizing that both Britain and the EU are very different to what they were,” he said. “This will take time and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next parliament. At every stage, the British people will be the boss.” Andrew McDonald contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: Le Pen defends retirement reform plan as opponents mock her economic credibility
noticias.resumen: The far-right leader says her plan to lower the retirement age would be offset by savings and employer-funded pension schemes.
noticias.texto: PARIS — Far-right French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen pushed back against the latest accusations on Tuesday that the math behind her pension reform doesn’t add up, arguing she and her team had done “a painstaking meticulous job” to create a system that is both “fair” and “economically efficient.” “We are taking the situation seriously,” Le Pen said as she briefed reporters on the fine print of her proposal to bring down the retirement age to 62 for most workers. France’s retirement age is set to rise to 64 for most people in the coming years. Le Pen and her lieutenants argued that while their proposal would cost more than €18 billion, that bill would be offset by more than €23 billion in savings from efficiency adjustments, thighter qualification rules for part-time workers, incentives for older people to stay in work and a host of other measures. Le Pen also floated introducing some private pension schemes, financed by employers’ contributions, in addition to France’s state pension system. Yet Le Pen’s skeptics do not yet appear convinced by the figures and charts she presented. Le Pen and her party, the National Rally, have for years been accused of floating unrealistic or poorly constructed economic proposals, and their opponents and independent economists have repeatedly questioned whether her campaign pledge to lower the retirement age is feasible given the dire state of French public finances. Following Le Pen’s press conference, conservative presidential hopeful Bruno Retailleau posted a picture of an ostrich burying its head in the sand . A spokesperson for center-right presidential candidate Edouard Philippe wrote on X that the National Rally was “out of control” and taking “demagoguery to new heights.” During a presidential debate on Monday, Le Pen’s opponents also attacked her economic policies , including her proposal to enact €140 billion in savings by 2032. “It doesn’t add up,” said Retailleau. On Tuesday, Le Pen turned her fire on her opponents, accusing presidential candidates from President Emmanuel Macron’s political family of “deploying the heavy artillery” in proposing to push back the legal age of retirement. “Instead of repairing the pensions system, they want to make the French pay,” she said. She also accused the far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who could reach the runoff the presidential election of promising “all kinds of nonsense” with a pensions project that is “eye-watering”.

noticias.titulo: Polish far-right lawmaker Braun charged over hospital ‘citizen’s arrest’
noticias.resumen: Grzegorz Braun faces up to five years in prison for allegedly detaining a doctor who had performed an abortion.
noticias.texto:
Polish prosecutors charged far-right European Parliament lawmaker Grzegorz Braun on Tuesday over an alleged incident in which he tried to carry out a “citizen’s arrest” of a doctor who had performed an abortion.
The Wrocław regional prosecutor’s office said it had sent an indictment to the court in the southwestern town of Oleśnica, accusing Braun of depriving the doctor of her liberty, violating her bodily integrity and insulting her. The charges carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison, prosecutors added.
Braun and several supporters entered the Oleśnica hospital in April 2025 to confront a gynecologist who had carried out a late-term abortion on a patient whose life was at risk. The doctor said Braun held her for more than an hour by blocking the exit with his body.

noticias.titulo: Crimea bridge destruction will impair Russian supply chains, says Ukraine
noticias.resumen: The Ukrainian president gave details of a weeks-long operation aimed at crippling a crucial Russian transport route that also has symbolic meaning for Vladimir Putin.
noticias.texto: KYIV — Ukraine’s destruction of part of the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea was the result of a carefully planned operation involving Ukrainian weapons, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. Zelenskyy described the bridge strike as a response to Russian attacks against Ukrainian bridges that began a month ago. “We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region. We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began,” Zelenskyy said in a statement . The Russia-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksenov, confirmed the strike, saying the bridge was closed until further notice, but provided no details of the damage. Russia launched a bombing campaign against Ukrainian bridges on Oct. 1, choking logistics and causing huge public transport problems. The Russian defense ministry reported hitting Kyiv’s North and South bridges across the Dnipro River, linking the two sides of the Ukrainian capital. Ukraine said its attack against the $3.7 billion Kerch Bridge is part of its response to the Russian campaign. The road and rail bridge is a key supply line for the 2.5 million people living on the Crimean Peninsula, illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, as well as for Russian forces stationed there. The road portion has collapsed, and the extent of damage to the parallel rail bridge is uncertain, although the Russian transport ministry said Tuesday that limited traffic will resume on a single railway track. Without the bridge, Russia will have to rely on ferries and overland transport through occupied Ukraine — both routes subject to attack by Kyiv. “Partial destruction of the bridge affects logistics, supply chains, and the morale and psychological state of the families of Russian military personnel, intelligence officers, and officials,” said Andrii Klymenko, head of the Black Sea and Baltic Strategic Research Monitoring Group. Zelenskyy said the operation was carefully planned and gave a long list of the missiles and drones used. “Our warriors gradually destroyed air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective. For this, they used Dovbush, Vendetta, Da Vinci, Sichen, Mich-2000, Ruta, Palianytsia, An-197, FP-1, FP-5 Flamingo, and R-360 Neptune,” the president said. For the final stage, the Ukrainian army used Palianytsia drones to strike a road section of the bridge, while Neptune missiles, Ruta cruise missiles and FP-5 Flamingo heavy missiles struck the railway section. “Using Flamingo, our warriors carried out a precision-guided strike — and the communications uplink worked flawlessly until the very last seconds,” Zelenskyy said, thanking Ukrainian weapons manufacturers. Dutch-Ukrainian defense startup Destinus Group said that its Ruta missiles were used over two consecutive days. “Today, seven RUTA missiles hit the bridge, causing one span to collapse.” “For years, the Russians convinced the entire world that the Crimean Bridge was one of the most heavily protected structures on the planet. Today, parts of it lie on the seabed,” said the press service of Ukraine’s SBU security agency. Russian pro-war bloggers confirmed the scale of the attack. “More than 10 Flamingo cruise missiles hit the target, plus a large number of drones. Given Russia’s air defense problems, the bridge could be ‘crushed’ by sheer numbers, without needing to overpower the defenses,” said the Rybar and Dva Mayora channels. Russian officials downplayed the attack, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying the bridge would be rebuilt even better than it was before. Russia-installed Sevastopol Governor Mikhail Razvozhaev said : “Supplies of food, fuel, diesel and other necessary goods continue. The bridge was not used for the delivery of goods that much, so the incident did not affect the supply of the city. Deliveries continue as usual.” He said the bridge is largely used by private cars and buses. “Now the main task is to work out alternative logistical solutions for people who need to return home or continue their journey,” Razvozhaev said, asking people not to travel to Crimea until the authorities announce alternative routes. Since Oct. 10, Ukrainian forces have targeted six other bridges near Crimea, creating growing problems for Russian logistics. “The problem of destabilizing the rear in Crimea — and the entire southern grouping of forces— will only intensify if the railway section of the bridge is destroyed or significantly damaged, as this route is the most efficient one,” said Klymenko. Disabling the bridge could make it more difficult for Russian forces to attack Odesa, Kherson and other regions along the Black Sea, said Ukrainian navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk. “With the bridge damaged and land routes to Crimea under Ukrainian operational control, it would now be significantly harder to deliver those drones Russia sends to Ukraine from the peninsula,” he said. This article has been updated.

noticias.titulo: Rwanda hits back at asylum-seeker return hub criticism
noticias.resumen: NGOs say Rwanda's human rights record means deportation hub plans fail EU and international law requirements.
noticias.texto: VIENNA — Rwanda’s interior minister has rebuked criticism of a plan by five European Union countries to deport failed asylum-seekers to his country. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands on Monday announced a partnership with Rwanda to set up a deportation hub. They aim to send the first asylum-seekers to the African country in 2027. The plan comes after the EU adopted legislation that allows countries to negotiate deals to build such “return hubs” outside the bloc — as long as they meet human rights standards. The announcement led to a storm of protest from civil society and human rights groups, which said the fundamental rights of people sent to Rwanda cannot be guaranteed. Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, disagreed. “Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country,” Biruta said Tuesday, speaking on a panel at a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. He argued his country’s migration policies are among the “most progressive” as they allow refugees to work and start a business. In a joint warning against the plan Monday , 47 organizations pointed to a 2023 court decision that slapped down the United Kingdom’s plans to process asylum seekers’ claims in Rwanda. It cited “substantial grounds” to believe that people sent to the African nation would be exposed “to a real risk of ill-treatment by reason of refoulement” — referring to a practice whereby people are forcibly moved to countries where they face real threats. Under a 2013 deal with Israel, people sent to Rwanda “were routinely moved clandestinely to Uganda,” the court added. Biruta said he was “not surprised” by NGOs’ warnings and said the government faced “the same issue” when it was making plans with the U.K. Those plans “didn’t work but … helped to improve our asylum system,” he added. NGOs “always … say that nothing is working, that our human rights record is bad,” Biruta said, “but I’d like them to come forward with an alternative solution.” EU ministers repeatedly stressed Monday that their partnership with Rwanda would meet international and European standards. Biruta said his country would put in place an independent monitoring mechanism and that it wants to involve the International Organization for Migration and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees. Details about such mechanisms and cooperation, as well as how the EU countries and Rwanda will divide responsibilities for the refugees’ wellbeing, have not yet been revealed. “There are still some technical things that have to be solved, including where [the responsibility of ] Europe ends and where Rwanda starts,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told POLITICO after the plan’s announcement. Human rights groups don’t believe the countries can come up with a framework that will guarantee migrants’ rights are respected. Rwanda has an abysmal human rights record, is responsible for serious abuses and war crimes in eastern Congo and engages in transnational repression, Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO. “No amount of nominal safeguards will be sufficient to mitigate the risks of serious human rights violations, particularly as there is unlikely to be any way to implement effective monitoring or seek accountability,” she said. “Given its track record, the fact that Rwanda was even considered, much less chosen, justifies deep skepticism about EU rhetoric about respecting people’s rights.” Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting .

noticias.titulo: EU countries postpone vote to lift Brazilian chicken ban
noticias.resumen: The vote was postponed after it became clear that enough member countries were likely to oppose the agreement, according to three EU diplomats.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Brazilian poultry meat won’t return to European supermarket shelves for now, after EU countries on Tuesday put off a vote that would have lifted a ban that has been in place since September. A committee with representatives of the EU’s member countries had been set to vote on the decision, but this was canceled as they failed to reach an agreement, European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said. The Commission said it would address the issue with the aim to discuss it again Dec. 7-8 at the next meeting of the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed (PAFF). Brazil failed to prove it complies with EU rules on antimicrobials and the EU halted poultry imports on Sept. 3. A subsequent Commission audit at the end of that month found that Brazil’s controls again meet the necessary requirements. Still, a number of countries “requested further clarifications on the system put in place by Brazil,” Hrncirova said. Tuesday’s vote was postponed after it became clear that enough member countries were likely to oppose the agreement to form a blocking minority, according to three EU diplomats familiar with the matter. The poultry dispute has added to tensions over the EU’s trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc, which includes Brazil and took effect in May. Farmers in countries including France and Poland have opposed the agreement, warning that cheaper South American imports would expose them to unfair competition. Bartosz Brzeziński and Camille Gijs contributed reporting.

noticias.resumen: In a voice from Gaza, Ahmed Abu Jami, a 28-year-old doctor, who lives in Khan Younis, told EUobserver via WhatsApp: "Things are bad, really Gaza is descending into hell."
noticias.texto:
New UK sanctions against Israel have spotlighted the EU’s inaction on the “man-made catastrophe” in Gaza and raging aggression in the West Bank.
The UK blacklisted eight Israeli construction firms which build homes for West Bank settlers on Tuesday (17 November), as well as the Tzav 9 activist group, which blocks humanitarian aid to Gaza.
“My message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build,” said British foreign secretary Ed Miliband, referring to the new ‘E1’ settlement designed to cut the West Bank in half and kill off the prospect of a two-state solution.
Israel is currently being led by a caretaker government amid post-election coalition talks.
Miliband noted that “more settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government [of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu] than in the previous 20 years.”
Floods in Gaza, after Israel destroyed its EU-funded water-management infrastructure, have left 4,000 people homeless, while 1.4 million people are living in tents in wintry weather, but Israel was blocking deliveries of tarpaulins and timber, Miliband added.
EU foreign minsters are also clear-eyed about what Israel is doing in Gaza and the West Bank.

noticias.titulo: EU asylum agency floats idea of foreign ‘processing centres’ to handle asylum claims
noticias.resumen: Innovative solutions is a catch all phrase that describes return hubs in Rwanda and Italy's controversial deal with Albania. Now it also applies to "process centres" for asylum seeker hopefuls.
noticias.texto:
Late last year, the EU tweaked laws allowing member states to have a person’s claim for asylum heard somewhere abroad.
Now, discussions are taking place to create a so-called “processing centre” in a foreign country, where the asylum seekers who initially landed in Europe would have their case for protection heard.
Nina Gregori, who heads the Malta-based European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), floated the idea in a passing remark about possible innovative solutions on migration control at the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD) conference in Vienna on Tuesday (17 November).
‘Innovative solutions’ is a catch-all phrase that has also applied to return hubs in Rwanda and Italy’s controversial deal with Albania.
Asked to further elaborate, she told EUobserver that the idea is already backed by European law, citing the so-called “safe-third country concept”.
The concept essentially shifts EU member states’ responsibility for processing asylum claims to foreign states, even if the asylum seeker has never set foot in the country. The concept itself is not new.

noticias.titulo: France dethrones Sweden as EU gender equality leader — but overall progress is slowing
noticias.resumen: Europe still has a significant gender gap. It's in employment, in who takes care of children, in places of power. It's stronger in places like Cyprus and Bulgaria, while Spain and Denmark prioritised its gender politics. But full gender equality is still a distant goal, as Europe still lags behind pre-pandemic levels of parity.
noticias.texto: France is leading the way on gender equality in the EU, according to a study published on Tuesday (17 November), with more female representation at decision-making levels becoming the main push for gender equality. The European institute for gender equality ( EIGE ) publishes an annual index measuring how close the EU is to equality between men and women. This year’s report shows a small improvement, though noting European societies are yet to recover from a post-pandemic slump in progress. The agency says this is “a sign that the momentum built over the past decade is losing strength”. The proportion of women in positions of power has grown faster than in any other sector, with increased representation in economic and social decision-making positions across several member states. Even so, it is still the lowest-scoring area of the index. While still remaining severely underrepresented in leadership positions, particularly compared to the Nordic countries, France and Spain have encouraged more policy action on gender equality. Read more EU reduces funds for women’s rights groups, in wider budget bonfire of good causes However, some of the Nordic nations have started to fall back. Sweden, whose 13-year record in leading the gender equality struggle was overtaken this year by France, is “kind of stagnating,” EIGE’s statistics officer, Davide Barbieri, told EUobserver. “We are going in a good direction, but we can do even better, and we need to do that together, member states as well, its regions, civil societies, companies, employers,” said EU commission executive vice-president for social rights, Roxana Mînzatu, at Tuesday’s launch event for the index in Brussels. “How we make sure that gender equality contributes and fuels growth, it’s always three levels that we need to act upon: it’s skills and education, it’s the quality of jobs, and it’s the availability of care” This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: EU freezes €62.5m of Slovakia’s recovery funds over plans linked to ousted environment minister
noticias.resumen: Internal government warnings, downgraded wind plans and controversial zoning tweaks by ousted environment minister Taraba’s team now emerge at the heart of the Commission’s decision, exposing how months of behind-the-scenes manoeuvring may have sabotaged Slovakia’s own green transition money.
noticias.texto: The European Commission has suspended €62.5m from Slovakia’s eighth recovery-plan payment over inadequacies in the zoning of national parks and preparation of a wind energy zone. The sum concerns the Recovery and Resilience Facility , part of the EU’s plan to emerge stronger from the Covid-19 pandemic by issuing funds for the green transition and country-specific investments. After the commission’s decision on Monday (16 November), the Slovak government now has two months to prepare its position and send the missing documentation to Brussels. The commission confirmed it only partially approved the eighth recovery-plan payment worth €735m, adding that Slovakia had not fulfilled two commitments concerning national park zoning and preparation of a wind farm zone. In its plans, Slovakia had not classified all threatened forests under the highest level of protection available. And the country also failed to show that the area chosen for a wind energy acceleration zone was suitable for building wind farms with a capacity of at least 300 megawatts. As a result, €62.5m is expected to be withheld. “Should the Commission, following Slovakia’s observations, confirm its assessment that the milestones in question have not been satisfactorily fulfilled, it will proportionally reduce the amount corresponding to this milestone and target, out of the total €548m under this payment request,” read an EU press release . Read more MEPs warn against EU rush to restarting funds for Hungary while corruption and plurality concerns remain Ex-environment minister to blame? Both problematic milestones are linked to steps taken by the former Slovak environment minister Tomáš Taraba. Taraba was removed from office in September 2026 after falling out with the right-wing Slovak National Party who had appointed him in 2023. Slovak prime minister Robert Fico has taken over his office for the time being. The office of the deputy prime minister, temporarily headed by education minister Tomáš Drucker (belonging to the left-wing Voice party), blames the previous cabinet for forest and wind energy zoning plan problems. noticias.resumen: Temu failed to take sufficient action to stop illegal or unsafe products being put on sale, the EU Commission has found preliminarily. It comes as part of a probe into the company's compliance with the Digital Services Act. The Chinese shopping website has disputed the latest findings.
noticias.texto: Temu failed to take sufficient action to stop illegal or unsafe products being put on sale, the EU Commission concluded on Tuesday (17 November), as part of a lengthy probe to assess its compliance with EU law launched in 2024. The commission found that the online marketplace had “ineffective controls” in place to ensure that products sold on its platform met EU safety requirements. It also says this amounts to a breach of the Digital Services Act , the EU’s rulebook for online platforms, which has been in force since August 2023. The commission’s latest findings of insufficient mitigation against the sale of illegal items follow a decision in May that Temu’s risk assessments were inadequate, leading Temu to pay a €200m fine . The Chinese online shopping retailer has been investigated over the alleged listing of illegal products, as well as addictive design, recommendation algorithms and data-sharing. Temu has more than 120 million users in the EU, according to commission officials. “We’re happy to see the Commission has taken consumer organisations complaints and evidence seriously regarding how Temu’s fails to meet its obligations. Consumers should be able to shop safely on these very large online marketplaces,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer protection body BEUC .
