noticias.titulo: [Interview] Czech MEP Niedermayer slams Babiš opposition to new EU budget revenue: ‘It’s short-sighted’
noticias.resumen: From missed IT revolutions to costly nuclear bets, EU Parliament's economic policy vice-chair Luděk Niedermayer sketches a stark choice for European capitals: keep blaming Brussels for their woes, clinging to national budgets, or allow the EU to levy its own targeted taxes on negative externalities to better compete with the US and China.
noticias.texto: The EU should introduce its own taxes to discourage the consumption of harmful products such as tobacco and strengthen its ability to compete with the US and China, Czech MEP Luděk Niedermayer said in an interview. A member of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), Niedermayer is a former vice-governor of the Czech central bank and vice-chair of the European Parliament’s committee on economic and monetary affairs. The 2024 report of former Italian prime minister Mario Draghi delivered a n unflattering assessment of the EU’s competitiveness . Do you fear that divisions between national capitals in the EU means the union will have to rely on enhanced cooperation more often? Luděk Niedermayer: I would not describe enhanced cooperation as something to fear — in many cases, it is a useful solution when all countries simply do not agree on something that would in fact move the EU forward. As an MEP, I worked on a mechanism to promote equity financing for companies instead of loans. In my view, that mechanism is very good and has clear economic justification. It stalled in the Council, blocked by the unanimity requirement for tax matters. “National leaders declare their support for Draghi’s findings, but do precisely the opposite in negotiations on the European budget.” But if, through enhanced cooperation, a workable concept could be created for a group of countries without undermining the single market, it would clearly add value. The same applies to the so-called 28th legal regime [ EU Inc ]. If someone offered me a choice between a weak compromise and a strong regime for half of the EU’s member states, I would choose the latter. The red line is fragmentation of the single market itself, for instance by protectionist barriers between member states. It cannot be that someone says: ‘I am in the single market, but I do not import apples from Poland,’ or, ‘I am in the single market, but I will not import cars from Czechia and Slovakia.’ That would be the end of the road, but nobody is considering that. So what follows from this? The Draghi report focuses on key European sectors for economic growth. Many member states blame their economic failures on EU regulations, while other countries operating within the same legislative framework achieve excellent results, prosper and reduce their debt. National leaders declare their support for Draghi’s findings, but do precisely the opposite in negotiations on the European budget. [Another former Italian prime minister] Enrico Letta’s report on the single market is equally crucial. It outlines changes that could be implemented more quickly. You are working on the 28th regime with former Slovak prime minister and current Renew MEP Ľudovít Ódor with the aim to enable companies to grow without having to hire dozens of tax advisers in each EU country. Given that taxation falls within national competence, is it realistic to establish a workable model? I consider the EU Commission’s initial proposal to simplify the establishment of companies across borders good. Digitalisation, simplification and acceleration are a good direction to take as a starting point. Read more EU unveils ’28th regime’, creating bloc-wide business code I do not think it is essential for the 28th regime to be used by tens of thousands of companies across the EU; it would be most effective for start-ups and expanding companies, for which the costs of extending across Europe are greatest. Limiting this regime to a specific type of company in exchange for its high effectiveness is an acceptable compromise. Looking at the wider business environment, 60 of the world’s 100 largest companies are from the US and fewer than 20 are European. And Chiness giants are growing faster than us. Why is Europe unable to produce global giants like Google or Anthropic ? One reason we are absent from these rankings is that rapid growth needed took place in the IT sector, where Europe simply fell asleep. Parts of our economy and politics remained stuck in the analogue era, and we did not realise how important this was. “Rapid growth needed took place in the IT sector, where Europe simply fell asleep.” And when high-quality IT know-how emerged in Europe, it moved to the US at a certain stage of growth. I see three reasons for this. What are those three reasons? First, the US has an incomparably larger financing market than the EU. Second, other legal environments are more certain. The US state Delaware has created the world’s best commercial legal system, under which most large US companies are incorporated. Not because of taxes, but because of legal certainty. Delaware has a commercial law system that no one can match. Read more MEPs back new EU‑wide ‘28th regime’ businesses plan — but fear a ‘European Delaware’ Third, non-EU markets have higher demands for new players. The US market is far more willing to buy products from young start-ups, while Europe prefers established suppliers. But I will add a caveat: a larger company does not mean a better company. Our weakness in the IT sector has cost us economic growth and created a dangerous technological dependency. The Draghi report warns of Europe’s strategic vulnerabilities in raw materials, chips and security. How should the EU respond to Chinese dominance in these fields? China has made good decisions and backed them with massive state aid for industrial sectors. This would not be possible in Europe. China also disregards ethical and environmental standards in extracting raw materials. But its technologies are of high quality. There are areas in which we can benefit from the fact that China has invested heavily and produces an excess supply of quality goods. Solar panels are one example. Cheap solar panels are helping us move towards achieving our climate goals. In critical sectors, we must use a combination of supportive and protective measures to build our own capacity or diversify suppliers. Where there are unfair state subsidies, we must impose duties to offset them, but not blanket protectionism, the cost of which consumers would bear in the form of higher prices for goods. Read more One supply scare pushed China into renewables. Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up Chinese technology is also a threat… In terms of security, we must ask ourselves the extent to which there is a risk that China will use technology as a weapon, like [Russian president] Vladimir Putin does with gas. We must be careful not to use security arguments as a pretext for closing the market. We would deprive ourselves of competition that could bring down the prices of goods. If we neglect this, it also becomes a security risk. Czech EPP-group MEP Luděk Niedermayer (Source: Tomáš Benedikovič, Denník N) Is the growth of China’s electric-vehicle sector a threat to the automotive industry in Eastern Europe? I have the impression that this concern stems from the situation a few years ago. Dependence on batteries has gradually decreased thanks to dozens of new investments and research projects in the EU, although it remains significant. In 10 to 20 years, recycling will play a key role, reducing dependence on raw materials. European carmakers made a huge strategic mistake by suppressing the development of electric vehicles and promoting combustion engines. noticias.titulo: Listen: What do France’s centre-right candidates want for Europe?
noticias.resumen: In the race for the French presidential election, there are already four names on the centre-right: Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard and Édouard Philippe. For now, they haven't reached an agreement to join forces and put forward a single candidate.
noticias.texto: Production: By Europod , in co-production with Sphera Network . EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms . Find the full transcript below : In the race for the French presidential election, there are already four names on the centre-right: Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard and Édouard Philippe. For now, they haven’t reached an agreement to join forces and put forward a single candidate. But do they share the same vision of Europe? None of these candidates question France’s membership of the European Union, or the fundamental rules governing it. Nor do they call for changes to the EU treaties, unlike some other candidates. The differences are more about how critical they are of the EU’s current functioning. For example, both David Lisnard and Bruno Retailleau believe the European Commission sometimes goes beyond its original remit. Retailleau wants to make it possible to bring cases before the Court of Justice of the European Union when the commission is accused of overstepping its powers. Lisnard, meanwhile, wants to strengthen the role of the Council and the European Parliament, which he considers more legitimate institutions. Read more What Marine Le Pen and Alice Weidel are planning for Brussels He also takes a particularly strong stance on national sovereignty. He opposes situations in which EU law prevents member states from taking certain decisions. When that happens, he believes the question should be put to the people through a referendum. As for the biggest issue of the moment, the EU’s multiannual budget, none of the four candidates has set out a clear position on the size of the EU budget, or on how much France should contribute to it. This is quite different from Marine Le Pen’s pledge to halve France’s contribution to the EU budget. You won’t find anything of the sort in the centre-right candidates’ programmes. Édouard Philippe puts considerable emphasis on mobilising private investment to finance innovation. That’s a position often associated with the more fiscally conservative EU member states: rather than injecting more public money into the economy, they want to make better use of private savings. Gabriel Attal takes a somewhat different approach. For example, he proposes a common European artificial intelligence policy, backed by its own dedicated budget, much like the Common Agricultural Policy. Read more Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down And he explicitly suggests that this could be financed through common European borrowing. Speaking of the Common Agricultural Policy, do they agree on what should happen to EU farming subsidies? Very much so. All four candidates place considerable importance on the CAP and want to protect France’s share of the funding. That’s hardly surprising: France is one of the biggest beneficiaries of the Common Agricultural Policy, which provides substantial financial support to French farmers. When it comes to agriculture, there’s one proposal from Bruno Retailleau that stands out: he doesn’t want Ukraine to join the EU’s agricultural market. This isn’t particularly surprising, actually. Many Europeans share this view, especially in countries where agriculture plays a major role. But unlike Retailleau, the other centre-right candidates don’t openly state this position. And what about Ukraine more broadly? Do they have clear positions on the war and European support? All in all, yes, although they don’t go into much detail. Their programmes are almost silent on this issue. Read more Europe’s centre parties are collapsing – and, for the first time, the far-right are collaborating, rather than fighting However, their public statements are clear: all four have consistently supported Ukraine, including through weapons deliveries and the possible use of frozen Russian assets to finance the country’s reconstruction. They also agree on the need to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities. One way to do this, they argue, is to give preference to European-made military equipment. In other words, European countries should prioritise buying weapons and defence systems from European manufacturers rather than relying on American suppliers. Gabriel Attal talks about this extensively, and Édouard Philippe also explicitly supports the idea. Attal goes a step further, proposing an investment fund specifically designed to support small and medium-sized businesses in the defence sector. So, while the four candidates don’t have identical programmes, their overall vision of Europe is relatively similar. The main differences lie in how they want to reform the EU institutions, finance common priorities and protect national sovereignty.

noticias.titulo: Vacancy: Senior Editor, EUobserver
noticias.resumen: EUobserver is looking for a Senior Editor to support our daily newsroom and help shape the next chapter of independent pan-European journalism
noticias.texto: EUobserver is looking for a Senior Editor to support our daily newsroom and help shape the next chapter of independent pan-European journalism. You will join a cross-border team of journalists in an expanding newsroom with over 25 years of experience covering EU affairs. What you’ll do Editing articles from reporters and contributors Guide and support reporters and contributors Ensure accuracy, quality and editorial standards in everything we publish Work with the Editor-in-Chief on editorial strategy, new formats and newsroom growth What we’re looking for Solid editorial and leadership experience in a newsroom (3-5 years of experience) Strong knowledge of the EU institutions and European politics Excellent English writing and editing skills French, German, Polish, Hungarian, Czech, Slovak and any other European languages are an asset. Flexibility to adapt to a fast-changing news agenda, including occasional early, late or weekend shifts when big stories break Calm under deadline pressure, with sharp news judgment Commitment to independent, fact-based journalism What we offer A senior role in an independent, journalist-owned newsroom A hand in EUobserver’s expansion into five new languages in 2027, bringing EU news to readers across Europe Short decision-making lines and a real say in the newsroom’s editorial direction A small, multilingual team where your work is visible and valued A newsroom in Residence Palace, in the heart of Brussels and the EU quarter, with flexible teleworking Additional information Expected start date: January or February 2027 Location: Brussels , on-site in Residence Palace (not a remote position) Engagement options: 1. Freelance / B2B (preferred option) or 2. Full-time employment (under Belgian law) How to apply Sounds interesting? Send your CV and a short cover letter (300 words) to our Editor-in-chief, Elena Sánchez Nicolás (jobs@euobserver.com), by 30 November , with “Senior Editor + your name” in the subject line.

noticias.titulo: Thaçi sentenced to 17 months in prison for obstructing the Hague court and disclosing protected witnesses
noticias.resumen: The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague sentenced former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leader and ...
noticias.texto: The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague sentenced former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leader and Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi to 17 months in prison for obstructing and showing contempt for the court by disclosing confidential information about protected witnesses. Thaçi, 58, was found guilty at first instance of attempting to obstruct public officials in the performance of their duties, violating the confidentiality of proceedings, and contempt of court. His co-accused associates Bashkim Smakaj and Fadil Fazliu were each sentenced to 12 months for attempted obstruction; both will be released immediately because they have already served the time in pre-trial detention. Hajredin Kuçi received a one-month suspended prison sentence with a one-year probation period for contempt of court, while Isni Kilaj was acquitted. Prosecutors seek six years for Thaçi over alleged witness interference in The Hague The court found that Thaçi disclosed information about six protected witnesses from his main war-crimes trial to associates who visited him in Hague detention in the summer and autumn of 2023, and that he used those visitors to instruct the witnesses on how to testify in his favour. In a separate proceeding, the same court sentenced Thaçi on 16 September 2026 to 25 years in prison for war crimes committed in Kosovo and Albania in 1998–99. Under today’s ruling, delivered by single judge Christopher Gosnell, the two sentences are to be served consecutively, as prosecutors requested. Hague Kosovo war crimes court sentences former president Hashim Thaçi to 25 years Judge Gosnell stated that evidence showed Thaçi, during separate meetings in detention, passed confidential details about protected witnesses to associates and gave them detailed instructions on how the witnesses should testify to benefit him. Smakaj and Fazliu then separately made unauthorised contact on Kosovo with prosecution witnesses – former KLA commanders Rustem Mustafa-Remi and Bislim Zyrapi – and relayed Thaçi’s instructions. The judgment also confirmed that Thaçi printed an earlier statement by Zyrapi on a computer in detention and gave it to Smakaj. Investigators later found that statement during a search of Smakaj’s car in Kosovo. Thaçi also provided confidential witness information to Kilaj and Kuçi, but both were cleared of the obstruction charge because they took no further action after returning to Kosovo. Kuçi was nonetheless convicted for sending an SMS to witness Mustafa, which the court had prohibited because Kuçi was then a member of the defence team for co-accused Kadri Veseli in the main war-crimes case. Specific incidents included a 2 July 2023 request by Thaçi to Fadil Fazliu to convey instructions to Rustem Mustafa-Remi; they arranged for Fahri Fazliu (Fadil’s son) to meet the witness. The day after the visit, Fahri exchanged messages with Mustafa and proposed a meeting that day involving both Fazlius, consistent with Thaçi’s directions. Father and son Fazliu had already met Mustafa on 29 June 2023, before the visit to Thaçi. On 9 September 2023, Thaçi gave Smakaj detailed instructions on how Bislim Zyrapi should testify; the judge cited a secretly recorded conversation. Smakaj later contacted Zyrapi in Kosovo. Thaçi provided further instructions for Zyrapi during a subsequent visit on 7 October 2023. Fazliu, Smakaj and Kilaj were arrested in Kosovo on 5 December 2023 and transferred to Hague detention the next day. Kuçi was not arrested but appeared voluntarily. All defendants pleaded not guilty. The obstruction trial began in late February 2026, with closing arguments in mid-September. Smakaj headed Kosovo’s Intelligence Service from 2017 to 2020 and worked for Thaçi while the latter was president. Kilaj is a KLA co-founder and head of Thaçi’s party in Malisheva. Fazliu is a former KLA member from the Podujeva area. Hajredin Kuçi previously served as Kosovo’s deputy prime minister and justice minister in Thaçi’s cabinet. The main war-crimes trial of Thaçi and his co-accused (for events in Kosovo and Albania in 1998–99) began in April 2023 and concluded in February 2026. The first-instance judgment on 16 September sentenced Thaçi and Jakup Krasniqi to 25 years each, Kadri Veseli to 18 years, and Rexhep Selimi to 13 years. This article draw on reporting by EUalive’s partner BETA . Caption: Supporters react as they show solidarity with former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders ahead of their upcoming trial verdict, in Pristina, Kosovo, 16 September 2026. The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague, Netherlands, sentenced Hashim Thaci, Kadri Veseli, Rexhep Selimi, and Jakup Krasniqi to long prison terms on ten counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1998–1999 Kosovo War. EPA/ARBEN LLAPASHTICA

noticias.titulo: Russia’s foreign intelligence issues statement alleging EU concerns regarding Serbia’s Student List
noticias.resumen: On 17 November 2026, Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs amplified a statement from the press ...
noticias.texto: On 17 November 2026, Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs amplified a statement from the press bureau of the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) on X and Telegram. The text claimed that EU leaders are “concerned by the unwillingness of Serbia’s Student List to blindly follow instructions from Brussels” and are prepared to use “every dirty trick in the book” to bring its leaders into line. ⚡️ Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service: The EU leadership is concerned by the unwillingness of Serbia's Student List to blindly follow instructions from Brussels. ❗️ They are ready to use every dirty trick in the book to bring their leaders into line. https://t.co/YWlvYlxzii pic.twitter.com/biRXRINd3F — MFA Russia 🇷🇺 (@mfa_russia) November 17, 2026 This form of communication is atypical for most foreign ministries. Intelligence services rarely issue real-time public commentary on another country’s domestic politics in this direct style. Russia has made the practice more frequent in recent years: the SVR’s press bureau has previously released statements framing protests or political shifts in Serbia, Moldova, and Georgia as Western-orchestrated “Maidan” scenarios or pressure campaigns, which the MFA then publicizes. In this instance, the timing – days after the Student List’s representatives appeared at EU forums – fits that pattern. Moscow’s alleged concerns According to the SVR, Brussels is particularly irritated that the Student List has refused to sever ties with Russia or join EU sanctions. The service further claimed that the intelligence services of Germany and France intend to isolate the movement’s leaders and split its ranks in order to force compliance. A related SVR formulation stated that European attempts to impose their will would meet resistance from the “steadfast and wise Serbian people,” invoking historical resistance to Nazi Germany and the 1999 NATO bombing. These claims present the Student List’s positions as a surprising defiance that has triggered covert EU planning. The SVR offers no specific evidence in the public statements. Verified facts on the election and Student List positions The Republic Electoral Commission confirmed the final results of the 25 October 2026 snap parliamentary election on 5 November. The Student List (“Students Are Winning”) received approximately 53 percent of the vote and 140 of 250 seats, securing an absolute majority. Aleksandar Vučić’s United Serbia list (led by the Serbian Progressive Party) finished second with about 39 percent and 103 seats. Turnout was roughly 69 percent. The outcome ended more than 14 years of SNS-led rule. The list emerged from nearly two years of student-led protests that began after the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. Student plenums selected 250 candidates – primarily academics, experts, and public figures rather than students themselves – creating a leaderless electoral platform focused on accountability, anti-corruption, media freedom, judicial independence, and education. On EU accession, Student List representatives have publicly engaged Brussels. A member spoke at the EU Enlargement Forum in mid-November 2026 and stated that the movement intends to accelerate fulfillment of interim benchmarks under Chapters 23 and 24 (judiciary and fundamental rights). EU officials, including Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, welcomed the election result and indicated readiness to move forward on reforms, while noting that foreign-policy alignment remains a condition for significant progress. Previous accession steps had been stalled under the Vučić government partly over democratic standards and limited alignment with the EU’s common foreign and security policy. Serbia’s European path is also its path of reforms. This was the clear message from representatives of the Student List, whom I met in Brussels today. We share the same goal of a democratic Serbia. We are ready to work together on the reforms needed to make this ambition a… pic.twitter.com/5W1TUgoG8X — Marta Kos (@MartaKosEU) November 16, 2026 On Russia, the Student List’s published program and statements by its candidates are explicit: Serbia will preserve its traditional partnership with Moscow (including coordination in the UN Security Council on territorial integrity) and will not introduce sanctions. Representatives have cited Serbia’s own historical experience with sanctions and a preference for dialogue. This stance continues the policy maintained under the previous government and has been acknowledged as a continuing point of friction with the EU. The movement’s program prioritises domestic governance and describes the EU as Serbia’s most important economic partner, while maintaining military neutrality and the constitutional position that Kosovo remains part of Serbia. It does not frame membership as an unconditional goal but signals intent to advance the existing accession process through internal reforms. EU reactions have cantered on welcoming the opportunity for progress on democracy and judiciary benchmarks rather than public threats. Bottom line Overall, the SVR statement reads as a calculated PR move, underscoring the enduring strength of pro-Russian sentiment in Serbia after the elections and quietly mocking the EU’s inability to secure any meaningful shift on core issues such as Kosovo or sanctions against Russia. As the statement portrays the Student List as resisting external control and anticipates dirty tricks, it should be reminded that when Russia warns of impending dirty tricks, this should mean is already preparing them itself. Caption: Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos met with representatives of the Student List in Brussels on 16 November 2026

noticias.titulo: Turkey takes pro-opposition TV channel Sözcü off air in raid, appoints trustee
noticias.resumen: Turkish authorities took pro-opposition Sözcü TV off air in a pre-dawn raid on Tuesday and ...
noticias.texto: Turkish authorities took pro-opposition Sözcü TV off air in a pre-dawn raid on Tuesday and appointed a trustee to run the channel and its website, prosecutors said, extending a crackdown on the opposition and renewing concerns about media freedom. The move significantly restricts Turks’ access to pro-opposition media, with the last two mainstream channels giving prominence to opposition views — Halk TV and Sözcü TV — effectively brought under government oversight since last month. The opposition is facing an unprecedented legal crackdown with restrictions and bans imposed on opposition and independent media, and dozens of elected mayors and officials removed from duty, detained or arrested. The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said it had ordered police raids at the Sözcü offices in Istanbul in connection with a case launched nearly 10 years ago over alleged links between Sözcü media group owner Burak Akbay and the network of Fethullah Gülen, a late US-based Muslim cleric whom Ankara blamed for a failed coup attempt in 2016. It said four executives from Sözcü, including its chairwoman Funda Tuncer Sıdalı, had been detained. Özgür Özel, head of the main opposition New Party, said the move showed the government had “no tolerance for even the smallest criticism,” while İYİ Party chair Müsavat Dervişoğlu called it a blow against democracy and freedom of information. “They are trapped in a corner, they are sinking in the swamp. This is why they are trying to drown whoever is not with them,” Özel said on X. “If we give in to these would-be dictators, if we hand over this nation to them, then may our hearts wither away.” Media freedom concerns Tuesday’s move makes Sözcü TV the sixth major Turkish news outlet to have a trustee appointed since 2022, following similar action at Halk TV, Flash TV, Eko Türk, Habertürk and Tele1. Authorities have also appointed trustees in recent years to take over many municipalities, previously seizing those run by pro-Kurdish opposition mayors in southeastern Turkey and more recently major municipalities, including Istanbul and its districts, won by the opposition, prompting some mayors to join President Tayyip Erdoğan’s ruling AK Party. The prosecutor’s office said Turkey’s Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) had been appointed as trustee of Sözcü TV and its news website, adding that its print newspaper and affiliated newspapers Tavır and Korkusuz had not been affected. While pro-opposition print newspapers still exist and operate, their reach is considerably less than television and online news. Rights groups and Western countries have criticised the government over its use of the judiciary, its record on rights, and its crackdown on press freedom. The government says that actions taken against news outlets follow regular judicial practices and that Turkey’s judiciary is independent. Turkey’s Progressive Journalists Association (PJA) accused the government of seeking to silence media through its trustees. “You cannot cover up the truth, you cannot destroy reality by silencing journalists,” it said. With Reuters Caption: The logo of TV channel Sözcü [@BirGun_Gazetesi on X]

noticias.titulo: Spanish hard right coalition poised for majority as snap election nears
noticias.resumen: Three opinion polls published on Monday indicate that an alliance between Spain’s conservative People’s Party ...
noticias.texto: Three opinion polls published on Monday indicate that an alliance between Spain’s conservative People’s Party and the far-right Vox would secure a parliamentary majority in the 29 November general election, even as Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s socialists gain modest ground at this stage of the campaign. The surveys, the first released since campaigning formally began last week, project that the right-wing bloc could win more than 190 seats in the 350-seat lower house, enough to form a government without other partners. Spaniards will vote in the country’s sixth general election in eleven years, a contest that could end eight years of Socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into national government for the first time since the restoration of democracy after the death of General Francisco Franco. A daily poll by 40dB for El País showed the Socialists rising to 30.3 percent from 29.9 percent, crossing the 30 percent threshold for the first time in that survey since the 2023 election. The People’s Party stood at 31.5 percent and Vox at 18 percent, a combination that would deliver more than 190 seats. An NC Report poll for La Razón projected between 201 and 205 seats for the PP and Vox together, against 102 to 104 for the Socialists, whose support rose half a percentage point to 26.1 percent. An IMOP poll for El Confidencial put Socialist support at 26.9 percent, up one point from the previous week, while the right-wing bloc was forecast to take 194 seats to the Socialists’ 109. Other recent surveys, including those by SocioMétrica for El Español and Sigma Dos for El Mundo, have pointed to similar outcomes, with the combined right winning around 199 to 200 seats and the Socialists recovering only marginally after the late-October high-speed train crash. Housing crisis and parliamentary deadlock triggered the vote Sánchez called the snap election on 5 October after the People’s Party, Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts joined forces to defeat emergency housing measures his minority government had proposed. Spain faces one of Europe’s most severe housing affordability crises. The issue gained national urgency with the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman forced from her Madrid home of seven decades after an investment fund demanded a 230 percent rent increase. Large protests followed, and more than three million people took part in a general strike last week over soaring housing costs. Sánchez has argued that only a stronger progressive mandate can deliver effective solutions, while the right has accused his government of failing to address the shortage of affordable homes. The defeat of the housing decrees exposed the fragility of the coalition Sánchez has led since 2018 with the left-wing Sumar alliance. His government has not passed a budget since 2023 and has repeatedly struggled to advance legislation in a fractured Congress. Junts, which provided conditional support after the 2023 election, has frequently extracted concessions before withdrawing its backing. The administration has also faced intense criticism over its handling of the mass border crossing into the North African exclave of Ceuta earlier this year and over two deadly rail crashes on the same high-speed line within nine months. The second crash, on 28 October, killed 69 people and prompted the resignation of Transport Minister Óscar Puente, who said neither the country nor he could bear another such tragedy. Corruption allegations surrounding Sánchez’s party and inner circle over the past two years have further eroded public trust in a prime minister who once cast himself as a reformer determined to root out graft. Sánchez has sought to frame the election as a defence of social rights against a right-wing advance that would reverse progressive gains on equality, environmental policy and workers’ protections. At a rally in Seville he spoke of an “epic comeback” driven by popular mobilization. Yet the left of his own party remains divided. The Broad Front, uniting several former allies including groups linked to former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau, is projected to win only 10 to 15 seats, while Podemos contests the election separately and risks falling below the threshold for representation. Together they are unlikely to provide the numbers needed for another left-wing coalition. Right-wing platform and Socialist counter-proposals shape the contest Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the People’s Party, has promised a return to “decency as a basic principle” and has sharpened his attacks on what critics call “sanchismo.” The PP, which once kept Vox at arm’s length, now governs jointly with it in four regions and has adopted a more accommodating tone toward its partner’s hard line on immigration. Vox leader Santiago Abascal has campaigned on “national priority,” giving Spanish citizens precedence in access to subsidized housing, social benefits and grants, along with deregulation, tax cuts and the removal of people who entered the country illegally, committed crimes or rely on welfare. Although the party earlier floated far broader “remigration” ideas, it has since narrowed the scope. Feijóo has insisted that any agreement must respect the constitution and European law, defining national priority in terms of rootedness rather than strict nationality. The Socialists, for their part, have unveiled an ambitious platform centered on higher taxes on large property owners, “vulture funds” and high capital income, accelerated social-security contributions from top earners, and a commitment to mobilize the equivalent of 1 percent of GDP annually for housing. They propose progressive taxes on vacant residential properties and tourist rentals, an increase in the financial-transaction tax, and measures to strengthen the pension system. Sánchez presents these steps as necessary for fair taxation and sustained social spending while meeting European fiscal rules. Critics on the right argue the plans lack detail and risk further burdening businesses and middle-income households. With less than two weeks remaining, the campaign has already been marked by sharp exchanges over housing affordability, immigration, infrastructure safety and the legacy of eight years of Socialist governance. The state-run CIS poll continues to stand as an outlier, suggesting the Socialists could still assemble a broader left-wing majority, but most independent surveys point in the opposite direction. Sources: El País, El Mundo, La Razón, EFE Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election for 29 November after housing defeat Caption: Leader of the People’s Party (PP) and prime ministerial candidate for the upcoming general election Alberto Nunez Feijoo (L) poses with a supporter (C) and the leader of the PP in Galicia region Alfonso Rueda (R) during an electoral meeting in Santiago de Compostela, Galicia, Spain, 14 November 2026. Spain will hold general elections on 29 November. EPA/Lavandeira jr

noticias.titulo: Dutch minority coalition to continue after four days of crisis talks
noticias.resumen: The Dutch governing coalition of D66, the Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA) and the VVD has ...
noticias.texto: The Dutch governing coalition of D66, the Christian Democratic Appeal (CDA) and the VVD has decided to continue as a minority government after four days of intensive crisis talks, Prime Minister Rob Jetten’s office announced on Monday evening. The marathon discussions had “restored trust” between the three parties, the statement said. Party leaders issued no separate comments. The talks followed a sharp breakdown over the 2027 tax plan. D66 and the CDA had reached a deal with the left-wing opposition parties Pro and Volt to raise roughly €1 billion through higher taxes on wealth (a new top rate of 38.5% on returns above €60,000 in box 3) in order to limit the planned rise in the lowest income-tax rate. The VVD, whose finance minister Eelco Heinen had prepared the original package, opposed the amendment, arguing it breached the coalition agreement and was negotiated behind its back. On Thursday the tax plan passed the lower house by the narrowest possible margin (76–74) with VVD votes against it. VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz subsequently described the minority government as “a failed experiment” and demanded a “fundamental reset,” including possible changes to both policy and the coalition’s composition. Jetten called for thorough discussions to improve cooperation on substance, politics and personal relations. After the first day of crisis talks on Friday he expressed cautious optimism; Yeşilgöz immediately dampened expectations. The three party leaders maintained a media blackout while continuing talks through the weekend and Monday. According to Dutch media reports, the eventual agreement does not bring an additional party into government – an option Yeşilgöz had floated – and leaves the existing three-party minority intact. Details of any changes to working methods or future dealings with parliament are expected after Tuesday’s cabinet meeting. The coalition, formed earlier this year and lacking a parliamentary majority from the outset, had already been operating under strain as it sought ad-hoc majorities for key legislation. The wealth-tax row exposed the practical limits of that approach and left relations between the partners visibly damaged, even if the immediate threat of collapse has been averted. Caption: Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten speaks to the press following crisis talks at the top of the Dutch cabinet in The Hague, Netherlands, 13 November 2026. Coalition tensions peaked after D66 and CDA secured a majority for an amendment to the tax plan proposed by PRO and Volt. EPA/ROBIN UTRECHT

noticias.titulo: EU, Black Sea, South Caucasus and Central Asia advance connectivity agenda at Brussels meeting
noticias.resumen: Foreign ministers and senior officials from the European Union, the Black Sea region, the South ...
noticias.texto: Foreign ministers and senior officials from the European Union, the Black Sea region, the South Caucasus and Central Asia met in Brussels on 16 November for the second Ministerial Meeting on Cross-Regional Security and Connectivity. Hosted by EU High Representative Kaja Kallas, Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos and Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Síkela, the gathering reaffirmed commitments to deepen cooperation on transport, energy and digital links while addressing shared security challenges. Participants included representatives from EU member states as well as Armenia, Azerbaijan, Moldova, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan. They underlined that stronger cross-regional connectivity and joint responses to security threats are essential for peace, stability, resilience and sustainable growth. Georgian authorities confirmed they stayed away. This follows a pattern of reduced high-level EU engagement with Georgia linked to concerns over democratic backsliding. Georgia was also absent from the first such ministerial meeting in Luxembourg in October 2025 for the same reason. A central focus was the Middle Corridor (Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor), described by the European Commission as a flagship initiative announced by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The route aims to connect Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and onward to European markets via Turkey and the Black Sea. The stated objectives are to diversify trade routes, triple trade volumes and significantly reduce freight transit times by 2030. Work under the Connectivity Agenda Platform, launched in June 2026, prioritises turning the corridor into a resilient, efficient and commercially competitive multimodal link, with emphasis on border procedures, customs cooperation and trade facilitation. Kazakhstan is key to the Middle corridor. The country’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi took part in the discussions. According to the Kazakh Foreign Ministry, he stressed that developing the country’s transit and transport potential and modernising infrastructure remain strategic priorities set by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Tileuberdi reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s interest in closer cooperation with European and regional partners in transport, logistics, energy and digitalisation, highlighting the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route as a key link between Europe and Asia. Kazakhstan has been actively upgrading ports and related infrastructure along the corridor, consistent with earlier bilateral steps with partners such as Azerbaijan to strengthen the Caspian segment. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan advance the “Caspian Bridge” as core upgrade to the Middle Corridor The meeting also addressed security dimensions, including maritime risks, protection of critical infrastructure, hybrid threats and demining in the Black Sea. The planned Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, co-hosted by Bulgaria and Romania and supported by up to €50 million in EU funding, was noted as a contribution to a safer maritime environment. Broader discussions covered digital connectivity, electricity grids, renewable energy projects and the need for more resilient alternative routes in light of disruptions to traditional maritime passages. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, speaking after the meeting, underlined his country’s role as a natural hub linking Europe, the Black Sea, the Caucasus and Central Asia, and called for concrete steps to improve the flow of trade, energy and data. Turkmenistan’s representatives advocated the creation of a single transport connectivity space spanning Central Asia, the South Caucasus and the Black Sea region. The second ministerial meeting builds on the first, held in Luxembourg in October 2025, and on the Cross-Regional Connectivity Agenda under the EU’s Global Gateway strategy. Officials indicated that the format is expected to continue, with a regional connectivity summit planned for Sofia in 2027. Implementation work, including private-sector dialogue on the Trans-Caspian corridor, is already under way. The gathering reflects growing EU interest in diversifying connectivity with Central Asia and the wider region amid geopolitical disruptions, while partner countries seek practical upgrades to infrastructure and procedures that can turn political commitments into operational corridors. Caption: Family photo of participants in the second Ministerial Meeting on Cross-Regional Security and Connectivity [Council Newsroom]

noticias.titulo: Second attack on the Crimean Bridge in two days: what is known
noticias.resumen: This article was updated with the post on X of president Zelenskyy containing details of ...
noticias.texto: This article was updated with the post on X of president Zelenskyy containing details of the operation In occupied Crimea, the Crimean Bridge (also known as the Kerch Bridge) was attacked for the second time in two days. Occupation authorities said road and rail traffic had been suspended. One of the bridge’s arches was destroyed, and part of the railway section was also damaged, according to preliminary reports. This was confirmed on Tuesday by the Russian-appointed head of Crimea, Sergey Aksyonov. He urged “residents and guests of Crimea” to refrain from travelling towards the bridge and to take the restrictions into account when planning routes. Russia’s Ministry of Transport stated that movement of both trains and cars across the Crimean Bridge had been halted. “As a result of a repeated UAV attack on the night of 17 November, traffic on the road and railway sections of the Crimean Bridge has been temporarily suspended. Specialists are assessing the damage. According to preliminary information, there are no casualties as a result of the incident. Drivers are advised not to travel towards the Crimean Bridge,” the ministry said. Denis Shtilerman, co-founder of the Ukrainian private defence technology company Fire Point, reposted on X a message by former Ukrainian MP Anton Gerashchenko claiming that the bridge had been attacked with a Flamingo missile. “We dedicate this to the memory of our friends and colleagues Andriy and Yuriy, without whom this would not have been possible. R.I.P.,” Shtilerman wrote. Присвячуємо це памʼяті наших друзів і колег Андрія і Юрія без яких це було б неможливо. R.I.P. https://t.co/qYH3HBRvNU — Denys Shtilierman (@DenShtilierman) November 17, 2026 Ukrainian open-source intelligence analyst “Harbuz” published a video reconstructing the consequences of the overnight combined attack on 17 November. “As a result of multiple hits, the arched span of the road section of the Kerch Bridge, more than 270 metres long, collapsed. Damage to the railway track was also recorded,” the post said. Monitoring Telegram channels “Crimean Wind” and “Exilenova+” published photos and videos from eyewitnesses showing the aftermath, including footage of the moment of the attack. “Crimean Wind” reported that the entire road span collapsed along with the arch, and that the navigable fairway was completely blocked by debris, making shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov impossible. The previous day, on 16 November, Aksyonov had already reported damage to the Crimean Bridge, with road traffic restricted until the evening. Why the bridge matters The Kerch Bridge is the only direct road and rail link between mainland Russia and the Crimean peninsula, which Russia seized and annexed in 2014. Opened in 2018 after years of construction, it was a flagship project for President Vladimir Putin, who personally inaugurated it. Roughly 19 km long, it consists of parallel road and rail sections and has served both as a vital logistics artery for Russian forces in southern Ukraine and as a powerful political symbol of Moscow’s control over Crimea. Ukraine has targeted the bridge repeatedly since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, viewing it as a legitimate military objective because of its role in supplying Russian troops and sustaining the occupation. Earlier major strikes in 2022 and 2023 caused significant temporary disruption. The latest attacks come amid a wider wave of Ukrainian strikes, with Russia claiming to have intercepted more than 2,000 drones in a single 24-hour period. Grateful to the Security Service of Ukraine, all units of Ukraine’s Defense Forces involved, Ukraine’s Minister of Defense, the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine and the General Staff, and all our weapons manufacturers for an unprecedented operation in response to… pic.twitter.com/pgUxGrE61K — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) November 17, 2026 This article draws on reporting by EUalive’s partner Suspilne . Caption: The Kerch bridge after the double attack [Suspilne]

noticias.titulo: Cyber-meltdown in Europe’s cold chains: an expert opinion
noticias.resumen: To protect the refrigeration megasector against potential catastrophic disruptions, the most urgent measure recommended by ...
noticias.texto: To protect the refrigeration megasector against potential catastrophic disruptions, the most urgent measure recommended by leading cybersecurity agencies is completely eliminating direct access to refrigeration automation via the public internet, writes Kostadin Fikiin. Dr. Kostadin Fikiin is a refrigeration and cold-chain expert, scientist and international R&D project manager, affiliated with the global professional organisations and European technology and innovation platforms in the sector. To most people, refrigeration equipment appears to be robust stand-alone hardware. Recent incidents across Europe have exposed how easily cold storage facilities can now have their temperatures altered remotely. Modern refrigeration systems are managed by electronic controllers connected to cloud-based SCADA/IoT platforms. Today, this is standard practice across the industry, as remote access enables continuous monitoring, energy optimisation, and rapid service diagnostics. However, when these control interfaces are left directly accessible via the public internet, the equipment becomes a vulnerable target for external interference. The 110°C blood plasma speculation Spectacular media reports claimed that hackers managed to set a –30°C blood plasma cold store to 110°C. From a thermodynamic and engineering standpoint, however, no standard refrigeration unit can physically heat a storage room to 110°C. The operating principle of the refrigeration cycle does not allow it either on the condenser side (in heat-pump mode) or, even less so, on the evaporator side. Defrost heaters are designed solely to melt frost and are restricted by thermal protection switches, which is why the affected French National Blood Service (Établissement français du sang – EFS) did not confirm that this speculative temperature figure was actually reached. The presence of such a value in the program menu is a software configuration oversight: manufacturers use universal controllers for various industrial processes and sometimes fail to lock the software limits to the actual operating temperature range of the specific cold store. Food and medical cold chains: shared and specific protection Cyberattacks also reveal that refrigerated storage and retail facilities for foods and medicines face similar underlying risks. For basic refrigeration components and controllers, equipment diversification is often lacking. Both retail chains and medical facilities rely heavily on automation from the same leading manufacturers – such as the Danfoss, Copeland, and Dixell platforms cited in official reports by European cybersecurity agencies – where the issue stems not from a defect in the refrigeration equipment itself, but from the unprotected network exposure of the controllers. This high technological and market concentration among automation suppliers creates a systemic risk of simultaneous disruption. The key difference in medical storage facilities – such as the EFS – lies in strict regulatory supervision, independent backup alarm systems, and on-duty response teams. It was precisely these additional layers of protection that enabled EFS staff to detect the temperature deviation in time and relocate the blood plasma without losses, unlike many affected supermarkets. Beyond conventional breakdowns: cyberattacks aggravate spoilage Deliberate parameter tampering via network intrusion poses a new threat to stored goods in addition to traditional system breakdowns. During a power outage or mechanical failure, large thermal masses of goods and the thermal insulation of stores slow down warming. The system immediately alerts staff, leaving hours to activate backup power or relocate commodities. In a coordinated cyberattack, however, spoilage is actively accelerated by forcing defrost cycles on. Simultaneously, alarm notifications are suppressed or temperature readings are spoofed across multiple sites at once. This requires a quite different emergency response: immediately disconnecting controllers from the network, manually verifying actual temperatures on-site, and operating the equipment in local emergency override mode. Safeguarding critical infrastructure Addressing this wave of attacks is urgent because refrigeration and air-conditioning technology is critical infrastructure of immense societal and economic importance. According to the International Institute of Refrigeration (IIR), over 5.4 billion refrigeration, air-conditioning, and heat-pump systems operate worldwide. Refrigeration consumes around 20% of global electricity, and when heat pumps are included, this share reaches 25–30%. The capacity of industrial refrigerated warehouses exceeds 720 million cubic meters, as reported by the Global Cold Chain Alliance (GCCA). Nearly 50% of all food requires refrigeration (up to 70% in Europe), and the global financial value of chilled and frozen foodstuffs surpasses EUR 3 trillion. The lack of an adequate cold chain results in the annual loss of over 500–600 million tonnes of food – enough to feed over 950 million people. In healthcare, temperature control is vital for biologics, blood plasma, and vaccines, where 25–40% of doses worldwide are compromised due to cold-chain failures. To protect this megasector against potential catastrophic disruptions, the most urgent measures – also recommended by leading cybersecurity agencies – are completely eliminating direct access to refrigeration automation via the public internet and isolating it within a separate operational network (network segmentation). Remote access must rely exclusively on encrypted VPN connections with multi-factor authentication, combined with changing default passwords and regularly updating firmware. Alongside this, the industry must implement hard software locks on operating temperature ranges, physically independent safety thermostats, and greater diversification of equipment and control platforms so that a single software vulnerability cannot paralyse key supply chains simultaneously. Further to technical safeguards, we must also rethink the public availability of data on these facilities. Within European research projects such as CryoHub and ICE-E, our team mapped thousands of large refrigerated warehouses across Europe by location, capacity, and power consumption to improve energy efficiency and integrate renewable energy. In the new cyber-threat landscape, however, such geospatial datasets on critical infrastructure should now be protected with restricted access. Ultimately, addressing these emerging vulnerabilities opens up a broad field for research, development, and innovation (R&D&I) – with joint endeavours of academics and industrialists both across Europe and around the world – to build smarter, cleaner, and more cyber-resilient cold-chain systems. Caption: An Intermarché supermarket in Asnieres, near Paris, France, 12 October 2026. A cyberattack has affected refrigeration systems at several supermarkets, with large quantities of frozen food and fresh produce expected to be destroyed. EPA/CHRISTOPHE PETIT TESSON

noticias.titulo: Two centres, one Black Sea hub. Who will take the decisions?
noticias.resumen: Sofia and Bucharest have already divided the security tasks in the Black Sea. What remains ...
noticias.texto: Sofia and Bucharest have already divided the security tasks in the Black Sea. What remains is to agree how they will jointly run the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub. During her visit to Varna on 10 November, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed a commitment of up to €50 million for the joint hub, announced the previous day in Bucharest. The idea of the centre was included in May 2025 in the EU’s Strategic Approach to the Black Sea, which Bulgaria and Romania had pushed for. From Bucharest Von der Leyen vows EU response to Black Sea attacks Centres in Varna and Constanța, joint command “We have two centres, we have joint command,” Romanian Defence Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea told Digi24 on 12 November. According to him, work has already started and the Romanian centre in Constanța could be ready in a few months. In response to questions from EUalive, Bulgaria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs described the hub as a “civilian analytical network structure” with “two equal and mutually complementary thematic elements”. Varna will focus on hybrid and cyber threats, civilian crisis management and environmental security. Constanța will handle maritime surveillance and the protection of critical infrastructure. “Negotiations are under way to finalise a bilateral memorandum of understanding,” the ministry said. It did not specify how joint decisions will be taken or from where the hub will be directed. A second Bulgarian city may also be involved. “Border security is part of the joint concept, and the unit for it could be located in Burgas,” Yordan Bozhilov, director of the Sofia Security Forum, told EUalive. As a former deputy defence minister, he worked on the hub concept. In his view, the Naval Academy in Varna could take on the hybrid threats work. Where the hub is physically based is a secondary question, Bozhilov believes. “The point is to have operational capacity. The idea is to analyse and put forward ideas on how to mitigate the risks,” he told EUalive. Who will take the decisions On 9 November, former Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu listed what still lies ahead: the legal form of the hub, a governing board, a joint director, and national contributions in the two countries’ 2027 budgets. Three days later, Romanian Defence Minister Ștefan-Radu Oprea was already speaking of “joint command”. He also indicated who would coordinate the work on the Romanian side – the Interior Ministry through the coast guard, with support from the defence ministry. The Bulgarian newspaper Capital reported that Bulgaria has proposed rotational leadership, which Bucharest and the European Commission have opposed. According to the paper, the Commission has also asked for a short, fixed deadline to conclude the talks. In its response to EUalive, the Bulgarian Foreign Ministry stated that the network structure will be “under the joint hosting of Bulgaria and Romania”. The ministry clarified that the bilateral arrangements “are not subject to possible approval” by the European institutions. It did not say whether rotation had been proposed or whether a deadline had been set. In August the Bulgarian government recorded in its governing programme that the Black Sea Maritime Security Centre should be established by May 2030. Three months later the European Commission set the goal of the hub becoming operational as early as 2027. Sofia and Bucharest are still negotiating the memorandum that is supposed to define how the joint centre will work. Bulgaria and Romania jointly pressed for a European strategy for the Black Sea, but on the question of hosting Bucharest took the initiative. As early as October 2025, Oana Țoiu presented Romania’s proposal to host the centre to her EU colleagues. In February she introduced the hub at a maritime security discussion in Munich involving Norway, and in June she announced the joint project with Bulgaria for centres in Constanța and Varna. Who will react in the event of an attack Yordan Bozhilov describes the hub’s task as civilian – to collect and analyse information and propose measures against identified risks. When it comes to the physical protection of commercial vessels, he points to the example of Operation Aspides in the Red Sea, where European warships have a mandate from the EU Council to protect shipping from attacks in a defined area. In the Black Sea, the first signal of a drone heading toward a commercial ship will raise two questions with different responsible authorities: who warns the crew, and who has the authority to order intervention if the vessel is outside territorial waters. On 20 August a commercial vessel reported a sea drone near the Neptune Alpha gas platform in Romania’s exclusive economic zone. Romanian F-16s struck the device and naval divers neutralised it. On 6 October Bulgaria launched a rescue operation after drones hit two commercial ships in the Bulgarian economic zone. The joint hub in Varna and Constanța could shorten the time between detecting a drone and warning the crew. To stop an attack, however, the signal must also reach the service that has the equipment to intercept it, and the authority to give the order must be settled in advance. The drone will not wait for Sofia and Bucharest to decide who gives the command. Caption: Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen and Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev aboard a warship in Varna [Ursula von der Leyen on X]

noticias.titulo: Five EU countries open talks with Rwanda on deportation hub for rejected asylum seekers
noticias.resumen: Austria, Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece have launched negotiations with Rwanda to establish a ...
noticias.texto: Austria, Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece have launched negotiations with Rwanda to establish a deportation, or “return,” hub there under a new European Union legal framework, with the aim of beginning transfers of rejected asylum seekers in 2027. Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the initiative in Vienna on Monday, joined by ministers from the participating countries and Rwanda’s Interior Minister Vincent Biruta. Stocker described the move as a historic shift in European migration policy, arguing that the asylum system is undermined when people with no right to remain cannot be removed. Frederiksen called the planned hub a “game changer” that would help dismantle smugglers’ business models and restore control over borders. Under the scheme, which remains under negotiation, the five countries would transfer adults whose asylum claims have been fully rejected and who face enforceable return orders but cannot be sent back to their countries of origin. The facility is envisaged as a pilot with capacity for around 100 people at a time. Those transferred would receive residence permits and be offered the option of integrating into Rwandan society – with support for housing, language and vocational training – or returning home. Officials have stressed it would not be a closed detention centre. Minors would be excluded. Some participating states have indicated initial preferences, such as the Netherlands focusing on single men from the region and Germany prioritising non-cooperative individuals from countries that refuse readmission. The plan became feasible after the EU adopted a new Return Regulation earlier this year. The regulation accelerates deportations, introduces a European Return Order enforceable across member states, and explicitly permits member states to establish return hubs in third countries, provided fundamental rights standards are met. Low return rates – official estimates suggest fewer than 30 per cent of people ordered to leave the EU actually do so – have long frustrated governments. Proponents argue the hubs will serve primarily as a deterrent, signalling that irregular journeys to Europe may end in transfer to a third country rather than settlement. EU proposes major expansion of Frontex powers to bolster deportations Previous hesitations over externalising asylum and returns European governments have debated externalising elements of asylum and return policy for decades, but concrete offshoring of people who have already reached EU territory has repeatedly stalled over legal, political and practical objections. In the early 2000s, the United Kingdom (then an EU member) under Tony Blair and Germany under Interior Minister Otto Schily floated ideas of processing centres outside Europe. These proposals gained little traction amid doubts about feasibility and compatibility with international refugee law. Denmark explored similar concepts as early as the 1980s and later legislated for transfers, but its own Rwanda plans were shelved amid domestic opposition. After the 2015–16 migration peak, further ideas – including “disembarkation platforms” and expanded “hotspot” processing – surfaced but did not materialise into large-scale extraterritorial facilities on EU soil or beyond. More recent attempts have highlighted the obstacles. The United Kingdom’s 2022 Rwanda asylum partnership, which aimed to send irregular arrivals for processing and potential settlement in Rwanda, was ruled unlawful by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 over risks of refoulement and inadequate safeguards. The incoming Labour government abandoned the scheme in 2024 after substantial costs and no operational flights. Italy’s 2023 agreement with Albania to process asylum claims in Italian-run centres on Albanian territory has faced court challenges and limited implementation, though it differs by keeping jurisdiction with the transferring state. Broader EU deals with countries such as Turkey, Tunisia and Libya have focused on external border control and interception rather than transferring people already inside the EU for return or processing. Human rights organisations and the UN refugee agency have consistently warned that third-country hubs risk reduced oversight, potential abuse and violations of non-refoulement. Rwanda’s human rights record – including concerns over political repression and its role in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo – has drawn particular scrutiny. Previous African Union opposition to extraterritorial detention centres on the continent further complicated such projects. Until the recent Return Regulation, EU law also imposed stricter requirements, such as needing a meaningful connection between the individual and the third country in some contexts. The current initiative deliberately differs from the abandoned UK model: it targets only those whose claims have already been rejected after full procedures, not people still seeking asylum, and frames the hub as a return facility rather than an asylum-processing centre. Officials insist it will comply with EU and international law, with involvement from organisations such as UNHCR and the IOM envisaged. Rights groups have nonetheless condemned the plan as a “grave moral failing” and a dangerous precedent that could place vulnerable people at risk far from effective legal remedies. Rwanda, which has long cultivated selective partnerships on its own terms and has shown little urgency to expand migration-related cooperation with Europe, is hardly a country that needs fresh encouragement from the EU to open new deals – particularly while it remains locked in a prolonged confrontation with the Democratic Republic of the Congo over the conflict in eastern Congo. Italy-Albania protocol on migrant centres gets nod from the EU Advocate General Caption: (L-R) Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta, Greek Minister of Migration and Asylum Athanasios Plevris and Danish Minister of Immigration and Integration Morten Boedskov hold a press conference following a working meeting of the ‘Implementers Group’ at the Austrian Chancellery in Vienna, Austria, 16 November 2026. EPA/CHRISTIAN BRUNA

noticias.titulo: Revolut data breach via compromised email system reopens cybersecurity questions in Italy and Europe
noticias.resumen: At least 700 Revolut customer accounts were exposed after hackers compromised an Italian government certified ...
noticias.texto: At least 700 Revolut customer accounts were exposed after hackers compromised an Italian government certified email system and used it to obtain confidential data from the online bank, the Financial Times reported, citing company sources. Revolut, the UK-founded fintech that operates across several European countries including Italy, confirmed it had shared customer information in response to requests that appeared to come from Italian authorities. A person or group using the handle “iamnotavillain” told the FT via Telegram that they first contacted Revolut “a couple of months ago, posing as an Italian law-enforcement agency.” Over subsequent weeks they repeatedly requested sensitive account details – addresses, phone numbers and transaction histories – claiming the information was needed for ongoing police investigations. Late on Monday the group published a website displaying partially redacted screenshots of material they said had been obtained from the bank. The screenshots indicated that Revolut had exchanged information with an office of Italy’s Interior Ministry through the Posta Elettronica Certificata (PEC) system over a period of several months. PEC is Italy’s certified email system, which gives messages legal status by certifying the date and time of sending and delivery. It is widely used for official communications with public administrations, companies and professionals and is operated by private providers accredited by the Agency for Digital Italy (AgID). According to the hackers, most of the roughly 680 affected customers were based in Switzerland and France, although data relating to residents of 31 other countries – mainly European, including the United Kingdom, Germany and Spain – were also involved. A banking-sector observer contacted by FocusEurope.it argued that the episode highlights long-standing structural weaknesses in the way Italian public authorities request information from banks, rather than solely the responsibility of the current government. “The volume of requests that authorities send to banks, and the quality of those requests, has been out of control for decades,” the source said. Each individual case can generate large numbers of queries from police, judicial police, tax authorities, regulators and bodies involved in insolvency proceedings. The processes by which PEC messages are generated and transmitted are, the observer added, “mostly unaudited,” both in terms of efficiency and security. Problems include redundant requests (for example, documents relating to all suspects being sent simultaneously to multiple banks) and access points to PEC mailboxes where the true sender can be difficult to establish. Some public bodies have also used PEC for purposes that are not sufficiently discouraged or sanctioned, such as a debt-collection agency that for months sent banks lists of people subject to asset freezes in order to identify and block accounts. The source noted that relying primarily on manual human checks to manage such a large volume of communications is unlikely to provide effective verification at scale. The result, the observer said, is “an enormous and poorly defended attack surface.” Before adding more controls, the priority should be to reduce the number and extent of vulnerable points and then systematically strengthen defences. The case also sits within a European cybersecurity framework that has strengthened common rules and tools in recent years without creating a centralised structure. The NIS2 directive has raised and harmonised security requirements for a wide range of essential and important public and private entities and requires member states to designate competent national authorities, establish cyber-crisis management structures and maintain Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). The EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) plays a coordinating and support role, while the network of national CSIRTs enables information exchange and coordinated handling of cross-border incidents. Concrete responsibility for prevention, supervision, intervention and crisis management remains largely with the member states. Newer instruments follow the same logic: the Cybersecurity Reserve under the Cyber Solidarity Act makes specialised services available to help states and EU institutions respond to significant or large-scale incidents, but it supports rather than replaces national capabilities. The overall architecture is therefore one in which the European Union sets common standards, promotes cooperation, provides shared tools and coordinates responses to cross-border incidents, while the actual resilience of systems continues to depend heavily on the administrations, infrastructures and security procedures of individual member states. As the story has developed, it has taken on greater political weight in Italy. Opposition figures have called on the government for explanations. Giulia Pastorella, a member of parliament for the Azione party, wrote on X that if the Interior Ministry’s PEC was indeed compromised and used to obtain confidential bank documents, “we could be looking at the tip of the iceberg.” She asked how many other emails had been sent from the compromised government address, how many other companies had been targeted, and said she would raise the matter in parliament with an urgent question. Revolut Group Holdings Ltd, known as Revolut,is a British multinational neobank and financial technology company headquartered in London, England. It was founded in July 2015 by Nik Storonsky and Vlad Yatsenko.
